//! A node: a member, its clock, and the connections that carry its
//! messages to the other members.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;

use kv::{Change, Condition, Entry, Written};
use kvd::api::ApiError;
use parking_lot::Mutex;
use raft::{Member, Message, NodeId, Outgoing, Role};
use tokio::sync::watch;
use tokio::task;
use tokio::time::{interval, timeout};
use tonic::transport::{Channel, Endpoint};

use crate::rpc::{ElectionClient, ReplicationClient, appended, proto, voted};

/// The length of a tick of the member's clock.
pub const TICK: Duration = Duration::from_millis(100);

/// How long a member waits for the answer to one message.
const ANSWER: Duration = Duration::from_millis(500);

/// How long a write waits for its record to be committed.
const COMMIT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1);

pub struct Node {
    pub member: Mutex<Member>,
    /// A connection to each of the other members.
    peers: BTreeMap<NodeId, Channel>,
    /// Held by the write that is in progress.
    turn: tokio::sync::Mutex<()>,
    /// The committed sequence, for writes that wait for it to advance.
    committed: watch::Sender<u64>,
}

impl Node {
    pub fn new(
        member: Member,
        addresses: BTreeMap<NodeId, String>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<Node>, tonic::transport::Error> {
        let mut peers = BTreeMap::new();

        for (id, address) in addresses {
            peers.insert(
                id,
                Endpoint::from_shared(address)?
                    .connect_timeout(ANSWER)
                    .connect_lazy(),
            );
        }

        Ok(Arc::new(Node {
            member: Mutex::new(member),
            peers,
            turn: tokio::sync::Mutex::new(()),
            committed: watch::Sender::new(0),
        }))
    }
}

impl Node {
    /// Runs one operation on the member and publishes the committed
    /// sequence. The member waits for the disk, so the operation runs where
    /// blocking is allowed.
    fn with_member<T>(&self, operation: impl FnOnce(&mut Member) -> T) -> T {
        task::block_in_place(|| {
            let mut member = self.member.lock();
            let result = operation(&mut member);
            self.committed
                .send_replace(member.committed());

            result
        })
    }
}

impl Node {
    /// Sends each message in a task of its own, so that a member that does
    /// not answer delays nothing else.
    fn dispatch(self: &Arc<Node>, messages: Vec<Outgoing>) {
        for message in messages {
            tokio::spawn(Arc::clone(self).send(message));
        }
    }

    /// Carries one request to a member and gives the answer to this member.
    async fn send(self: Arc<Node>, outgoing: Outgoing) {
        let Some(channel) = self
            .peers
            .get(&outgoing.to)
            .cloned()
        else {
            return;
        };

        let answer = match outgoing.message {
            Message::Append(request) => {
                let call = async move {
                    ReplicationClient::new(channel)
                        .append(proto::AppendRequest::from(request))
                        .await
                };

                timeout(ANSWER, call)
                    .await
                    .ok()
                    .and_then(Result::ok)
                    .map(|answer| appended(outgoing.to, answer.into_inner()))
            }
            Message::Vote(request) => {
                let call = async move {
                    ElectionClient::new(channel)
                        .request_vote(proto::VoteRequest::from(request))
                        .await
                };

                timeout(ANSWER, call)
                    .await
                    .ok()
                    .and_then(Result::ok)
                    .map(|answer| voted(outgoing.to, answer.into_inner()))
            }
            // An answer travels as the response of the call that asked.
            Message::Appended(..) | Message::Voted(..) => None,
        };

        if let Some(answer) = answer {
            self.deliver(answer);
        }
    }

    /// Gives the member a message and sends what the member returns.
    fn deliver(self: &Arc<Node>, message: Message) {
        match self.with_member(|member| member.handle(message)) {
            Ok(messages) => self.dispatch(messages),
            Err(error) => eprintln!("the member could not process a message: {error}"),
        }
    }
}

impl Node {
    /// The member's answer to a request that arrived over gRPC.
    pub fn answer(&self, request: Message) -> io::Result<Message> {
        let mut messages = self.with_member(|member| member.handle(request))?;

        messages
            .pop()
            .map(|outgoing| outgoing.message)
            .ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("the member gave no answer"))
    }

    /// Advances the member's clock, for as long as the node runs.
    pub async fn run_clock(self: Arc<Node>) {
        let mut ticks = interval(TICK);

        loop {
            ticks.tick().await;

            match self.with_member(Member::tick) {
                Ok(messages) => self.dispatch(messages),
                Err(error) => eprintln!("the member could not advance its clock: {error}"),
            }
        }
    }
}

impl Node {
    fn not_leader(member: &Member) -> ApiError {
        match member.leader() {
            Some(leader) => ApiError::Misdirected(format!("the leader is member {leader}")),
            None => ApiError::NoLeader,
        }
    }

    /// A write on the leader. It is acknowledged when its record is
    /// committed and this member has led the same term throughout.
    pub async fn write(
        self: &Arc<Node>,
        change: Change,
        condition: Condition,
    ) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
        let turn = self.turn.lock().await;

        let last = {
            let member = self.member.lock();

            if member.role() != Role::Leader {
                return Err(Node::not_leader(&member));
            }

            member.last_sequence()
        };

        self.wait_for(last).await?;

        let (written, term, messages) = self.with_member(|member| {
            if !member.is_settled() {
                return Err(Node::not_leader(member));
            }

            let created = match &change {
                Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => member.get(key).is_none(),
            };
            let version = member.propose(change, condition)?;

            Ok((
                Written { version, created },
                member.term(),
                member.replicate(),
            ))
        })?;

        self.dispatch(messages);
        self.wait_for(written.version)
            .await?;
        drop(turn);

        // A member that lost the leadership while it waited may hold another
        // leader's record at this sequence.
        let member = self.member.lock();

        if member.role() == Role::Leader && member.term() == term {
            Ok(written)
        } else {
            Err(ApiError::Unavailable(
                "the leadership changed before the record was committed".into(),
            ))
        }
    }

    async fn wait_for(&self, sequence: u64) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        let mut committed = self.committed.subscribe();

        let reached = committed.wait_for(|&committed| committed >= sequence);
        let in_time = timeout(COMMIT, reached)
            .await
            .is_ok_and(|reached| reached.is_ok());

        if in_time {
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(ApiError::Unavailable(format!(
                "record {sequence} is not on a majority of the members"
            )))
        }
    }

    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Result<Entry, ApiError> {
        let member = self.member.lock();

        if member.role() != Role::Leader {
            return Err(Node::not_leader(&member));
        }

        if !member.can_read() {
            return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(
                "this leader cannot confirm that it still leads".into(),
            ));
        }

        member
            .get(key)
            .cloned()
            .ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)
    }
}

Listing 4.50 The complete kvraft/src/main.rs. kvraft/src/main.rs

//! Command kvraft is a storage node whose shard elects its own leader.
//! Every node is started the same way, with its id and the replication
//! addresses of the other members.
//!
//! Run 3 nodes from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run -p kvraft -- --id 1 --listen 127.0.0.1:7001 --replication 127.0.0.1:7101 --data /var/tmp/m1 \
//!         --peer 2=http://127.0.0.1:7102 --peer 3=http://127.0.0.1:7103
//!
//! and the same for ids 2 and 3, each with its own ports and the other 2 as peers.

mod node;
mod rpc;

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::error::Error;
use std::net::SocketAddr;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::Arc;

use axum::body::Bytes;
use axum::extract::{DefaultBodyLimit, Path, State};
use axum::http::header::{CONTENT_TYPE, ETAG, IF_NONE_MATCH};
use axum::http::{HeaderMap, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};
use axum::routing::get;
use axum::{Json, Router};
use clap::Parser;
use kv::{Change, Condition};
use kvd::api::{ApiError, MAX_VALUE, etag, valid_key, version_header, write_condition};
use raft::{Member, NodeId, Role};
use serde::Serialize;
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tonic::transport::Server;

use crate::node::Node;
use crate::rpc::{ElectionServer, ReplicationServer, Service};

/// Reads `2=http://127.0.0.1:7102` as member 2 at that address.
fn parse_peer(text: &str) -> Result<(NodeId, String), String> {
    let (id, address) = text
        .split_once('=')
        .ok_or("a peer is written as id=address")?;
    let Ok(id) = id.parse() else {
        return Err("the id of a peer is a number".to_owned());
    };

    Ok((id, address.to_owned()))
}

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    /// The id of this member, a number that no other member has.
    #[arg(long)]
    id: NodeId,

    /// The address of the HTTP API.
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7001")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    /// The address on which this member accepts messages from the others.
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7101")]
    replication: SocketAddr,

    /// Another member and its replication address, as id=address.
    #[arg(long = "peer", value_parser = parse_peer)]
    peers: Vec<(NodeId, String)>,

    #[arg(long, default_value = "data")]
    data: PathBuf,

    /// Respond without waiting for the disk.
    #[arg(long)]
    no_sync: bool,
}

async fn put_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let condition = write_condition(&headers)?;

    let written = node
        .write(
            Change::Put {
                key,
                value: body.to_vec(),
            },
            condition,
        )
        .await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let condition = write_condition(&headers)?;

    node.write(Change::Delete { key }, condition)
        .await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

async fn get_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let cached = version_header(&headers, IF_NONE_MATCH)?;
    let entry = node.get(&key)?;
    let tag = [(ETAG, etag(entry.version))];

    if cached == Some(Condition::Version(entry.version)) {
        return Ok((StatusCode::NOT_MODIFIED, tag).into_response());
    }

    Ok((
        tag,
        [(CONTENT_TYPE, "application/octet-stream")],
        entry.value,
    )
        .into_response())
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Health {
    id: NodeId,
    role: &'static str,
    term: u64,
    /// The leader of the term, when this member knows it.
    leader: Option<NodeId>,
    last_sequence: u64,
    committed: u64,
}

async fn health(State(node): State<Arc<Node>>) -> Json<Health> {
    let member = node.member.lock();

    let role = match member.role() {
        Role::Leader => "leader",
        Role::Candidate => "candidate",
        Role::Follower => "follower",
    };

    Json(Health {
        id: member.id(),
        role,
        term: member.term(),
        leader: member.leader(),
        last_sequence: member.last_sequence(),
        committed: member.committed(),
    })
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let peers: BTreeMap<NodeId, String> = options.peers.into_iter().collect();
    let member = Member::open(
        &options.data,
        options.id,
        peers.keys().copied().collect(),
        !options.no_sync,
    )?;

    println!(
        "member {}, term {}, log ends at {}",
        member.id(),
        member.term(),
        member.last_sequence()
    );

    let node = Node::new(member, peers)?;

    let replication = ReplicationServer::new(Service {
        node: Arc::clone(&node),
    });
    let election = ElectionServer::new(Service {
        node: Arc::clone(&node),
    });

    tokio::spawn(
        Server::builder()
            .add_service(replication)
            .add_service(election)
            .serve(options.replication),
    );
    tokio::spawn(Arc::clone(&node).run_clock());

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route(
            "/v1/keys/{key}",
            get(get_key)
                .put(put_key)
                .delete(delete_key),
        )
        .route("/healthz", get(health))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(node);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

Listing 4.51 The complete probe/src/main.rs. probe/src/main.rs

//! Command probe measures how long a shard is unavailable when its leader
//! is lost. It writes keys for a number of seconds, trying each node in turn
//! until one accepts the write, and reports the longest pause between 2
//! acknowledged writes.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run --release -p probe -- --seconds 20 --acked acked.txt \
//!         --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --server http://127.0.0.1:7002 --server http://127.0.0.1:7003

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

use clap::Parser;
use ureq::Agent;

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    /// The HTTP address of a node. Given once for each node of the shard.
    #[arg(long = "server", required = true)]
    servers: Vec<String>,

    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 20)]
    seconds: u64,

    /// The file that receives the key of every acknowledged write.
    #[arg(long)]
    acked: PathBuf,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let agent: Agent = Agent::config_builder()
        .timeout_global(Some(Duration::from_secs(2)))
        .build()
        .into();
    let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&options.acked)?);

    let started = Instant::now();
    let (mut server, mut number, mut refused) = (0, 1, 0);
    let (mut last_success, mut longest, mut longest_at) = (started, Duration::ZERO, Duration::ZERO);

    while started.elapsed() < Duration::from_secs(options.seconds) {
        let key = format!("key-{number:06}");
        let address = format!("{}/v1/keys/{key}", options.servers[server]);

        if agent
            .put(&address)
            .send(format!("value of {key}"))
            .is_err()
        {
            // This node did not accept the write. Try the next one.
            refused += 1;
            server = (server + 1) % options.servers.len();
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));

            continue;
        }

        let pause = last_success.elapsed();

        if pause > longest {
            (longest, longest_at) = (pause, started.elapsed());
        }

        last_success = Instant::now();
        writeln!(file, "{key}")?;
        number += 1;
    }

    file.flush()?;

    println!(
        "{} writes acknowledged in {} seconds, {refused} attempts refused",
        number - 1,
        options.seconds
    );
    println!(
        "the longest pause between 2 acknowledged writes was {:.2} s, ending {:.1} s after the start",
        longest.as_secs_f64(),
        longest_at.as_secs_f64()
    );

    Ok(())
}

Further reading

  • D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, “In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm”, USENIX ATC 2014.
  • D. Ongaro, Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice, doctoral dissertation, Stanford University, 2014.
  • L. Lamport, “Paxos Made Simple”, ACM SIGACT News, 2001.
  • T. Chandra, R. Griesemer and J. Redstone, “Paxos Made Live: An Engineering Perspective”, PODC 2007.
  • M. Fischer, N. Lynch and M. Paterson, “Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process”, Journal of the ACM, 1985.
  • K. Kingsbury, the Jepsen analyses, jepsen.io.

Summary

  • Every member starts as a follower, and a follower that hears nothing from a leader for its election timeout becomes a candidate and asks all the others for their votes.
  • A member votes at most once in a term, so that a term has at most 1 leader, and the term and the vote are stored on disk before any answer that depends on them is sent.
  • A member votes only for a candidate whose log ends at least as far as its own, with terms compared before sequences, from which it follows that an elected leader holds every acknowledged record.
  • A term marker, the first record of a leader, records the term of every record without changing the format of the log, and commits the records of earlier terms.
  • Append carries the term of the record that precedes its new records. A follower whose record at that position has a different term refuses, the leader steps back, and the follower replaces its differing records with the leader’s.
  • Only uncommitted records are ever removed from a log.
  • In 200 simulated runs with crashes and lost messages, 480 leaders were elected with no term having 2, and all 504 acknowledged writes were present after recovery.
  • The simulation detected 2 disabled voting rules, and did not detect a disabled commit condition for earlier terms.
  • With 3 nodes, killing the leader interrupted writes for 1.05 seconds, and none of 1443 acknowledged writes was lost.

Key-Value Store: Router (Low-Level Design)

With chapter 4 complete, we have a shard that survives the loss of its leader without anybody’s help. Measured against the design of chapter 1, 2 things are still wanting. A client has to discover for itself which member of the shard is the leader, as the program probe did by trying each node in turn and collecting 51 refusals in the process. And all the data is in a single shard, whereas the design calls for the keys to be divided among many.

A single small component supplies both. The router stands between the clients and the shards. Clients send every request to it, and for each request it works out which shard owns the key and which member of that shard is at present the leader, and passes the request on. The clients are thereby relieved of all knowledge of the cluster. They know 1 address, and neither the number of shards nor a change of leader is visible to them.

The router is the least intricate program in this part of the book, and it contains 1 decision that is easy to get wrong and expensive when it is: what to do when the member it has asked does not give a clear answer. A router that retries too readily will perform a write twice, and a router that retries too reluctantly will report failures that it could have concealed. The chapter builds the router, states the rule that settles this question, and then repeats the experiment of chapter 4, killing a leader under load, with the router in front.

This chapter covers

  • what a router does, and why it holds no data
  • a ring file that lists the shards and their members
  • finding the shard of a key with the ring of chapter 1
  • finding the leader, and the rule that decides when another member may be asked
  • 2 shards behind 1 router, measured
  • the loss of a leader behind the router, as a client sees it

What a router does

A router keeps no data. Everything it knows comes from a ring file, read when it starts, and from what the members tell it in the course of its work. This is the statelessness that chapter 1 required of routers, and its practical value is considerable: any number of routers may be run side by side, and any of them may be stopped or restarted at any time, since a router that has lost its memory rebuilds it from the first few answers it receives.

The ring file

$ cat ring.json
{
  "virtual_nodes": 256,
  "shards": [
    { "name": "shard-a", "members": ["http://127.0.0.1:7011", "http://127.0.0.1:7012", "http://127.0.0.1:7013"] },
    { "name": "shard-b", "members": ["http://127.0.0.1:7021", "http://127.0.0.1:7022", "http://127.0.0.1:7023"] }
  ]
}

Each shard is a group of 3 kvraft members, listed in the order of their ids. In the design of chapter 1, the ring is held by a coordinator and changes while the system runs. Here it is a file that the router reads once at startup. That is sufficient for routing requests, and it leaves changes to the ring, which are a substantial subject in themselves, outside this chapter.

Listing 5.2 The ring file, and what the router keeps for each shard. kvrouter/src/main.rs

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7000")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    /// A JSON file that lists the shards and the addresses of their members.
    #[arg(long)]
    ring: PathBuf,
}

/// The contents of the ring file.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Config {
    virtual_nodes: u32,
    shards: Vec<ShardConfig>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ShardConfig {
    name: String,
    /// The HTTP address of each member, in the order of their ids: member 1 first.
    members: Vec<String>,
}

/// A shard, as the router knows it.
struct Shard {
    members: Vec<String>,
    /// The position in `members` of the member that led when the router last asked.
    leader: AtomicUsize,
}

struct Routes {
    ring: Ring,
    shards: HashMap<String, Shard>,
    client: reqwest::Client,
}

For every shard the router remembers a single number, the position in the list of the member that was the leader when it last asked. This is a guess and nothing more. The sections that follow show what happens when the guess is wrong, and the important property of the design is that a wrong guess costs an extra request and never a wrong result.

Finding the shard

Each shard is placed on the ring of chapter 1 with 256 tokens. To look up a key then takes 2 steps: the ring is asked for the name of the owner, and the shard of that name is fetched.

Listing 5.3 Building the ring, and finding the shard of a key. kvrouter/src/main.rs

impl Routes {
    /// Builds the ring from the file: every shard receives its tokens.
    fn load(config: Config) -> Routes {
        let mut ring = Ring::new(config.virtual_nodes);
        let mut shards = HashMap::new();

        for shard in config.shards {
            ring.add(&shard.name);
            shards.insert(
                shard.name,
                Shard {
                    members: shard.members,
                    leader: AtomicUsize::new(0),
                },
            );
        }

        Routes {
            ring,
            shards,
            client: reqwest::Client::new(),
        }
    }

    /// The shard that owns a key.
    fn shard_of(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Shard> {
        self.shards
            .get(self.ring.owner(key)?)
    }
}

Finding the leader

The router sends the request to the member that it believes to be the leader. Usually the belief is correct. When it is not, the answer of the member tells the router what to do next.

All the cases are decided by a single rule: the router asks another member only if the first attempt has certainly changed nothing. A follower that answers 421 did not touch its log. Nor did a member that reports that the shard is electing a leader, nor one whose process is not running and whose connection was refused. In all 3 cases, to ask another member is safe, since whatever that member does will be the only effect of the request.

A timeout is a different matter altogether. The leader may have appended the record, and even committed it, before the connection failed, and the router cannot know. If it were to send the request to another member, a write might be performed twice, and a conditional write that had succeeded might be reported as failed. The router therefore answers 503 and leaves the decision to the client, which is the only party that knows whether its request is safe to repeat. This is the lost response of chapter 1 once again, and the router’s rule is a refusal to guess about it on somebody else’s behalf.

In the code, the possible outcomes of asking a member are the variants of an enum.

Listing 5.4 The 3 outcomes of asking a member. kvrouter/src/main.rs

/// What a member said about a request it did not serve.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Problem {
    #[serde(rename = "type")]
    kind: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    detail: String,
}

impl Problem {
    /// The position of the leader in the shard's list of members, when the
    /// member named it, as in "the leader is member 3".
    fn named_leader(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        let id: usize = self
            .detail
            .rsplit(' ')
            .next()?
            .parse()
            .ok()?;

        id.checked_sub(1)
    }
}

/// The result of asking one member.
enum Attempt {
    /// The member served the request. This is its response.
    Served(Response),
    /// The member changed nothing. It may have named the leader.
    Refused(Option<usize>),
    /// The request may or may not have taken effect.
    Unknown(String),
}

ask sends the request to 1 member and classifies what comes back as 1 of the outcomes.

Listing 5.5 Asking 1 member. kvrouter/src/main.rs

const NO_LEADER: &str = "/problems/no-leader";

impl Routes {
    /// Sends the request to one member and classifies what comes back.
    async fn ask(
        &self,
        member: &str,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Attempt {
        let conditions = [IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH]
            .into_iter()
            .filter_map(|name| {
                headers
                    .get(&name)
                    .map(|value| (name, value))
            });
        let request = self
            .client
            .request(method, format!("{member}/v1/keys/{key}"))
            .body(body);
        let request = conditions.fold(request, |request, (name, value)| {
            request.header(name, value)
        });

        let response = match request.send().await {
            Ok(response) => response,
            Err(error) if error.is_connect() => return Attempt::Refused(None),
            Err(error) => return Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        };

        let status = response.status();
        let redirected = status == StatusCode::MISDIRECTED_REQUEST;

        if !redirected && status != StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE {
            return Attempt::Served(relay(response).await);
        }

        match response.json::<Problem>().await {
            Ok(problem) if redirected || problem.kind == NO_LEADER => {
                Attempt::Refused(problem.named_leader())
            }
            Ok(problem) => Attempt::Unknown(problem.detail),
            Err(error) => Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        }
    }
}

/// Passes a member's response on to the client: status, version and body.
async fn relay(response: reqwest::Response) -> Response {
    let status = response.status();
    let headers: HeaderMap = [ETAG, CONTENT_TYPE]
        .into_iter()
        .filter_map(|name| {
            response
                .headers()
                .get(&name)
                .map(|value| (name, value.clone()))
        })
        .collect();

    match response.bytes().await {
        Ok(body) => (status, headers, body).into_response(),
        Err(error) => ApiError::Unavailable(error.to_string()).into_response(),
    }
}

forward is the loop around it. A refusal moves the guess to the member that the refusal named, or failing that to the next in the list. When every member has refused once, an election must be in progress, and the router then waits 150 ms between further attempts, so that it does not flood a shard which is busy choosing a leader.

Listing 5.6 Trying members until one serves the request. kvrouter/src/main.rs

/// How many times the router asks a member before it gives up.
const ATTEMPTS: usize = 12;

/// How long the router waits before it asks again, once every member of a
/// shard has refused.
const PAUSE: Duration = Duration::from_millis(150);

impl Routes {
    /// Sends a request to the leader of the key's shard. A member that
    /// refuses has changed nothing, so the router asks another.
    async fn forward(
        &self,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
        valid_key(key)?;

        let shard = self
            .shard_of(key)
            .ok_or(ApiError::NoLeader)?;

        for attempt in 1..=ATTEMPTS {
            let tried = shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
            let member = &shard.members[tried];

            let named = match self
                .ask(member, method.clone(), key, headers, body.clone())
                .await
            {
                Attempt::Served(response) => return Ok(response),
                Attempt::Unknown(detail) => return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(detail)),
                Attempt::Refused(named) => named,
            };

            let next = named
                .filter(|&position| position < shard.members.len())
                .unwrap_or((tried + 1) % shard.members.len());

            shard
                .leader
                .store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);

            // Every member has refused once: the shard is electing a leader.
            if attempt >= shard.members.len() {
                sleep(PAUSE).await;
            }
        }

        Err(ApiError::NoLeader)
    }
}

Listing 5.7 The HTTP handlers, and the start of the program. kvrouter/src/main.rs

async fn key(
    State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>,
    method: Method,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    routes
        .forward(method, &key, &headers, body)
        .await
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ShardHealth<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    /// The address the router currently sends this shard's requests to.
    leader: &'a str,
}

async fn health(State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>) -> Json<serde_json::Value> {
    let mut shards: Vec<ShardHealth> = routes
        .shards
        .iter()
        .map(|(name, shard)| ShardHealth {
            name,
            leader: &shard.members[shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)],
        })
        .collect();
    shards.sort_by_key(|shard| shard.name);

    Json(serde_json::json!({ "status": "ok", "shards": shards }))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let config: Config = serde_json::from_str(&fs::read_to_string(&options.ring)?)?;
    let routes = Arc::new(Routes::load(config));

    println!("routing to {} shards", routes.shards.len());

        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", get(key).put(key).delete(key))
        .route("/healthz", get(health))
        .with_state(routes);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;

    Ok(())
}

2 shards behind 1 router

We start 6 kvraft members in 2 groups of 3, then the router, and write 400 keys through it.

$ ./target/release/kvrouter --listen 127.0.0.1:7000 --ring ring.json &
routing to 2 shards
listening on 127.0.0.1:7000
$ ./target/release/kvctl load --server http://127.0.0.1:7000 --count 400 --acked acked.txt
400 writes acknowledged
$ for port in 7013 7023; do curl http://127.0.0.1:$port/healthz; echo; done
{"id":3,"role":"leader","term":1,"leader":3,"last_sequence":206,"committed":206}
{"id":3,"role":"leader","term":1,"leader":3,"last_sequence":196,"committed":196}
$ ./target/release/kvctl verify --server http://127.0.0.1:7000 --acked acked.txt
400 acknowledged, 400 found, 0 missing
OutputWhat it shows
logs end at 206 and 196The 400 keys were divided 205 to 195. Each log also contains 1 term marker.
400 found, 0 missingA read through the router reaches the shard that holds the key.

The client used a single address throughout. It never learned how many shards exist, or which members lead them.

A leader is lost behind the router

probe, from chapter 4, is now given the router’s address and no other. While it is writing, the leader of shard-a is killed.

$ ./target/release/probe --seconds 12 --acked acked.txt --server http://127.0.0.1:7000 &
$ sleep 4; kill -9 <pid of member 3 of shard-a, its leader>
780 writes acknowledged in 12 seconds, 0 attempts refused
the longest pause between 2 acknowledged writes was 1.08 s, ending 5.2 s after the start
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:7000/healthz
{"shards":[{"leader":"http://127.0.0.1:7011","name":"shard-a"},{"leader":"http://127.0.0.1:7023","name":"shard-b"}],"status":"ok"}
$ ./target/release/kvctl verify --server http://127.0.0.1:7000 --acked acked.txt
780 acknowledged, 780 found, 0 missing
OutputWhat it shows
0 attempts refusedThe client saw no error of any kind. In chapter 4, without a router, the same experiment produced 51 refusals.
longest pause 1.08 sRequests for shard-a waited inside the router while the shard elected a leader.
leader of shard-a is now member 1The router found the new leader by asking, and remembered it.
780 found, 0 missingNo acknowledged write was lost.

The comparison with chapter 4 shows what the router contributes. The election took as long as it did before, about a second, since the router does nothing to hasten it. What has changed is what the client experiences. A second of refusals, which every client would have had to be written to handle, has become a second of waiting, which requires nothing of the client at all.

Writes to shard-b were at no time affected. probe sends its keys in turn, and so it waited behind the 1 request for shard-a that was being held. Independent clients writing to shard-b would have noticed nothing.

What is still missing

MissingEffect
The ring is a file read at startup.To add a shard, the router has to be restarted, and existing keys do not move to the new shard.
Members do not check which shard a key belongs to.A router with a wrong ring file could write a key to the wrong shard. Chapter 1 prevents this by sending the version of the ring with every request.
Listing keys by prefix is not routed.The router would have to ask every shard and merge the answers.

//! Command kvrouter sends each request to the shard that owns its key, and
//! within that shard to the member that leads. Clients talk to the router
//! and need to know nothing about shards or leaders.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run -p kvrouter -- --listen 127.0.0.1:7000 --ring ring.json

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::net::SocketAddr;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::time::Duration;

use axum::body::Bytes;
use axum::extract::{Path, State};
use axum::http::header::{CONTENT_TYPE, ETAG, IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH};
use axum::http::{HeaderMap, Method, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};
use axum::routing::get;
use axum::{Json, Router};
use clap::Parser;
use kvd::api::{ApiError, valid_key};
use ring::Ring;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::time::sleep;

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7000")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    /// A JSON file that lists the shards and the addresses of their members.
    #[arg(long)]
    ring: PathBuf,
}

/// The contents of the ring file.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Config {
    virtual_nodes: u32,
    shards: Vec<ShardConfig>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ShardConfig {
    name: String,
    /// The HTTP address of each member, in the order of their ids: member 1 first.
    members: Vec<String>,
}

/// A shard, as the router knows it.
struct Shard {
    members: Vec<String>,
    /// The position in `members` of the member that led when the router last asked.
    leader: AtomicUsize,
}

struct Routes {
    ring: Ring,
    shards: HashMap<String, Shard>,
    client: reqwest::Client,
}

impl Routes {
    /// Builds the ring from the file: every shard receives its tokens.
    fn load(config: Config) -> Routes {
        let mut ring = Ring::new(config.virtual_nodes);
        let mut shards = HashMap::new();

        for shard in config.shards {
            ring.add(&shard.name);
            shards.insert(
                shard.name,
                Shard {
                    members: shard.members,
                    leader: AtomicUsize::new(0),
                },
            );
        }

        Routes {
            ring,
            shards,
            client: reqwest::Client::new(),
        }
    }

    /// The shard that owns a key.
    fn shard_of(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Shard> {
        self.shards
            .get(self.ring.owner(key)?)
    }
}

/// What a member said about a request it did not serve.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Problem {
    #[serde(rename = "type")]
    kind: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    detail: String,
}

impl Problem {
    /// The position of the leader in the shard's list of members, when the
    /// member named it, as in "the leader is member 3".
    fn named_leader(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        let id: usize = self
            .detail
            .rsplit(' ')
            .next()?
            .parse()
            .ok()?;

        id.checked_sub(1)
    }
}

/// The result of asking one member.
enum Attempt {
    /// The member served the request. This is its response.
    Served(Response),
    /// The member changed nothing. It may have named the leader.
    Refused(Option<usize>),
    /// The request may or may not have taken effect.
    Unknown(String),
}

const NO_LEADER: &str = "/problems/no-leader";

impl Routes {
    /// Sends the request to one member and classifies what comes back.
    async fn ask(
        &self,
        member: &str,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Attempt {
        let conditions = [IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH]
            .into_iter()
            .filter_map(|name| {
                headers
                    .get(&name)
                    .map(|value| (name, value))
            });
        let request = self
            .client
            .request(method, format!("{member}/v1/keys/{key}"))
            .body(body);
        let request = conditions.fold(request, |request, (name, value)| {
            request.header(name, value)
        });

        let response = match request.send().await {
            Ok(response) => response,
            Err(error) if error.is_connect() => return Attempt::Refused(None),
            Err(error) => return Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        };

        let status = response.status();
        let redirected = status == StatusCode::MISDIRECTED_REQUEST;

        if !redirected && status != StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE {
            return Attempt::Served(relay(response).await);
        }

        match response.json::<Problem>().await {
            Ok(problem) if redirected || problem.kind == NO_LEADER => {
                Attempt::Refused(problem.named_leader())
            }
            Ok(problem) => Attempt::Unknown(problem.detail),
            Err(error) => Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        }
    }
}

/// Passes a member's response on to the client: status, version and body.
async fn relay(response: reqwest::Response) -> Response {
    let status = response.status();
    let headers: HeaderMap = [ETAG, CONTENT_TYPE]
        .into_iter()
        .filter_map(|name| {
            response
                .headers()
                .get(&name)
                .map(|value| (name, value.clone()))
        })
        .collect();

    match response.bytes().await {
        Ok(body) => (status, headers, body).into_response(),
        Err(error) => ApiError::Unavailable(error.to_string()).into_response(),
    }
}

/// How many times the router asks a member before it gives up.
const ATTEMPTS: usize = 12;

/// How long the router waits before it asks again, once every member of a
/// shard has refused.
const PAUSE: Duration = Duration::from_millis(150);

impl Routes {
    /// Sends a request to the leader of the key's shard. A member that
    /// refuses has changed nothing, so the router asks another.
    async fn forward(
        &self,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
        valid_key(key)?;

        let shard = self
            .shard_of(key)
            .ok_or(ApiError::NoLeader)?;

        for attempt in 1..=ATTEMPTS {
            let tried = shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
            let member = &shard.members[tried];

            let named = match self
                .ask(member, method.clone(), key, headers, body.clone())
                .await
            {
                Attempt::Served(response) => return Ok(response),
                Attempt::Unknown(detail) => return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(detail)),
                Attempt::Refused(named) => named,
            };

            let next = named
                .filter(|&position| position < shard.members.len())
                .unwrap_or((tried + 1) % shard.members.len());

            shard
                .leader
                .store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);

            // Every member has refused once: the shard is electing a leader.
            if attempt >= shard.members.len() {
                sleep(PAUSE).await;
            }
        }

        Err(ApiError::NoLeader)
    }
}

async fn key(
    State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>,
    method: Method,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    routes
        .forward(method, &key, &headers, body)
        .await
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ShardHealth<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    /// The address the router currently sends this shard's requests to.
    leader: &'a str,
}

async fn health(State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>) -> Json<serde_json::Value> {
    let mut shards: Vec<ShardHealth> = routes
        .shards
        .iter()
        .map(|(name, shard)| ShardHealth {
            name,
            leader: &shard.members[shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)],
        })
        .collect();
    shards.sort_by_key(|shard| shard.name);

    Json(serde_json::json!({ "status": "ok", "shards": shards }))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let config: Config = serde_json::from_str(&fs::read_to_string(&options.ring)?)?;
    let routes = Arc::new(Routes::load(config));

    println!("routing to {} shards", routes.shards.len());

    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", get(key).put(key).delete(key))
        .route("/healthz", get(health))
        .with_state(routes);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;

    Ok(())
}

Summary

  • A router hashes the key, finds the shard on the ring, and forwards the request to the leader of that shard, and it holds no data of its own.
  • The router keeps a guess at the leader of each shard and corrects the guess from the answers it receives.
  • It asks another member only when the first attempt certainly changed nothing: after a follower’s 421, after a 503 that reports no leader, or after a refused connection.
  • After a timeout it answers 503, since the write may have been performed, and only the client knows whether the request is safe to repeat.
  • With 2 shards, 400 keys were divided 205 to 195, and every key was found again through the router.
  • When a leader was killed, clients behind the router experienced a pause of 1.08 seconds and no errors.

Key-Value Store: Group Commit (Low-Level Design)

The capacity estimate of chapter 1 arrived at 24 nodes by assuming that a node stores 20 writes with every wait for its disk. Without that assumption the same calculation gave 325 nodes. Nothing built so far does anything of the kind. The storage node of chapter 2 waits once for every write, and reaches its limit at about 180 writes per second however many clients are sending to it, since each must wait its turn for a disk that confirms 185 times a second.

This chapter adds the missing technique. Under group commit, a node stores all the writes that are waiting at a given moment with a single wait for the disk. The change is small, some 60 lines in the store and 1 thread in the server, and its effect is out of all proportion to its size: the measured rate rises from 180 writes per second to almost 5000 with 64 clients, and beyond 17000 with 256. It is among the best examples in systems programming of a large gain obtained by rearranging work, with no part of the work made faster.

This chapter covers

  • why a single wait for the disk can serve many writes
  • a committer thread that forms batches without a timer
  • conditional writes within a batch
  • measurements with 1, 8, 64 and 256 clients
  • a crash in the middle of a batch

The idea

A wait for the disk takes about 5.4 ms whether it stores 1 record or 100. Nearly all of that time is spent by the disk in confirming that the data is safe, and very little in transferring the data, so that the cost is close to a fixed charge for each wait and almost independent of how much is written. Writes that arrive while 1 wait is in progress can therefore share the next.

The design uses no timer, and the point deserves emphasis because the alternative is common. Some systems hold a write back for a millisecond or so in the hope that others will arrive to share its wait. This improves throughput under heavy load and penalises every write under light load, when no others are coming. Here a batch is formed only from writes that are already waiting. A write that arrives alone is stored at once, with no delay, and the batches grow of their own accord as the load grows, since the busier the node is, the more writes accumulate during each wait. The mechanism adjusts itself to the load without any parameter that an operator has to tune.

A batch in the store

Store::commit takes a list of writes and returns a result for each of them.

Listing 6.1 The imports of kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::ops::Bound;
use std::path::Path;

use thiserror::Error;

use crate::log::Log;
use crate::record::{Change, Record};

Listing 6.2 Storing a batch of writes with a single wait for the disk. kv/src/store.rs

/// One write of a batch: the change, and the condition it carries.
pub struct Write {
    pub change: Change,
    pub condition: Condition,
}

impl Store {
    /// Performs several writes with a single wait for the disk. Each write
    /// is checked as if the writes before it in the batch had already
    /// happened. The result of each is returned in the same order.
    pub fn commit(&mut self, writes: Vec<Write>) -> Vec<Result<Written, StoreError>> {
        // The versions that keys will have once the accepted writes of this
        // batch are applied. `None` is a key that a write of the batch deletes.
        let mut pending: BTreeMap<String, Option<u64>> = BTreeMap::new();
        let mut records = Vec::new();
        let mut results = Vec::new();
        let first = self.log.last_sequence() + 1;

        for write in writes {
            let key = match &write.change {
                Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => key.clone(),
            };
            let current = match pending.get(&key) {
                Some(version) => *version,
                None => self.version(&key),
            };
            let deletes = matches!(write.change, Change::Delete { .. });

            let checked = if deletes && current.is_none() {
                Err(StoreError::NotFound)
            } else {
                check(write.condition, current)
            };

            if let Err(error) = checked {
                results.push(Err(error));

                continue;
            }

            let sequence = first + records.len() as u64;
            let version = if deletes { None } else { Some(sequence) };

            pending.insert(key, version);
            results.push(Ok(Written {
                version: sequence,
                created: current.is_none(),
            }));
            records.push(Record {
                sequence,
                change: write.change,
            });
        }

        // One write and one wait for the disk, for the whole batch.
        if let Err(error) = self.log.append_records(&records) {
            let failure = error.to_string();

            return results
                .into_iter()
                .map(|result| result.and(Err(StoreError::Log(io::Error::other(failure.clone())))))
                .collect();
        }

        for record in records {
            apply(&mut self.entries, record);
        }

        results
    }
}

The method works in 3 passes.

PassWhat happens
CheckThe condition of each write is checked, and the writes that are accepted receive the next sequence numbers.
StoreAll the accepted records go to the log in 1 write, followed by 1 wait for the disk.
ApplyThe records are applied to the map, and the results are returned.

Conditional writes need care in the first pass. Suppose that a batch contains 2 writes to user-1, each carrying If-None-Match: *, which means “create only”. The first ought to succeed and the second to fail, although neither is yet in the map, and a check against the map alone would accept both. The pending map resolves the difficulty. It records the version that each key will have once the accepted writes of the batch have been applied, and a later write in the same batch is checked against it. The batch thus behaves, as far as any client can tell, exactly as if its writes had been performed in sequence, which is the property that makes batching invisible.

The order of the passes preserves invariant 1 of chapter 2. No result leaves commit before the wait for the disk has ended, and so no client is answered early.

The committer

A single thread, the committer, owns the store. The handlers of requests do not touch the store at all. Each hands its write to the committer through a channel and waits for the result.

Listing 6.3 The imports of kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

use std::error::Error;
use std::net::SocketAddr;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::thread;

use axum::Router;
use axum::body::Bytes;
use axum::extract::{DefaultBodyLimit, Path, State};
use axum::http::header::ETAG;
use axum::http::{HeaderMap, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};
use axum::routing::put;
use clap::Parser;
use kv::{Change, Store, StoreError, Write, Written};
use kvd::api::{ApiError, MAX_VALUE, etag, valid_key, write_condition};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::sync::oneshot;

Listing 6.4 The options, and a write on its way to the committer. kvgroup/src/main.rs

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7001")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    #[arg(long, default_value = "data")]
    data: PathBuf,

    /// The largest number of writes stored with one wait for the disk.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 256)]
    batch: usize,
}

/// A write on its way to the committer, with the channel for its result.
struct Request {
    write: Write,
    reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<Written, StoreError>>,
}

Listing 6.5 The committer thread. kvgroup/src/main.rs

/// The committer: the one thread that owns the store. It takes the write
/// that has waited longest, adds every write that arrived meanwhile, and
/// stores them together.
fn run_committer(mut store: Store, requests: Receiver<Request>, limit: usize) {
    let (mut batches, mut writes) = (0u64, 0u64);

    while let Ok(first) = requests.recv() {
        // The first request, and whatever else is already waiting.
        let mut batch = vec![first];

        batch.extend(requests.try_iter().take(limit - 1));

        let (changes, replies): (Vec<Write>, Vec<_>) = batch
            .into_iter()
            .map(|request| (request.write, request.reply))
            .unzip();

        batches += 1;
        writes += changes.len() as u64;

        // A handler that has gone away no longer wants its result.
        store
            .commit(changes)
            .into_iter()
            .zip(replies)
            .for_each(|(result, reply)| drop(reply.send(result)));

        if batches.is_multiple_of(200) {
            let average = writes as f64 / batches as f64;
            println!("{writes} writes in {batches} batches, {average:.1} writes per batch");
        }
    }
}

This loop is the whole of group commit. recv blocks until a write arrives. try_iter then yields every write that is already in the channel, without waiting for more, up to a limit of 256 for the batch. While commit is waiting for the disk, new writes accumulate in the channel, and the next turn of the loop takes all of them.

Giving the store to 1 thread has a further merit. Since no other thread touches it, the store needs no lock, and the question of what 2 concurrent writers might do to the map does not arise. Concurrency has been confined to the channel, where it is handled by a well-tested library, and the logic of the store remains sequential.

Listing 6.6 Handing a write to the committer, and the HTTP handlers. kvgroup/src/main.rs

/// Hands a write to the committer and waits for its result.
async fn submit(committer: &Sender<Request>, write: Write) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
    let (reply, result) = oneshot::channel();
    let stopped = || ApiError::Unavailable("the committer has stopped".into());

    if committer
        .send(Request { write, reply })
        .is_err()
    {
        return Err(stopped());
    }

    let Ok(outcome) = result.await else {
        return Err(stopped());
    };

    Ok(outcome?)
}

async fn put_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Put {
            key,
            value: body.to_vec(),
        },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    let written = submit(&committer, write).await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Delete { key },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    submit(&committer, write).await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

Listing 6.7 Starting the committer and the server. kvgroup/src/main.rs

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (store, applied, discarded) = Store::open(&options.data, true)?;

    println!("recovered {applied} records, cut {discarded} bytes from the end of the log");

    let (committer, requests) = mpsc::channel();
    thread::spawn(move || run_committer(store, requests, options.batch));

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", put(put_key).delete(delete_key))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(committer);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

Measurements

kvbench runs a number of clients simultaneously. Each client sends its writes in succession and waits for every answer before sending the next.

Listing 6.8 The imports of kvbench/src/main.rs. kvbench/src/main.rs

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

use clap::Parser;
use ureq::Agent;

Listing 6.9 Writing from several clients at once. kvbench/src/main.rs

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long)]
    server: String,

    /// The number of clients that write at the same time.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 8)]
    clients: u32,

    /// The number of writes each client makes.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 200)]
    writes: u32,

    #[arg(long)]
    acked: PathBuf,
}

/// The writes of one client. It returns the keys that were acknowledged.
fn client(server: &str, number: u32, writes: u32) -> Vec<String> {
    let agent = Agent::new_with_defaults();
    let mut acknowledged = Vec::new();

    for write in 1..=writes {
        let key = format!("key-{number:03}-{write:06}");
        let address = format!("{server}/v1/keys/{key}");

        if agent
            .put(&address)
            .send(format!("value of {key}"))
            .is_ok()
        {
            acknowledged.push(key);
        }
    }

    acknowledged
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (server, writes) = (options.server.as_str(), options.writes);
    let started = Instant::now();

    let acknowledged: Vec<String> = thread::scope(|scope| {
        let clients: Vec<_> = (1..=options.clients)
            .map(|number| scope.spawn(move || client(server, number, writes)))
            .collect();

        clients
            .into_iter()
            .flat_map(|client| client.join().unwrap_or_default())
            .collect()
    });

    let seconds = started.elapsed().as_secs_f64();
    let rate = acknowledged.len() as f64 / seconds;

    fs::write(&options.acked, acknowledged.join("\n") + "\n")?;

    println!(
        "{} clients: {} writes acknowledged in {seconds:.2} s, {rate:.0} writes per second",
        options.clients,
        acknowledged.len()
    );

    Ok(())
}
$ ./target/release/kvd --data /var/tmp/kvd &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 12 --acked acked.txt
64 clients: 768 writes acknowledged in 4.27 s, 180 writes per second

$ ./target/release/kvgroup --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 400 --acked acked.txt
64 clients: 25600 writes acknowledged in 5.13 s, 4993 writes per second
25535 writes in 800 batches, 31.9 writes per batch
ClientsWithoutWith group commitWrites in a batch
11671651.0
81817124.0
64180499331.9
256not measured17218119.9

Several things can be read from the table. A single client gains nothing, since it sends its next write only when the previous one has been answered, and there is consequently never a second write with which a wait could be shared. Group commit improves throughput under concurrency and does nothing for the latency of an individual write, which remains 1 wait for the disk.

The size of a batch is about half the number of clients: 4 of 8, 32 of 64, 120 of 256. The explanation is that the clients fall into 2 groups that alternate. While 1 half is waiting in the batch that is being stored, the other half has just been answered and is sending its next writes, which form the following batch.

And the assumption of chapter 1 is confirmed with something to spare. The estimate supposed 20 writes for each wait and 3700 writes per second. With 64 clients the node achieved 31.9 writes for each wait and 4993 writes per second.

A crash in the middle of a batch

The server is killed while 64 clients are writing. The program kvd of chapter 2 then opens the same data directory, which incidentally demonstrates that the 2 programs use the same format for the log.

$ ./target/release/kvgroup --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 2000 --acked acked.txt &
$ sleep 2; kill -9 <pid of kvgroup>
64 clients: 9341 writes acknowledged in 2.74 s, 3412 writes per second
$ ./target/release/kvd --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
recovered 9366 keys from 9366 records, cut 0 bytes from the end of the log
$ ./target/release/kvctl verify --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --acked acked.txt
9341 acknowledged, 9341 found, 0 missing

Every one of the 9341 acknowledged writes is present. The log contains 25 more, which are the batch that had reached the disk when the process was killed and whose answers had not yet been sent. These are the durable and unacknowledged writes of chapter 2, the third case of its figure of crash points, now occurring 25 together. Group commit has not altered the guarantee in any respect. It has enlarged the number of writes that may be in that uncertain state at the moment of a crash from 1 to the size of a batch, and each of the 25 clients concerned resolves the uncertainty in the usual way, by repeating its request.

What is still missing

MissingEffect
kvgroup serves writes only.Reads need access to the map, which the committer thread owns. A shared view of the map for reading would provide it.
The replicated nodes of chapters 3 and 4 still store 1 write for each round trip.Their leaders could send a whole batch in 1 Append, which the protocol already permits, and the followers already store the records of a message with 1 wait.

The complete programs

Store::commit is part of kv/src/store.rs, which is listed in full in chapter 2.

Listing 6.10 The complete kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

//! Command kvgroup is the storage node of chapter 2 with group commit: one
//! thread writes the log, and it stores every write that is waiting with a
//! single wait for the disk.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run --release -p kvgroup -- --listen 127.0.0.1:7001 --data /var/tmp/kvgroup

use std::error::Error;
use std::net::SocketAddr;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::thread;

use axum::Router;
use axum::body::Bytes;
use axum::extract::{DefaultBodyLimit, Path, State};
use axum::http::header::ETAG;
use axum::http::{HeaderMap, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};
use axum::routing::put;
use clap::Parser;
use kv::{Change, Store, StoreError, Write, Written};
use kvd::api::{ApiError, MAX_VALUE, etag, valid_key, write_condition};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::sync::oneshot;

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7001")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    #[arg(long, default_value = "data")]
    data: PathBuf,

    /// The largest number of writes stored with one wait for the disk.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 256)]
    batch: usize,
}

/// A write on its way to the committer, with the channel for its result.
struct Request {
    write: Write,
    reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<Written, StoreError>>,
}

/// The committer: the one thread that owns the store. It takes the write
/// that has waited longest, adds every write that arrived meanwhile, and
/// stores them together.
fn run_committer(mut store: Store, requests: Receiver<Request>, limit: usize) {
    let (mut batches, mut writes) = (0u64, 0u64);

    while let Ok(first) = requests.recv() {
        // The first request, and whatever else is already waiting.
        let mut batch = vec![first];

        batch.extend(requests.try_iter().take(limit - 1));

        let (changes, replies): (Vec<Write>, Vec<_>) = batch
            .into_iter()
            .map(|request| (request.write, request.reply))
            .unzip();

        batches += 1;
        writes += changes.len() as u64;

        // A handler that has gone away no longer wants its result.
        store
            .commit(changes)
            .into_iter()
            .zip(replies)
            .for_each(|(result, reply)| drop(reply.send(result)));

        if batches.is_multiple_of(200) {
            let average = writes as f64 / batches as f64;
            println!("{writes} writes in {batches} batches, {average:.1} writes per batch");
        }
    }
}

/// Hands a write to the committer and waits for its result.
async fn submit(committer: &Sender<Request>, write: Write) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
    let (reply, result) = oneshot::channel();
    let stopped = || ApiError::Unavailable("the committer has stopped".into());

    if committer
        .send(Request { write, reply })
        .is_err()
    {
        return Err(stopped());
    }

    let Ok(outcome) = result.await else {
        return Err(stopped());
    };

    Ok(outcome?)
}

async fn put_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Put {
            key,
            value: body.to_vec(),
        },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    let written = submit(&committer, write).await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Delete { key },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    submit(&committer, write).await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (store, applied, discarded) = Store::open(&options.data, true)?;

    println!("recovered {applied} records, cut {discarded} bytes from the end of the log");

    let (committer, requests) = mpsc::channel();
    thread::spawn(move || run_committer(store, requests, options.batch));

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", put(put_key).delete(delete_key))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(committer);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

            .put(&address)
            .send(format!("value of {key}"))
            .is_ok()

        }
    }

    acknowledged
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {

        let clients: Vec<_> = (1..=options.clients)
            .map(|number| scope.spawn(move || client(server, number, writes)))
            .collect();

            .collect()
