Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Rate limitera component that refuses requests from a caller that has sent too many
Ratethe number of requests per unit of time that a caller may send indefinitely
Bursta group of requests sent at the same moment, or the largest such group that is allowed
Keythe identity under which requests are counted together, such as a client id
Windowa span of time over which requests are counted
Fixed window countera count for each clock window, beginning again at 0 in every window
Sliding window loga list of the arrival times of recent requests, counted exactly
Sliding window counteran estimate of the sliding count, made from the counts of 2 fixed windows
Token bucketa rule with a refill rate and a capacity, in which each request removes 1 token
Leaky bucketa queue that releases requests at a fixed pace
GCRAthe generic cell rate algorithm, which decides from 1 stored time
Load sheddingdropping requests, whoever sent them, when a service is close to overload
429 Too Many Requeststhe HTTP status for a request refused by a limit
Retry-Afterthe HTTP header that states how long to wait before trying again
Thundering herdmany clients retrying at the same moment
Jittera random additional wait that spreads retries out
Fail opento let requests pass when the check itself cannot be made
Fail closedto refuse requests when the check itself cannot be made

Summary

  • Every limit contains a rate and a permitted burst, and the phrase “5 per second” specifies only the first.
  • The fixed window counter is the cheapest algorithm and admits twice the limit across a window boundary, which confines it to long quotas.
  • The sliding window log is exact and keeps a timestamp for every request, which suits it to small, strict limits.
  • The sliding window counter estimates the log from 2 counts, with a small error in either direction.
  • The token bucket sets rate and burst independently in 2 numbers of state, and forwards up to capacity + rate × time.
  • The leaky bucket queues requests and releases them at a fixed pace, shaping the traffic at the cost of waiting.
  • On many machines the buckets are kept in a shared store, and each update is a single indivisible operation timed by the store’s clock.
  • A refusal carries Retry-After, and well-written clients add jitter before retrying.
  • General limits fail open with local buckets, and limits that act as security controls fail closed.

Unique ID Generator: System Design

Almost every record that a system stores needs a name by which the rest of the system can refer to it. An order is mentioned in an invoice, a message in a reply, a user in a thousand other rows, and each of these references works only if the name it uses belongs to exactly 1 record and will never belong to another. Such a name is an identifier, or id, and for as long as a system consists of a single database the question of where ids come from hardly arises, because the database keeps a counter and hands out the next number with every insert.

The question becomes interesting when records are created on many machines at once. The counter that served 1 database so well now has to be shared, and a shared counter is a place where every creation of every record in the system must queue, and a machine whose failure stops all of them. This chapter is about producing identifiers without that shared point. We examine 4 ways of doing it, of which the last, an id composed of a timestamp, a node number and a counter, is the one we then design in full, and we give particular attention to the ways in which each scheme can quietly produce the same id twice.

This chapter covers

  • what an identifier is required to do, beyond being unique
  • a counter in 1 database, and what it costs at scale
  • random identifiers, the probability that 2 of them collide, and their effect on an index
  • blocks of numbers handed out by a coordinator
  • identifiers composed of time, node number and counter
  • clocks that run backwards, restarts, and node numbers given out twice
  • what an id reveals to the people who see it
  • why the order of ids from different nodes is only approximate

What an identifier has to do

Uniqueness is the one property that cannot be compromised, and it is worth being precise about its scope. An id has to differ from every other id of the same kind that has ever been issued or ever will be, on any machine, including machines that have since been replaced and machines that were restarted a moment ago and have forgotten what they did before. Most of the difficulties in this chapter come from that last clause, since it is easy to design a generator that never repeats itself while it is running and considerably harder to design one that does not repeat itself after it has lost its memory.

Several further properties are desirable, and the 4 schemes differ mainly in which of them they provide. An id should be small, because it is stored not only in its own record but in every record that refers to it and in every index over those references, so that the difference between 8 bytes and 16 is multiplied many times over. It should be obtainable without a network call, since a call adds latency to every insert and a dependency that may be unavailable. And it is very useful if ids increase with time, so that an id issued later is larger than one issued earlier.

This last property deserves an explanation, because its value is not obvious until one considers how a database stores an index. An index keeps its entries in sorted order, divided among pages of fixed size, and an insert has to write the page into which the new entry falls. If new ids are always larger than existing ones, every insert falls on the last page, which is therefore the only page that needs to be in memory, and the index grows by appending. If new ids are scattered at random across the whole range, each insert falls on a different page, nearly every page of the index is being modified at any moment, and once the index has outgrown memory each insert costs a read from disk.

Time-ordered ids bring smaller conveniences as well. Sorting by id is sorting by age, so that “the newest 20 orders” can be read from the end of the primary index without a separate index on the creation time, and an engineer looking at 2 ids in a log can tell at a glance which came first.

A counter in 1 database

The traditional source of ids is a counter kept by the database, usually called an auto-increment column or a sequence. Its ids are as small as ids can be, they are strictly increasing, and uniqueness is guaranteed by the simplest possible argument, namely that 1 component gives out each number once.

The cost lies entirely in the phrase “1 component”. Every insert anywhere in the system must reach that database, which bounds the rate at which the whole system can create records by what 1 machine can do, and adds a network round trip for every service that is not in the same data centre. If the database is unavailable, nothing can be created at all. A system that has divided its data among many shards, as the key-value store of chapter 1 does, would be reintroducing through its ids the single point of failure that sharding was meant to remove.

A well-known refinement keeps the counter and removes some of the dependence on 1 machine. 2 databases each maintain a counter, the first giving out odd numbers and the second even numbers, so that either can serve requests when the other is down and their ids never coincide. The idea extends to n databases, each stepping by n from a different starting point. Its weakness is rigidity. The number of databases is built into every id that has been issued, and to add a third database to a pair one must change the step on machines that are in service, without ever letting 2 of them issue the same number during the change. The ids are also no longer ordered in time, since one database may be far ahead of the other.

Random identifiers

At the opposite extreme is the idea of using no coordination whatsoever. Each machine picks a number at random from a range so large that 2 machines are extremely unlikely ever to pick the same one. The best-known form is the universally unique identifier, or UUID, a 128-bit value, and in its version 4 all but 6 of those bits are random, which leaves 122 random bits.

Whether “extremely unlikely” is unlikely enough can be calculated. Among n ids drawn at random from 2 to the power 122 possible values, the probability that at least 2 are equal is approximately n squared divided by 2 to the power 123. A system that generates a million ids every second for 30 years produces about 10 to the power 15 ids, and the probability of a single collision among all of them comes to roughly 1 in 10 million. For nearly every purpose this is as good as certainty, provided the random numbers are truly random. That proviso is the practical risk of the scheme: a generator seeded from the clock, or 2 virtual machines cloned from the same image with the same internal state, will produce identical “random” ids with a probability that has nothing to do with the calculation above.

Random ids have 2 real costs. They occupy 16 bytes where a counter needs 8, and that is paid again in every reference and every index. And they are scattered uniformly over their range, which is the worst case for index locality shown in the figure above. Many teams have adopted random UUIDs as primary keys while their tables were small and have discovered the second cost only when the index no longer fitted in memory and insert throughput fell sharply.

The response to this has been to give up some random bits in exchange for order. Version 7 of the UUID standard places a 48-bit timestamp in milliseconds at the front and fills the rest with random bits, so that ids generated later sort after ids generated earlier, to the precision of a millisecond, while 2 ids from the same millisecond are distinguished by 74 random bits. This keeps the great advantage of random ids, which is that a machine needs nothing from anybody in order to make one, and removes the scattered inserts. What it cannot remove is the size, and if ids must fit in 64 bits, as they must wherever they are to be stored as an ordinary integer column, there is not enough room for both a useful timestamp and enough random bits to make collisions negligible.

Blocks of numbers

A third scheme returns to the counter and reduces the cost of sharing it. A coordinator holds a single durable counter. A node that needs ids asks the coordinator for a block of them, 1000 at once for example, upon which the coordinator advances its counter by 1000 and the node gives out the numbers of its block one by one from memory. The node contacts the coordinator again only when the block is used up.

Uniqueness follows from the fact that no number belongs to 2 blocks, and the coordinator is consulted once per 1000 ids, so that its load and its influence on latency are a thousandth of what they were with a plain shared counter. If the coordinator fails, every node can continue until its current block is exhausted, which with a suitable block size gives operators ample time to restore it.

2 properties are lost. The ids contain gaps, because a node that crashes or is restarted discards the unused remainder of its block, and anyone who assumed that ids are consecutive, for instance in order to count records by subtracting one id from another, will be misled. And the ids are no longer ordered in time across nodes, since a slow node may still be giving out numbers from an old block long after a busy node has moved on to much larger ones. Where neither property is needed, this is a simple and dependable scheme, and it yields the smallest ids of any distributed method.

Time, node number and counter

The fourth scheme obtains uniqueness without any communication while a node is running, keeps the id within 64 bits, and preserves the order of time. It does so by composing each id from 3 numbers that the node already has at hand: the current time in milliseconds, the node’s own number, and a counter of the ids the node has made in the current millisecond. The arrangement became widely known through a generator that a large social network published in 2010 under the name Snowflake, and ids of this form are often called by that name.

The argument for uniqueness considers the ways in which 2 ids might be related, and shows that in each case they differ in at least 1 field. If they were made by different nodes, they differ in the node number, provided every node has a number of its own. If they were made by the same node in different milliseconds, they differ in the time, provided the node’s clock does not return to a millisecond it has already used. And if they were made by the same node in the same millisecond, they differ in the counter, provided the node does not issue more ids in a millisecond than the counter can count. The 3 provisos are the whole of the engineering problem. Each corresponds to a way in which the scheme fails if it is neglected, and the 3 sections after the next deal with them in turn.

The order of the fields within the id is what makes ids sortable by time. Because the time occupies the most significant bits, comparing 2 ids as integers compares their times first, and only when the times are equal does the comparison fall through to the node number and the counter.

The sizes of the fields are a budget of 63 bits to be divided, and the division shown is the common one. 41 bits of milliseconds last for 69 years, counted from a starting date that the service chooses for itself, and choosing a recent date in place of the conventional 1970 gives the scheme its full 69 years from the day it goes into service. 10 bits allow 1024 nodes. 12 bits allow each node 4096 ids per millisecond, or about 4 million per second. A system with few nodes and a very high rate might prefer 8 bits of node and 14 of counter, and a system spread over many small machines the reverse, and the only firm rule is that the division must be fixed before the first id is issued, since ids made under 2 different divisions cannot safely coexist.

When a millisecond is full

A node that has issued 4096 ids within 1 millisecond has no counter values left for that millisecond. The correct response is to wait until the clock has advanced and to continue with a counter of 0, which delays the caller by less than a millisecond. In the simulation for this chapter, 3 nodes are each asked for 5000 ids in every one of 100 milliseconds, and each makes exactly 4096 per millisecond, so that 1228800 ids are made in all, every one of them different, and 271200 requests have to wait.

The response to avoid is letting the counter overflow. An overflowing counter carries into the adjacent field, which in this layout is the node number, and the node then issues ids that appear to come from its neighbour and may coincide with ids that the neighbour has really made.

The clock

The second proviso, that a node’s clock never returns to a millisecond it has already used, is not one that a computer’s clock satisfies without help. The clock of a machine drifts, by an amount that is typically some tens of milliseconds a day, and a time service corrects it periodically by comparison with better clocks. When the machine’s clock is found to be ahead, the correction may set it back, and for a brief period afterwards the clock shows times that it has shown before.

The defence shown in these steps is for the node to remember the time of the last id it issued and to refuse to issue an id for any earlier time. A step backwards of a few milliseconds is then waited out. A step of seconds or minutes indicates that something is wrong with the machine or its time service, and it is better for the node to report itself unhealthy, so that callers go elsewhere and an operator is alerted, than to stall silently for as long as the step lasts.

This defence depends on the node’s memory of its last id, and that memory is lost when the node restarts. Consider a node that issues an id at a time its clock calls 5000, crashes, and is running again 20 ms later with a clock that has meanwhile been corrected backwards by 50 ms. The restarted node remembers nothing, reads 4970 from its clock, and issues ids for milliseconds that its former self has already used. 2 precautions are taken against this. The node can record on disk, every few seconds, a time somewhat in the future before which it promises not to issue ids after a restart, and on starting it waits until its clock has passed the recorded time. Alternatively, or in addition, a starting node can wait for longer than the largest clock correction that is considered possible before it issues its first id. Both cost a short delay at startup and nothing afterwards.

It is tempting to avoid the problem by using the machine’s monotonic clock, which the operating system guarantees never to run backwards. That clock, however, measures time from an arbitrary starting point, commonly the moment the machine was switched on, and its readings are therefore meaningless on any other machine and after any reboot. It can serve to detect that the wall clock has jumped, by comparing the progress of the 2, and it cannot replace the wall clock as the source of the timestamp.

The node number

The first proviso requires that no 2 nodes that are making ids ever hold the same number. Of the 3 provisos it is the one whose violation is most damaging, because 2 nodes with the same number and reasonably accurate clocks produce identical ids continuously, and nothing in an id or in either node can reveal that this is happening. The duplicates surface later and elsewhere, as rejected inserts if the ids are primary keys with a uniqueness constraint, or as 2 different records answering to 1 name if they are not.

Node numbers therefore need an authority. The usual arrangement is the one of our design, in which a starting node obtains its number from a coordinator of the kind described in chapter 1, which records the numbers in use and gives each to 1 node only. The alternatives are to write the numbers into the configuration of each machine, which is workable for a handful of machines administered by hand and dangerous wherever machines are created from a common image, or to derive the number from something assumed to be unique to the machine, such as part of its network address, which holds only as long as the assumption does.

Reusing a number requires care for the same reason that restarting a node does. When a node has been retired and its number is given to a new node, the new node must not issue ids for any millisecond that the old one used, and since the 2 clocks may disagree, the coordinator should withhold a released number for longer than the largest clock difference that is thought possible. With 1024 numbers available and far fewer nodes in service, there is rarely any pressure to reuse a number quickly.

What an id reveals

An id that is handed to the outside world, in a URL or an API response, tells its recipient whatever its construction encodes, and it is as well to decide in advance whether that is acceptable.

An id of the time, node and counter form discloses exactly when the record was created, to the millisecond, to anyone who knows the layout, and the layout of such ids is common knowledge. For a public post this hardly matters, while for a medical record or an account it may. Sequential ids from a counter disclose something of commercial interest: a competitor who places an order today and another a week later, and subtracts the 2 order numbers, learns how many orders the business took in that week.

Ordered ids are also guessable. Given one valid id, neighbouring values are likely to be valid as well, and a service that returns a record to anyone presenting its id, without checking that the caller is entitled to see it, can be read from end to end by counting. The proper remedy is the authorisation check, and an id should never be relied upon as a secret. Where an unguessable reference is truly required, as in a link for resetting a password, it should be a separate random token, kept apart from the id of the record.

The order of ids is approximate

Since the time is the leading field, it is natural to read the order of 2 ids as the order in which 2 events occurred, and within a single node that reading is correct. Between nodes it holds only to the accuracy of their clocks. If the clock of node 1 is 15 ms ahead of the clock of node 2, an id that node 2 makes now is smaller than an id that node 1 made 10 ms ago, although it was made later.

Ids of this kind are accordingly described as roughly sorted: any 2 ids made further apart in time than the largest difference between clocks are in the right order, and ids made closer together than that may be in either order. This is entirely adequate for the purposes mentioned at the start of the chapter, such as index locality and listing recent records. It is inadequate as evidence that one event caused or preceded another. A system that needs to know the true order of 2 writes, for example in order to decide which of them should prevail, must obtain that order from a mechanism that establishes it, such as the sequence numbers that a leader assigns in chapter 3, and must not infer it from identifiers.

The 4 schemes compared

Counter in 1 databaseRandom (UUID version 4)Blocks of numbersTime, node, counter
Size64 bits128 bits64 bits64 bits
Network call1 per idnone1 per blocknone, after startup
Ordered by timeexactlynonoroughly
What uniqueness rests on1 machinethe quality of random numbersthe coordinator’s counterdistinct node numbers and a clock that does not repeat
Fails silently whenit does notrandom state is clonedit does not2 nodes share a number, or a clock repeats
When the shared component is downno idsnot applicableids until blocks run outrunning nodes are unaffected

The row on silent failure explains why the last scheme, for all its advantages, asks for more care than the others. The counter and the block schemes derive uniqueness from a single durable number and cannot produce a duplicate without losing that number. The schemes that need no coordination purchase their independence with assumptions about the environment, and when an assumption fails, no component is in a position to notice.

Our design uses time, node number and counter, because the requirements below ask for 64-bit ids, rough ordering by time, and continued operation when every other component is down, and no other scheme provides all 3.

Use cases

Services ask for ids, at a very high rate and with no interest in how they are made. Operators have a single duty, which is to see that every node receives a number of its own.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0Each caller receives an id that no other caller has received or will receive.
1Ids fit in 64 bits, so that they can be database keys.
2An id made later is larger than an id made earlier, to within a few milliseconds.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0AvailabilityAny node can make ids while every other node is down.
1LatencyMaking an id takes microseconds and involves no network call.
2ConsistencyUniqueness is absolute. Order between nodes is approximate, limited by how far their clocks differ.
3ScaleUp to 1024 nodes, each making 4 million ids per second.

The consistency models of chapter 1 do not apply to this design in the ordinary sense, because the nodes share no data that could be consistent or inconsistent. The uniqueness of ids follows from their layout. The only fact that nodes must agree on is which number belongs to which node, and that fact is established once, at startup, by a coordinator that is strongly consistent.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 1 node can make 4096 ids per millisecond, and the 41 bits of time last 69 years.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Ids per node per millisecond2 to the power 124096
Ids per node per second4096 × 10004096000
Nodes2 to the power 101024
Years of time2 to the power 41 ms ÷ (1000 × 60 × 60 × 24 × 365)69.7

The API

The service has a single operation. Callers that need ids in very large numbers often link the generator into their own process as a library, each such process being a node with its own number, and thereby avoid the network altogether.

Get an id

POST /v1/ids HTTP/1.1
Host: ids.example

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": "8388636672" }

We send the id as a string, because JSON numbers lose precision above 2 to the power 53.

The id is returned as a string for a reason that has caught many APIs unprepared. JSON itself places no limit on the size of a number, but the most widely used JSON parsers, those of web browsers, read every number as a 64-bit floating-point value, which represents integers exactly only up to 2 to the power 53. A larger id is silently rounded to a nearby value, so that 2 different ids can arrive in the browser as the same number.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Id nodemakes ids from its clock, its number and a counterits number and the time of its last idthe others carry on; its number is not reused while it may return
Coordinatorgives each starting node a number that no other node holdsthe numbers in userunning nodes are unaffected; new nodes cannot start

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 8.8.

  1. When an id node starts, it asks the coordinator for a node number. The coordinator gives out each number once. This is the only time a node needs anyone else.
  2. A service sends POST /v1/ids to any id node. The node reads its clock, takes the next counter value for that millisecond, and joins time, node number and counter into 1 number.

It is the absence of arrows between the id nodes that characterises this design. Once a node holds its number, it needs nothing from the coordinator or from any other node, and the availability of the service as a whole is that of whichever single node a caller manages to reach.

The design, deployed

The id nodes are spread over 3 zones and placed behind a load balancer only as a convenience for callers, since any node can answer any request. Each zone is given a range of node numbers, so that the number in an id also says where the id was made, which helps when a duplicate has to be traced. The coordinator is consulted when a node starts and at no other time. Callers with very high rates do not use the network at all: they link the generator into their own processes, each of which then holds a node number of its own.

How real systems do it

The scheme of time, node number and counter is the one that Twitter announced in June 2010 under the name Snowflake, with exactly the division used here: 1 unused bit, 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits for the machine and 12 for a sequence. Twitter adopted it when it moved its tweets from a single database to a sharded store and could no longer rely on the database’s counter. The layout has been widely copied with different divisions. Instagram described a variant in 2012 with 41 bits of time, 13 bits for the logical shard and 10 for a sequence, generated inside the database itself, so that no separate service is needed. Discord uses the original layout with its own starting date.

The counter in a pair of databases, stepping by 2, is the scheme that Flickr published as its ticket servers. Blocks of numbers handed out by a coordinator are how many database sequences are cached in practice.

Version 7 of the UUID, with a millisecond timestamp in its first 48 bits, was standardised in RFC 9562 in 2024, and it exists because of the problem of index locality described at the start of this chapter.

There is an important case in which the advice of this chapter is reversed. In a store that partitions its data by ranges of keys, as Spanner, CockroachDB and Bigtable do, keys that increase with time send every insert to the last range, and that 1 range and the machines holding it become a bottleneck however large the cluster. The documentation of such stores warns against time-ordered primary keys for exactly this reason, and recommends keys whose leading bits are spread out, by a hash or by reversing the bits of a sequence. The locality that helps an index on 1 machine becomes a hot spot on many, and which of the 2 effects governs depends on how the store beneath partitions its keys.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Giving 2 nodes the same numberBoth issue identical ids for as long as they run, and nothing reports it.Let 1 coordinator assign the numbers, and hold a released number back before reusing it.
Trusting the clock to move forwardsAfter a correction backwards, a node repeats ids it has already issued.Remember the time of the last id and refuse to issue one for an earlier time.
Forgetting the last time on restartA restarted node with a corrected clock reuses milliseconds from before the crash.Record a time on disk before which no id will be issued, or wait at startup for longer than any possible correction.
Letting the counter overflowThe overflow carries into the node number, and the ids collide with another node’s.Wait for the next millisecond when the counter is used up.
Sending ids as JSON numbersBrowsers round integers above 2 to the power 53, and 2 ids become equal.Send ids as strings.
Using random ids as the key of a large tableInserts are scattered over the whole index, which must then stay in memory.Use ids that begin with a timestamp.
Treating an id as a secretNeighbouring ids are valid and can be guessed.Check on every request that the caller may see the record.
Reading the order of ids as the order of eventsIds from 2 nodes can be out of order by the difference between their clocks.Take the order of events from a log’s sequence numbers.
Changing the sizes of the fields after launchIds made under the old and the new layout can coincide.Fix the layout before the first id is issued.

The coordinator is downnothingrunning nodes keep their numbers

Simulation in the repository. The program code/idgen simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p idgen in the code directory.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Identifier, ida value that names 1 record and no other
Sequencea counter kept by a database that gives out the next number on request
UUIDa 128-bit identifier, of which version 4 is random and version 7 begins with a timestamp
Collision2 records receiving the same id
Blocka range of consecutive numbers given to 1 node to hand out
Node numbera small number that belongs to exactly 1 generator node
Counterthe count of ids that a node has made in the current millisecond

Roughly sortedin the right order except among ids made within a short time of each other

Summary

  • An id must be unique across every machine and every restart, and it is the restarts that make this hard.
  • A counter in 1 database is exact and small, and makes every insert depend on 1 machine.
  • Random 128-bit ids need no coordination and collide with negligible probability, at the cost of size and of scattered inserts unless they begin with a timestamp.
  • Blocks of numbers reduce a shared counter to 1 call per block, and give up consecutive numbers and order in time.
  • An id composed of time, node number and counter fits in 64 bits, needs no communication, and sorts roughly by time.
  • That scheme is correct only if node numbers are distinct, the clock never repeats a millisecond, and the counter does not overflow, and it fails silently when one of these does not hold.
  • The order of ids from different nodes is accurate only to the difference between their clocks.

Distributed Cache: System Design

A database answers a question by doing work: it locates pages on disk, follows an index, perhaps joins several tables and sorts the result. When the same question is asked again a moment later, it does all of that work again, although nothing has changed and the answer will be the same. A cache is a component that remembers recent answers, keeps them in memory, and returns them without consulting the database, so that a question which took 20 ms the first time takes less than 1 ms on every subsequent occasion and places no load on the database at all.

That description contains the whole appeal of caching and conceals nearly all of its difficulty. The remembered answer is a copy, and from the moment it is made the original is free to change without the copy’s knowledge. A cache also has less room than the data it copies from, so that it must continually decide what to forget. And because a system that has a cache soon comes to rely on it, the moments at which the cache cannot help, when an entry has just expired or a cache node has just been lost, are precisely the moments at which the database receives a load it has not carried for months. This chapter treats each of these in turn: what to keep, how a copy and its original drift apart and how far that can be controlled, and how a cache fails and takes other things with it.

This chapter covers

  • what a cache is worth, as a function of how often it can answer
  • 4 ways of arranging a cache and a database, and what each guarantees
  • which entries to remove when memory is full: least recently used, least frequently used, and their relatives
  • how a cached value becomes stale, including a race that defeats the usual precautions
  • time limits, and why they are the last line of defence
  • the stampede, penetration by keys that do not exist, and the avalanche
  • spreading a cache over many nodes with the hash ring of chapter 1
  • what happens to the database when the cache is lost

What a cache is worth

The fraction of reads that a cache is able to answer is called its hit ratio, a read answered from the cache being a hit and a read that has to go on to the database a miss. Almost everything about the value of a cache follows from this single number, and the relationship is less linear than intuition suggests.

Suppose that a read from the cache takes 1 ms and a read from the database 20 ms. The average read then costs the hit ratio times 1 ms plus the miss ratio times 20 ms.

A cache that answers half of all reads has barely halved the average, since the slow half still dominates. At 90% the average has fallen to 2.9 ms, and at 99% to 1.19 ms. The more important effect, however, is on the database. Between a hit ratio of 90% and one of 99%, the reads reaching the database fall from 10% of the total to 1%, which is a tenfold reduction, and it is usually this reduction, more than the gain in latency, that a cache is installed to obtain. A database that could not possibly serve the whole read load directly is able to serve the 1% that the cache passes on.

The same arithmetic contains a warning that the rest of the chapter develops. A system whose database is sized for 1% of the read load is a system that cannot survive without its cache. If the hit ratio falls from 99% to 90%, the load on the database multiplies by 10, and if the cache is emptied altogether it multiplies by 100.

Whether a high hit ratio is attainable depends on the traffic. Caching works because requests are unevenly distributed, a small number of keys being asked for again and again while the great majority are asked for rarely. The simulation for this chapter sends a million requests for 100000 keys, with popularity concentrated on a few, to a cache of various sizes.

Size of the cacheRequests answered from the cache
1% of the keys5.7%
5% of the keys24.7%
10% of the keys42.2%
25% of the keys72.7%

A cache holding a quarter of the keys answers nearly 3 quarters of the requests. With traffic more sharply concentrated than this, which is common, the same hit ratio would be reached with a much smaller cache, and with requests spread evenly over the keys a cache of 25% would answer only 25%. The distribution of real traffic should therefore be measured before a cache is sized, and no figure quoted from elsewhere, including the figures above, is a substitute.

Arranging a cache and a database

There are 4 established ways of placing a cache beside a database, which differ in who is responsible for filling the cache and in what order the 2 are written.

In the first and commonest arrangement, called cache-aside, the application manages everything. To read, it asks the cache, and on a miss it reads the database and stores the result in the cache for the benefit of later readers. To write, it updates the database and then removes the corresponding entry from the cache, so that the next reader will miss and fetch the new value. The cache is a passive store that knows nothing of the database. The great merit of this arrangement is that the cache is optional: if it is unreachable, the application reads the database directly and continues to work, only more slowly.

Read-through moves the same logic into the cache. The application asks the cache for a key, and the cache, on a miss, fetches the value from the database itself. The behaviour is that of cache-aside, with the advantage that the fetching code exists in 1 place, where every application shares it, and the disadvantage that the cache must be taught how to query the database.

In write-through, the application writes to the cache, and the cache writes to the database before confirming. Every write thus refreshes the cache, which consequently always holds the latest value of whatever has been written through it. The cost is that every write pays for 2 stores, and that entries are cached on writing whether or not anybody will read them.

Write-behind is write-through with the database write postponed. The cache confirms the write at once and passes it to the database later, usually in batches. Writes become very fast, and a burst of them is smoothed into a steady stream. The price is durability: writes that the cache has confirmed and has not yet passed on are lost if the cache node fails, which is the kind of loss that chapter 2 went to such lengths to prevent. Write-behind is appropriate for data whose occasional loss is tolerable, such as counters of page views, and for little else.

ArrangementWho fills the cacheOn a writeStalenessIf the cache is down
Cache-asidethe application, after a missdatabase first, then the entry is removedpossible, bounded by the time limitreads go to the database
Read-throughthe cache, on a missas for cache-asidepossible, bounded by the time limitreads fail unless the application has a fallback
Write-throughthe cache, on every writecache and database togethernone for data written this waywrites fail
Write-behindthe cache, on every writecache now, database laternone in the cache; the database lagsconfirmed writes can be lost

The design of this chapter uses cache-aside, because requirement by requirement it is the arrangement in which a failure of the cache does the least harm.

What to remove when memory is full

In steady operation a cache is always full, since it has less memory than there is data and something is inserted on every miss. Each insertion therefore requires an eviction, the removal of an existing entry, and the rule by which the victim is chosen determines the hit ratio that a cache of a given size achieves. The ideal rule would remove the entry that will not be needed for the longest time to come. As the future is unknown, practical rules estimate it from the past, and they differ in which aspect of the past they consult.

Least recently used

The rule known as least recently used, or LRU, removes the entry that has gone longest without being read or written. Its justification is the observation that requests come in clusters, so that something used a moment ago is likely to be used again soon, and something untouched for a long time is likely to remain so. The cache keeps its entries in order of last use, moves an entry to the front whenever it is used, and evicts from the back.

The final step exhibits the characteristic weakness of the rule. A had been requested 3 times in succession and was plainly the most popular key, and yet a single pass over 3 other keys, each requested once, was enough to push it out. In practice this happens when a job scans a large number of keys once, for a report or a backup: the scan passes through the cache, evicting the truly popular entries in favour of entries that will never be requested again, and the hit ratio collapses until ordinary traffic has restored the popular entries.

Least frequently used

Least frequently used, or LFU, consults how often an entry has been used and disregards when. Every entry carries a count of its uses, and the entry with the lowest count is evicted.

On this sequence the rule does better, since the count of 3 protects A from the single requests for B, C and D, and the last request is a hit. A scan can no longer displace popular entries, because the scanned keys never accumulate a count.

LFU has the opposite weakness. A count, once earned, lasts indefinitely, so that an entry which was requested 10000 times last month and has not been requested since continues to occupy its place, while a newly popular entry begins at 1 and is in danger of eviction before it has had time to prove itself. Practical versions therefore let the counts decay, halving them at intervals, so that popularity has to be maintained to be kept.

Other rules

First in, first out evicts the entry that was inserted longest ago, without regard to use. It needs no bookkeeping on reads, which makes it the cheapest rule, and it evicts popular and unpopular entries alike, which generally makes it the least effective.

Evicting an entry chosen at random sounds like no rule at all and performs surprisingly close to LRU on many workloads. A refinement that several in-memory stores have adopted is to pick a handful of entries at random and evict the least recently used among them. This approximates LRU closely while avoiding the ordered list that true LRU must update on every single read, an update which becomes a point of contention when many threads read the cache at once.

The most effective rules in current use combine recency and frequency. One widely adopted approach admits a new entry to the main part of the cache only if an approximate count of its past requests exceeds that of the entry it would displace, so that keys seen once, whether from a scan or from the long tail of unpopular keys, are turned away at the door. The details are beyond this chapter, and the principle is the one the 2 pictures above have already shown, namely that recency and frequency each catch what the other misses.

RuleEvictsStrengthWeakness
Least recently usedthe entry unused for longestadapts quickly when popularity shiftsa scan of cold keys flushes the popular ones
Least frequently usedthe entry with the fewest usesscans do no harmformerly popular entries linger, and new ones struggle
First in, first outthe oldest insertionno work on readsignores popularity altogether
Random sample, then least recently usedthe stalest of a few random entriesclose to LRU without an ordered listslightly lower hit ratio

Our design uses least recently used, as most caches do. It is simple, it suits traffic in which popularity changes from hour to hour, and its weakness can be avoided by keeping scans away from the cache.

How a copy becomes stale

A cached value is stale when the database holds a newer one. Some staleness is inherent in caching and has to be accepted, and the purpose of the design is to bound it and to make sure that it is never permanent.

Under cache-aside, staleness is addressed by the rule that a writer, having updated the database, removes the entry from the cache. It may be asked why the writer does not place the new value in the cache directly, which would spare the next reader a miss. The reason is that 2 writers can then interfere. If writer 1 sets the database to 11 and writer 2 sets it to 12, and their subsequent writes to the cache happen to arrive in the opposite order, the database ends at 12 and the cache at 11. Removing the entry is immune to this, because removing something twice, in either order, leaves it removed.

The order of the 2 steps of a write also matters, the database being written before the entry is removed. If the entry were removed first, a reader arriving between the removal and the database write would miss, read the old value from the database, and put it back into the cache, where it would remain after the write had completed.

Even with both precautions observed, a stale value can become established, through an interleaving of a reader and a writer that is rare and entirely possible.

What makes this race instructive is that neither request did anything wrong. The reader followed the rule for reads and the writer the rule for writes, and the result is a cache that disagrees with the database and will go on disagreeing, since no further event is scheduled to correct it. The race needs a read to be delayed, between fetching from the database and storing in the cache, for longer than an entire write takes, which is unusual, and on a busy system unusual events occur many times a day.

There are 3 defences, of increasing strength. The first is to give every entry a time limit, discussed in the next section, so that even an entry that should have been removed disappears eventually. The second is for the writer to remove the entry a second time after a short delay, which catches a reader that stored its stale value just after the first removal. The third makes the reader’s store conditional. On a miss the cache hands the reader a token, the removal of an entry invalidates any token outstanding for it, and a store that presents an invalidated token is rejected. In the steps above, request 2’s removal would have invalidated the token of request 1, whose attempt to store 10 would then have failed, leaving the cache empty and correct.

Time limits

Every entry in a cache should carry a time to live, or TTL, after which the cache discards it regardless of anything else. The TTL is what converts every failure of invalidation, whether the race just described, a removal that was lost because the cache was briefly unreachable, or a code path that updates the database and forgets the cache, from a permanent error into a temporary one. It is the single mechanism that bounds staleness unconditionally, and for that reason it should be present even where explicit removal is believed to be complete.

Choosing the value is a judgement about the data. A long TTL gives a higher hit ratio and allows stale values to live longer, and a short one the reverse. The question to ask of each kind of data is how long a wrong answer could be shown before somebody is harmed. A product description may tolerate an hour, the number of items in stock a few seconds, and an account balance nothing at all, which is another way of saying that it should not be cached in this manner.

3 ways in which a cache fails under load

The failures considered so far concern correctness. The 3 considered next concern load, and each of them has brought down systems whose caches were functioning exactly as designed.

The stampede

When a popular entry expires or is removed, every request that arrives before it has been restored is a miss. For an entry that is read 500 times per second and takes 100 ms to recompute, some 50 requests will arrive during the recomputation, and under plain cache-aside every one of them queries the database for the same value.

If the query is expensive, the database slows down under 50 simultaneous copies of it, the recomputation takes longer, still more requests arrive during it, and the situation feeds on itself. This is called a stampede.

The principal remedy is to ensure that only 1 request recomputes a given entry. The first request to miss takes a short-lived lock on the key and proceeds to the database, and the others, finding the lock taken, wait briefly and read the cache again, by which time the value is usually there. A complementary technique avoids the miss altogether by refreshing popular entries shortly before they expire: a request that finds an entry close to its expiry may, with a probability that rises as the expiry approaches, recompute it early while all other requests continue to be served the existing value. A third approach is to serve the expired value for a short grace period while a single request fetches a fresh one in the background, which trades a little staleness for the complete absence of a stampede.

Penetration by keys that do not exist

A cache stores answers, and a request for something that does not exist has, on the face of it, no answer to store. Consequently every request for a nonexistent key misses the cache and reaches the database, which searches and finds nothing, and the next request for the same key does the same. An attacker who requests random ids, or merely a defective client that keeps asking for a deleted record, thus obtains unimpeded access to the database, the cache contributing nothing. This is known as cache penetration.

The straightforward remedy is to cache the absence. When the database reports that a key does not exist, the application stores a marker to that effect under a short TTL, and subsequent requests for the key are answered from the cache. Where the set of possible nonexistent keys is very large, as with random ids, the markers themselves could fill the cache, and a more economical structure is placed in front: a Bloom filter, which is a compact summary of the set of keys that do exist. It can state with certainty that a key is absent, and it occasionally reports an absent key as possibly present, in which case the request proceeds to the cache and the database as usual. A filter covering a billion keys occupies little more than a gigabyte.

The avalanche

The third failure arises when a large part of the cache becomes empty at once. This happens when many entries were loaded together and given the same TTL, for example by a job that warms the cache at startup, so that they all expire in the same instant. It happens on a larger scale when a cache node fails or is restarted. In either case the hit ratio falls abruptly, and by the arithmetic of the first section a fall from 99% to 90% multiplies the load on the database by 10.

Against synchronised expiry the remedy is to add a random amount to each TTL, so that entries loaded together expire over a spread of time. Against the loss of a node, the remedies are structural and are the subject of the next section. In both cases the database should be defended independently, by a limit on the number of concurrent queries that the application will send to it, so that an empty cache results in slow responses and some refusals while the database itself stays up. The rate limiter of chapter 7 and load shedding serve exactly this purpose.

A cache on many nodes

With 100 GB of entries and nodes of 16 GB, the cache has to be spread over several machines, and each key must be assigned to one of them in a way that every client computes identically. This is the problem that chapter 1 solved for the key-value store, and the solution is the same: a consistent hash ring on which each node owns many small ranges, so that adding or removing a node moves only the keys of that node.

The argument for consistent hashing is, if anything, stronger for a cache than for a store. A key that moves to a different node is, from the cache’s point of view, a key that has been forgotten, since the new node does not have it. Were keys assigned by taking a hash modulo the number of nodes, the addition of a single node would move nearly all keys, which is to say that it would empty the cache, with the consequences just described. On the ring, adding an eighth node to 7 moves about an eighth of the keys.

In this design the ring lives in a library inside each service, and the cache nodes are unaware of one another. A node holds entries, evicts and expires them, and that is all. There is no leader and no replication between nodes in the basic design, on the reasoning that every entry is a copy of something held durably elsewhere, so that the loss of a node loses nothing that cannot be fetched again.

That reasoning is sound with respect to data and incomplete with respect to load. The loss of 1 node in 8 turns an eighth of all reads into misses until those entries have been fetched again, and the database must be able to bear this. Where it cannot, each entry can be written to 2 nodes, the next one clockwise on the ring serving as a standby, at the cost of half the cache’s capacity. A related precaution concerns a node that returns after a restart with its memory empty: its entries can be loaded gradually by admitting only a fraction of its normal traffic at first, so that its misses arrive at the database as a trickle.

A last difficulty on many nodes is the hot key, a single entry so popular that the 1 node holding it is overloaded while the others are idle. No arrangement of the ring helps, since the ring spreads keys and this is 1 key. The usual answers are to keep a copy of such entries in the memory of each application process for a second or 2, in front of the distributed cache, or to store the entry under several derived keys on different nodes and have readers choose among them at random.

Use cases

Services read through the cache and inform it when the data behind an entry has changed. Operators add and remove nodes.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A service can store a value under a key for a limited time.
1A service can read a value, and learns whether the cache had it.
2A service can delete a key when the data behind it changes.
3When memory is full, the cache drops the entries that were used longest ago.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0LatencyA read takes under 1 ms.
1AvailabilityThe loss of a cache node loses no data that matters, because every entry is a copy.
2ConsistencyEventual. A cached value can be older than the database for as long as its time limit.
3Scale100 GB of entries and 200000 reads per second.

A cache is eventually consistent by its nature, and non-functional requirement 2 says so openly. For some period after a write, a reader may still receive the previous value, and the TTL of the entry is the bound on that period. The design does not attempt to remove this window. It attempts to make its length a deliberate choice for each kind of data, and to ensure, by means of the TTL, that no failure can extend it indefinitely.

The API

Values are opaque bytes, as in the key-value store of chapter 1, and the time limit of an entry travels in a header.

Store a value for 60 seconds

PUT /v1/entries/user-42 HTTP/1.1
Host: cache.example
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Content-Length: 9

ada, 1815

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

After 60 seconds the entry is gone, whether or not it was read.

Read a value that is not cached

GET /v1/entries/user-43 HTTP/1.1
Host: cache.example

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

Misses are ordinary answers: the caller reads the database and stores the result.

A miss is reported with 404, since from the point of view of HTTP the resource does not exist at that address. It is an ordinary outcome and no error, and the caller responds to it by reading the database and storing the result.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Cache libraryhashes a key and talks to the node that holds ita copy of the ringnothing to recover: it is part of the service
Cache nodekeeps entries in memory and drops the least recently usedentries, in memory onlyits keys miss until they are fetched again
Databaseholds the real dataeverythingoutside the scope of the cache

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 9.8.

  1. A service asks the cache library for user-42.
  2. The library hashes the key on its ring and asks the 1 cache node that owns it. That node answers with the value, or with 404.
  3. On 404, the service reads user-42 from the database, which is slower.
  4. The service stores the value in the cache with a time limit, so that the next reader gets a hit.

A write follows the complementary path. The service updates the database first, and when the database has confirmed, it sends DELETE for the key to the cache node that owns it. If that DELETE fails because the node is unreachable, the entry survives with the old value until its TTL expires, which is the case the TTL exists for.

The design, deployed

The deployment has a feature that distinguishes it from most others in this book, which is the absence of a load balancer. Each of the 400 service instances contains the cache library with its copy of the ring, and sends every request directly to the 1 cache node that owns the key. The 8 nodes are spread over 3 zones. With a hit ratio of 99%, about 2000 of the 200000 reads per second go on to the database, whose followers serve them. The figure makes the dependence plain: the database tier is sized for the traffic that passes the cache, and would receive 100 times as much if the cache tier were lost.

How real systems do it

The most thorough public account of a cache at scale is Facebook’s paper on its use of memcached, and nearly every difficulty in this chapter appears in it with the remedy that Facebook adopted.

The stale value left by an overlapping read and write, and the stampede on a missing entry, are both solved there by 1 mechanism, the lease. On a miss, the cache gives the client a token that entitles it to fill the entry. A delete invalidates any outstanding token, so that a late fill with an old value is rejected, which is the conditional store described above. And the cache issues a token for a given key only at intervals, telling other clients that miss in the meantime to wait briefly and try again, which prevents the stampede. The paper reports that leases reduced the peak rate of database queries for a set of keys prone to stampedes from 17000 per second to 1300.

The paper also describes what it does about the avalanche. When a cache server fails, its keys are not moved to the remaining servers, which might then be overloaded in turn. Requests for them go to a small set of idle machines kept for the purpose, called the gutter. Invalidation is driven from the database’s own log of committed changes, which is more dependable than relying on every application to issue its deletes, and a cluster that starts empty is warmed by reading from a neighbouring cluster’s cache before it is allowed to reach the database.

On eviction, the rule of sampling a few entries and removing the least recently used among them is what Redis does by default, with 5 samples. The admission policy that compares the estimated frequency of a newcomer with that of the entry it would replace is TinyLFU, implemented in the Caffeine library. A study of the cache clusters at Twitter found, among other things, that for many workloads at realistic cache sizes plain first in, first out performed about as well as LRU, which has since led to a family of simple queue-based policies. The technique of refreshing an entry early with a probability that rises towards its expiry has been analysed formally and shown to be optimal in a certain sense.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Entries without a time limitA missed or lost removal leaves a wrong value in place permanently.Give every entry a TTL, even where removal on write is believed to be complete.
Writing the new value into the cache on update2 writers can leave the cache holding the older of their values.Remove the entry and let the next reader fetch it.
Removing the entry before writing the databaseA reader in between restores the old value.Write the database first, then remove.
Assuming that removal after writing closes every raceA delayed reader can store an old value after the removal.Rely on the TTL, and where it matters make the reader’s store conditional.
Letting every miss query the databaseAn expired popular entry produces a stampede.Let 1 request recompute while the others wait or are served the old value.
Not caching absencesRequests for nonexistent keys reach the database every time.Cache a marker for “does not exist” with a short TTL, or put a Bloom filter in front.
The same TTL on entries loaded togetherThey expire together, and the hit ratio drops at once.Add a random amount to each TTL.
Sizing the database for the load that passes the cacheThe loss of the cache multiplies the database’s load beyond what it can serve.Limit concurrent queries to the database, and test with the cache empty.
Assigning keys by hash modulo the number of nodesAdding a node moves nearly every key, which empties the cache.Use a consistent hash ring.
Scanning through the cacheA batch job evicts the popular entries.Let scans read the database directly, without storing what they read.
Caching data that must be exactReaders act on a balance or a permission that has changed.Read such data from the database, or use the write-through arrangement.
