Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Cachea store of copies kept in memory so that repeated reads are fast
Hit, missa read that the cache answers, and a read that it cannot
Hit ratiothe fraction of reads that are hits
Cache-asidethe arrangement in which the application reads the database on a miss and fills the cache
Read-throughthe arrangement in which the cache fetches from the database on a miss
Write-throughthe arrangement in which a write goes to the cache and the database together
Write-behindthe arrangement in which the cache confirms a write and passes it to the database later
Evictionremoving an entry to make room for another
Least recently used, LRUevicting the entry that has gone longest without use
Least frequently used, LFUevicting the entry with the fewest uses
Staleolder than the value now in the database
Invalidationremoving or replacing an entry because its original has changed
Time to live, TTLthe time after which the cache discards an entry
Stampedemany requests recomputing the same entry at once after a miss
Cache penetrationrequests for keys that do not exist, which the cache cannot answer
Bloom filtera compact summary of a set that can say for certain that a key is absent
Avalanchea large part of the cache becoming empty at once
Hot key1 entry popular enough to overload the node that holds it

Summary

  • The value of a cache lies in its hit ratio, and going from 90% to 99% reduces the load on the database tenfold.
  • A system sized for the load that passes its cache cannot run without the cache, so the database needs its own protection.
  • In cache-aside, a reader fills the cache after a miss, and a writer updates the database and then removes the entry.
  • Least recently used adapts quickly and is flushed by scans, while least frequently used resists scans and holds on to entries that are no longer popular.
  • A read and a write can overlap so that the cache keeps an old value, and the time limit on every entry is what bounds the damage.
  • A stampede is prevented by letting 1 request recompute an entry, penetration by caching absences, and an avalanche by spreading expiry times.
  • Keys are assigned to cache nodes with a consistent hash ring, so that a change of nodes forgets only a small share of the entries.

Distributed Lock: System Design

Some operations must be performed by 1 party only. A nightly billing run that charges every customer should execute once, on 1 machine, a file that is being rewritten should not be rewritten by 2 processes whose changes would interleave, and of the replicas of a database exactly 1 should accept writes. Within a single process this need is met by a lock, an object that 1 thread holds while it works and that makes every other thread wait, and the operating system guarantees that the lock behaves as advertised.

A distributed lock attempts to offer the same service to processes on different machines, and it has to do so under conditions that a lock inside 1 process is spared. The holder of a distributed lock may crash without releasing it. It may be cut off from the network and continue working in the belief that it still holds the lock. It may stop for a while, through no fault of its own, and resume later with no awareness that time has passed. In each case the other participants can observe only that the holder has fallen silent, and they cannot tell which of these things has happened. The central result of this chapter is that under these conditions a lock service cannot, by itself, guarantee that only 1 process acts at any moment, however carefully it is built, and that the guarantee has to be completed by the resource which the lock protects.

This chapter covers

  • the 2 purposes of a lock, and why they call for different amounts of care
  • a lock as an entry in a shared store, and why it has to expire
  • the paused holder, which no lease can exclude
  • fencing tokens, by which the protected resource rejects a late holder
  • releasing a lock safely, and renewing a lease
  • why the lock service itself must store each lock on a majority
  • waiting for a lock without a stampede
  • when a lock is the wrong tool

What a lock is for

Locks are taken for 2 quite different reasons, and it is necessary to know which one applies before deciding how much machinery a lock deserves.

In the first case the lock serves efficiency. Its purpose is to avoid doing the same work twice: sending a reminder email from 2 machines, or having 5 servers recompute the same expensive report. If the lock occasionally fails and 2 processes do proceed together, the consequence is some wasted effort or a duplicated email, which is regrettable and nothing more. A lock of this kind may be simple and may be wrong once in a long while.

In the second case the lock serves correctness. Here 2 processes acting together would corrupt something: a file written by both, an account debited twice, 2 database nodes both accepting writes as leader. When such a lock fails, the result is lost or damaged data, and “once in a long while” is not an acceptable frequency.

Much of the confusion surrounding distributed locks arises from applying a mechanism that is adequate for the first purpose to the second. The simple designs described in the next 2 sections are perfectly serviceable for efficiency. The remainder of the chapter concerns what must be added for correctness, and it turns out to be a good deal.

A lock as an entry in a store

The basic construction requires nothing more than a store that all the parties can reach and that offers 1 atomic operation: create this key, provided it does not already exist. To acquire the lock named nightly-billing, a worker asks the store to create that key with the worker’s own name as its value. If the creation succeeds, the worker holds the lock. If the key already exists, another worker holds it, and the creation fails. To release the lock, the holder deletes the key.

The atomicity of “create if absent” is what makes this a lock. Were the worker to read the key first and create it afterwards, in 2 separate operations, 2 workers could both read that the key was absent and both proceed to create it, which is the same race that chapter 7 found between 2 rate limiter nodes sharing a bucket.

This lock has an obvious and fatal defect. If the worker that holds it crashes, or loses its network connection, the key is never deleted, and the lock remains taken for ever. Every other worker waits indefinitely on a holder that no longer exists.

Leases

The remedy is to let the lock expire. The key is created with a time limit, 10 seconds for example, and the store deletes it automatically when that time has passed. A lock that expires in this way is called a lease. A worker that needs the lock for longer than the lease must renew it periodically, by asking the store to extend the time limit while the worker’s name is still on the key, and a worker that crashes ceases to renew, so that its lease runs out and the lock becomes available to others.

The lease repairs the defect of the previous section and in doing so introduces the difficulty that occupies the rest of this chapter. The lock can now pass to a second worker without the first having agreed to give it up. Whenever a lease ends, there are 2 possibilities which the store cannot distinguish: the holder is dead, in which case handing the lock to someone else is exactly right, or the holder is alive and has merely been prevented from renewing, in which case there will shortly be 2 workers that each consider themselves the holder.

The duration of the lease expresses a trade between these cases. A short lease means that a crashed holder is replaced quickly and that a slow or briefly disconnected holder is more often presumed dead. A long lease means the opposite. No duration makes the second case impossible.

The holder that pauses

It might seem that a careful worker could protect itself against the second case. It knows when its lease ends, so it could check the clock before each step of its work and stop if the lease has run out.

This fails, and the reason is fundamental. No amount of careful programming removes it. Between the moment at which the worker checks its lease and the moment at which the effect of its next action reaches the protected resource, an arbitrary amount of time can pass without the worker being aware of it. The process may be suspended by its runtime in order to reclaim memory, which in some languages can take seconds. The virtual machine in which it runs may be paused by its host, for instance while being moved to another physical machine. The operating system may be short of memory and spend a long time reading the process’s pages back from disk. Or the worker’s write may be on its way through a congested network, delayed in a buffer for longer than the lease has left to run. In every one of these cases the worker performed its check correctly, found the lease valid, and acted in good faith, and the action took effect after the lease had ended and the lock had been given to someone else.

Nor can the worker rely on its clock to notice. A lease is measured on the clock of the lock service, while the worker reads its own, and chapter 8 has already shown that the clocks of 2 machines differ and that either may be corrected at any moment.

The conclusion has to be stated without qualification. A worker can never be certain, at the instant its action takes effect, that it still holds the lock. Any design in which correctness depends on that certainty is unsound, and the degree of unsoundness is merely a question of how often pauses of sufficient length occur.

Fencing tokens

Since the lock service cannot prevent a late holder from acting, and the holder cannot detect its own lateness, the only remaining party that can intervene is the resource being protected. It needs some means of recognising that a request comes from a holder whose lease has been superseded, and the lock service can supply that means at very small cost.

Each time the service grants the lock, it also issues a number that is larger than any it has issued before. This number is the fencing token. The holder attaches its token to every request it sends to the protected resource, and the resource remembers the highest token it has seen and refuses any request that carries a lower one.

The picture follows the scenario of the previous section to its end. Worker A was suspended, its lease expired, B was granted the lock with token 2 and wrote, and A then resumed and attempted to write with token 1. The storage refused, on the simple ground that 1 is less than 2. Nothing in this depends on clocks, on the length of the pause, or on A’s noticing anything.

The token changes the nature of what the lock service provides. Without tokens, the service is asked to guarantee that 2 workers never act together, which it cannot. With tokens, it is asked only to issue increasing numbers and to grant the lock to 1 worker per number, which it can, and the exclusion is enforced at the 1 place where it can be enforced, namely the resource itself.

There is a requirement hidden in this arrangement, and it is the reason fencing is used less often than it should be. The protected resource must take part. It has to accept a token with each request, store the highest, and compare. A database can do this readily, by keeping the token in a column and making each write conditional on the token’s being no lower than the stored one, which is the compare-and-set operation of chapter 1. A resource that cannot be made to check tokens, such as a third-party API that merely accepts requests, cannot be protected for correctness by any distributed lock at all, and in that case one must either accept the risk or redesign the operation so that performing it twice does no harm.

Releasing and renewing

Releasing a lock looks like the simplest of the operations and conceals a well-known error. A worker that releases by deleting the key, without regard to its contents, may delete a lock that it no longer holds.

The correct release is conditional: delete the key only if its value is still my name. The comparison and the deletion have to be a single atomic operation in the store, for the usual reason that the lock might change hands between a separate read and delete. The same condition applies to renewal, which must extend the lease only if the caller is still the holder.

Renewal raises a question of timing. A worker normally renews at intervals of about a third of the lease, so that 2 consecutive renewals may be lost before the lease is in danger. The renewing is commonly done by a separate thread, so that the work itself need not be interrupted, and this has a hazard of its own. If the working thread becomes stuck while the renewing thread continues happily, the lock is held for ever by a worker that is accomplishing nothing, which is the original defect returned by another route. A sound implementation ties the 2 together, for example by renewing only while the work reports progress.

The lock service must not lose locks

Everything so far has treated the store that holds the lock as reliable, and a lock service on a single machine is as reliable as that machine. For availability the service is therefore replicated, and how it is replicated matters a great deal.

Many in-memory stores replicate in the manner that chapter 3 called asynchronous: the leader confirms a write to the client at once and forwards it to its followers afterwards. For a cache this is a sensible choice. For a lock it is a flaw.

The lock service is the 1 component in this design that requires strong consistency in the full sense of chapter 1. A granted lock has to survive the failure of any single node, which means that it has to be stored on a majority of nodes before it is confirmed, exactly as chapter 3 stores a record and chapter 4 elects a leader. Token numbers must likewise come from the replicated log, so that a new leader continues from the highest token ever issued and does not start again from a lower one. In practice this means building the lock service on a consensus system of the kind developed in chapters 3 and 4, and the coordinator of chapter 1 is such a system and commonly offers locks as one of its services.

An alternative that is sometimes proposed avoids consensus by using several independent stores. The worker attempts to create the lock on each of 5 unrelated nodes and regards itself as the holder if it succeeds on at least 3 within a short time. This is more dependable than a single node, since no 1 failure loses the lock. Its safety, however, rests on assumptions about time: that the clocks of the 5 nodes advance at nearly the same rate, and that the worker is not paused between acquiring the lock and using it. The previous sections have shown that neither assumption can be relied upon, and so this approach is suitable for locks taken for efficiency and should be combined with fencing, like any other, when correctness is at stake. It cannot itself supply fencing tokens, since 5 independent nodes have no common counter.

Waiting for a lock

A worker that fails to acquire a lock generally wishes to obtain it as soon as it is free. The crude method is to try again at intervals, which either wastes requests if the interval is short or wastes time if it is long.

Lock services therefore let a worker watch a key and be notified when it is deleted. The naive use of this facility has a defect at scale. If 100 workers are all watching the same lock, its release wakes all 100, all of them attempt to acquire it, 1 succeeds, and 99 resume watching, so that every release costs 100 notifications and 100 attempts. This is the thundering herd that chapter 7 met among retrying clients.

The established remedy arranges the waiters in a queue. Each worker, on arriving, creates an entry of its own that the service numbers in order of arrival. The worker whose entry bears the lowest number holds the lock. Every other worker watches only the entry immediately ahead of its own. When the holder finishes and deletes its entry, exactly 1 worker is notified, the next in line, and it becomes the holder. The entries are tied to the sessions of their workers, so that the entry of a worker that crashes is removed by the service and the queue closes up behind it. As well as avoiding the herd, this arrangement is fair, since the lock is granted in the order in which it was requested.

When a lock is the wrong tool

A distributed lock used for correctness requires a consensus system, fencing tokens, and the cooperation of the protected resource. It is worth asking, before paying that price, whether the problem can be solved without mutual exclusion.

Often it can. If the operation can be made idempotent, so that performing it twice has the same effect as performing it once, then 2 workers doing it together is harmless and no lock is needed: chapter 19 uses this approach for payments. If the operation is an update to a single record, a conditional write expresses “change this only if nobody else has changed it since I read it” directly, and the loser of a race reads again and retries, which is the compare-and-set of chapter 1 and is called optimistic concurrency. And if work can be partitioned so that each item has exactly 1 owner, as the message queue of chapter 11 assigns each partition to 1 consumer, then exclusion is achieved by the assignment and need not be negotiated for each item.

It will be observed that fencing is itself a conditional write, and this is no coincidence. In a correct design the resource’s own check does the real work of protection, and the lock in front of it serves chiefly to keep workers from wasting effort on attempts that would be refused. Seen in this light, a lock is an optimisation layered over a conditional write, and a design that has the conditional write may find that it needs the lock less than it supposed.

Use cases

The lock service has a single kind of user, a worker that must be alone during some critical step.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A worker can acquire a named lock. At most 1 worker holds a lock at any time.
1A lock is held for a limited time, a lease, and the holder can renew it.
2A lock whose lease has ended can be acquired by another worker.
3Every lease comes with a token that is larger than the token of every earlier lease.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0ConsistencyStrong. At any moment, the lock service grants a lock to at most 1 worker.
1AvailabilityThe service survives the loss of 1 of its 3 nodes.
2LatencyAcquiring a lock takes 1 round trip to a majority, a few milliseconds.

This is one of the few designs in the book that demands strong consistency without reservation. A cache may be stale and a rate limiter may be off by a few requests, but a lock service that grants 1 lock to 2 holders has failed at the only thing it is for. The lock and its token are therefore stored on a majority of the service’s nodes before a grant is confirmed, and when a majority cannot be reached the service refuses to grant locks at all, preferring unavailability to error.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. A lock is about 100 bytes, so a million locks fit in 100 MB, and 3 small nodes are enough.

Memory per lockname 50 bytes + holder 30 + token 8 + expiry 8about 100 bytes

The API

A lock is a resource with a name. Acquiring it creates the resource, renewing it replaces the expiry, and releasing it deletes the resource.

Acquire a lock for 10 seconds

POST /v1/locks/nightly-billing HTTP/1.1
Host: locks.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "holder": "worker-a", "seconds": 10 }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{ "token": 1, "expires_in": 10 }

Workers have to pass the token on to whatever the lock protects.

Acquire a lock that is held

POST /v1/locks/nightly-billing HTTP/1.1
Host: locks.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "holder": "worker-b", "seconds": 10 }

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/lock-held",
  "title": "The lock is held",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "held for 9 more seconds"
}

409 Conflict is the status for a request that is valid but cannot be carried out in the current state.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Workeracquires the lock, then does its workthe token of its leaseits lease runs out, and another worker can acquire the lock
Lock servicegrants leases and counts tokensthe locks, replicated on 3 nodesthe other 2 nodes continue
Storagethe thing the lock protects; checks the tokenthe highest token it has acceptedoutside the scope of the lock service

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 10.6.

  1. A worker sends POST /v1/locks/nightly-billing. The lock service, a group of 3 nodes that agree by majority, records the worker as holder for 10 seconds and returns token 1.
  2. The worker does its protected work and sends token 1 with every write to the storage. The storage compares the token with the highest it has accepted.

The scenario, simulated

The simulation for this chapter plays out the paused holder with and without help from the storage. Its output for the fenced case reads as follows.

TimeEventResult
0 sworker A acquires the locktoken 1, lease until 10 s
1 sworker B asks for the lockrefused
2 sworker A is paused for 15 seconds
12 sthe lease has ended, and worker B acquires the locktoken 2
13 sworker B writes with token 2accepted
17 sworker A resumes and writes with token 1refused

At the end the storage holds what worker B wrote.

The design, deployed

The lock service is small. It has 3 nodes, 1 in each zone, which form a single consensus group of the kind built in chapter 4, and workers reach whichever of them is the leader. It needs no more machines than this, because a well-designed system takes locks rarely and holds them for long periods, so that the rate of requests is low. What the figure is chiefly meant to show is the second arrow. The workers write to the protected storage directly, and the lock service is not on that path at all, which is why the last line of defence has to be in the storage.

How real systems do it

The lock service of this chapter is modelled on Chubby, which Google described in 2006 and which is the origin of most of the vocabulary. Chubby is a small replicated store whose locks are leases renewed by periodic messages, and its paper makes 2 observations that bear directly on this chapter. It introduces the sequencer, a token obtained with a lock that the holder passes to the servers it uses and that they check, which is the fencing token under its original name. And it reports that the service was designed for coarse locks held for hours or days, chiefly for electing leaders, and that using it for fine-grained locking is discouraged.

ZooKeeper provides the queue of waiters described above as a standard recipe. Each waiter creates a node that is numbered in sequence and tied to its session, and watches only the node immediately before its own. In etcd, a lock is a key attached to a lease, and the revision number at which the key was created, which increases with every change to the store, serves as a fencing token.

The approach of acquiring a lock on a majority of independent in-memory stores is the Redlock algorithm proposed by the author of Redis. Martin Kleppmann’s analysis of it in 2016 set out the argument of this chapter: that a pause of the process or a jump of a clock can leave 2 clients each believing that it holds the lock, that no lease-based lock can prevent this, and that safety therefore requires fencing, which Redlock does not provide since it has no source of increasing numbers. The author of Redis replied in defence of the algorithm, and the exchange remains the clearest public discussion of what a distributed lock can and cannot promise.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
A lock without a time limitA holder that crashes keeps the lock for ever.Make every lock a lease.
Believing that a lease guarantees 1 holderA paused or delayed holder acts after its lease has ended.Have the protected resource check a fencing token.
Checking the lease and then writingThe pause can fall between the check and the write.Let the resource decide, on the token, at the moment of the write.
Releasing by deleting the key unconditionallyA late holder deletes the lock of its successor.Delete only if the key still carries the caller’s name, in 1 operation.
Reading the key and then creating it2 workers both find it absent and both create it.Use the store’s atomic create-if-absent.
A lock store that confirms before replicatingA failover forgets the lock, and it is granted twice.Store each lock on a majority before confirming.
Renewing from a thread that ignores the workA stuck worker holds the lock indefinitely.Renew only while the work makes progress.
Every waiter watching the lock itselfEach release wakes all of them.Queue the waiters, each watching the one ahead.
A lease shorter than the usual length of the workThe lock changes hands in the middle of ordinary runs.Set the lease well above the normal duration, and renew.
Taking a lock where a conditional write would doMachinery and a dependency that add no safety.Use compare-and-set or an idempotent operation.

A worker pauses for longer than its leasenothing wrong: its late writes are refusedthe worker sees the refusal and stops
A lock service node is lostnothingthe remaining 2 nodes form a majority

Trade-offs

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Locka right, held by 1 party, to act alone on something
Mutual exclusionthe property that at most 1 party acts at any moment
Leasea lock that expires unless its holder renews it
Renewalextending a lease before it expires
Process pausea period in which a process does not run and is unaware of it
Fencing tokena number, larger with every grant of a lock, that the protected resource checks

Summary

  • A lock taken for efficiency may occasionally fail, and a lock taken for correctness may not, and the 2 need very different designs.
  • A lock in a shared store has to be a lease, since a holder that crashes would otherwise keep it for ever.
  • A lease can end while its holder is paused or delayed, and the holder cannot detect this, so a lease alone does not guarantee 1 holder.
  • A fencing token, which grows with every grant and is checked by the protected resource, rejects the late holder.
  • Release and renewal must be conditional on the caller still being the holder.
  • The lock service stores each lock and token on a majority, because a lock forgotten in a failover is a lock granted twice.
  • Waiters are queued so that a release notifies 1 of them.
  • Idempotent operations and conditional writes often remove the need for a lock.

Message Queue: System Design

When one service needs another to do something, the direct course is to call it and wait for the answer. An order service that has accepted an order calls the billing service to issue an invoice, then the warehouse to reserve the goods, then the mail service to send a confirmation, and replies to the customer when all 3 have answered. This works, and it binds the 4 services together more tightly than is good for any of them. The order service is now as slow as the slowest of the 3 and as available as all of them together, so that an outage of the mail service, which is surely the least important of the 3, prevents customers from placing orders.

A message queue loosens this binding. The order service records the fact that an order was created by writing a short message to the queue, and its part is then finished. Billing, the warehouse and the mail service each read the message when they are able to, at their own pace, and a service that is down for an hour reads it an hour late and is otherwise none the worse. The sender and the receivers need not be running at the same time, need not be equally fast, and need not know of one another’s existence.

What the queue takes on in exchange is a set of promises that are easy to state and hard to keep: that a message once accepted is not lost, that it reaches every party entitled to it, that related messages arrive in the order in which they were sent, and that all of this continues to hold when machines fail in the middle of things. This chapter designs a queue of the kind that keeps its messages in a log, and most of it is devoted to stating exactly what can and what cannot be promised about delivery.

This chapter covers

  • what a queue changes in the relationship between 2 services
  • 2 kinds of queue: one that hands out tasks, and one that keeps a log
  • partitions, keys, and what ordering a queue can preserve
  • consumer groups, and how partitions are shared and reassigned
  • at most once, at least once, and why “exactly once” needs the consumer’s help
  • what a producer must do so that a retry does not duplicate a message
  • how a queue stays durable, using the replication of chapter 3
  • messages that can never be processed, consumers that fall behind, and publishing together with a database write

What a queue changes

A queue placed between 2 services alters their relationship in 3 respects, each of which is a reason for introducing one.

It separates them in time. The sender, called the producer, hands its message to the queue and proceeds without waiting for anybody to act on it, and the receiver, called the consumer, takes the message whenever it is ready. Neither depends on the other being available at that moment, and the availability of the producer is no longer limited by that of its consumers.

It absorbs differences in speed. If orders arrive in a burst of 1000 per second for a minute while the billing service can process 200 per second, direct calls would overwhelm billing or force the order service to refuse customers. With a queue between them, the burst accumulates as a backlog of 48000 messages, which billing works through in the following 4 minutes. The queue has levelled the load, turning a peak that billing could not meet into a delay that it can.

And it permits several independent receivers. The order service publishes a single message, “order 7 created”, and has no need to know who is interested. A new service, written next year to compute sales statistics, can begin reading the same messages without any change to the producer.

These benefits come at a definite cost, which should be acknowledged at the outset. The producer no longer learns whether its message was acted upon, or when. Errors that a direct call would have reported immediately now occur later, in another service, and have to be found there. And the system as a whole has become eventually consistent in the sense of chapter 1: for some time after an order is accepted, no invoice exists for it, and every part of the system has to be designed in the knowledge that this interval exists and is sometimes long.

2 kinds of queue

The word “queue” is applied to 2 designs that share the vocabulary of producers and consumers and differ in almost everything else.

The older design, which we may call a task queue, treats a message as a piece of work to be done once. Consumers take messages from the front, and each message is given to exactly 1 of them. When the consumer reports that it has finished, by sending an acknowledgement, the queue deletes the message. If the consumer fails to acknowledge within a set time, the queue assumes it has crashed and makes the message available to another. The queue holds only what has not yet been done, and a message that has been processed is gone.

The newer design is a log. Messages are appended to the end of a file and stay there, each identified by its position, which is called its offset. Reading a message does not remove it. A consumer keeps track of the offset it has reached, reads onward from there, and periodically records its position with the queue. Messages are deleted only when they exceed a configured age or the log exceeds a configured size, quite independently of whether anybody has read them.

Task queueLog
After a message is processedit is deletedit remains until it is old
Several independent readerseach message goes to 1 of themeach reader sees every message
Reading old messages againimpossiblestart from an earlier offset
What the queue tracks per consumerwhich messages are outstanding1 number, the offset
Order of processinglost when consumers work in parallelkept within a partition
Typical usedistributing jobs among workerspublishing events to many services

The log has become the more common basis for communication between services, chiefly on account of the second and third rows. Because reading does not consume, any number of services can read the same messages, each at its own offset. Because messages are retained, a consumer that had a defect can be corrected and set back to reprocess the last day’s messages, and a newly written service can begin from the start of the log and build its state from history. The log is also the structure this book already knows best: it is the append-only log of chapter 2, replicated as in chapter 3, and offered to other services as a product.

The task queue remains the better choice for what its name describes, the distribution of independent jobs among a pool of workers, and it reappears in chapter 12. The remainder of this chapter concerns the log.

Partitions and order

A single log has a single end to which every message is appended, and is therefore limited to the rate at which 1 machine can write and to the capacity of 1 disk. To go beyond that, a named stream of messages, called a topic, is divided into several logs, called partitions, which can be placed on different machines and written concurrently.

Dividing the topic raises the matter of order. Within 1 partition, messages have a definite order, that of their offsets, and every consumer reads them in that order. Between partitions there is no order at all: if one message is in partition 0 and another in partition 1, nothing records which was published first, and 2 consumers may process them in either sequence.

For many messages this is of no consequence. For some it matters a great deal. “Order 7 created”, “order 7 paid” and “order 7 shipped” must be processed in that order, while the order of “order 7 paid” relative to “order 8 created” is immaterial. The requirement, in other words, is for order among messages about the same thing, and the queue provides exactly this by means of a key. The producer attaches a key to each message, here the order number, and the queue chooses the partition by hashing the key, so that all messages with the same key are appended to the same partition, where their order is preserved.

3 consequences of this arrangement tend to be discovered later than they should be. The first is that the choice of key is a design decision with lasting effects, since it fixes which messages are ordered relative to which. The second is that the number of partitions cannot be changed casually: the partition of a key is its hash modulo the number of partitions, so that adding partitions sends new messages for an existing key to a different partition from the old ones, and their order across the change is lost. The third is that a key which accounts for a large share of all messages, such as a single very large customer, makes its partition far busier than the others, and no number of additional partitions relieves it.

Consumer groups

A topic with 4 partitions can be read by 4 consumers working in parallel, and the mechanism that coordinates them is the consumer group. All instances of 1 service, for example the 4 running copies of the billing service, belong to 1 group, and the queue ensures that each partition is read by exactly 1 member of the group at any moment. Different services form different groups, and each group reads the whole topic independently, with its own offsets.

Confining each partition to 1 reader per group is what preserves order during processing. If 2 members of the same group read the same partition, one might process “order 7 paid” before the other had finished with “order 7 created”. The rule has the further consequence, shown in the fourth step, that the number of partitions is an upper limit on parallelism. A fifth consumer in a group that reads 4 partitions has nothing to do.

The redistribution of partitions when a member joins or leaves is called a rebalance, and it is a regular source of trouble in operation. The group detects a failed member by the absence of its periodic heartbeat, a short message that says only “I am alive”. While a rebalance is in progress, the partitions being moved are read by nobody. A consumer that is merely slow, taking longer over a batch of messages than the heartbeat timeout allows, is declared dead, loses its partitions, and rejoins, which triggers another rebalance, and a group can spend a large part of its time rebalancing in this way without any member having actually failed. The remedies are to send heartbeats from a thread separate from the one doing the work, and to limit the number of messages fetched at once so that a batch is always finished well within the timeout.

What “delivered” can mean

A consumer that handles a message does 2 things: it performs the work that the message calls for, and it records with the queue that the message has been dealt with, which in a log is done by committing an offset. These are separate operations on separate systems, and a consumer can crash between them. The order in which it performs them determines what the system guarantees, and there are only 2 orders to choose from.

If the consumer does the work first and commits afterwards, a crash between the 2 leaves the work done and the offset not advanced.

The replacement consumer begins from the last committed offset and repeats work that was already done. No message is ever skipped, and some are processed more than once. This guarantee is called at least once.

If the consumer commits first and does the work afterwards, a crash between the 2 leaves the offset advanced and the work not done.

Now the replacement begins after the message that was never processed, and that message is lost for good. Nothing is processed twice, and some messages are not processed at all. This guarantee is called at most once.

There is no third order, and it follows that a queue cannot on its own deliver each message exactly once. One naturally asks whether the work and the commit could be made a single atomic step, and in general they cannot, because they affect different systems: the invoice is sent by a mail server, and the offset is stored by the queue. Making 2 independent systems change together or not at all is the hard problem of distributed transactions, and for something like sending an email it is impossible, since an email cannot be unsent.

What can be achieved, and what careful systems mean when they speak of exactly-once processing, is an effect that occurs exactly once. The queue delivers at least once, and the consumer is built so that processing a message a second time changes nothing. An operation with this property is idempotent, and there are 2 standard ways of obtaining it. Some operations are idempotent by nature: “set the status of order 7 to paid” may be applied any number of times with the same result, whereas “add 1 to the count of paid orders” may not. For the others, the consumer records the identifier of every message it has processed, in the same database transaction as the effect of the message, and on receiving a message it has already recorded it does nothing. The simulation for this chapter uses this second method: a consumer crashes after acting on 6 messages and before committing, its successor is given the same 6 messages again, recognises each of them, and the total number of actions taken remains 6.

The choice between the 2 guarantees should be made by asking which failure is the more tolerable. For most business events it is plainly better to risk a duplicate, which idempotency can neutralise, than a loss, which nothing can repair, and at least once with idempotent consumers is the standard combination. At most once is appropriate where a late or repeated message is worthless or harmful, such as a reading from a sensor that will be superseded by the next reading a second later.

The producer’s side

The same difficulty exists on the producing side, where it is less often noticed. A producer sends a message and waits for the queue to confirm that it has been stored. If no confirmation arrives within the expected time, the producer cannot tell whether the message was lost on the way to the queue or stored successfully with only the confirmation lost on the way back. If it does not send again, the message may be lost, and if it does, the message may be stored twice.

The solution again consists in making the repetition harmless. Each producer is given an identity by the queue, and numbers its messages to each partition consecutively. The partition remembers the highest number it has stored for each producer and discards any message whose number it has already seen. A producer can then resend without hesitation, and the log contains each message once.

The producer also decides how much durability to wait for, by choosing what constitutes a confirmation. It may send without waiting for any confirmation, which is fastest and loses messages whenever a machine fails. It may wait until the leader of the partition has written the message, in which case a message is lost if the leader fails before its followers have copied it. Or it may wait until the message is stored on a majority of the replicas, which is the rule of chapter 3 and the only setting under which a confirmed message survives the failure of a machine. Our design uses the third.

Durability and replication

Each partition is a log, and it is kept durable and available by precisely the means that chapter 3 applied to the log of a key-value shard. One of the machines that hold a copy of the partition, the machines being called brokers, is its leader and receives all appends. The others are followers, which copy the leader’s log, and a message counts as stored when a majority holds it. If the leader fails, a follower that holds every stored message is elected in its place, by the procedure of chapter 4.

Consumers are permitted to read a message only once it is stored on a majority. The reason is the one given in chapter 3 for not applying a record before it is committed. If a consumer were allowed to read a message that existed on the leader alone, and the leader then failed, the new leader’s log would not contain that message, and the consumer would have acted on something that, as far as the queue is concerned, never happened.

The committed offsets of consumer groups are themselves data that must survive failures, since losing them would cause every group to reprocess its entire topic. They are small and frequently updated, and are kept in a replicated store of their own, shown in the design as the offset store.

Difficulties in operation

Messages that cannot be processed

Suppose a message is malformed in a way the consumer does not anticipate, so that every attempt to process it raises an error. Under at least once delivery the consumer does not commit past it, and so it receives the same message again, fails again, and continues to do so indefinitely. A single such message, known as a poison message, halts its entire partition, since no later message in the partition can be reached.

The remedy is to limit the number of attempts. After a message has failed a set number of times, 5 for example, the consumer publishes it to a separate topic reserved for failures, called a dead-letter queue, commits past it, and continues. An alert draws an engineer’s attention to the dead-letter queue, where the message can be examined and, once the defect is corrected, published again. The cost is that the failed message has been overtaken by its successors, so that the order within its key is broken, and whether that is acceptable has to be decided for each topic.

Consumers that fall behind

The difference between the offset of the newest message in a partition and the offset that a group has committed is the group’s lag. It is the most informative single measurement in the operation of a queue, because it states directly how far a consumer is behind its producers. A lag that fluctuates around a small value indicates health. A lag that rises steadily indicates that messages arrive faster than they are consumed, and since messages are retained only for a limited period, a lag that continues to rise ends with the oldest unread messages being deleted before the consumer has reached them, which is a loss of data that no setting on the producer can prevent.

Publishing together with a database write

A service very often needs to do 2 things in response to 1 request: change its own database and publish a message announcing the change. The order service inserts an order and publishes “order 7 created”. Performed as 2 separate operations, these can come apart. If the service writes the database and crashes before publishing, an order exists of which no other service will ever hear. If it publishes first and the database write then fails, other services act on an order that does not exist.

The outbox pattern makes the 2 operations one. The service writes the message, as an ordinary row, into a table of its own database called the outbox, in the same transaction as the order itself, so that the database guarantees that both are written or neither is. A separate process then reads the outbox and publishes its rows to the queue.

The relay may crash between publishing a row and marking it as published, and will in that case publish it again on restarting. The pattern therefore delivers at least once, which returns us to the idempotent consumer, and it will be noticed how many of the questions in this chapter have ended at that same answer.

Keeping the latest value only

Retaining messages for a fixed period suits a stream of events. Some topics, however, carry the current state of things, each message being the latest value for its key, such as a customer’s current address. For these, old values are of no interest and the latest must be kept however old it is. A log can be compacted for this purpose: a background process rewrites it, keeping for every key only the most recent message. A new consumer reading a compacted topic from the beginning thereby obtains the current value of every key, and can construct a complete copy of the data from the topic alone.

Use cases

Producers publish, consumers fetch and commit, and operators decide how many partitions a topic has.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A producer can publish a message to a topic. Messages with the same key are delivered in the order they were published.
1A consumer can fetch messages starting from an offset.
2A group of consumers shares a topic: each message goes to 1 member of the group.
3A consumer can commit an offset, and after a restart it continues from the committed offset.
4Messages are kept for 7 days, whether or not they were read.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DurabilityA published message survives the loss of 1 broker.
1ConsistencyStrong within a partition: every consumer sees the same messages in the same order.
2DeliveryAt least once. A message can be delivered again after a consumer crash.
3Scale100000 messages per second of 1 KB each.

The queue is strongly consistent within a partition, which means that all consumers see the same messages at the same offsets, and that a message which has been confirmed to its producer will be seen by every consumer. It makes no promise about the relative order of messages in different partitions. The system built from the queue and its consumers is eventually consistent, as the opening section explained, since a consumer acts on a message some time after it was published.

Core entities

The API

Publishing creates a message within a topic. Fetching reads from a partition, starting at an offset. Committing replaces the stored offset of a group.

Publish a message

POST /v1/topics/orders/messages HTTP/1.1
Host: queue.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "key": "order-7", "body": "paid" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{ "partition": 1, "offset": 2 }

Its key chooses the partition, and the response says where the message now lives.

Commit an offset

PUT /v1/topics/orders/partitions/1/offsets/billing HTTP/1.1
Host: queue.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "committed": 6 }

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

PUT is idempotent, so committing the same offset twice is harmless.

Consumers fetch messages, and the queue does not push them. This allows each consumer to proceed at its own pace and to ask for as many messages as it can handle, where a queue that pushed would have to guess at the capacity of every consumer. So that an idle consumer does not issue requests continuously, a fetch that finds no new messages is held open by the broker for a short time and answered as soon as a message arrives.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Brokerstores partitions as logs and serves fetchesthe logsa follower of each partition it led takes over
Consumerfetches, acts, commitsnone that must surviveanother member of its group takes over its partitions
Offset storeremembers each group’s committed offsetsthe offsets, replicatedconsumers keep working and commit later

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 11.8.

  1. A producer sends a message with the key order-7. A hash of the key picks partition 0, and the request goes to the broker that leads it.
  2. The leader appends the message to the partition’s log and copies it to a follower, as in chapter 3. Then it answers with the offset.
  3. A consumer asks the leader for messages from its committed offset onward.
  4. The consumer acts on each message. When the batch is done, it stores the new offset in the offset store.

The design, deployed

The 12 brokers are divided among 3 zones, and each partition has 1 replica in each zone. Leadership is spread evenly, so that every broker leads roughly a third of the partitions it holds, and the failure of a broker moves the leadership of only those. Producers and consumers hold a list of the brokers and connect directly to the leader of each partition they use, so that here too there is no load balancer on the path of the data. The offsets of the consumer groups are kept in a small replicated store of their own.

How real systems do it

The log-structured queue of this chapter is Kafka, which LinkedIn described in 2011. The partitioned log, the offset kept by the consumer, the consumer group and the retention of messages by age all come from that design, as do the compaction of a log by key and the producer that numbers its messages so that a retry is not stored twice, which was added in 2017 together with transactions.

In 1 respect Kafka differs from this chapter, and the difference is instructive. This chapter replicates a partition as chapter 3 does, confirming a message when a majority of replicas hold it. Kafka uses a different rule. The leader keeps a list of the replicas that are fully caught up, the in-sync replicas, and confirms a message when every one of them has it. A replica that falls behind is removed from the list, and the partition continues with those that remain. With this rule, f + 1 replicas tolerate f failures, where a majority rule needs 2f + 1, which matters for a system that stores a great deal of data. The cost is that the list itself must be agreed upon by some other means, for which Kafka relied on ZooKeeper and now on a Raft-based controller of its own, and that a setting for the smallest permitted size of the list has to be chosen with care, since a list that has shrunk to the leader alone confirms messages that exist on 1 machine.

The task queue described at the start of the chapter is the model of Amazon’s SQS, whose visibility timeout is the period after which an unacknowledged message is given to another consumer, and of RabbitMQ. Pulsar separates the brokers, which serve requests, from the storage of the log, which is delegated to a separate replicated service. And the outbox pattern is commonly implemented without a relay process, by reading the database’s own log of changes and publishing from that, a technique called change data capture.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Expecting each message to arrive exactly onceA consumer that crashes before committing receives its messages again and repeats their effects.Deliver at least once and make the consumer idempotent.
Committing before the workA crash after the commit loses the message.Do the work, then commit, unless losing messages is acceptable.
Publishing without a key, or with a random oneMessages about the same thing land in different partitions and are processed out of order.Use as the key the thing whose messages must stay in order.
Adding partitions to a topic in useNew messages for a key go to a different partition from the old ones.Choose the number of partitions generously at the start.
More consumers than partitionsThe extra consumers receive nothing.Size the partitions for the parallelism that will be needed.
Retrying a failing message without limit1 message stops its whole partition.After a fixed number of attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue.
Writing the database and publishing as 2 stepsA crash between them leaves the 2 in disagreement.Write the message to an outbox in the same transaction.
Waiting only for the leader’s confirmationA message is lost when the leader fails before its followers have it.Wait for a majority.
Heartbeats from the thread that does the workA slow batch is taken for a crash, and the group rebalances repeatedly.Send heartbeats separately, and fetch small batches.
Not watching lagA consumer falls so far behind that unread messages are deleted.Raise an alert when lag grows steadily.
Processing 1 partition with several threadsMessages of the same key are handled out of order.Use 1 thread per partition, or distribute within the consumer by key.
