Summary

  • A queue separates services in time, absorbs bursts, and lets any number of services read the same messages, and the system becomes eventually consistent in return.
  • A task queue deletes a message once it is processed, and a log keeps messages and lets each reader hold its own offset.
  • Order exists within a partition only, and the key of a message decides which messages are ordered relative to each other.
  • A consumer group gives each partition to 1 of its members, so the number of partitions limits parallelism.
  • Working before committing gives at least once, committing before working gives at most once, and there is no other order.
  • An effect that happens exactly once is obtained by delivering at least once to an idempotent consumer.
  • A producer waits for a majority and numbers its messages, so that a confirmed message survives a failure and a retry is not stored twice.
  • A database write and a message are made 1 step by writing the message to an outbox in the same transaction.

Job Scheduler: System Design

A good deal of the work that a system does is not done while anybody waits for it. A user uploads a video and receives an immediate confirmation, while the conversion of the video into several resolutions takes place over the following minutes. An account is closed today, and its data is to be erased in 30 days. A report on yesterday’s sales is to be compiled every night at 2 o’clock. In each case a piece of work, which we shall call a job, has to be remembered now and carried out later, by some machine other than the one that asked for it, and it has to be carried out even if that machine, or the one that accepted the request, fails in the meantime.

A job scheduler is the service that takes responsibility for such work. It accepts jobs, stores them durably, hands them to workers when their time has come, and keeps track of what became of them. The essential difficulty is that the scheduler can never observe a job being executed. It gives a job to a worker and thereafter knows only what the worker reports, and a worker that has stopped reporting may have crashed, may be slow, or may have completed the job and failed only in delivering the news. Everything in the design follows from the need to make progress in spite of this uncertainty without either losing jobs or running them more often than can be tolerated.

This chapter covers

  • the life of a job, as a small set of states and transitions
  • leases, by which a job is lent to a worker for a limited time
  • why a job may run more than once, and how to make that harmless
  • giving 1 job to 1 worker when many workers ask together
  • retries, increasing pauses, and jobs that never succeed
  • jobs that are due at a later time, and how to find them efficiently
  • recurring jobs, and the hazards of firing twice or not at all
  • priorities, fairness among customers, and long-running jobs

The life of a job

Every job in the scheduler is in exactly 1 of a small number of states, and the whole behaviour of the system can be described by the permitted movements between them.

A newly submitted job is waiting. When a worker takes it, the job becomes running, and from that state there are 3 ways out. If the worker reports success, the job has succeeded and nothing more will happen to it. If the worker reports failure, or reports nothing before a deadline, the job returns to waiting in order to be tried again. And if it has already been tried a fixed number of times without success, it becomes dead, which means that the scheduler has given up on it and that a person will have to look at it.

The value of describing the system in this way is that every question about its correctness becomes a question about a transition. Jobs are not lost if every job is always in 1 of the states and no transition discards a job. A job is not run by 2 workers at once if the transition from waiting to running can be made by 1 worker only. The 3 sections that follow take the transitions out of the running state one by one, beginning with the least obvious.

Lending a job: the lease

Suppose that a worker takes a job and the scheduler marks it as running and does nothing further. If the worker completes the job, all is well. If the worker crashes, the job remains marked as running indefinitely, and since only waiting jobs are handed out, it will never be given to anyone else. The job has in effect been lost, although it is still in the store.

The scheduler therefore does not give a job to a worker outright. It lends it for a limited period, and the loan is called a lease. The worker must report the result before the lease ends. If the period passes without a report, the scheduler concludes that the worker is not going to finish and returns the job to the waiting state, from which another worker will take it. Chapter 10 used a lease for the same reason, to recover a lock from a holder that has vanished.

The simulation for this chapter runs this scenario with 6 jobs and 3 workers, 1 of which crashes 2 seconds into its first job. All 6 jobs are completed. The job held by the crashed worker is recovered when its lease expires at 3 seconds and is finished by another worker at 6, and the record shows 2 attempts for that job and 1 for each of the others.

The length of the lease involves the compromise that chapter 10 described. If it is short, a crashed worker’s job is recovered quickly, and a worker that is merely slow has its job taken away and given to another while it is still working. If it is long, slow workers are safe and a crashed worker’s job sits idle for a long time before anyone notices. For jobs whose duration is predictable, the lease is set comfortably above the usual duration. For jobs that may take minutes or hours, a fixed lease of sufficient length would delay recovery intolerably, and the worker takes a short lease and renews it at intervals for as long as it is making progress, as with the renewal of a lock.

A job may run twice

The lease brings with it a consequence that has to be faced squarely. The expiry of a lease does not prove that the worker has stopped. The worker may be running slowly, or may have been paused in the manner described in chapter 10, or may have finished the job and been unable to report because of a fault in the network. In each of these cases the scheduler gives the job to a second worker while the first is still executing it or has already executed it, and the job is performed twice.

This is the same situation that chapter 11 called delivery at least once, and it is unavoidable for the same reason. The scheduler must choose between reissuing a job whose worker has fallen silent, which risks a second execution, and not reissuing it, which risks no execution at all, and since a job that is never run is nearly always the worse outcome, schedulers reissue. It follows that a scheduler guarantees that a job will be run at least once, and cannot guarantee that it will be run exactly once.

The responsibility for making this harmless lies with the author of the job. A job should be idempotent, which is to say that running it twice should leave the world in the same condition as running it once. Some jobs have this property without effort: resizing an image and storing the result under a fixed name can be repeated indefinitely. Others must be given it. A job that charges a customer has to carry a unique reference that the payment system uses to recognise a repeated charge, as chapter 19 describes, and a job that sends an email should record that it has done so and check the record before sending.

One further precaution limits the damage that a late worker can do. When a worker reports a result, it presents the number of the lease under which it was working, and the scheduler accepts the report only if that lease is still the current one for the job. The slow worker of the scenario above, reporting success under lease 771 after the job has been reissued under lease 772, is told that its lease is no longer valid and its report is ignored. The lease number plays the part of the fencing token of chapter 10: it cannot prevent the late worker from having done the work, and it does prevent the late worker from overwriting the state recorded by its successor.

Giving 1 job to 1 worker

The transition from waiting to running must be made by 1 worker only, and when many workers ask for jobs at the same time this requires care.

The natural way of writing the operation is in 2 steps: find a job that is waiting, then mark it as running. Between the 2 steps there is a gap, and a second worker’s request can fall into it.

The remedy, shown in the last step, is to make the transition a single conditional operation in the job store, of the form “set this job to running, under my lease, if it is still waiting”. The store performs each such operation in its entirety before beginning the next, so that when 2 workers attempt it on the same job, the second finds the condition no longer true and is refused. This is the compare-and-set of chapter 1 once more.

A conditional change is correct and, with many workers, not yet efficient. If 50 idle workers all identify the oldest waiting job and all attempt to take it, 1 succeeds and 49 have wasted a round trip and must try again, upon which they all converge on the next job. Databases used as job stores offer a remedy in the form of a query that selects waiting rows while passing over any row that another transaction has locked, so that each worker is given a different job at the first attempt. Where no such facility exists, workers can be made to choose at random among the first few waiting jobs, which reduces the collisions considerably.

Retries and jobs that never succeed

A job may fail for reasons that will have passed in a moment, such as a brief network fault or a service that was restarting, and for such failures the right response is to try again. The scheduler counts the attempts made on each job and, after a failure, returns the job to the queue.

It should not be returned for immediate execution. If a job has failed because some service it depends upon is overloaded, then retrying at once adds to the overload, and thousands of jobs doing the same can prevent the service from recovering at all. The job is therefore made to wait before its next attempt, and to wait longer after each successive failure: 1 second, then 2, then 4, and so on, which is called exponential backoff. A random amount is added to each pause, so that jobs which failed together do not all return together. Chapter 13 examines these pauses in detail.

Some jobs fail for reasons that will never pass. The input is malformed, or the code has a defect that this particular input exposes, and the hundredth attempt will fail exactly as the first did. Retrying such a job for ever would waste capacity and, worse, would conceal the problem. The number of attempts is therefore limited, and a job that exhausts its attempts is moved to the dead state, where it is kept with its last error for an engineer to examine. This is the dead-letter queue of chapter 11 under another name. An alert on the number of dead jobs is among the most useful that a scheduler can provide, since a sudden increase usually means that a defect has been deployed.

It is helpful if workers can distinguish the 2 kinds of failure where the cause is evident. A job that fails because its input cannot be parsed will not improve with repetition, and a worker that reports it as permanently failed spares the system the remaining attempts.

Jobs that are due later

A job may be submitted with a time before which it is not to run. The scheduler must then, at every moment, be able to find the jobs that have become due, and it must do so without examining all the jobs that are not.

The straightforward method is to store the due time of each job and to keep the waiting jobs in an index ordered by that time. The scheduler asks the store, every second or so, for waiting jobs whose time is not later than the present, and since the index is ordered, the store answers by reading from its beginning and stopping at the first job that is not yet due. The cost is proportional to the number of jobs that are due, however many millions are waiting for later.

2 limitations of this method should be understood. The first is precision: a job may start up to a polling interval late, which is of no importance for a job due in 30 days and matters for one that is meant to fire at a precise second. The second is that all scheduler nodes query the same index, which becomes a point of contention at high rates. A common refinement divides responsibility. Jobs due in the distant future remain in the durable store, and a scheduler node periodically loads those due within the next minute into its own memory, where it keeps them in a structure ordered by time and can release each at its exact moment. If that node fails, nothing is lost, since the jobs are still in the store and another node loads them.

Recurring jobs

A recurring job is a rule, such as “every day at 02:00”, from which a new job is to be created at each of the times the rule names. Creating those jobs is itself a piece of work that must be done exactly once per occasion, and with several scheduler nodes running for the sake of availability, the obvious implementation does it once per node.

One remedy is to elect 1 scheduler node as the only one that evaluates schedules, using the lock service of chapter 10. This works, and it inherits the weakness of every lock, namely that for a short time during a change of leader there may be 2 nodes that each believe themselves elected. The more dependable remedy does not rely on there being a single creator. Each run of a recurring job is given a name constructed from the rule and the scheduled time, and the job is created only if no job of that name exists. Any number of nodes may then attempt the creation, and the store admits the first and rejects the rest. The creation has been made idempotent, which, as so often in this book, is more reliable than trying to ensure that it is attempted only once.

The opposite hazard is the run that is missed. If every scheduler node is down from 01:55 to 02:10, the question arises of what should happen at 02:10 to the run that was due at 02:00. There is no universally right answer. A nightly report should probably be run late, since a late report is better than none. A job that sends a “good morning” notification should probably be skipped if it is already afternoon. And a job due every minute that has missed 3 hours should certainly not be run 180 times in succession. The policy for missed runs, whether to run once on recovery, to run every missed occasion, or to skip, has to be stated for each recurring job, and a scheduler that leaves it unstated has made the choice on its users’ behalf.

Schedules expressed in local time have a further peculiarity that causes a failure once or twice a year. On the night when clocks are set forward, the time 02:30 does not occur, and a job scheduled for it is either skipped or run at an unexpected hour. On the night when clocks are set back, 02:30 occurs twice, and the job may run twice. Schedules are best expressed in coordinated universal time, which has no such discontinuities, and converted for display only.

Priorities and fairness

When more jobs are waiting than the workers can take, the order in which jobs are handed out becomes a matter of policy. The simplest policy is first come, first served, and 2 situations call for something more.

Some jobs are more urgent than others. An email carrying a password reset should not wait behind 100000 jobs that regenerate thumbnails. Jobs are accordingly given a priority, and the scheduler hands out the highest priority first. Strict priority has a well-known defect, which is that a continuous supply of high-priority jobs prevents low-priority jobs from ever running, a condition called starvation. It is countered by letting the effective priority of a job rise with the time it has waited, or by reserving a share of the workers for each level.

Fairness among customers presents a similar problem. If 1 customer submits a million jobs and they are served in order of arrival, every other customer’s jobs wait behind all of them. The remedy is to keep a separate queue for each customer and to take from the queues in rotation, so that a customer who submits a great deal delays chiefly its own jobs. A limit on the number of jobs of 1 customer that may be running at once serves the same end.

Use cases

Developers submit jobs and ask about their state. Workers take jobs and report results.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A developer can submit a job, to run now or at a later time.
1A worker can take a waiting job. A job is given to 1 worker at a time.
2A worker reports success or failure. A failed job is tried again, up to 5 times.
3A job whose worker stops responding is given to another worker.
4A developer can read the state and the number of attempts of a job.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DurabilityA submitted job is not lost when a scheduler node fails.
1ConsistencyStrong for job state: 2 workers are not given the same job at the same time.
2DeliveryAt least once. A job can be started a second time.
3Scale10 million jobs per day.

The state of a job has to be strongly consistent. Were 2 scheduler nodes to hold different views of whether a job is waiting or running, each could hand it to a worker, and the lease, on which all recovery depends, would mean nothing. The job store is therefore replicated in the manner of chapters 3 and 4, and a transition is acknowledged only when a majority has recorded it. What remains eventual is the relationship between the store and the world: a job recorded as running may in fact have finished a moment ago, and the design accepts this by allowing a job to run more than once.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 10 million jobs per day are 116 per second on average, which 1 replicated job store handles.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Jobs per second, average10000000 ÷ 86400116
Jobs per second, at a peak of 10 times the average116 × 101160
Storage for 30 days10000000 × 30 × 1 KB300 GB

The API

A worker takes a job by creating a lease, which is why the request is a POST to the collection of leases, and it reports by writing the result that belongs to its lease, which is a PUT to an address that names the job and the lease.

Submit a job

POST /v1/jobs HTTP/1.1
Host: jobs.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "kind": "resize-image", "payload": { "image": "cat.jpg" }, "run_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/jobs/8231
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 8231, "state": "waiting", "attempts": 0 }

Location gives the URL of the new job, as HTTP expects after a 201.

Take a job: create a lease

POST /v1/leases HTTP/1.1
Host: jobs.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "worker": "worker-2", "seconds": 30 }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/leases/771
Content-Type: application/json

{ "lease": 771, "job": { "id": 8231, "kind": "resize-image", "payload": { "image": "cat.jpg" } }, "expires_in": 30 }

A worker takes a job by creating a lease, so the path names a thing and the method says what happens to it. The scheduler picks the job. When no job is waiting, the answer is 204 No Content.

Report the result

PUT /v1/jobs/8231/results/771 HTTP/1.1
Host: jobs.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "outcome": "succeeded" }

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

The lease number proves that this worker still holds the job. A report with an expired lease is answered 409 Conflict.

Workers ask the scheduler for jobs, and the scheduler does not push jobs to workers. A worker that asks is by that fact ready to work, and one that is overloaded or shutting down merely stops asking, so that no separate mechanism is needed for the scheduler to learn the capacity of each worker.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Scheduleraccepts jobs and hands out leasesnone of its ownanother scheduler node serves the API
Job storeholds every job and its statethe jobs, replicateda follower takes over, as in chapter 4
Workertakes a job, runs it, reportsnone that must surviveits jobs return to the queue when their leases end
Reclaimerreturns jobs with expired leases to the queuenoneleases are reclaimed late, by the next reclaimer run

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 12.7.

  1. A developer sends POST /v1/jobs. The scheduler checks the request and gives the job an id.
  2. The scheduler writes the job to the job store in the state waiting. The store keeps it on a majority of its nodes, as in chapter 3.
  3. A worker sends POST /v1/leases. The scheduler picks a waiting job, marks it running with this worker and a deadline, and returns it.
  4. Every few seconds the reclaimer looks for running jobs whose deadline has passed and sets them back to waiting.

The design, deployed

The scheduler nodes hold no state and stand behind a pair of load balancers, through which both submitters and workers reach them. All state is in the job store, a leader with 2 followers in 3 zones. The reclaimer, which returns jobs with expired leases to the queue, runs as 2 instances of which 1 is active, chosen through the lock service of chapter 10, and since reclaiming is itself a conditional write, a moment in which both believe themselves active does no harm. The 200 workers are the only tier whose size follows the amount of work, and it can be changed freely.

How real systems do it

Google has published an account of its distributed cron service that agrees with this chapter on the essentials and is frank about the same limits. The service keeps its state in a store replicated by Paxos, and only the leader launches jobs. The authors state that the system cannot guarantee that a job is launched exactly once, since the leader may fail between launching and recording the launch, and that the owners of each job must therefore decide whether it is worse for the job to be skipped or to run twice. They recommend making launches idempotent, and naming each launch after its scheduled time so that a repeat can be recognised, as this chapter does.

The remedy for many workers competing for the same waiting job, a query that passes over rows locked by other transactions, is the clause SKIP LOCKED, which PostgreSQL has offered since version 9.5 and which is the basis of several job queues built on that database. For keeping very large numbers of timers in memory, the classical structure is the timing wheel, in which timers are placed in slots by their expiry time and a pointer advances 1 slot at each tick, so that starting and stopping a timer take constant time.

A more recent development goes beyond anything in this chapter. Systems such as Temporal, which descends from Uber’s Cadence, record every step of a long-running piece of work in a durable history, and recover a failed worker by replaying that history to the point it had reached. A job in such a system is a program that appears to run for days without interruption, and the leases, retries and idempotency of this chapter are handled beneath it. The underlying guarantee is unchanged: each step runs at least once, and the steps must tolerate repetition.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Marking a job as running with no deadlineA worker that crashes keeps the job for ever.Lend the job under a lease, and requeue it when the lease runs out.
Assuming a job runs exactly onceA slow or disconnected worker and its replacement both run it.Write jobs to be idempotent.
Finding a waiting job and marking it in 2 steps2 workers take the same job.Make the change conditional on the job still being waiting.
Accepting a result from any workerA late worker overwrites the state set by its successor.Accept a result only under the current lease.
Retrying at onceJobs that failed because a service is overloaded keep it overloaded.Wait longer after each failure, with a random addition.
Retrying without limitA job that can never succeed occupies workers and hides a defect.Move it to the dead state after a fixed number of attempts, and raise an alert.
A fixed lease shorter than the jobThe job is reissued while it is still running, every time.Renew the lease while the job makes progress.
Each scheduler node creating recurring jobsEvery run is created once per node.Name each run after its scheduled time and create it only if absent.
No stated policy for missed runsAfter an outage, runs are silently skipped or all fire together.Decide for each recurring job whether to run once, run all, or skip.
Schedules in local timeA run is skipped or doubled when the clocks change.Use coordinated universal time.
Strict prioritiesLow-priority jobs never run.Let waiting raise a job’s priority, or reserve workers for each level.
1 queue for all customersA large customer delays everyone.Keep a queue per customer and serve them in rotation.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
A worker crashes during a jobthe job finishes laterits lease ends and another worker takes the job
A worker stalls and finishes latenothing, if the job is safe to repeatits late report is refused
A job fails every timethe job stops after 5 attemptsit is marked failed for a person to inspect

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Leases with deadlinesno job is stuck with a dead workera slow worker can cause a second run
Workers pull jobsa worker takes work only when it has rooma job waits until some worker asks
At-least-once executionno job is lostjobs must be safe to repeat

Simulation in the repository. The program code/jobsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p jobsim in the code directory.

Summary

  • A job is always in 1 of 4 states, and the design consists in making each transition between them safe.
  • A job is lent to a worker under a lease, so that the job of a crashed worker returns to the queue.
  • A lease can run out while its worker is still running the job, so a job may be executed more than once and has to be idempotent.
  • A job is taken with a single conditional change, and a result is accepted only under the current lease.
  • Failed jobs are retried after increasing pauses, and jobs that keep failing are set aside as dead.
  • Due jobs are found through an index on their time, and recurring jobs are created under a name that makes a second creation fail.
  • Priorities need protection against starvation, and customers need separate queues to be treated fairly.

Notification Service: System Design

Nearly every service in a large system has occasion to tell a person something. The order service wishes to say that a parcel has been shipped, the security service that a login was attempted from a new device, the billing service that a payment has failed. If each of these services dealt with email, text messages and push notifications for itself, each would need to know the user’s preferred channel and language, to hold credentials for the outside companies that carry the messages, to handle their failures, and to refrain from disturbing the user at 3 in the morning. A notification service gathers all of this into 1 place. Other services tell it what should be said and to whom, and it sees to the saying.

The peculiar character of this system comes from the fact that its most important work is done by parties it does not control. An email is delivered by an email provider, a text message by a telephone network, a push notification by the company that makes the phone’s operating system. These providers are slow at some times and unavailable at others, they impose limits on how fast they may be called, and they reply to a request in ways that leave real doubt about what has happened. The design of a notification service is therefore, to a large extent, a study in calling an unreliable dependency well: when to try again and how long to wait, when to stop trying, how to avoid sending the same message twice, and how to avoid making a struggling provider’s condition worse.

This chapter covers

  • the path of a notification, from a request to a phone
  • why a request is accepted first and sent later
  • repeated requests, and the key that identifies them
  • failures that will pass and failures that will not
  • retries with pauses that double, and why the pauses are made random
  • the circuit breaker, which stops calling a provider that is down
  • the limits that providers impose, and a second provider as a fallback
  • the difference between sent and delivered
  • preferences, quiet hours, priorities, and sending to millions at once

The path of a notification

A notification passes through a sequence of decisions before anything is sent, and laying them out in order shows where the service’s responsibilities lie.

A calling service submits a request that names a user, a kind of message and the data to be inserted into it, for example “tell user 42 that order 7 has shipped”. The notification service first establishes that it has not already received this request. It then consults the user’s preferences to learn whether the user wishes to receive messages of this kind at all and by which channel. It finds the address for that channel, which may be an email address, a telephone number, or the device token by which a push provider identifies a particular installation of an app on a particular phone. It selects the template for this kind of message in the user’s language and fills in the data. Only then is there something to send, and it is placed in a queue from which a pool of senders takes messages and hands them to the appropriate provider.

The division into a part that accepts requests and a part that sends them, with a queue between, is the central structural decision, and it follows from the first section of chapter 11. A provider may take several seconds to answer, or may not answer at all. If the calling service had to wait for the provider, an outage at a text message provider would make the order service slow, which is exactly the coupling a notification service exists to remove. The service therefore answers the caller as soon as the request has been stored durably, with the status 202 Accepted, whose meaning in HTTP is precisely “received, and not yet acted upon”, and does the sending afterwards.

The same request twice

The calling service is itself a distributed program and will sometimes send the same request more than once. It may time out while waiting for the 202 and try again, or it may be a consumer of a message queue that, as chapter 11 explained, delivers its messages at least once. From the user’s side the result of treating both requests as new would be 2 identical text messages, which is a visible defect and, for some kinds of message, an alarming one.

The notification service cannot recognise a repeat by comparing contents, since 2 separate and legitimate notifications may have identical text. The caller must therefore say which requests are the same, and does so by attaching an idempotency key, a name of the caller’s own choosing that identifies the event being reported, such as order-7-shipped. The service records every key it has accepted, and when a request arrives with a key that is already recorded, it returns the original response and sends nothing.

The recording of the key and the placing of the message in the queue must succeed or fail together. If the key were recorded and the service then crashed before queueing the message, the caller’s retry would be dismissed as a repeat and the notification would never be sent. This is the problem of writing to a database and publishing a message as 1 step, and the outbox of chapter 11 solves it here as it did there. Keys need not be kept for ever. A retry arrives within seconds or minutes of the original, and a key that is retained for a day covers every realistic case.

Failures that pass and failures that do not

When a sender hands a message to a provider, the provider’s reply falls into 1 of 3 classes, and the proper response is different for each.

The provider may accept the message. The sender records the fact and is finished.

The provider may refuse the message for a reason that is permanent. The telephone number does not exist, the email address is malformed, or the device token belongs to an app that the user has since removed. Sending the same request again will yield the same refusal, so the sender must not retry. It should record the failure and, in the case of an invalid address or token, mark it so that no further notifications are attempted there. Continuing to send to dead addresses is more than wasteful: providers of email in particular observe what proportion of a sender’s messages are undeliverable and begin to treat a sender with a high proportion as a source of unwanted mail, to the detriment of its deliverable messages.

Or the provider may fail in a way that is probably temporary. It answers that it is overloaded, or that the sender has exceeded its permitted rate, or it does not answer within the time allowed. These are the cases for trying again, and they include the 1 that is most awkward. When a request times out, the sender does not know whether the provider never received it or received it, sent the message, and lost only the reply. A retry in the second case sends the user a duplicate. Where the provider’s API accepts an idempotency key of its own, the sender should supply one, so that the provider can recognise the retry, and where it does not, an occasional duplicate after a timeout is a risk that has to be accepted, since the alternative is an occasional message that is never sent.

The provider’s replyWhat it meansWhat the sender does
Acceptedthe provider has taken the messagerecords success
Refused: invalid address, unknown token, malformed requestrepeating the request cannot helprecords failure, marks the address, does not retry
Overloaded, rate exceeded, internal errorthe condition will probably passretries after a pause
No reply in timeunknown: the message may or may not have goneretries after a pause, with the provider’s own idempotency key if it has one

Retrying with pauses that double

Having decided to retry, the sender must decide when. The answer that comes first to mind, immediately, is the worst available.

A provider that reports overload is receiving more requests than it can handle. A sender that responds by repeating its request at once has increased the load on a system that has just said it has too much, and if a thousand senders do the same, the provider is held in its overloaded condition by the very traffic that its failures generate. Systems have been kept down for hours in this way after the original cause of the trouble had gone.

The sender should therefore wait, and the question of how long is settled by the observation that each successive failure is evidence that the previous wait was too short. The wait is accordingly doubled after every failure: 1 second, then 2, then 4, then 8. This is exponential backoff. It has the property that a brief disturbance is overcome quickly, by the first or second retry, while in a prolonged outage the sender’s requests become rapidly less frequent and soon impose almost no load.

The simulation for this chapter sends 5 notifications to a provider that fails a set number of times for each. One succeeds at the first try. One fails twice and is sent on the third try, 3 seconds after the first, and one fails 4 times and is sent on the fifth, after 15 seconds, as in the picture. One fails every time and is set aside after 5 tries. The remaining request carries a key that has been seen before and causes nothing to be sent.

2 limits complete the scheme. The pause is capped at some maximum, a minute for instance, so that it does not grow to absurd lengths. And the number of tries is bounded, so that a notification which can never be sent leaves the system. What should be done with a notification that has exhausted its tries depends on its kind. A code for logging in is worthless after a few minutes and may be dropped, whereas a notice that a payment has failed should be set aside, in the manner of the dead-letter queue of chapter 11, and looked at by a person.

Why the pauses are made random

Doubling the pause protects a provider from a single sender. It does not protect the provider from many senders that failed at the same moment, which is the usual situation, since a provider’s difficulty affects all of its callers together.

Suppose that 1000 notifications fail in the same second. All 1000 wait 1 second and return together, and if the provider has not recovered they fail together, wait 2 seconds, and return together again. The doubling has spaced the waves further apart and has done nothing to diminish them: each wave strikes the provider with the full 1000 requests, and a provider that is on the point of recovering is knocked down afresh by each.

The remedy is to make each sender’s pause random, which is called jitter. In the simplest effective form, where the plain scheme would wait 4 seconds, the sender waits for a time chosen at random between 0 and 4 seconds. The 1000 retries are then spread evenly over the interval and reach the provider as a steady flow of about 250 per second. The average wait has been halved, and the peak load on the provider has been reduced by a far larger factor. This thundering herd and its cure appeared in chapter 7 from the other side, as the advice a rate limiter gives its clients.

The circuit breaker

Backoff governs the retries of a single notification. It leaves untouched a further problem, which arises when a provider is not merely slow but down. Every new notification that arrives is then tried for the first time, and each such first try waits for the full length of the timeout before failing. Senders are occupied with calls that cannot succeed, the queue lengthens behind them, and notifications for other channels, whose providers are perfectly healthy, are delayed because all the senders are waiting on the provider that is not.

A circuit breaker is a small mechanism that remembers the recent behaviour of a dependency and, when the dependency is plainly failing, stops calling it for a time. It takes its name from the electrical device that cuts off a circuit in which too much current is flowing.

The breaker has 3 states. While it is closed, calls pass through to the provider and the breaker counts consecutive failures. When the count reaches a threshold, the breaker becomes open, and in that state it rejects every call at once without contacting the provider. After a set interval it becomes half open and admits a single trial call. If the trial succeeds, the breaker closes and normal operation resumes, and if the trial fails, the breaker opens again for another interval.

2 benefits follow. The senders fail fast, in microseconds, where they would otherwise have waited out a timeout of many seconds, and so remain free to serve the other channels. And the failing provider is relieved of all traffic but the occasional trial, which gives it the best chance of recovering. A notification rejected by an open breaker has not been lost. It returns to the queue to be tried later, or is directed to another provider.

Providers’ limits and a second provider

Providers restrict the rate at which they may be called, and a sender that exceeds the permitted rate is refused, usually with the status 429 that chapter 7 described. A well-behaved notification service does not discover the limit by running into it. It paces its own calls to each provider slightly below that provider’s limit, using the leaky bucket of chapter 7, which is the algorithm designed for exactly this purpose of feeding a consumer at a steady rate. Notifications that arrive faster than the provider will take them wait in the queue, which is what the queue is for.

For channels on which delivery matters greatly, such as the text messages that carry login codes, a service commonly holds accounts with 2 providers. When the circuit breaker for the first is open, messages are directed to the second. This raises the availability of the channel considerably and brings a small complication with it: a message that timed out at the first provider and was then sent through the second may arrive twice, since the 2 providers know nothing of each other and cannot recognise the duplicate.

Sent is not delivered

When a provider accepts a message, it has undertaken to try to deliver it, and nothing more. The email may yet be rejected by the recipient’s mail server, the text message may wait for a phone that is switched off, and the push notification may be addressed to an app that was removed last week. None of this is known at the moment the provider replies to the sender.

Providers report the later fate of a message after the event, by calling an address that the notification service has registered with them. Such a call from a provider back to its customer is known as a webhook. The service must be prepared to receive these reports at any time, in any order, and more than once, and uses them to bring the recorded state of each notification up to date. They are also the principal means by which the service learns that an address has gone bad, so that it can stop sending to it.

The practical consequence is that a notification service should be careful in what it claims. It can truthfully state that a message was handed to a provider. Whether the message was delivered is known only later and only for some channels, and whether it was read is hardly ever known. A system that requires certainty that a person has seen something, such as an alert to an engineer on call, cannot rely on a notification alone. It must require an explicit acknowledgement from the person and escalate to someone else when none arrives.

Preferences, quiet hours and priorities

Not every notification that is requested ought to be sent, and the service is the place where this is decided.

Users choose which kinds of message they wish to receive and by which channels, and in many countries the law requires that every promotional message offer a means of refusing further ones and that the refusal be honoured. The check against preferences belongs in the notification service itself, where no calling service can omit it by oversight. Users may also set hours during which they are not to be disturbed, and a message that falls within them is held and released when they end, unless it is of a kind, such as a security alert, that overrides them.

A limit on frequency protects users from the combined enthusiasm of many calling services, each of which considers its own messages important. A user who receives 30 notifications in a day will turn all of them off, the important ones included, and so the service limits the number of non-urgent notifications per user per day and discards or combines the excess.

Notifications differ enormously in urgency. A login code is useless unless it arrives within seconds, and a weekly digest may arrive at any time today. If both wait in the same queue, a campaign that addresses 10 million users will delay every login code until it has been worked through. The service therefore keeps separate queues for separate priorities, each with senders of its own, so that the bulk traffic cannot occupy the capacity on which urgent traffic depends.

Sending to very many users

A single request sometimes asks that millions of users be notified, of a change to the terms of service for example. Treated naively as 1 unit of work, it would occupy a sender for hours and would have to begin again from the start if that sender failed.

The request is fanned out. A first stage divides the list of recipients into batches of perhaps 1000 and places 1 message per batch in the queue, and a second stage expands each batch into individual notifications. The work is thereby spread across all the senders, a failure affects 1 batch only, and the progress of the whole is the number of batches completed. Each individual notification is given an idempotency key derived from the campaign and the user, so that a batch which is processed twice does not send anything twice. Such campaigns are sent at low priority and paced over minutes or hours, both to respect the providers’ limits and because a notification that brings a million users to the app within the same minute is an overload of one’s own making.

Use cases

Other services ask for notifications to be sent. Users decide which they are willing to receive.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A service can ask for a notification to a user on a channel: email, text message or push.
1A request carries a key. A second request with the same key sends nothing.
2A failed send is tried again, up to 5 times, with a longer pause each time.
3A notification that fails 5 times is set aside and reported.
4A user’s choice of channels is respected.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DeliveryAt least once to the provider, and once per key from the caller’s point of view.
1LatencyA notification leaves within 5 seconds of the request when the provider is healthy.
2ConsistencyStrong for the set of keys already seen. Eventual for delivery state.
3Scale50 million notifications per day.

The guarantee offered to callers is that an accepted request leads to at least 1 attempt to hand the message to a provider, and that a request repeated with the same key leads to no more than the first one did. The record of keys must be strongly consistent, since 2 nodes that disagreed about whether a key had been seen would between them send a duplicate. The state of a notification, by contrast, is eventually consistent with reality, since delivery is learned of after the fact, from the provider’s reports.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 50 million notifications per day are 580 per second on average, and the queue absorbs peaks of 10 times that.

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Per second, average50000000 ÷ 86400579
Per second, peak579 × 105790
Senders, at 50 sends per second each5790 ÷ 50116

The API

A request creates a notification. The reply does not say that anything was sent, only that the request has been stored and will be acted upon.

Send a notification

POST /v1/notifications HTTP/1.1
Host: notify.example
Idempotency-Key: order-7-shipped
Content-Type: application/json

{ "user": "user-42", "channel": "email", "body": "Your order has shipped." }

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /v1/notifications/5512
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 5512, "state": "queued" }

202 Accepted says that the request was taken and the work will happen later.

The same request again

POST /v1/notifications HTTP/1.1
Host: notify.example
Idempotency-Key: order-7-shipped
Content-Type: application/json

{ "user": "user-42", "channel": "email", "body": "Your order has shipped." }

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 5512, "state": "sent" }

Our service returns the same id and sends nothing.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
APIaccepts requests and drops repeats by keythe keys seen, replicatedanother API node serves requests
Queueholds notifications until a sender takes themthe messages, as in chapter 11a follower broker takes over
Sendercalls the provider and retriesnoneits message is delivered again to another sender
Provideran outside email, text or push serviceoutside our controlsenders retry, then set the message aside

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 13.7.

  1. A service sends POST /v1/notifications with the header Idempotency-Key: order-7-shipped.
  2. The API looks the key up. A key it has seen gets the earlier answer and nothing else happens. A new key is recorded, and the notification goes into the queue.
  3. A sender takes the notification from the queue.
  4. The sender calls the provider. On failure it waits and tries again, with a pause that doubles.
  5. After 5 failed tries the sender moves the notification to a separate list for a person to look at.

The design, deployed

The deployment falls into 2 halves joined by queues. The upper half, the API nodes with their key store, must always be available, since it is what the calling services depend on, and it does very little. The lower half, the senders, is where the slow and uncertain work is done, and it is divided into separate pools for each channel and each priority, so that a pool blocked on a failing provider cannot starve the others. The providers at the bottom are outside the system, and for the channel that matters most there are 2 of them.

How real systems do it

The treatment of retries in this chapter follows an article from Amazon that has become the standard reference. It simulates many clients contending for a resource and compares several ways of randomising the pause. The form used in this chapter, a random time between 0 and the full exponential value, is the one the article calls full jitter, and it found that this did the least total work, with a variant that keeps half of the pause fixed close behind and a third variant, in which each pause is derived from the previous one, somewhat worse. The author has since added the caution that backoff and jitter spread a burst of load out and do not reduce a sustained overload, for which the load itself must be reduced.

That further step is the retry budget. Google’s book on site reliability engineering recommends that a client limit its retries to a fixed proportion of its ordinary requests, 10% for example, in addition to a limit for each request, so that when a dependency is failing completely, the retries add a tenth to the load, where unlimited retries would multiply it. A circuit breaker achieves a similar end by different means.

The circuit breaker was described by Michael Nygard in his book on production failures and was made widely known by a library from Netflix. The same book treats its companions, the timeout and the bulkhead, which is the separation of pools used in the deployment above.

For push notifications, the providers are Apple’s and Google’s services, each of which reports a token that is no longer valid in its reply to a send, so that sending is also the means by which dead tokens are discovered. Most providers of email and text messages report delivery by webhook, and they retry their webhooks for hours when the receiver is down, so that the receiver must be idempotent, in a reversal of the usual roles.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Calling the provider while the caller waitsA slow provider makes every calling service slow.Store the request, answer 202, and send from a queue.
No idempotency keyA caller’s retry sends the user the same message twice.Require a key and record the keys accepted.
Recording the key and queueing the message as 2 stepsA crash between them loses the notification, and the retry is dismissed as a repeat.Do both in 1 transaction, through an outbox.
Retrying every failureInvalid addresses are tried again and again, and the sender’s reputation suffers.Retry only failures that may pass, and mark addresses that are permanently refused.
Retrying at onceRetries keep an overloaded provider overloaded.Double the pause after each failure.
The same pauses for everyoneSenders that failed together return together, in waves.Choose each pause at random within its range.
Retrying without limitA notification that can never be sent circulates for ever.Stop after a fixed number of tries and set it aside.
No circuit breakerSenders wait out timeouts on a dead provider, and healthy channels are delayed.Stop calling a provider after repeated failures, and test it with single trial calls.
Reporting “delivered” when the provider acceptsUsers are told of messages that never arrived.Record “handed to the provider”, and update from the provider’s reports.
1 queue for everythingA large campaign delays login codes.Keep separate queues and senders for each priority.
Checking preferences in each calling serviceA service forgets, and a user who refused messages receives them.Check preferences in the notification service.
Sending a campaign as fast as possibleThe providers refuse the excess, and the users who respond overload the app.Pace campaigns over time at low priority.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
The provider is downnotifications arrive latesenders retry with growing pauses; the queue holds the backlog
A sender crashes after the provider accepted a messagethe user may get that message twicethe queue redelivers; providers that accept a key drop the repeat
A caller retries its requestnothingthe idempotency key identifies the repeat

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
A queue between API and providercallers are not slowed by the providerdelivery is no longer immediate
Retriesbrief failures are invisiblea message can be sent twice without a key on the provider’s side
Setting aside after 5 triesa bad message does not block the otherssomeone has to look at what was set aside

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/notifysim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p notifysim in the code directory.

  • B. Beyer and others (editors), Site Reliability Engineering, O’Reilly, 2016, chapter 22, “Addressing Cascading Failures”.

Summary

  • A notification service accepts a request, stores it, answers 202, and sends from a queue, so that slow providers do not slow down the callers.
  • A caller identifies each request with an idempotency key, and a repeated key sends nothing.
  • A provider’s refusal is either permanent, in which case retrying is harmful, or temporary, in which case the sender tries again.
  • The pause before each retry doubles, so that a failing provider receives less and less traffic.
  • The pauses are random, so that senders which failed together do not return together.
  • A circuit breaker stops calls to a provider that is down and tests it with single trial calls.
  • Acceptance by a provider is not delivery, which is learned of later from the provider’s reports.
  • Preferences, limits on frequency and priorities are enforced in the service, and very large sends are fanned out in batches and paced.

URL Shortener: System Design

A URL shortener accepts a long web address and returns a short one, such as sho.rt/4C92, which leads to the same place. Anyone who opens the short address is redirected to the long one. The service does 2 things only, creating a link and following a link, and its data is a single table with 2 columns. It is nevertheless a standard exercise in system design, and deservedly so, because within that small compass it raises several questions that recur in much larger systems: how to generate identifiers that are short, unique and hard to guess; how to serve a load that consists almost entirely of reads; how to count events without slowing down the operation being counted; and how to run a public service that people will certainly try to misuse.

The quantities involved shape every decision. Links are created at a modest rate and followed at a far higher one, typically a hundred times higher, and a link once created is never changed. A system with these characteristics is designed around its read path, which must be fast and must stay available, while the write path may be slower and may, if necessary, be briefly unavailable without great harm. A link that fails to open is a failure visible to everyone who was sent it, and a link that cannot be created for a minute inconveniences 1 person.

This chapter covers

  • how long a code has to be
  • 3 ways of making a code: from a hash, at random, and from a counter
  • writing a number in base 62, step by step
  • why codes from a counter can be guessed, and how to prevent it
  • the 2 kinds of redirect, and what each means for speed and for counting
  • a read path built from a cache and a key-value store
  • counting clicks without writing on every redirect
  • custom names, expiry, and the same address submitted twice
  • the misuse of a public redirect service

How long a code must be

The code is the part of the short address that follows the domain, and its length is the first thing to be settled, since shortness is the product.

A code is a string over some alphabet, and the number of distinct codes of a given length is the size of the alphabet raised to that length. The customary alphabet consists of the 10 digits, the 26 capital letters and the 26 small letters, 62 characters in all, each of which may appear in a web address without special encoding. With 62 characters, codes of length 6 number about 57 billion and codes of length 7 about 3.5 trillion.

The service of this chapter expects 100 million new links per month, or 6 billion in 5 years. Codes of 6 characters would suffice for that in principle, with about 10 times as many codes as links. We choose 7, which provides nearly 600 times as many, for 2 reasons. The service should not approach exhaustion within its lifetime, since lengthening the codes later is disruptive. And, as will appear below, a code space that is sparsely occupied is considerably harder to explore by guessing.

Some alphabets omit characters that are easily confused in print or over the telephone, such as the digit 0 and the capital O, or the digit 1 and the small l. This reduces the alphabet to 58 or fewer characters and the number of codes accordingly. It is worth doing where links are likely to be read aloud or copied by hand.

Making a code

A code must be unique, because a code that referred to 2 addresses would send some visitors to the wrong one. There are 3 established ways of producing codes, and they differ in how uniqueness is obtained and in what the codes reveal.

From a hash of the address

The first idea is to compute a hash of the long address and take its first 7 characters. The method has the attraction of needing no state at all: the code is a function of the address, and any server can compute it.

Its defect is that 2 different addresses can produce the same 7 characters. This is the collision that chapter 8 calculated for random identifiers, and the same arithmetic applies: among n codes drawn from N possibilities, the expected number of colliding pairs is about n squared divided by twice N. The simulation for this chapter shortened 2 million addresses to 6 characters of a hash, a form that allows about 20 billion different codes, and 97 of the addresses received a code that another address already had.

A collision rate of 97 in 2 million sounds small, and a service cannot send even 1 visitor in 20000 to the wrong destination. Every newly computed code must therefore be checked against the store, and when it is found to be taken by a different address, the service must derive another, for instance by appending a counter to the address and hashing again. The method thus requires a read before every write and a loop for retries, and the collisions become more frequent as the store fills.

Deriving the code from the address has a further consequence that is sometimes wanted and sometimes not. The same address always yields the same code, so that 2 people who shorten the same address receive the same link, and neither can have statistics or an expiry date of their own.

At random

The second method draws 7 characters at random and checks whether the resulting code is already in use, drawing again if it is. As with the hash, a check before each write is unavoidable. With 6 billion links among 3.5 trillion codes, about 1 draw in 600 finds its code taken, so the retries are rare and remain rare for the life of the service.

Random codes have an important virtue, which is that they disclose nothing. A code says nothing about when its link was created or how many others exist, and knowing 1 valid code is of no help in finding another. The cost is the check, which on a replicated store must be an atomic “create if absent” of the kind described in chapter 10, since 2 servers might otherwise draw the same code at the same moment and both find it free.

From a counter

The third method abandons chance. Each new link is assigned the next number from a counter, and the code is that number written in a compact notation. Since no 2 links are given the same number, no 2 receive the same code, and uniqueness requires no check and no retry.

The compact notation is base 62, which uses the 62 characters of the alphabet as digits in the way that decimal notation uses 10.

The simulation confirms the round trip for a selection of numbers: 0 is written as 0, 61 as z, 62 as 10, a million as 4C92, and the largest number that fits in 7 characters, 3521614606207, as zzzzzzz, and each code reads back as the number from which it came. It also shortens 2 million addresses by counter and finds no collision among them, as must be the case.

The counter itself must be shared by all the servers that create links, and chapter 8 was devoted to that problem. The method of blocks suits this service well. Each web server obtains a block of, say, 1000 consecutive numbers from the counter and assigns them from memory, returning for another block when the first is used up. The counter is consulted once per 1000 links, and the numbers lost when a server restarts in the middle of a block are of no consequence when 3.5 trillion are available.

What a counter gives away

Codes that are consecutive numbers have a property that is unacceptable in a public service. They can be guessed.

Anyone who holds 1 link can obtain others by adding or subtracting 1, and can walk through the entire collection in order. Short links are routinely created for addresses that carry a secret within them, such as a shared document that anyone with the link may read or a page for resetting a password, on the assumption that the address cannot be found by a stranger. Sequential codes destroy that assumption. They also reveal the volume of the business, since the difference between a code created today and one created a week ago is the number of links made in the week.

The remedy keeps the counter and conceals its order. Before the number is written in base 62, it is passed through a fixed scrambling function that maps each number below 62 to the power 7 to a different number in the same range. Because the mapping sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs, the codes remain unique without any check, and because it is designed so that neighbouring inputs give unrelated outputs, consecutive links receive codes with no visible relation to one another. Such a function is in effect a small cipher with a secret key, and anyone without the key cannot recover the sequence.

Even with scrambled or random codes, a stranger can still try codes blindly, and the fraction of attempts that succeed equals the fraction of the code space in use. This is the second reason for preferring 7 characters to 6. With 6 billion links in 57 billion codes, 1 guess in 10 would find a link. With 3.5 trillion codes, 1 guess in 600 does, and a rate limit on requests for codes that do not exist, of the kind described in chapter 7, makes systematic exploration impractical.

From a hashAt randomFrom a counter, scrambled
Uniquenessby check and retryby check and retryby construction
A read before each writeyesyesno
Shared statenonenonea counter, consulted once per block
The same address twicethe same codedifferent codesdifferent codes
Can codes be guessednonono, while the key is secret

The design of this chapter uses a counter with blocks and a scrambling step. It avoids the read before each write, and it never has to retry.

Following a link

When a visitor’s browser requests sho.rt/4C92, the service looks up the code and replies with a redirect, a response that carries no page and names another address to which the browser should go. HTTP provides 2 principal kinds, and the choice between them is a real design decision with consequences for load and for measurement.

A reply with status 301 Moved Permanently tells the browser that the short address has been replaced by the long one for good. Browsers are entitled to remember this, and they do: the next time the same person opens the same short link, the browser goes directly to the long address without contacting the shortener at all. A reply with status 302 Found states that the redirect is temporary, and the browser asks the shortener again on each occasion.

301 Moved Permanently302 Found
Repeat visits by the same browsergo straight to the destinationreturn to the shortener each time
Load on the shortenerlowerhigher
Click countscount each browser oncecount every visit
Changing or disabling the link laterdoes not reach browsers that remembered ittakes effect immediately

The last row is the one most often overlooked. A link that has been served with 301 cannot reliably be withdrawn, because browsers that have stored the redirect will continue to follow it. A service that must be able to disable links, which, as the section on misuse explains, every public shortener must, should prefer 302, or should send 301 with a short limit on how long it may be remembered. Our design sends 301 together with a header that limits the browser’s memory of it to a day, which removes most repeat requests while ensuring that a disabled link stops working within 24 hours.

The read path

Redirects outnumber creations by a hundred to 1 and must be answered in a few milliseconds, so the read path is built for speed in layers.

The mapping from code to address is a pure lookup by key, with no queries by any other attribute, and it is therefore kept in a key-value store of the kind built in chapters 1 to 6, divided among shards by a hash of the code. At 6 billion links of about 500 bytes each, the data amounts to 3 TB, which is too much for 1 machine and entirely ordinary for a sharded store.

In front of the store stands a cache, as described in chapter 9. Traffic to short links is extremely uneven: a link shared by a popular account may be opened a million times in an hour, while most links are opened a few times in their whole existence. A cache holding a small fraction of the links therefore answers the great majority of requests. Links are also the ideal content for a cache, because a link is never modified after creation, so that the problem of stale entries, which occupied much of chapter 9, scarcely arises. The 1 change that can occur is the disabling of a link, and it is handled by deleting the cache entry at that moment.

Requests for codes that do not exist deserve attention, since they are what an exploring stranger or a mistyped address produces. As chapter 9 explained under the name of cache penetration, such requests pass straight through an ordinary cache to the store. The service therefore caches the fact that a code is absent, for a short time, and limits the rate at which any 1 client may request absent codes.

The web servers themselves hold no data. Each request can be served by any of them, and the load balancer in front distributes requests without regard to who is asking. Servers can accordingly be added and removed freely, and the failure of 1 is of no consequence to visitors.

Counting clicks

Authors wish to know how often their links are followed. The obvious implementation, incrementing a counter in the database on every redirect, would convert the read path into a write path. Every redirect would cost a durable write, a hundred times more writes than link creation produces, all contending on the rows of the popular links.

The redirect and the count are therefore separated. On each redirect the web server appends a small record, consisting of the code and the time, to a message queue of the kind described in chapter 11, and replies to the visitor without waiting for anything further. A separate consumer reads these records and maintains the counts, typically adding up the clicks for each link over a minute and applying the sum in a single write. The visitor’s redirect is delayed by nothing, the store receives 1 write per link per minute in place of 1 per click, and if the counting consumer fails, redirects continue undisturbed and the counts are brought up to date when it returns.

The price is that the counts are eventually consistent. They lag behind reality by up to a minute, and since the queue delivers at least once, a consumer that crashes and repeats a batch may count some clicks twice unless it records which batches it has applied. For a statistic shown on a dashboard this is entirely acceptable. It would not be acceptable if clicks were being billed for, in which case each click record would need an identifier and the counting would have to be made idempotent in the manner of chapter 11.

Further features

Authors sometimes wish to choose the code themselves, as in sho.rt/spring-sale. A custom name is stored in the same table as a generated code and must be reserved with an atomic “create if absent”, since 2 authors may ask for the same name at the same moment. Custom names and generated codes have to be kept from colliding, which is most arranged by making them differ in form: generated codes are exactly 7 characters, and custom names are required to be longer or to contain a hyphen.

A link may be given an expiry, after which it ceases to work. The expiry time is stored with the link, and the web server compares it with the clock on each redirect, so that an expired link is refused from the correct moment even though its row has not yet been removed. A periodic job deletes expired rows later, at leisure. Codes of expired links should not be given to new links, since old messages and documents containing the code would then lead to an unrelated destination.

When the same long address is submitted twice, the service may return the existing link or create a new one. Returning the existing link saves storage and requires an additional index from addresses to codes, and it means that the 2 submitters share 1 link, with shared statistics. Most services create a new link each time, on the grounds that links belong to their authors and that storage is the cheaper resource.

Misuse

A service that will redirect anyone to anywhere is useful to people with bad intentions, and a design that ignores this will not survive contact with the public.

The principal abuse is concealment. A short link hides its destination, and so it is used to disguise addresses that the recipient would not knowingly open: pages that imitate a bank’s login form, or downloads of harmful software. Mail filters and messaging services respond by treating all links of a shortener that carries much of this as suspect, at which point the legitimate links of the service stop working in practice. A public shortener therefore checks each submitted address against lists of known harmful sites when the link is created, checks again periodically, since a destination may turn harmful after the link was made, and provides a means of reporting links. A link found to be harmful is disabled, and this is the reason the service must retain the ability to disable a link promptly, which the earlier discussion of 301 and 302 turned upon.

Creation must be rate limited, per account and per network address, to prevent a single party from generating links by the million. And the service must refuse to shorten its own short links, since chains of redirects are used to defeat the checks just described and a link that redirects to itself would loop.

Use cases

Authors create links and read their statistics. Visitors follow links, in far greater numbers.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0An author can create a short link for a URL and receives a code of 7 characters.
1Opening a short link redirects the visitor to the URL.
2A code, once given out, always leads to the same URL.
3An author can read how often a link was opened.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0Availability99.99% for redirects. A link that does not open is the worst failure.
1LatencyA redirect takes under 10 ms.
2ConsistencyStrong for creating a link: each code belongs to exactly 1 URL. Eventual for click counts.
3Scale100 million new links per month, and 100 redirects for every new link.

The mapping from a code to its address must be strongly consistent in 1 specific respect: once a link has been created and its code returned to the author, every subsequent lookup must find it, since the author will share the code immediately. The key-value store provides this by confirming a write only when a majority holds it. Click counts, by contrast, are eventually consistent by design, as the section on counting explained.

Core entities

Arithmetic ahead. 5 years of links are 6 billion codes and 3 TB, and redirects average 3900 per second.

The API

Creating a link is an ordinary POST to the collection of links. Following one is a GET on the shortest path the service can offer, the code itself.

Create a link

POST /v1/links HTTP/1.1
Host: sho.rt
Content-Type: application/json

{ "url": "https://example.com/a/very/long/address?with=parameters" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/links/4C92
Content-Type: application/json

{ "code": "4C92", "short_url": "https://sho.rt/4C92" }

Its code is the base 62 form of the link’s id.

Open a link

GET /4C92 HTTP/1.1
Host: sho.rt

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/a/very/long/address?with=parameters
Cache-Control: max-age=86400

Browsers follow Location by themselves.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Web servercreates links and answers redirectsnonethe load balancer uses the others
Cacheholds the most opened linkscopies, in memoryits links are read from the store once more
Key-value storemaps a code to its URLevery link, replicateda follower takes over, as in chapter 4
Id generatorgives each new link a numbersee chapter 8another id node is asked

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 14.6.

  1. A visitor’s browser sends GET /4C92.
  2. The load balancer passes the request to a web server.
  3. The web server asks the cache for 4C92. Popular links are found here.
  4. On a miss, it reads 4C92 from the key-value store and puts the answer in the cache.
  5. When an author creates a link, the web server takes the next number from the id generator and writes it in base 62.
  6. The visitor receives 301 with the long address in Location, and the browser goes there.

The design, deployed

Visitors reach a pair of load balancers in front of 12 web servers in 3 zones, any of which can answer any request. A redirect reads the cache and, on a miss, 1 of the 8 shards of the key-value store, each of which has a replica in every zone. The counter that supplies numbers for new links is consulted once for each block of 1000 and stands to 1 side. Below the line, the click queue and its counters form a separate tier, which a redirect writes to and never waits for. In front of all this, a service of this kind normally places the edge servers of a content delivery network, which can answer a popular redirect without reaching the origin at all.

How real systems do it

The published material on URL shorteners is thinner than on most systems in this book, since their operators have written little about them, and this section is accordingly short and confined to what can be supported.

The semantics of the redirects are fixed by the HTTP standard, which also defines 2 further status codes, 307 and 308. These are the temporary and permanent redirects that additionally require the browser to repeat the request with the same method, where 301 and 302 allow a POST to be turned into a GET. For a link that is only ever followed with GET, the difference does not arise.

The scrambling of a counter described above is an instance of format-preserving encryption, a cipher whose output lies in the same range as its input. The construction generally used for small ranges is a Feistel network of a few rounds, and it should be distinguished from libraries that merely obfuscate numbers by a fixed shuffle of the alphabet, which resist casual inspection and do not resist analysis.

The alphabet of 58 characters that omits the easily confused ones is known as Base58, and Flickr has described using it for its short addresses. The checking of submitted addresses against lists of harmful sites is offered as a public service by the makers of the major browsers.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Codes cut from a hash, without a check2 addresses receive the same code, and some visitors reach the wrong page.Check every code against the store, or use a counter.
Checking for a free code and then writing it2 servers find the same code free and both take it.Use an atomic create-if-absent.
Codes that are consecutive numbersAnyone can walk through all links by counting.Scramble the number before encoding it, or use random codes.
Codes only just long enoughBlind guesses find real links often, and the codes run out.Choose a length that leaves the code space sparsely used.
301 with unlimited cachingA link that has been disabled keeps working in browsers that remembered it.Use 302, or limit how long 301 may be remembered.
Incrementing a counter on every redirectEvery read becomes a write, and popular links contend.Record clicks in a queue and count them in batches.
Not caching absent codesRequests for nonexistent codes all reach the store.Cache absence briefly, and rate limit such requests.
Giving the code of an expired link to a new linkOld references lead to an unrelated destination.Do not reuse codes.
Accepting any addressThe service carries links to harmful pages and is blocked by mail filters.Check addresses against lists of harmful sites, and be able to disable a link.
Shortening the service’s own linksRedirects chain or loop.Refuse addresses on the service’s own domain.

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
The cache is lostredirects are slower for a few minuteslinks are read from the store and cached again
The id generator is unreachablenew links cannot be created; redirects workanother id node is used
A store leader failsabout 1 second without new links for its sharda follower is elected

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs

  • M. Bellare and others, “Format-Preserving Encryption”, Selected Areas in Cryptography, 2009.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Short linka short address that redirects to a longer one
Codethe part of a short link that identifies it
Base 62a way of writing numbers with 62 digits: 0 to 9, A to Z and a to z
Collision2 addresses receiving the same code
Redirecta response that tells the browser to go to another address
