Summary

  • Codes of 7 characters over 62 symbols give 3.5 trillion possibilities, far more than the links expected, which keeps guessing unrewarding.
  • Codes cut from a hash or drawn at random must be checked against the store before use, while codes from a counter are unique by construction.
  • A counter’s numbers are written in base 62 after a scrambling step, since consecutive codes could be guessed.
  • 301 lets browsers skip the shortener on repeat visits, and 302 keeps every visit visible and every link revocable.
  • Redirects are served from a cache in front of a sharded key-value store, by web servers that hold no data.
  • Clicks are written to a queue and counted in batches, so that a redirect never waits for a write.
  • A public shortener checks destinations, limits creation, and can disable a link quickly.

News Feed: System Design

A news feed is the page that a member of a social service sees on opening it: the recent posts of the accounts that the member follows, gathered into a single list with the newest at the top. Described as a query, it is brief. Take the accounts this member follows, take their posts, sort by time, and return the first 20.

The difficulty is that this query must be answered for every member, at every visit, within a fraction of a second, and that its cost grows with numbers which have no natural bound. A member may follow thousands of accounts, an account may be followed by millions of members, and a busy service receives far more requests to read feeds than to write posts. A naive evaluation of the query touches the posts of every followed account on every visit and cannot meet these demands. The standard remedy is to do the work in advance, at the moment a post is written, and this in turn becomes ruinously expensive for the small number of accounts that have a very large following. The design of a feed is a matter of choosing, for each post, when the work of delivering it should be done, and this chapter develops the 2 pure answers and the mixture that practical systems adopt.

This chapter covers

  • the feed as a query, and why it cannot be evaluated as written
  • copying a post to every follower’s list when it is written
  • collecting posts from every followed account when the feed is read
  • the account with millions of followers, and the mixture of both schemes
  • what a feed list contains, and how much of it is kept
  • reading a feed in pages, with a cursor
  • the delays and anomalies that members can see, and which of them matter
  • following, unfollowing, deleting, and ranking by something other than time

The feed as a query

Suppose that posts are kept in 1 table and the relation of who follows whom in another. The feed of a member is then the result of joining the 2: all posts whose author is among the accounts the member follows, ordered by time, newest first, limited to the first page.

On a single database with a modest number of members, this query can be executed, and a service in its early days should do exactly that. Its cost is dominated by the number of accounts the member follows, since the recent posts of each have to be located before the newest overall can be chosen. For a member who follows 200 accounts this means 200 separate lookups in an index, or a scan that is equivalent to them, on every visit.

The arrangement breaks down as the service grows, for 2 reasons that reinforce each other. The data no longer fits on 1 machine, so that the posts of 200 authors lie on many different shards, and the query becomes 200 network requests whose results must be merged. And feeds are read very often. A member may publish 2 posts a day and open the feed 20 times, so that the expensive operation is also the frequent one. A design in which the common operation is costly and the rare one cheap has its costs the wrong way round, and the natural response is to move work from reading to writing.

Copying when a post is written

In the first scheme, every member has a feed list that is stored and kept ready. The list contains references to the posts the member should see, in order, and reading the feed consists of nothing more than fetching this list. The work is done at the time of writing. When an author publishes a post, the service looks up the author’s followers and adds a reference to the new post at the front of each follower’s list. Delivering 1 post to many lists in this way is called fan-out, and this scheme is fan-out on write, or informally the push model.

Reading under this scheme is as inexpensive as reading can be. A single lookup by the member’s identifier returns a list that is already assembled and already sorted, and the feed service has only to fetch the posts it refers to. The feed can be served in a few milliseconds regardless of how many accounts the member follows.

The cost has been transferred to publishing, where it is proportional to the number of followers. For an author with 200 followers, a post gives rise to 200 small writes, which is perfectly acceptable. The copying is not done while the author waits. The post is stored, the author receives a reply, and a task describing the copying is placed in a message queue, from which workers perform it in the background, in the manner of chapters 11 and 12. A follower’s list therefore receives the post some moments after it was published, and the feed is eventually consistent by construction.

2 further costs are less conspicuous. Lists are maintained for all members, including those who have not opened the service in months, so that much of the copying is done for readers who will never see its result. And the lists occupy memory in proportion to the number of members, which obliges the service to bound the length of each.

Collecting when the feed is read

The second scheme stores no feed lists at all. Each author’s posts are kept together, indexed by author and time, and publishing a post is a single write to the author’s own collection. The feed is assembled when it is requested: the service looks up the accounts the reader follows, fetches the recent posts of each, and merges the results by time. This is fan-out on read, or the pull model, and it is the query of the first section carried out against data arranged to make each of its parts efficient.

Publishing is now trivially cheap and its cost is independent of the size of the author’s following. No work is done on behalf of members who never read. A post is visible to its readers the instant it is stored, there being no copying to wait for. And when a member follows a new account or stops following one, the feed reflects the change immediately and without any repair, since it is computed afresh from the current list of followed accounts.

The cost is borne by every read, and is proportional to the number of accounts the reader follows. With 200 followed accounts, a visit to the feed requires 200 fetches, which can be issued in parallel and must nevertheless all be awaited, so that the response is as slow as the slowest of them. Since reads are far more numerous than writes, the total work is much greater than under the first scheme for a typical population of accounts.

The account with millions of followers

The choice between the 2 schemes would be straightforward, in favour of copying on write, if all accounts resembled one another. They do not. In every social service the number of followers is distributed with extreme inequality: the great majority of accounts have a few hundred followers or fewer, and a small number have millions.

For such an account, copying on write is a very different proposition. A single post by an account with 2 million followers gives rise to 2 million writes. Performed by a pool of workers at 10000 writes per second, this takes more than 3 minutes, during which some followers have the post and others do not, and the queue of copying tasks is occupied to the detriment of everybody else’s posts. If several such accounts post at about the same time, as they tend to during events of general interest, the backlog grows to many minutes.

The simulation for this chapter makes the imbalance concrete. It models 1000 ordinary accounts, each with 200 followers, publishing 2 posts and reading the feed 20 times a day, together with a single account that has 2 million followers and publishes 10 posts a day.

Under copying on write, the 1000 ordinary accounts cause 400000 copies a day between them, and the 1 large account causes 20 million. A single account is responsible for 98% of all the work in the system. Under collecting on read, the total is about 4 million fetches, nearly all of them attributable to the ordinary accounts’ 20000 daily reads of 200 lists each.

The figures suggest the remedy, which is to treat the 2 kinds of account differently. Posts by ordinary accounts are copied to their followers’ lists on writing, as in the first scheme. Posts by accounts whose following exceeds some threshold, 10000 in the simulation, are not copied at all. When a member’s feed is read, the service takes the member’s stored list and merges into it the recent posts of the few large accounts that the member follows, which it fetches at that moment as in the second scheme. In the simulation this mixture requires 400000 copies and 20005 fetches a day, about a fiftieth of the work of either pure scheme.

The mixture succeeds because it assigns each scheme to the case in which it is cheap. Copying on write costs in proportion to an author’s followers, and is applied where followers are few. Collecting on read costs in proportion to the number of accounts fetched, and is applied to the handful of large accounts that any 1 member follows. It helps, too, that the recent posts of a very large account are requested by so many readers that they are almost always in a cache, so that the additional fetches at reading time are inexpensive.

Copy on writeCollect on readMixture
Cost of publishing1 write per follower1 write1 write per follower, for ordinary authors only
Cost of reading1 list1 fetch per followed account1 list, and 1 fetch per large account followed
Delay before a post is visibleuntil the copying is donenonenone for large accounts, brief for others
Work for inactive memberswastednonewasted for ordinary authors’ posts only
After following or unfollowingthe list has to be repairedcorrect at oncepartly repaired, partly correct at once

What a feed list contains

A feed list could in principle hold complete posts. It holds only references, each consisting of the identifier of a post and its time, about 16 bytes in all, and the posts themselves are stored once and fetched by identifier when a page of the feed is displayed. The reasons are those of any normalised design. A post with a million readers would otherwise exist in a million copies, and an edit or deletion would have to find and alter every one of them. With references, an edited post is changed in 1 place, and a deleted post is found to be absent when the feed service tries to fetch it and is omitted from the page.

The length of each list is bounded, commonly at a few hundred entries, the oldest being discarded as new ones arrive. Hardly any member scrolls back further than this, and for the rare one who does, the service falls back on collecting on read for the older portion. With 500 entries of 16 bytes for each of 10 million members, the lists occupy 80 GB, which is held in a cache spread over several nodes as described in chapter 9.

Because the lists are held in a cache, outside durable storage, a list can be lost, through the failure of a cache node or through eviction. This is acceptable only because a list can always be reconstructed from the durable data, by running the collect-on-read procedure once for that member and storing the result. The lists of members who have been inactive for some weeks may deliberately be allowed to lapse and be rebuilt in this way on their return, which recovers much of the wasted work noted above.

Reading a feed in pages

A feed is delivered in pages, and the method by which the client asks for the next page deserves more attention than it usually receives.

The obvious method is by position: the first request asks for items 1 to 20 and the second for items 21 to 40. This fails in a characteristic way on any list to which items are being added at the front, which a feed always is.

Every insertion at the front shifts all existing items down by 1 position, so that the boundary between pages moves under the reader’s feet and the second page begins with items from the end of the first. Deletions shift items the other way and cause items to be missed. The remedy is to ask for the next page by reference to an item, in the form “20 items older than the last one I have”. The identifier of that last item, returned by the service with each page for use in the next request, is called a cursor. Since it denotes a fixed point in the sequence, insertions before it have no effect on what follows it. A request by cursor is also cheaper for the store to answer, since an ordered index can be entered directly at the cursor, whereas a request for position 10000 obliges the store to count past 10000 entries. Chapter 1 used the same technique for listing keys.

What members can observe

Since the feed is eventually consistent, members can observe states of affairs that a strongly consistent system would exclude, and it has to be decided which of these are tolerable.

After publishing a post, an author expects to see it at once. Under copying on write, the author’s own list is updated by the same background process as everyone else’s, and a quick reload might not yet show the post, which authors interpret as its having been lost. The property that is wanted is called read your own writes, and it is usually secured for this 1 case by having the feed service add the author’s own most recent posts to the author’s feed at reading time, without waiting for the copying.

Followers receive a post at slightly different moments, as the copying proceeds. This passes unnoticed in itself and becomes visible through replies: a member may be shown a reply to a post that has not yet reached the member’s own list. Services deal with this by fetching the original together with any reply to it, so that the pair is always displayed together.

A subtler requirement is that a member who has seen a post should not find it gone on the next reload. This can occur when 2 successive requests are answered by 2 cache replicas of which the second is behind the first. Directing all of a member’s requests within a session to the same replica is generally sufficient to prevent it.

None of these anomalies does lasting harm, and that is the justification for choosing eventual consistency here. A feed that is a few seconds stale is still a perfectly good feed, whereas a feed service that refused to respond until every replica agreed would be unavailable on many occasions when a slightly stale answer would have served.

Following, deleting and ranking

Changes in who follows whom require the stored lists to be repaired. When a member follows a new account, that account’s recent posts should appear in the member’s feed, and so the service merges them into the member’s list as a background task. When a member stops following an account, the posts of that account should disappear, and the simplest method is not to remove them from the list and to filter them out at reading time, by checking each entry against the member’s current list of followed accounts.

The same filtering at reading time disposes of several other cases at once: posts that have been deleted, authors whom the reader has blocked, and posts withdrawn by moderators. A design that depended on locating and removing every copy of a reference from millions of lists would be slow and unreliable, while a check at the moment of display is immediate and certain. The general principle is that anything which must take effect at once should be enforced when the feed is read, and the stored lists should be regarded as a hint about what to show, subject to verification.

Finally, many services order the feed by an estimate of what the member will find interesting, and no longer strictly by time. This alters the pipeline less than might be supposed. The stored list becomes a pool of candidates, perhaps the 500 most recent references, and at reading time a ranking function assigns a score to each candidate and the highest are shown. Fan-out, storage and the treatment of large accounts are unchanged. What changes is that paging by cursor becomes harder, since the order is no longer fixed, and services commonly rank a batch of candidates once, at the start of a session, and page through that fixed result.

Use cases

A member publishes posts, reads the feed, and chooses whom to follow.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A member can publish a post.
1A member can follow and unfollow an account.
2A member can read a feed of recent posts from followed accounts, newest first, in pages.
3A new post appears in followers’ feeds within 5 seconds.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0LatencyReading a feed takes under 200 ms.
1Availability99.9% for reading feeds.
2ConsistencyEventual. Followers may see a post a few seconds apart, and in slightly different order.
3Scale10 million members, 20 feed reads for every post.

The feed is eventually consistent, and deliberately so. A post may take some seconds to reach all of its author’s followers, and 2 followers may see it at different moments. The posts themselves and the relation of who follows whom are stored durably and consistently in a replicated store, and the feed lists are a derived and disposable view of that data, which can be rebuilt whenever they are lost.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. A feed entry is 16 bytes, so the newest 500 entries for 10 million members are 80 GB of cache.

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Feed entrypost id 8 bytes + time 8 bytes16 bytes

The API

Publishing creates a post in the collection of posts. Every member has a news feed, so the feeds form a collection too, /v1/newsfeeds, in which a feed is identified by its owner, and reading a feed returns a page of its posts together with the cursor for the page that follows.

Publish a post

POST /v1/posts HTTP/1.1
Host: feed.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "body": "Shipped the new release." }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/posts/90210
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 90210, "time": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z" }

We store the post before the response and copy it to followers afterwards.

Read a page of the feed

GET /v1/newsfeeds/ada/posts?limit=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: feed.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "posts": [
    { "id": 90210, "author": "ada", "body": "Shipped the new release." },
    { "id": 90188, "author": "grace", "body": "Found the bug." }
  ],
  "next_after": "90188"
}

next_after is the id of the last post on the page.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Post servicestores a post and queues the copyingposts, in the key-value storeanother instance serves requests
Fan-out workersadd a post to each follower’s listnonetheir tasks are delivered again, as in chapter 11
Feed cache1 list of recent post ids per memberlists, in memorylists are rebuilt from the posts on the next read
Feed servicereads a member’s list and fetches the postsnoneanother instance serves requests

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 15.7.

  1. An author sends POST /v1/posts.
  2. The post service stores the post once and puts a small task on the queue: “post 90210 by ada”.
  3. A fan-out worker takes the task and looks up ada’s followers.
  4. For each follower, the worker adds the post’s id to that follower’s list in the feed cache.
  5. A reader sends GET /v1/newsfeeds/{user}/posts.
  6. The feed service reads the reader’s list, merges in recent posts of any very large accounts the reader follows, and fetches the posts themselves.

For a reader who follows a very large account, the feed service adds 1 step to this path. Having read the stored list, it fetches the recent posts of each large account the reader follows, from a cache in which they are nearly always present, and merges them into the list by time before returning the page.

The design, deployed

The feed service is the largest stateless tier, since reads dominate, and it stands with the post service behind load balancers in 3 zones. Below them are 3 stores of different kinds: the feed cache, in memory, holding 1 list for each member, and the post store and follow store, both sharded and replicated across the zones. The fan-out workers at the bottom take 1 task for each post from the queue and are the only component that writes to the feed cache, which keeps the read path free of any concern with copying.

How real systems do it

The best documented feed is Twitter’s home timeline, described in a talk of 2012 that is the source of the arrangement in this chapter. Twitter then had about 150 million active users. Timelines were read some 300000 times per second and written a few thousand times per second, a ratio that settled the choice in favour of doing the work on writing. Every tweet was inserted, by its identifier, into a list held in an in-memory store for each follower, exactly as the feed lists here. The talk gives the aim of delivering a tweet to all followers within 5 seconds, and acknowledges that for accounts with tens of millions of followers this was not always achieved, and that the company was therefore moving to merge the tweets of such accounts at reading time, which is the mixture this chapter recommends.

Facebook’s news feed has taken the other course from the beginning. Its feed is assembled when it is requested, by aggregator servers that query a set of leaf servers holding recent activity and rank what they collect, which suits a feed that is ordered by predicted interest and drawn from many kinds of story. The social graph beneath it, who is connected to whom, is served by a system called TAO, a read-optimised cache over a sharded database, whose paper is the standard account of storing a graph of followers at scale.

The 2 examples show that the choice between the schemes is not settled by size alone. Twitter’s feed, chronological and with extremely skewed followings, favoured copying with an exception for the largest accounts. Facebook’s, ranked and with bounded numbers of friends, favoured collecting. LinkedIn has described a feed for its own service that is likewise assembled at reading time.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Evaluating the feed query on every visitEach read touches every followed account and is slow at scale.Keep a feed list per member, prepared when posts are written.
Copying every post to every follower1 post by an account with millions of followers produces millions of writes and delays all other posts.Above a threshold of followers, collect that author’s posts at reading time.
Copying while the author waitsPublishing takes as long as the copying.Store the post, reply, and copy from a queue.
Storing whole posts in the listsEdits and deletions must find every copy.Store references, and fetch posts by identifier.
Lists of unlimited lengthMemory grows without bound for entries nobody reads.Keep the newest few hundred, and collect on read beyond that.
Treating the lists as the only copyA lost cache node loses feeds.Rebuild a list from the durable posts and follows.
Paging by positionA new post shifts everything, and the next page repeats an item.Page with a cursor that names the last item seen.
Removing references when a post is deleted or an account unfollowedMillions of lists must be searched, slowly and unreliably.Filter at reading time.
The author’s own post arriving with everyone else’sThe author reloads and concludes the post was lost.Add the author’s recent posts to the author’s own feed at reading time.
Maintaining lists for members who never returnMost copying is done for nobody.Let inactive members’ lists lapse, and rebuild on return.

Failures

The feed cache is lostthe first read of each feed is slowlists are rebuilt by collecting on read

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Feedthe recent posts of the accounts a member follows, newest first
Followthe relation between a member and an account whose posts the member wishes to see
Feed lista stored list of references to the posts 1 member should see
Fan-outdelivering 1 post to many readers

Summary

  • A feed is a join of posts and follows that is too costly to evaluate on every visit once the data is spread over many machines.
  • Copying on write prepares a list for every member, so that reading is 1 lookup and publishing costs 1 write per follower.
  • Collecting on read prepares nothing, so that publishing is 1 write and reading costs 1 fetch per followed account.
  • An account with millions of followers makes copying on write impractical, and such accounts are few.
  • The mixture copies the posts of ordinary accounts and collects those of large accounts at reading time, at about a fiftieth of the work in the measured example.
  • Feed lists hold references, are bounded in length, live in a cache, and can be rebuilt from durable data.
  • Pages are requested by cursor, and deletions, blocks and unfollows are enforced by filtering when the feed is read.

Object Store: System Design

An object store keeps files of any size, from a thumbnail of a few kilobytes to a video of many gigabytes, and returns them on request by name. Photographs, backups, logs, the trained weights of machine learning models and the videos of chapter 17 all end up in a system of this kind, and a large one holds hundreds of petabytes on tens of thousands of disks.

At that scale the governing fact is that hardware fails continuously. A disk drive has perhaps a 2% chance of failing in any given year, so that among 20000 disks about 1 fails every day, as a matter of routine. Disks also fail in a quieter and more dangerous manner, by returning data that differs from what was written without reporting any error. A system that is to keep data for decades on such components cannot treat failure as an exceptional event to be handled when it occurs. It has to be built so that the loss of any disk, or any machine, or any rack of machines, at any moment, destroys nothing, and so that the damage is repaired automatically before a second failure can compound the first. This chapter is chiefly about how that is arranged, and about the related question of how to keep track of where everything is.

This chapter covers

  • what distinguishes an object store from a file system
  • keeping the names of objects apart from their bytes
  • cutting objects into chunks, and naming a chunk by its contents
  • surviving lost disks with copies, and with parity at less than half the space
  • where copies are placed, and why it matters as much as how many there are
  • silent damage, checksums, and the scrubber that looks for it
  • repair, and why its speed decides how durable the store is
  • uploading very large objects in parts
  • deleting, and collecting the chunks that nothing uses any more

What an object store is

It is easiest to say what an object store is by contrast with the file system that every reader has used. A file system offers a tree of directories, files that can be opened and modified at any position, appended to, renamed and locked, and it is expected to make all of these operations consistent with one another. These features are costly to provide across many machines, and most large collections of data do not need them.

An object store offers much less and can therefore scale much further. An object is a sequence of bytes with a name, held in a container called a bucket. The name is a plain string. It may contain slashes, as in 2026/10/holiday.mp4, and tools display such names as if they were folders, yet the store itself knows of no directories and treats the name as a single key. An object is written whole and read whole or in ranges, and it is never modified in place: to change an object, one uploads a replacement under the same name. There is no appending, no partial overwriting and no renaming other than by copying.

File systemObject store
Namesa tree of directoriesa flat key within a bucket
Changing part of a filesupportednot possible: the whole object is replaced
Renaming a directory1 operationa copy of every object beneath it
Typical size of a deployment1 machine, or a fewthousands of machines
Accesssystem calls on an open fileHTTP requests for a whole object or a range

The restriction to whole, immutable objects is what makes the rest of the design tractable. Data that never changes after it is written can be copied freely to several places without any risk of the copies diverging, can be verified against a checksum computed once, and can be cached anywhere.

Names in one place, bytes in another

An object store has 2 quite different things to remember about every object: what it is called and where its bytes are, which together are its metadata, and the bytes themselves. The 2 kinds of information have such different characteristics that they are kept in separate systems.

Metadata is small, a few hundred bytes per object, and is needed for every operation. It is updated when objects are created and deleted, it must be listed in the order of names, and it has to be strongly consistent, since an application that has just uploaded an object and been told so must find it when it asks. These are the requirements of a database, and the metadata is kept in a replicated, sharded key-value store of the kind built in chapters 1 to 6, keyed by bucket and object name.

The bytes are large, are written once and never altered, and are read sequentially. They need no ordering, no transactions and no queries. What they require is a great deal of cheap disk space and protection against the loss of disks. They are kept on storage nodes, which are machines with many disks and very simple software that stores and returns pieces of data by identifier.

This separation has a practical consequence for every request. A download first asks the metadata store where the pieces of the object are, and then fetches the pieces from storage nodes. An upload proceeds in the opposite order, writing the pieces to storage nodes first and recording the object in the metadata store last. The order of an upload is deliberate. The metadata entry is the single point at which an object comes into existence, and it is created only when all the bytes are safely stored, so that an upload interrupted in the middle leaves behind some unreferenced pieces, to be cleaned up later, and never an object that claims to exist and cannot be read.

Chunks

Objects range in size over 9 orders of magnitude, and it is impractical to handle a 5 TB object as 1 unit: it would not fit on a single disk together with others, could not be read in parallel, and would have to be copied in its entirety to repair the loss of any part. Objects are therefore cut into chunks of a fixed maximum size, a few megabytes, and each chunk is stored and protected independently. The metadata of an object lists its chunks in order.

A chunk needs an identifier under which storage nodes can keep it, and a particularly useful choice is to name each chunk by a hash of its contents. Naming data by its own hash is called content addressing, and it has 2 valuable consequences. The first is that integrity can be checked by anyone at any time: whoever holds a chunk can recompute the hash and compare it with the name, and a mismatch proves that the bytes have been altered. The second is that identical chunks receive identical names and so are stored only once, however many objects contain them, which is called deduplication.

The simulation for this chapter uploads a file of 10 MB, which is cut into 3 chunks of at most 4 MB, each stored on 3 of 6 nodes. It then uploads the same bytes again under another name, and the second upload writes no chunks at all, the 3 it needs being already present. The store holds 2 objects and the bytes of 1.

Content addressing demands a hash function for which it is not feasible to find 2 different inputs with the same output, since 2 different chunks with the same name would be treated as the same chunk and 1 of them would be lost. The simulation uses a short checksum for brevity, and a real store uses a cryptographic hash of 256 bits.

Surviving the loss of disks

Every chunk must survive the failure of the disks that hold it, and there are 2 ways of arranging this.

Copies

The simple way is replication: each chunk is stored in full on 3 different storage nodes. Any 1 of the copies suffices to read the chunk, so that the chunk survives the loss of any 2 nodes. Reading is fast, since any copy will serve, and repairing a lost copy consists of reading 1 of the survivors and writing it elsewhere. The cost is space. Every terabyte of objects occupies 3 terabytes of disk, and at 100 petabytes this overhead is 200 petabytes of disks that hold nothing but duplicates.

Parity

The economical way stores extra information from which lost pieces can be recomputed, in place of whole copies. The principle can be shown with ordinary addition.

In this small example, 4 disks protect 3 disks’ worth of data against the loss of any 1 disk. To protect the same data against 1 loss by replication would require 2 full copies and therefore 6 disks.

Practical systems extend the idea to tolerate several losses. A chunk is divided into k data pieces, and m additional parity pieces are computed from them, each by a different combination, in such a way that any k of the k + m pieces are sufficient to reconstruct the original. The technique is called erasure coding. Its arithmetic is carried out in a number system devised so that the necessary equations can always be solved, which is more elaborate than addition and rests on the same idea. A common choice is 10 data pieces and 4 parity pieces, stored on 14 different nodes.

The comparison is striking. The coded chunk occupies 1.4 times its own size where replication occupies 3 times, and it survives the loss of any 4 pieces where replication survives the loss of 2. At 100 petabytes of objects, the difference is 160 petabytes of disks.

Erasure coding exacts its price elsewhere. Computing parity takes processor time on every write. Reading normally touches only the data pieces, and when 1 of them is unavailable the reader must fetch 10 other pieces and compute the missing one, which makes reads of damaged chunks slow. Repair is costlier in the same way: to rebuild a single lost piece, 10 pieces must be read over the network, where replication reads 1. And the scheme is unsuitable for small objects, for which the fixed work of dealing with 14 nodes outweighs the saving in space.

Large stores accordingly use both. Small objects and recently written, frequently read data are replicated, for speed. Large objects, and data that has grown cold, are erasure coded, for economy, and a background process converts data from the first form to the second as it ages.

Where the copies go

The number of copies is only half of durability. Their placement is the other half. 3 copies on 3 disks of the same machine are all lost when that machine’s power supply fails, and 3 copies on 3 machines in the same rack are all unreachable when the rack’s network switch fails. Failures of this kind, in which many components go down together for a common reason, are called correlated, and they are far more common than a calculation that treats disks as independent would suggest.

A group of components that may fail together is called a failure domain, and the rule for placement is that the copies or pieces of a chunk are spread over as many failure domains as possible: on different machines, in different racks, and for the most valuable data in different buildings. The system must know the physical arrangement of its machines in order to apply this rule, and the rule has to be reapplied whenever data is moved for repair or rebalancing.

Silent damage

The failures discussed so far announce themselves. A dead disk returns errors, and a dead machine does not respond. A more insidious failure is the disk that works and returns the wrong bytes. Magnetic media decay, firmware has defects, and a write is occasionally directed to the wrong place. The rate of such events is low for any 1 disk and, across tens of thousands of disks and many years, they are a certainty. Because the disk reports success, nothing prompts anybody to look, and the damage lies undiscovered until the data is next read, which for an archive may be years later.

The defence has 2 parts. Every chunk is stored together with a checksum of its contents, and every read verifies the bytes against the checksum before returning them, so that damaged data is never served to a client. This alone is insufficient, since it finds damage only in data that happens to be read. The second part is therefore a background process, the scrubber, which reads every chunk on every disk in rotation, verifies it, and arranges for the repair of any that fails.

The simulation damages a single byte in 1 copy of 1 chunk and then reads the object. The read detects the mismatch, takes the chunk from another node, returns the correct 10485760 bytes, and repairs the damaged copy in passing.

The importance of scrubbing lies in the timing. A chunk with 3 copies survives the corruption of 1 or 2 of them provided the damage is found and repaired while a good copy still exists. If nothing looks for years, the damage accumulates unobserved, and the day arrives on which the last good copy of some chunk is found to be bad as well. Redundancy protects data only for as long as lost redundancy is promptly restored.

Repair

When a disk or node fails, every chunk that had a copy there is left with 1 copy fewer than it should have. A repair process detects this, from the absence of the node’s heartbeats or from the scrubber’s reports, and creates new copies on other nodes from those that remain.

The durability of the whole store depends more on the speed of repair than on any other single factor. A chunk with 3 copies is lost only if all 3 fail, and what matters is the length of the interval during which it is exposed. If a failed copy is replaced within an hour, the chunk is lost only if 2 further specific disks fail within that hour, which is extraordinarily improbable. If replacement takes a week, the window is 168 times longer and the probability of loss correspondingly greater. The remarkable durability figures quoted for large object stores are obtained less by keeping many copies than by repairing quickly.

Repair nevertheless has to be restrained in 2 respects. A node that has merely been restarted for maintenance will return in a few minutes with its data intact, and to begin copying terabytes the instant it disappears would be wasted effort, so repair waits for a short period before acting. And when an entire rack fails, the repair of all its chunks at once could saturate the network and disturb the service to clients, so repair is rate limited and proceeds in order of urgency, attending first to the chunks that have the fewest surviving copies.

Very large objects

An object of 50 GB cannot sensibly be uploaded in a single HTTP request, since any interruption in several hours of transfer would oblige the client to begin again. Object stores therefore offer multipart upload. The client announces that it intends to upload a large object and receives an identifier for the upload. It then sends the object in numbered parts of some tens of megabytes each, in any order and several in parallel, and a part that fails is sent again by itself. When every part has arrived, the client sends a final request listing them, and the store assembles the object by writing a metadata entry that refers to the chunks of all the parts in sequence.

Until that final request, the object does not exist as far as readers are concerned, which preserves the rule that an object appears whole or not at all. Uploads that are begun and never completed leave their parts behind, and a store needs a policy for discarding them after a time, since they would otherwise accumulate invisibly and be charged for.

Downloads have a corresponding facility in the range request, by which a client asks for a stated range of bytes within an object. The store determines from the metadata which chunks cover the range and fetches only those. A video player uses this to jump to the middle of a film without downloading what precedes it, and an interrupted download can be resumed from the point it had reached.

Deleting, and collecting unused chunks

Deleting an object removes its metadata entry, upon which the object ceases to exist for clients at once. Its chunks cannot be deleted at the same moment, for 2 reasons. With deduplication, a chunk may also belong to other objects. And the deletion of chunks on many nodes is slow work that should not hold up the client’s request.

Chunks that are no longer referred to by any object are therefore removed afterwards, by a background process of garbage collection. It determines which chunks are in use, by examining the metadata, and deletes those on the storage nodes that are not. This process contains a race that has cost real systems real data.

The collector’s knowledge of what is unused is necessarily a little out of date, and an upload that arrives in the meantime may rely on a chunk that the collector has already condemned. The standard protection is a period of grace. A chunk is deleted only when it has been unreferenced continuously for a substantial time, a day for example, and an upload that reuses an existing chunk records the fact in a way that restarts the period. The store thus retains some garbage for a day longer than strictly necessary, which is a trivial price for the assurance that nothing in use is ever removed.

Many stores also offer versioning, under which replacing or deleting an object retains the previous version, the latest version being what a plain request returns. This protects against deletion by mistake and against software that overwrites good data with bad, and it is among the few defences against an operator’s or a program’s own errors, which replication does nothing to prevent, since a mistaken deletion is replicated as faithfully as anything else.

Use cases

Applications upload, download and list objects. Operators replace failed hardware, which in a store of this size is a daily task.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0An application can upload an object of up to 5 TB under a name in a bucket.
1An application can download an object, or a range of its bytes.
2An application can list the objects of a bucket by prefix.
3An object that was stored is returned unchanged, or the store reports an error. It does not return damaged bytes.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DurabilityAn object survives the loss of any 2 of the 3 nodes that hold a chunk, and damage on a disk.
1Availability99.9% for uploads and downloads.
2ConsistencyStrong for names: after an upload completes, a download returns the new object. Chunks do not change at all.
3Scale1 billion objects and 100 PB of data.

The store combines 2 consistency models. Metadata is strongly consistent: once an upload has been confirmed, every subsequent request for that name finds the new object, and a listing of the bucket includes it. This property, known as read-after-write consistency, is what applications expect, and its absence from some early object stores was a persistent source of defects in the software built on them. The chunks need no consistency model in the usual sense, because they are immutable. A chunk either exists under its name with the correct contents, or it does not exist, and no reader can ever observe an out-of-date version of one.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 100 PB in 3 copies is 300 PB, about 21000 disks of 16 TB, with 25 billion chunks to keep track of.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Raw storage100 PB × 3 copies300 PB
Disks of 16 TB, 90% full300 PB ÷ 14.4 TB20834
Chunks of 4 MB100 PB ÷ 4 MB25 billion
Metadata1 billion objects × 1 KB1 TB

The API

The API is that of HTTP applied directly to objects. PUT stores an object under a name, GET retrieves it, and DELETE removes it.

Upload an object

PUT /v1/buckets/holiday/video.mp4 HTTP/1.1
Host: objects.example
Content-Type: video/mp4
Content-Length: 10485760

(10485760 bytes)

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
ETag: "crc32:9a3f11c2-3"

Clients can compare the ETag, which names the content, with their own checksum.

Download part of an object

GET /v1/buckets/holiday/video.mp4 HTTP/1.1
Host: objects.example
Range: bytes=0-1048575

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Range: bytes 0-1048575/10485760
Content-Length: 1048576

(1048576 bytes)

With a range, a video player fetches only the part it is about to show.

Applications frequently wish to let a user’s browser upload or download an object directly, without the bytes passing through the application’s own servers. For this the application generates a presigned URL: an ordinary address for the object that carries an expiry time and a signature computed with the application’s secret key. Anyone holding the address may perform the 1 operation it describes until it expires, and the store verifies the signature without needing to consult the application.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
API servercuts uploads into chunks and puts downloads togethernoneanother API server is used
Metadata storemaps an object’s name to its chunksthe names, replicateda follower takes over, as in chapter 4
Storage nodekeeps chunks on its diskschunksevery chunk it held has 2 other copies
Repair workerfinds chunks with fewer than 3 good copiesnonerepairs wait for the next run

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 16.7.

  1. An application sends PUT /v1/buckets/holiday/video.mp4 with the file as the body.
  2. The API server reads the body 4 MB at a time. It computes each chunk’s checksum and stores the chunk on 3 storage nodes.
  3. When every chunk is stored, the API server writes 1 record to the metadata store: the object’s name and its list of chunk names.
  4. In the background, the repair worker checks that every chunk still has 3 good copies, and makes a new copy where 1 is missing.

The design, deployed

The front end is a large stateless tier of API servers behind load balancers. Below it the 2 kinds of storage are plainly separate: 60 machines of the metadata store, which is 20 shards of 3 replicas each, and 600 storage nodes with some 36 disks apiece, which hold the bytes. The bottom tier is peculiar to storage systems. It serves no request, and it runs all the time: a scrubber on every node reading its disks in rotation, a pool of repair workers, and the garbage collector. A store of this size loses a disk on most days, and this tier is what turns that from an event into routine.

How real systems do it

The published designs of large stores show a clear progression, and this chapter compresses several generations into 1.

The Google File System of 2003 established the pattern of a metadata service and many chunk servers, with chunks of 64 MB kept in 3 copies. Facebook’s Haystack, in 2010, addressed a problem that this chapter passes over: a store of billions of small photographs spends most of its disk operations on locating files and very few on reading them, and Haystack packed many photographs into each large file with an index held in memory, so that a read needs a single disk operation. Any store of small objects has to do something of the kind, and a design that kept every object as a separate file would not survive.

For data that is seldom read, Facebook then built f4, which replaces copies by erasure coding with exactly the scheme of this chapter, 10 data blocks and 4 parity blocks, at 1.4 times the size of the data within a data centre. The paper gives the effective overhead of Haystack as 3.6, since it kept 3 copies on disks that were themselves in redundant arrays, and that of f4 as 2.1 once a further coding across data centres is included. Microsoft’s storage system uses a variant, local reconstruction codes, which adds parity blocks that each cover half of the data blocks, so that the common case of a single lost block is repaired by reading 6 blocks where the plain scheme reads 10 or more.

On placement, a paper from Stanford made precise the danger of correlated failures. When replicas are placed on nodes chosen at random, almost any simultaneous loss of 3 nodes in a large cluster destroys some chunk, because nearly every combination of 3 nodes holds the replicas of something. Restricting placement to a limited number of fixed groups of nodes makes a simultaneous loss far less likely to hit all copies of anything, at the cost of losing more when it does.

The deduplication of identical chunks described in this chapter is characteristic of backup and file synchronisation systems, and public object stores generally do not practise it across customers, in part because it lets 1 customer discover whether another holds a given file. And the consistency that this chapter requires of metadata was for many years not provided by the largest public store, Amazon’s S3, which offered it only from the end of 2020.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Recording the object before its bytes are storedA crash leaves an object that exists by name and cannot be read.Write the chunks first and the metadata last.
Counting copies without regard to placementA rack or a machine fails and takes every copy of some chunks with it.Spread the copies over different failure domains.
Verifying data only when it is readDamage in rarely read data goes unnoticed until every copy is bad.Scrub all chunks continuously in the background.
Slow or unprioritised repairChunks remain exposed for days, and a second failure destroys them.Repair promptly, the chunks with fewest copies first.
Repairing the instant a node disappearsTerabytes are copied for a node that was only restarting.Wait a short period before starting repair.
Erasure coding everythingSmall objects and reads of damaged chunks become slow.Replicate small and hot data, and code large and cold data.
Deleting chunks as soon as an object is deletedA chunk shared through deduplication, or just reused by an upload, is destroyed.Collect garbage later, after a period of grace.
A weak hash for content addressing2 different chunks receive the same name, and 1 is lost.Use a cryptographic hash.
Uploading huge objects in 1 requestAny interruption restarts the entire transfer.Upload in parts that can be retried separately.
Never discarding unfinished uploadsTheir parts occupy space indefinitely.Expire incomplete multipart uploads.
Relying on replication against mistakesA mistaken deletion or overwrite is replicated faithfully.Keep earlier versions of objects.
Names with a common prefix written in orderAll new objects fall on the same shard of the metadata store.Spread names by a hash, or shard by a hash of the name.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
A disk returns damaged bytesnothingthe checksum fails, another copy is used, and the bad copy is replaced
A storage node is lostnothingthe repair worker makes a third copy of each of its chunks on other nodes
An upload stops half waythe object does not appearits chunks have no name pointing at them and are removed later

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
3 copies of every chunksimple, and fast to repair3 times the disk space; erasure coding needs about half of that
Chunks named by checksumdamage is detected, and equal data is stored oncea chunk cannot be changed in place
Names in a separate storelisting and renaming are cheap2 systems to keep in step

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/objectsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p objectsim in the code directory.

Summary

  • An object store keeps whole, immutable objects under flat names, and gains its scale from offering so little.
  • Names and locations are kept in a strongly consistent metadata store, and bytes on simple storage nodes, written first and recorded last.
  • Objects are cut into chunks named by a hash of their contents, so that damage is detectable and identical chunks are stored once.
  • 3 copies survive 2 losses at 3 times the space, and 10 data pieces with 4 parity pieces survive 4 losses at 1.4 times.
  • Copies are spread over failure domains, since components fail together more often than independence would predict.
  • A scrubber verifies every chunk in rotation, because disks return wrong data without reporting it.
  • Durability depends above all on repairing quickly, so that a chunk is exposed only briefly after a loss.
  • Chunks are deleted by garbage collection after a period of grace, so that a chunk being reused is not removed.

Video Streaming: System Design

A film of 2 hours in high definition occupies about 4.5 GB. A viewer who presses play expects the picture to appear within a second and to continue without interruption, on a phone connected through a mobile network whose speed changes from moment to moment as readily as on a television connected by cable, and a popular film is watched by millions of such viewers at once, in every part of the world. Video accounts for the greater part of all the bytes carried by the internet, and a service that delivers it is, before it is anything else, a system for moving very large quantities of data to very many places under conditions it cannot control.

The observation on which every such system rests is that a video does not have to be delivered as a video. It can be cut into short pieces, each an ordinary file of a few megabytes, and delivered as files. Once this is done, the difficult parts of the problem turn out to have been solved already. Files of this size can be kept in the object store of chapter 16, served by ordinary web servers, and held in caches close to the viewers, and the player, which is the only component that knows how fast the viewer’s connection is at this instant, can decide for itself, piece by piece, which quality of picture to ask for. This chapter follows a video from the moment it is uploaded to the moment it is watched, and explains each of these steps.

This chapter covers

  • why a video is delivered as a sequence of small files
  • encoding 1 upload at several qualities, and dividing that work among many machines
  • the manifest, which tells a player what pieces exist
  • how a player chooses a quality for each piece, and what it does when the connection worsens
  • the buffer, and the balance between quality and interruptions
  • edge servers that keep copies of pieces near the viewers
  • what determines the cost of the service
  • how live video differs from video on demand

Why a video is delivered in pieces

The earliest method of delivering video over the internet treated it as a single file. The browser requested the file and played it as it arrived, and for a short clip on a fast connection this is adequate. For anything longer it has several defects, all of which follow from the indivisibility of the file. The quality is fixed when the download begins, so that a viewer whose connection deteriorates must either wait for the picture to catch up or abandon it. A viewer who wishes to skip to the middle must wait for everything before it, unless the server supports requests for ranges of bytes. And a viewer who leaves after 2 minutes may by then have received 20 minutes’ worth of data, which was paid for and never watched.

A second method, common for some years, used protocols designed especially for video, in which a server kept a connection open to each viewer and sent a continuous stream at whatever rate the connection would bear. This adapted well to changing conditions and scaled badly, since the server had to maintain state for every viewer and nothing between the server and the viewer was able to cache a stream.

The method that prevailed is simpler than either. The video is cut into pieces of a few seconds each, and every piece is stored as a separate file. The player fetches the pieces in order, by ordinary HTTP requests, and plays each as it arrives. The server keeps no state about any viewer, since each request is complete in itself and any server can answer any request. Skipping to the middle is a matter of requesting a later piece. And because pieces are ordinary files with ordinary addresses, the whole existing apparatus for delivering files over HTTP, caches above all, applies to video without modification.

Several qualities of 1 video

Viewers differ too widely for any single version of a video to suit them all. A phone on a weak mobile signal can receive perhaps 500 kilobits per second, while a television on a fibre connection can receive 50 times as much and has the screen to show the difference. A version small enough for the phone would look poor on the television, and a version suited to the television could not be played on the phone at all.

The service therefore prepares each video at several qualities. The process of producing a compressed video at a given picture size and data rate is called encoding, and each complete version so produced is a rendition. The data rate of a rendition, the number of bits it needs for each second of video, is its bitrate.

A detail of this figure is essential to everything that follows. All renditions are cut into pieces at exactly the same points in time, so that piece 17 covers the same 4 seconds of the film in each of them. A player can therefore take piece 17 from one rendition and piece 18 from another, and the picture continues without a break, changing only in sharpness. For this to work, every piece must begin with a complete picture. Most frames of a compressed video are stored only as a description of how they differ from the frame before, and the encoder is instructed to place a complete picture at the start of every piece.

The length of a piece is a compromise. Short pieces allow the player to change quality quickly and to begin playing sooner, and they compress less efficiently and multiply the number of requests. Long pieces are the reverse. Values between 2 and 6 seconds are usual, and this chapter uses 4.

From an upload to pieces

A creator uploads a single file, in whatever format their camera or editing software produced. Before anyone can watch it, the service must encode it at every quality and cut each result into pieces, and encoding is among the most computationally expensive operations in common use. To encode a film of 2 hours at 1 quality may take a single machine an hour or more, and there are 4 qualities.

The work is made tolerable by dividing it. The source is first cut into sections of about a minute, at points where a complete picture begins, so that each section can be encoded without reference to any other. Each section, at each quality, then becomes an independent job, and the jobs are distributed among a pool of encoding machines by a scheduler of the kind designed in chapter 12.

A film of 2 hours yields 120 sections and so 480 jobs, which 100 machines complete in roughly the time that 1 machine would need for 5 of them. The arrangement also confines the effect of failures. If an encoder crashes, the scheduler reissues that 1 job, as chapter 12 described, and a minute of video at a single quality is encoded again, the remainder being unaffected. Encoding jobs are idempotent without any special effort, since encoding the same section twice produces the same pieces under the same names.

The original upload is retained permanently, in the object store, although nobody will ever watch it directly. Encoding technology improves steadily, and a service will in time wish to encode its catalogue again in a more efficient format. This can be done well only from the source, since every encoding discards information, and to encode again from an already encoded version would compound the loss.

Not all videos need be treated alike. The distribution of views is extremely uneven, a small number of videos accounting for most of the watching and most uploads being watched a handful of times. A service may therefore encode every upload quickly at 2 or 3 qualities, so that it is soon available, and spend the considerable additional effort of a full set of carefully optimised renditions only on videos that prove popular.

The manifest

A player that is to fetch pieces must know what pieces exist. This information is supplied by a small text file called a manifest, which the player requests first. It lists the renditions available, with the bitrate and picture size of each, and, for each rendition, the addresses of its pieces in order together with their durations.

With the manifest in hand, the player needs nothing further from the service except the pieces themselves. It knows how long the video is, what qualities are offered, and the address of the piece that covers any given moment at any given quality. All subsequent decisions, including which quality to request and when, are taken by the player alone.

That the intelligence should reside in the player, with the server left ignorant, is a deliberate feature of the design and one of its chief strengths. The server answers requests for files and need not know that the files are video. The player is the 1 participant that can observe the speed of this particular viewer’s connection at this moment, the size of the screen, and the amount of video already downloaded, and it is therefore the participant best placed to choose.

Choosing a quality for each piece

Before requesting each piece, the player must decide which rendition to take it from. If it chooses too high a bitrate, the piece takes longer to download than it takes to play, the player eventually has nothing left to show, and the picture stops while the viewer waits. If it chooses too low a bitrate, the picture is needlessly poor. Choosing well, piece after piece, as conditions change, is called adaptive bitrate selection.

The player has 2 measurements to guide it. It knows how fast recent pieces were downloaded, which is an estimate of the present speed of the connection. And it knows how much video it has downloaded but has yet to play, an amount called the buffer.

The simplest rule uses the first measurement alone: request the highest bitrate that is comfortably below the measured speed. The simulation for this chapter applies this rule with a margin of 20%, taking the best rendition whose bitrate is at most 80% of the speed of the last download, to a connection whose speed drops twice and then recovers.

The steps show both the virtue of the rule and its inherent limitation. The player always acts on the speed of the previous download, and is consequently 1 piece behind events. When the speed fell from 6000 to 1500 at piece 4, the player had already committed itself to a piece at 2500, which took 6.7 seconds to arrive and consumed part of the buffer. It is the buffer that absorbed the error. The picture did not stop, because nearly 9 seconds of video were in hand when the slow download began. Over the 10 pieces, the only time without video was the fraction of a second before the first piece arrived.

The buffer is thus what allows the player to make mistakes without the viewer noticing, and the size at which to maintain it is another compromise. A large buffer tolerates long periods of poor connection. It also represents video that has been downloaded and may never be watched if the viewer leaves, and it delays the effect of a change of quality, since everything already in the buffer will be played at the quality at which it was fetched. Players commonly aim to hold between 10 and 30 seconds.

More refined rules take the buffer into account as well as the speed. When the buffer is nearly empty, such a rule chooses conservatively whatever the measured speed, because the cost of a mistake is an interruption. When the buffer is full, it can afford to try a higher quality, since an error will cost only some seconds of buffer. Some players ignore the measured speed altogether and select the quality as a function of the buffer alone, on the grounds that the level of the buffer already reflects everything the connection has recently done.

Whatever the rule, it must respect an asymmetry in what viewers will tolerate. An interruption, during which the picture freezes, is far more objectionable than a period of reduced sharpness, and viewers who experience interruptions stop watching. A change of quality is also somewhat disturbing in itself, so that a rule which switches up and down with every fluctuation of the measured speed is worse than one which holds a steady, slightly lower quality. A good rule accordingly steps down promptly, steps up cautiously, and prefers stability.

The first piece is a special case. The player has no measurement of the connection when it starts, and viewers are impatient for the picture to appear. Players therefore begin with a low bitrate, which arrives quickly whatever the connection, and improve within a few seconds as measurements accumulate.

Copies near the viewers

Pieces are stored in the object store, in 1 or a few locations. A viewer on another continent is separated from that location by a network path with a delay of perhaps 150 ms in each direction and a capacity shared with a great many others, and if every viewer fetched every piece from the origin, the origin’s network connection would have to carry the entire traffic of the service.

A content delivery network, or CDN, removes both problems. It consists of a large number of servers, called edge servers, placed in or near the networks of the internet providers that viewers use, in hundreds of cities. Each edge server is a cache, of the kind described in chapter 9, for the files of the origin.

A viewer’s request is directed to a nearby edge server, most often by the name resolution system returning the address of a server close to wherever the question came from. If that server holds the piece, it answers immediately. If not, it obtains the piece from the origin, answers, and retains a copy for subsequent viewers.

Video suits this arrangement exceptionally well, for 2 reasons. A piece, once encoded, never changes, so that the problem of stale copies, which dominated chapter 9, does not arise, and pieces can be cached for as long as there is room for them. And the demand for video is highly concentrated, so that an edge server which holds the pieces of the currently popular videos answers the great majority of the requests it receives. For a popular video the origin serves each piece once to each edge server, and the edge servers serve it to millions.

The manifest of an ordinary video is equally immutable and is cached in the same way. The requests that must reach the service itself are thus reduced to those that depend on who is asking, such as checking that the viewer is entitled to watch.

2 refinements are common. When a film is expected to be in great demand on its release, its pieces are copied to the edge servers beforehand, so that the first viewers do not all miss at once and produce at the origin the stampede described in chapter 9. And for videos that are rarely watched, an edge server may hold only the first few pieces, which is sufficient for playback to start promptly, and fetch the remainder from the origin when a viewer in fact continues.

What the service costs

It is instructive to ask where the money goes in such a service, since the answer shapes many decisions that would otherwise seem arbitrary.

Storage is not the principal cost. The renditions of a film amount to a few gigabytes, and a catalogue of 100 million videos to some hundreds of petabytes, which is substantial and, with the erasure coding of chapter 16, affordable. Encoding is a cost incurred once for each video.

The cost that recurs and dominates is the delivery of bytes. Every hour watched at 2500 kilobits per second is rather more than 1 GB transferred, and a service whose members watch a billion hours a month transfers more than an exabyte a year. Almost any measure that reduces the bytes delivered per hour watched therefore repays its cost: more efficient encoding formats, which convey the same picture in fewer bits and justify the expense of encoding the catalogue again; the avoidance of renditions beyond what a device’s screen can display; a limit on how far ahead the player buffers, so that less is wasted when viewers leave; and arrangements with internet providers to place edge servers inside their networks.

Live video

Everything described so far concerns video that exists in full before anyone watches it. A live broadcast uses the same machinery, with 1 important difference: the pieces are produced while the event is taking place.

The camera’s signal is encoded continuously at several qualities, and every 4 seconds a new piece of each rendition is completed and stored. The manifest is no longer fixed. It lists the most recent pieces, is revised as each new piece appears, and is fetched by players again and again, every few seconds, so that they learn of new pieces. It may accordingly be cached only very briefly.

The price of this simplicity is latency, the delay between an event and its appearance on the viewer’s screen. A piece cannot be delivered until it has been completed, which takes 4 seconds, and players hold several pieces in the buffer to guard against interruptions, so that viewers of a live stream built in this way are typically 15 to 30 seconds behind reality. For a concert this is immaterial. For a football match it means hearing the neighbours celebrate a goal that has not yet appeared, and for a conversation between 2 people it is unusable. Shorter pieces and the delivery of pieces while they are still being produced bring the delay down to a few seconds, and truly interactive video, such as a call, requires a different kind of protocol altogether, one which sends each frame as soon as it is captured and accepts occasional loss in exchange for immediacy.

Live video also changes the pattern of load on the caches. Every viewer wants the same new piece in the same instant, at the moment it comes into existence and before any edge server holds it. Edge servers must therefore ensure that the first request for a new piece fetches it from the origin once while the others wait for that fetch to complete, which is the remedy for the stampede given in chapter 9.

Use cases

Viewers play videos, in very large numbers. Creators upload them.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A creator can upload a video file of up to 10 GB.
1After processing, the video can be played on any device.
2Playback starts within 2 seconds.
3The quality adapts to the viewer’s connection while the video plays.
4A viewer can jump to any point of the video.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0Availability99.95% for playback.
1LatencyThe first piece arrives within 1 second of pressing play.
2ConsistencyEventual. A new video may take minutes to appear, and that is acceptable.
3Scale10 million viewers at the same time, and 500 hours of video uploaded per minute.

Consistency is scarcely an issue in the playback path, for the reason that has appeared repeatedly: pieces and the manifests of finished videos do not change after they are written, and unchanging data cannot be inconsistent. The catalogue of videos and their states is ordinary metadata and is kept in a strongly consistent store. The 1 window of eventual consistency a creator can observe is between completing an upload and the video’s becoming playable, which lasts as long as the encoding does.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 10 million viewers at an average of 2500 kbit/s need 25000 Gbit/s, far more than 1 site can send, so pieces are served from a CDN.

The API

A viewer’s player makes 2 kinds of request: 1 for the manifest, and then a long series for pieces.

Get the manifest of a video

GET /v1/videos/8842/manifests/default HTTP/1.1
Host: video.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "piece_seconds": 4,
  "pieces": 450,
  "qualities": [
    { "kbit": 400,  "url": "https://cdn.example/8842/400/piece-{n}.ts" },
    { "kbit": 1200, "url": "https://cdn.example/8842/1200/piece-{n}.ts" },
    { "kbit": 2500, "url": "https://cdn.example/8842/2500/piece-{n}.ts" },
    { "kbit": 5000, "url": "https://cdn.example/8842/5000/piece-{n}.ts" }
  ]
}

The manifest tells the player which qualities exist and how to build the URL of any piece.

Get 1 piece

GET /8842/1200/piece-17.ts HTTP/1.1
Host: cdn.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: video/mp2t
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
Content-Length: 600000

(600000 bytes)

immutable tells every cache that this piece will not change, so it can be kept for a year.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Upload servicereceives the source file and stores itnonethe creator’s upload resumes on another instance
Encodersturn the source into pieces at 4 qualitiesnonethe task is delivered again, as in chapter 11
Object storekeeps the source and every pieceeverything, see chapter 16chunks have 3 copies
Video APIreturns the manifestvideo recordsanother instance answers
CDNkeeps copies of pieces close to viewerscopies onlyviewers are served from the next nearest site

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 17.7.

  1. A creator uploads the source file. Large uploads are sent in parts, so that a broken upload continues where it stopped.
  2. The upload service stores the source in the object store and puts 1 task on the queue.
  3. An encoder takes the task and produces the video at 4 qualities, each cut into pieces of 4 seconds.
  4. Each piece is stored as its own object. When all are stored, the video is marked ready.
  5. A viewer presses play. The player asks the video API for the manifest.
  6. The player fetches pieces from the CDN, 1 after another. A CDN site that does not have a piece fetches it from the object store once and keeps it.

The design, deployed

The tiers of this system are separated by geography as much as by function. The edge servers number in the thousands and stand in hundreds of cities, inside or beside the networks of the internet providers. The origin is in a few places only, and consists of the video API, the object store that holds every piece, and the catalogue. The encoding tier is furthest from the viewers and is never reached by them. It is the largest consumer of computation in the system, and since its work is a queue of independent jobs with no deadline measured in milliseconds, it can use whatever machines are cheapest.

How real systems do it

Delivery in pieces over ordinary HTTP is standardised in 2 forms that differ in detail and agree in principle. Apple’s HTTP Live Streaming is specified in RFC 8216, and Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, usually called DASH, is an international standard. Both describe a manifest that lists renditions and their segments, and both leave the choice of rendition entirely to the player, as this chapter does.

The choice itself has been the subject of a good deal of research, and the simple rule of the simulation, which follows the measured speed with a margin, is the starting point, and the state of the art has moved well beyond it. A study carried out on Netflix’s service showed that estimates of capacity are unreliable enough that a player does better, once playback is under way, to choose the rendition from the level of the buffer alone, and reported between 10% and 20% fewer interruptions than the algorithm then in use, at a similar average quality. Later work formulated the choice as an optimisation over a short horizon of future pieces, and still later work trained a model to make it. A production player today usually combines an estimate of speed with the state of the buffer.

On the encoding side, Netflix has described abandoning a fixed list of bitrates for all titles. An animated film and a film of rapid action need very different numbers of bits for the same apparent quality, and each title, and later each scene, is analysed and given its own list. Netflix also places its own caching servers inside the networks of internet providers, under the name Open Connect, which is the arrangement with providers mentioned under the costs of the service.

For live video, the delay of 15 to 30 seconds described above is what the plain protocols give. Both standards have since gained low-latency modes, which publish a piece in smaller parts while it is still being produced and bring the delay down to a few seconds, and conversation in real time uses a different family of protocols altogether, of which WebRTC is the one built into browsers.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Delivering a video as 1 fileThe quality cannot change, and caches hold all of it or none.Cut it into pieces of a few seconds.
Cutting each quality at different momentsA change of quality causes a jump or a gap in the picture.Cut all renditions at the same times, each piece beginning with a complete picture.
Encoding a long video as 1 jobIt takes hours, and a failure starts it again from the beginning.Split the source into sections and encode them as separate jobs.
Discarding the uploaded sourceThe catalogue cannot later be encoded in a better format.Keep the source.
Choosing the quality on the serverThe server cannot see the viewer’s connection or buffer.Let the player choose, from its own measurements.
Requesting the highest quality the last measurement allowsAny drop in speed empties the buffer and stops the picture.Keep a margin, and take the buffer into account.
Changing quality with every fluctuationThe picture flickers between sharp and soft.Step down promptly and step up cautiously.
Serving every piece from the originDistant viewers start slowly, and the origin carries all the traffic.Serve pieces from edge servers near the viewers.
A popular release with cold cachesThe first viewers all miss and overload the origin.Copy the pieces to the edge beforehand.
Caching the manifest of a live stream for longPlayers do not learn of new pieces.Cache it for a second or 2 only.
Buffering as far ahead as possibleViewers who leave have downloaded video they never watched.Limit the buffer to some tens of seconds.
