Summary

  • A video is delivered as a sequence of small files, which makes it cacheable, stateless to serve, and adjustable in quality.
  • Each upload is encoded at several bitrates, all cut into pieces at the same moments, by many machines working on separate sections.
  • A manifest tells the player which pieces exist, and the player alone decides what to fetch.
  • The player chooses a quality for each piece from the measured speed and the state of its buffer, and gives up sharpness to avoid interruptions.
  • The buffer absorbs the player’s errors, since the player learns of a change in speed only after the next download.
  • Edge servers near the viewers hold copies of pieces, which never change and are in highly concentrated demand.
  • The dominant cost is the delivery of bytes, which is why efficient encoding and well-placed caches matter so much.
  • Live video uses the same pieces, produced as the event happens, at the price of some seconds of delay.

Chat: System Design

A chat service carries short messages between people, and its users hold it to a standard that few other systems are asked to meet. A message is expected to appear on the recipient’s screen within a moment of being sent, as though the 2 phones were directly connected. It is expected to arrive whether or not the recipient’s phone was reachable at the time, to arrive once, and to appear among the other messages of the conversation in the order in which they were sent. People notice at once when any of these expectations is disappointed, since a conversation in which replies precede their questions, or in which a remark is repeated, or in which something said an hour ago turns up now, is immediately felt to be broken.

The system has to meet this standard on a foundation that is distinctly unreliable. A mobile phone loses its connection many times a day, in lifts and tunnels and when passing from one network to another. Its operating system suspends applications that are not on the screen. A message, or the acknowledgement of a message, may be lost at any point, and neither party can tell which of the 2 was lost. The design of a chat service consists largely in arranging matters so that none of this is visible: so that every interruption is followed by an exact recovery, and no message is lost, repeated or misplaced in consequence.

This chapter covers

  • how a server can send to a phone that has not asked: 3 methods compared
  • gateways, which hold the open connections, and the record of who is connected where
  • numbering the messages of a conversation
  • how 1 number per message deals with gaps, repetitions and disorder
  • catching up after an absence, with a cursor
  • sending a message twice without storing it twice
  • sent, delivered and read
  • groups, several devices, presence, and recipients who are offline
  • what end-to-end encryption changes

Reaching a phone that has not asked

In the ordinary use of HTTP, every exchange is begun by the client. The client sends a request and the server replies, and a server has no means of addressing a client that has not just asked it something. For most applications this is no restriction. For chat it is the first obstacle, since the essential act of the service is to deliver a message to a phone at a moment the phone could not have predicted.

There are 3 ways round the obstacle, and they are best compared by what each costs in delay and in wasted effort.

The first method is for the phone to ask at regular intervals whether anything has arrived, which is called polling. It is trivially simple and unsatisfactory in both respects. A message waits, on average, for half the interval before the next request collects it, and nearly all the requests return nothing, so that a phone polling once a second makes 86400 requests a day in order to receive perhaps 50 messages. Shortening the interval reduces the delay and multiplies the waste, and across millions of phones the empty requests alone amount to a formidable load.

The second method, long polling, removes most of both defects by a simple change on the server. The phone sends a request as before, and the server, if it has nothing to report, refrains from answering and holds the request open. When a message arrives, the server answers the waiting request with it, and the phone, having received the answer, immediately sends another request to wait on. Messages are delivered as soon as they arrive, and no request is answered empty except when one has been held for so long, usually about half a minute, that it is released to prevent intermediate network equipment from concluding that the connection is dead.

The third method abandons the pattern of request and reply. The phone opens a single connection to the server and keeps it open, and either side may send on it at any time. The protocol that provides this over the same ports and through the same infrastructure as HTTP is called WebSocket. It has the lowest delay and the least overhead, since a message in either direction is a small frame on an existing connection and involves no new request.

PollingLong pollingOpen connection
Delay before a message is receivedup to 1 intervalnonenone
Requests when nothing happens1 per interval1 per half minute or sonone, apart from a periodic sign of life
What the server holds for each phonenothing1 waiting request1 connection
Sending from phone to servera separate requesta separate requeston the same connection

Chat services use the open connection, falling back on long polling in the rare environments where a connection of the third kind cannot be established. The price is in the third row of the table. The server must now maintain a connection for every phone that is online, and with 50 million phones online that is 50 million connections held open at once, most of them idle at any instant. This single fact shapes the architecture of the service.

Gateways and sessions

An open connection is a resource of an unusual kind. It consumes little processing and a modest amount of memory, and it is tied irrevocably to the particular machine on which it terminates: a message for a given phone can be written to its connection only by the 1 process that holds that connection. The service therefore sets aside a class of servers, called gateways, whose sole function is to hold connections. A gateway accepts connections from phones, authenticates them, relays what arrives on them to the rest of the service, and writes to them whatever the rest of the service asks it to deliver. It contains as little other logic as possible, so that the software which changes often, concerning messages and conversations, can be deployed without disturbing the millions of connections.

A properly configured machine can hold some hundreds of thousands of idle connections, and at 100000 each, 50 million phones require 500 gateways. A message addressed to a member must be handed to the particular gateway on which that member’s phone is connected, and so the service needs to know, for every member who is online, which gateway that is. This knowledge is kept in a session store, an in-memory store mapping each connected device to its gateway. A gateway writes an entry when a phone connects and removes it when the phone disconnects.

The session store can be wrong, and the design has to allow for it. A gateway that crashes has no opportunity to remove its entries, which continue to assert that 100000 phones are connected to a machine that no longer exists. Every entry is therefore given a time limit and must be renewed periodically by the gateway that owns it, so that the entries of a dead gateway lapse of their own accord, which is the lease of chapter 10 in another setting. More fundamentally, the session store is treated as a hint and nothing more. If the service forwards a message to a gateway and the phone proves not to be there, nothing has been lost, since the message is safely stored and the phone will collect it when it reconnects, by the mechanism described below. The correctness of delivery does not depend on the session store’s being accurate, only its speed.

When a gateway does fail, its 100000 phones all detect the loss within a few seconds and all attempt to reconnect. If they did so immediately, the surviving gateways would receive 100000 connection attempts in the same instant, each requiring a cryptographic handshake, and might themselves be overwhelmed, causing further disconnections and further attempts. Phones therefore wait for a random interval before reconnecting and lengthen the interval after each failure, which is the backoff with jitter of chapter 13 applied by the client.

Numbering the messages of a conversation

We come now to the central problem, which is to ensure that every member of a conversation sees the same messages in the same order, without omission or repetition, in spite of everything that can happen to connections.

It is necessary first to say what “the order” is, since the obvious definition does not survive examination. One might order messages by the time at which they were sent, as recorded by the sender’s phone. But the clocks of phones differ by seconds or minutes, and a phone whose clock is slow would have its messages placed before messages to which they are replies. Nor can the times at which messages arrive at the various recipients be used, since these differ from one recipient to another, and the members would see different orders.

The order is therefore defined by decree, at a single place. All messages of a conversation pass through 1 point in the service, which assigns to each the next number in a sequence belonging to that conversation: 1, 2, 3 and so on. The order of the conversation is the order of these numbers, for every member and on every device. A number of this kind is a sequence number, and the reader will recognise it as the sequence number that the leader of a shard assigned to each record in chapter 3. The message store that assigns it is, in fact, a replicated log for each conversation, and the requirement that 2 messages never receive the same number is met in the same way, by having a single leader accept all appends to a given conversation.

The effect of this decision is to reduce the whole problem of reliable, ordered delivery to a matter of arithmetic on the recipient’s device. Each device remembers 1 number for each conversation, the number of the last message it has displayed, and compares the number of every incoming message with it.

3 distinct faults occur in the course of these steps, and the same comparison disposes of each. A message whose number is exactly 1 greater than the last displayed is the next message, and is shown. A message whose number is greater than that has arrived ahead of others that are missing, and the device does not show it, since to do so would present the conversation out of order. It asks the server for everything after the last number it has. A message whose number is equal to or less than the last displayed has been seen before, and is discarded. The simulation for this chapter runs exactly this scenario, and ends with 4 messages on the server and the same 4, in the same order and each once, on the phone.

The number that a device remembers is called its cursor, and it is what makes recovery from an absence exact. A device that has been offline does not ask the server what it has missed, a question the server could answer only by keeping track of what each device has received. The device states its position, “I have everything up to number 1 in this conversation”, and the server replies with everything after that position. The server keeps no record of deliveries and has no need to know why the device was away or for how long. A phone that was switched off for a week recovers by the same request as a phone that passed through a tunnel.

Sending without duplicating

The preceding section dealt with messages travelling to a device. A similar hazard attends messages travelling from it. A phone sends a message and waits for the server’s confirmation. If none arrives, the phone cannot distinguish between a message that never reached the server and a message that was stored and whose confirmation was lost, and since an unsent message is the worse outcome, it must send again. In the second case the server now receives the same message twice, and a server that stored whatever it received would give the 2 copies 2 successive numbers, to be displayed twice on every member’s screen.

The remedy is the idempotency key that chapters 11 and 13 used for the same purpose. The phone generates a random identifier for each message before the first attempt and includes it in every attempt. The server records the identifier with the stored message, and on receiving an identifier it has already recorded for that conversation, stores nothing and returns the number it assigned originally. A message may then be sent any number of times and will be stored once.

The same identifier serves the phone in another way. A message that has been typed and sent should appear in the sender’s own view of the conversation at once, before the server has confirmed it, since any perceptible delay makes the application feel sluggish. The phone therefore displays the message immediately, marked as pending, and when the confirmation arrives with the server’s number, it uses the identifier to find the pending message and move it to its proper place in the sequence.

Sent, delivered and read

Chat applications commonly show the sender how far a message has progressed, and the 3 customary indications correspond to 3 different events in the system. A message is sent when the server has stored it and assigned its number, at which point it is safe and will not be lost. It is delivered when a device of the recipient has received it, which the device reports by informing the server of its new cursor. It is read when the recipient has opened the conversation, which the device reports similarly, as the number of the last message actually displayed on screen.

It will be seen that delivery and reading are both conveyed by a single number for each device, with no separate acknowledgement for every message. A cursor of 40 acknowledges messages 1 to 40 together. This economy matters in large and busy conversations, and it has the further merit of being idempotent, since reporting the same cursor twice has no additional effect.

These reports are themselves events that must be conveyed to the sender’s devices, and they pass through the same machinery as messages. They are, however, of less consequence. A message that is lost is a serious failure, whereas a read indication that arrives late or is occasionally lost is a blemish, and services accordingly transmit such indications with less ceremony, without storing each durably.

Recipients who are offline

When a message is stored and the recipient has no device connected, the service has done all that it can do directly. The message waits in the store, and will be delivered by the catching-up procedure when a device next connects.

To the recipient, however, a message that waits until the application is next opened has not really arrived. The service therefore asks the notification service of chapter 13 to send a push notification through the provider that serves the phone’s operating system, which is able to wake the device and display an alert even when the application is not running. The notification is merely a signal. It may be delayed or dropped by the provider, as chapter 13 explained, and it need not carry the message itself. When the user responds to it, the application opens its connection, reports its cursor, and obtains the messages in the ordinary way. Reliability thus continues to rest on the store and the cursor, and the notification serves only to bring the user back sooner.

Mobile operating systems reinforce this division. They suspend applications that are in the background and close their connections in order to save power, so that a phone is, from the service’s point of view, offline for most of the day although it is switched on and in its owner’s pocket. The combination of a push notification to attract attention and a cursor to recover the state is the pattern to which every mobile messaging application conforms.

Groups and several devices

A conversation with many members requires no new mechanism. The message is stored once, in the conversation’s sequence, and each member’s devices keep their own cursors. What differs is the work of delivery: the chat service must look up the sessions of every member and forward the message to the gateway of each one who is online, which is the fan-out of chapter 15.

For groups of ordinary size, a few dozen or a few hundred members, this is done directly. For very large groups, of tens of thousands, direct fan-out for every message becomes as expensive as it was for the accounts with millions of followers in chapter 15, and the same remedy applies. Devices are told only that the conversation has new messages, or discover it when the conversation is opened, and then fetch from their cursors.

A member who uses a phone, a tablet and a computer has 3 devices, each of which may be online or offline independently, and each must show the complete conversation. This too is already provided for, since every device has a cursor of its own and catches up separately. A message sent from the phone reaches the member’s own computer in the same way that it reaches the other members, by being stored in the sequence and delivered to every device that has not yet reached that number. The 1 thing that is shared among a member’s devices is the position up to which the member has read, so that a conversation read on the phone is not shown as unread on the computer.

Presence

Many applications show whether a contact is at present online, which is called presence. It appears a small feature and is, relative to its importance, among the most expensive.

The difficulty is one of fan-out. Whenever a member comes online or goes offline, every contact who might be displaying that member’s status must be informed, and with phones connecting and disconnecting continually, a member with 500 contacts produces 500 notifications at each change of state. Across all members, the traffic in presence updates can exceed the traffic in messages.

Services contain this in several ways. Presence is declared to be eventually consistent, and a status that is some seconds out of date is accepted. Updates are sent only to contacts who are themselves online and have the member in view, a device subscribing to the presence of the contacts it is currently displaying and to no others. And a brief disconnection is not announced at all: the service waits some seconds before declaring a member offline, so that a phone which drops its connection and restores it at once does not cause its owner to flicker in a thousand contact lists.

The indication that someone is typing is handled in the same spirit. It is forwarded to the other participants who are online and is stored nowhere, since if it is lost nothing of value is lost with it.

Storing messages

At 20 billion messages a day, the message store receives some 230000 writes a second and grows by terabytes daily. Its pattern of access is, fortunately, very regular. Messages are always appended to the end of a conversation and almost always read as a range from the end of a conversation, the most recent 50, or everything after a cursor.

The store is accordingly keyed by conversation and, within a conversation, by sequence number, so that the messages of a conversation lie together in order and a request for a range reads 1 contiguous run. It is divided among shards by a hash of the conversation identifier, in the manner of chapter 1, so that each conversation resides entirely on 1 shard and has 1 leader assigning its numbers. A very active conversation becomes a hot key in the sense of chapter 9, and the shards must be small enough that 1 busy group cannot overwhelm its neighbours.

Recent messages are requested constantly and old ones hardly ever, since people seldom scroll back more than a few days. The store can therefore keep recent messages on fast storage and move older ones to cheaper media, as the object store of chapter 16 does with cold data.

End-to-end encryption

In the design described, the service can read every message, since messages reach it in a form it is able to store, index and search. Many chat services now offer end-to-end encryption, in which a message is encrypted on the sender’s device with keys known only to the participants’ devices and is decrypted only on the recipients’ devices. The service transports and stores ciphertext that it has no means of reading.

Nothing in the architecture of this chapter is thereby altered. The service still numbers, stores, forwards and replays messages, which are now opaque to it. What changes is everything that depended on the server’s knowledge of the contents. The server can no longer search messages, so search must be performed on each device over its own copy. It cannot compose the text of a push notification, so the notification carries ciphertext or a bare signal, and the device decrypts or fetches. A newly added device cannot be given the history by the server in readable form, and must obtain the means of reading it from another of the member’s devices. The exchange and verification of keys, which is the difficult part of such a scheme, is a subject for a book on cryptography.

Use cases

A member sends messages, receives them, and returns after absences of every length.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A member can send a message to a conversation of 2 or more members.
1A member who is online receives a message within 500 ms.
2A member who was offline receives every missed message after reconnecting.
3Messages in a conversation are shown in the same order to every member.
4A message is shown once, even when it is delivered more than once.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DurabilityA message that the sender saw as sent is not lost.
1ConsistencyStrong within a conversation: 1 order of messages. Presence is eventual.
2Availability99.95% for sending and receiving.
3Scale50 million members online, and 20 billion messages per day.

Order is the property that members perceive most directly, and so the sequence of each conversation is strongly consistent. A message is confirmed to its sender only when a majority of the replicas of the conversation’s log has stored it under its number, and no 2 replicas ever disagree about which message bears a given number. Everything of secondary importance, presence, typing indications and read positions, is eventually consistent, on the principle that it is better for these to be briefly wrong than for the sending of messages to wait upon them.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 50 million open connections need about 500 gateway servers, and 20 billion messages per day are 230000 per second.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Connections per gatewaygiven100000
Gateways50000000 ÷ 100000500
Messages per second20000000000 ÷ 86400231000
Storage per day20 billion × 200 bytes4 TB

The API

Sending a message and catching up are ordinary HTTP requests, shown below. Live delivery takes place on the open connection, on which the server pushes each new message as a small frame carrying the conversation, the number and the content.

Send a message

POST /v1/conversations/301/messages HTTP/1.1
Host: chat.example
Idempotency-Key: phone-a-000512
Content-Type: application/json

{ "text": "are you coming?" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{ "number": 1, "time": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z" }

The server chooses the number. The key lets the phone send again after a lost answer without creating a second message.

Catch up after being offline

GET /v1/conversations/301/messages?after=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: chat.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "messages": [
    { "number": 2, "sender": "bob", "text": "hello?" },
    { "number": 3, "sender": "bob", "text": "we are starting" },
    { "number": 4, "sender": "bob", "text": "table 4" }
  ]
}

after=1 is the phone’s cursor: the last number it has shown.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Gatewayholds the open connections of many phonesconnections, in memoryits phones reconnect to another gateway and catch up
Chat servicenumbers and stores messages, and forwards themnoneanother instance takes the requests
Message storekeeps every conversation’s messages in ordermessages, replicateda follower takes over, as in chapter 4
Session storeremembers which gateway each online member is connected tosessions, in memoryphones re-register when they reconnect

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 18.6.

  1. The sender’s phone sends the message over the connection it keeps open to gateway A.
  2. Gateway A passes the message to the chat service.
  3. The chat service asks the message store to append it. The store gives it the next number of the conversation, and the sender is told that the message is sent.
  4. The chat service looks up the receiver in the session store, finds gateway B, and forwards the message there. A receiver who is offline is skipped: the message waits in the store.
  5. Gateway B pushes the message down the receiver’s open connection.

The design, deployed

The gateway tier is the one that this system has and most others lack. Its 500 machines hold 100000 connections each, and the load balancers in front of them distribute connections, which last for hours, where other systems distribute requests. Because a connection is tied to its gateway, this tier cannot be drained quickly: replacing the software on a gateway means disconnecting 100000 phones, and deployments are therefore made in small groups of gateways. Behind the gateways, the chat service is stateless and the message store is sharded by conversation, with 3 replicas of each shard in 3 zones.

How real systems do it

WhatsApp is the best known example of how few machines the connection tier needs when it is built with care. In 2012 its engineers reported more than 2 million connections held open on a single server, running a server written in Erlang on FreeBSD, and later accounts put the figure between 2 and 3 million. The figure of 100000 for each gateway used in this chapter is therefore conservative, and the difference is mostly a matter of memory for each connection and of how much work the gateway is asked to do beyond holding it.

For storage, Discord has published 2 accounts that follow the same service as it grew, first on Cassandra when it held billions of messages and later on ScyllaDB when it held trillions. In both, messages are keyed by channel and by a bucket of time, so that the messages of a channel for a given period lie together and a request for recent history reads 1 partition, which is the layout described under storing messages. The accounts are candid about the hot key: a single very large and active channel overloads the partition that holds it, and much of the later work concerns protecting the store from that.

The numbering of messages by the server within a conversation, and the client’s cursor, are the common practice of such services. Protocols differ in the transport. Facebook described building its mobile messenger on MQTT, a lightweight protocol of publishing and subscribing designed for unreliable networks, in order to keep the connection cheap in power.

End-to-end encryption, where it is offered, is nearly always the Signal protocol, whose central mechanism derives a fresh key for every message, so that the capture of 1 key exposes neither earlier messages nor later ones. For groups, each sender distributes a key of their own to the members, which is why adding and removing members of a large encrypted group is expensive.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Ordering messages by the sender’s clockPhones’ clocks differ, and replies appear before the messages they answer.Let the server number the messages of each conversation.
Displaying whatever arrivesA message that overtakes others appears out of order, and a repeat appears twice.Display a message only if its number follows the last one shown.
Sending only new messages after a reconnectionWhatever was sent during the absence is never delivered.Have the device report its cursor, and send everything after it.
Tracking on the server what each device has receivedThe server holds a great deal of state and still cannot know what was lost in transit.Let each device keep its cursor and report it.
Storing every message the server receivesA retry after a lost confirmation is stored as a second message.Have the phone attach an identifier, and store each identifier once.
Trusting the session storeA message is sent to a gateway where the phone no longer is, and is considered delivered.Treat sessions as a hint, and rely on the stored sequence and the cursor.
Session entries without a time limitA crashed gateway’s phones appear connected indefinitely.Give entries a lease that the gateway renews.
Reconnecting immediately after a gateway failsIts phones overwhelm the remaining gateways.Reconnect after a random, lengthening delay.
Relying on a push notification to deliver the messageNotifications are delayed and dropped, and messages with them.Use the notification as a signal, and fetch from the cursor.
Announcing every change of presence to every contactPresence traffic exceeds message traffic.Inform only contacts who are watching, and wait before declaring someone offline.
Putting message logic in the gatewaysEvery deployment drops millions of connections.Keep gateways minimal and deploy the logic separately.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
The receiver is offlinethe message arrives laterit waits in the message store until the phone reports its cursor
A gateway crashesits phones show ‘connecting’ for a momentthey reconnect elsewhere and catch up from their cursors
The answer to a send is lostthe sender’s phone sends againthe idempotency key returns the same message number

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Open connectionsmessages arrive at onceservers hold 1 connection per online phone
Numbers per conversationorder, gaps and repeats are handled by 1 mechanismevery message goes through the store that assigns numbers
Storing every messageoffline members catch upstorage grows with every message

Simulation in the repository. The program code/chatsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p chatsim in the code directory.

Summary

  • A phone keeps 1 connection open, so that the server can deliver a message the moment it arrives.
  • Gateways hold the connections, and a session store records which gateway each device is on, as a hint that may be wrong.
  • The server assigns every message the next number of its conversation, and that numbering is the order for everyone.
  • A device displays a message only if its number follows the last one displayed, which handles gaps, disorder and repetition alike.
  • After any absence, a device reports its cursor and receives everything after it, and the server keeps no record of deliveries.
  • A message carries an identifier chosen by the sending phone, so that a retry is stored once.
  • Push notifications call the user back, and the stored sequence and the cursor do the delivering.
  • The sequence is strongly consistent, and presence and read positions are eventually consistent.

Payment System: System Design

A payment system moves money from a customer to a shop. In its outward form it resembles many of the systems in this book, being a service that accepts requests, writes records and calls other services, and yet it differs from all of them in the consequences of its errors. When a news feed shows a post some seconds late, or a cache returns a slightly stale value, or a rate limiter admits a few requests too many, nobody is harmed, and the preceding chapters made deliberate use of that latitude in order to gain speed and availability. A payment system has no such latitude. If it charges a customer twice, real money has left a real account, and if it records a payment that did not take place, goods are shipped that were never paid for. Its errors are measured in currency, are noticed by the people affected, and in most jurisdictions are regulated by law.

The priorities of the design are in consequence the reverse of those that governed earlier chapters. Correctness is placed before availability, so that a payment system which is uncertain declines to act where another system would guess. Nothing is ever deleted or overwritten, so that every state the system has been in can be reconstructed and explained. And every operation is built on the assumption that it will be attempted more than once, since the networks and services on which payments depend fail in ways that leave the outcome of a request unknown. This chapter develops the 3 ideas on which a sound payment system rests: the idempotent request, the double-entry ledger, and the treatment of an unknown outcome as a state in its own right.

This chapter covers

  • the parties to a card payment, and the stages it passes through over several days
  • why a payment request must be safe to repeat, and how a key makes it so
  • representing money without losing fractions of a cent
  • the double-entry ledger, in which every movement is 2 entries that cancel
  • why entries are never changed, and how mistakes are corrected
  • a charge whose outcome is unknown, and why it is neither a success nor a failure
  • reconciliation, which compares our records with the bank’s
  • payments that span several services, and undoing what cannot be made atomic
  • keeping card numbers out of the system

The parties and the stages

A payment by card involves more parties than the 2 that are visible at the checkout. The customer’s card was issued by a bank, which holds the customer’s account. The shop has an account at another bank. Between the 2 banks stands a card network, which carries messages between them and lays down the rules. A payment system of the kind designed here acts on behalf of the shop: it receives the shop’s request to charge a card, communicates with the network, and keeps the records. For the purposes of this chapter, the banks and the network may be regarded as a single external service, slow and occasionally unavailable, whose behaviour we can observe and cannot change.

What appears to the customer as a single event is in fact spread over several days.

In authorisation, the customer’s bank is asked whether the card is valid and the funds are available, and, if so, sets the amount aside. No money moves. The customer sees “payment accepted” at this point, within a second or 2. In capture, the shop confirms that it wishes to collect the authorised amount, which it typically does when the goods are dispatched, and the amount captured may be less than the amount authorised if part of an order could not be fulfilled. In settlement, which takes place in batches some days later, the money is actually transferred between the banks. And for months afterwards the payment may be reversed, by a refund that the shop initiates or by a dispute in which the customer’s bank reclaims the money on the customer’s complaint.

The practical consequence is that a payment is not a single action with a result. It is an object with a long life and a series of states, and at each stage our system’s record of that state must be brought into agreement with what the banks have actually done. Much of the design follows from taking this seriously.

A request that is safe to repeat

Suppose a shop’s server sends a request to charge a customer 40 euros, and the connection fails before any reply is received. The shop does not know whether the charge was made. If it does nothing, it may have failed to collect payment for an order. If it sends the request again and the first had in fact succeeded, the customer is charged 80 euros. This is the dilemma of the lost reply, which has appeared in chapters 11, 13 and 18, and here it concerns money.

It is resolved in the same way. The shop attaches to each request an idempotency key, a string of its own choosing that uniquely identifies the business event concerned, such as the number of the order. The payment system records every key together with the result of its request, and when a request arrives bearing a key that has been seen before, it performs no action and returns the recorded result. The shop may then repeat a request as often as it needs to, in complete safety, until it obtains an answer.

Four details determine whether this protection is real.

The key and the effects of the request must be recorded atomically. If the system were to move the money in 1 step and record the key in another, a crash between the 2 would leave a completed charge with no record of its key, and the shop’s retry would be treated as new. Both are therefore written in a single database transaction.

The recorded result must include failures. In the simulation for this chapter, a charge of 9000 cents is refused because the customer’s account holds only 6000. That refusal is stored under the key, and a retry of the same request receives the same refusal, even if the customer has in the meantime received funds that would now cover it. The principle is that a retry must behave as a second delivery of the same request, which it is, since the shop, having perhaps already told the customer that the payment was declined, would otherwise find that it had succeeded after all.

Concurrent requests with the same key must be dealt with. A shop’s client may retry while the first attempt is still in progress, so that 2 requests bearing the same key are being processed at once. The system reserves the key, by an atomic “create if absent”, before doing anything else, and the second request, finding the key already reserved and no result yet recorded, is told to try again shortly.

And a key should be bound to the contents of its request. If a key that was first used for a charge of 40 euros arrives with a request for 400, something is wrong in the client, and the system should reject the request. To return the result of the earlier and different one would hide the fault.

The simulation sends 5 requests, of which 2 are repetitions. The 2 requests under the key order-7 leave the customer with the same balance of 6000, the second having moved nothing, and likewise for order-9. The total held across all accounts is 10000 cents at the start and 10000 at the end.

Representing money

A matter that seems too elementary to need discussion has caused a remarkable number of defects. Amounts of money must not be held in the floating-point numbers that programming languages offer for fractional values.

Floating-point numbers are stored in binary, and most decimal fractions have no exact binary representation, in the same way that a third has no exact decimal one. The value 0.10 is held as a number very slightly different from a tenth, and arithmetic on such values accumulates the differences: in most languages, the sum of 0.10 and 0.20 is not equal to 0.30. A single such discrepancy is far smaller than a cent. Across millions of transactions, in sums, percentages and currency conversions, the discrepancies round in different directions in different parts of the system, and totals that ought to agree fail to agree by a few cents, which in accounting is an error to be found and explained.

Amounts are therefore held as whole numbers of the smallest unit of the currency, so that 40 euros is the integer 4000, in cents. Arithmetic on integers is exact. The currency is always stored beside the amount, since 4000 means nothing without it, and since the smallest unit is not a hundredth in every currency: some have no subdivision and others divide into a thousand. Where a calculation yields a fraction of the smallest unit, as when a fee of 2.9% is computed or an amount is divided among 3 recipients, the rule for rounding is laid down explicitly, and the remainder is assigned to a specified party, so that the parts always add up to the whole.

The ledger

The core of a payment system is its record of where money is, and the form of that record has been settled for some 500 years. It is the double-entry ledger, and its governing rule is that every movement of money is recorded as 2 entries of equal amount and opposite sign, 1 against the account the money leaves and 1 for the account it enters.

The method has 3 properties, each of which answers a need that a simpler design would leave unmet.

It cannot create or destroy money. Since every movement consists of 2 entries that cancel, the sum of all entries in the ledger is 0 at all times, whatever has happened. Should the sum ever differ from 0, the ledger contains an error, and this is discovered by a single addition, with no need to understand any individual transaction. A design that kept only a balance for each account and adjusted the 2 balances in turn would have no such check. A defect that deducted from 1 account and failed to credit the other would cause money to vanish, and nothing would reveal it until a customer complained.

It explains every balance. The balance of an account is defined as the sum of that account’s entries, and so for any balance one can produce the complete list of movements that gave rise to it. When a shop asks why its balance is what it is, the answer is a list of entries, each referring to the payment that caused it.

And its history is permanent. Entries are added and never altered or removed, so that the ledger is an append-only log of the same kind as the log of chapter 2. An error is corrected by adding entries that reverse it, as the refund in the steps above reverses the first payment, and the record then shows both the error and its correction. This is what makes the system auditable. If a row could be edited, then a mistaken edit, or a dishonest one, would leave no evidence, whereas in an append-only ledger whatever has once been recorded remains for inspection.

The 2 entries of a movement must be written atomically, both or neither. This is the principal reason why the ledger is kept in a database with transactions and strong consistency, and why the weaker models that sufficed elsewhere in this book are out of place here.

Balances in practice

To define a balance as the sum of an account’s entries is correct and, taken literally, slow, since an account with a million entries would require a million additions for each reading. The system therefore keeps a stored balance for each account as well and updates it in the same transaction that adds the entries. The entries remain the authority. The stored balance is a cache of their sum, and it can be verified against them, or recomputed from them, at any time.

Checking that a customer has sufficient funds and then deducting the amount is a sequence of reading and writing, and it is exposed to the race that has appeared several times in this book: 2 simultaneous payments from the same account each read a balance of 6000, each conclude that 4000 can be afforded, and each deduct, leaving the account overdrawn. The check and the deduction have to be a single atomic step, which is obtained either by having the transaction lock the account’s row before reading it, or by making the update conditional, in the form “deduct 4000 if the balance is at least 4000”.

An account that takes part in a very large number of payments, such as that of a major shop, becomes a point of contention under this arrangement, since every payment to that shop must lock the same row. A usual remedy is to add the entries at once and to bring the shop’s stored balance up to date a little later, in batches. For an account that only receives money, a balance that lags by a few seconds is harmless. For the account from which a payment is made, the balance must be exact at the moment of the check.

A charge whose outcome is unknown

The ledger is under our control. The card network is not, and a request to it can come to 3 ends, of which the third is the source of most of the difficulty in the subject. The network may reply that the charge succeeded. It may reply that the charge was declined. Or no reply may arrive within the time allowed.

In the third case our system does not know whether the customer has been charged. Both of the natural reactions are mistaken. To treat the timeout as a failure and inform the shop that the payment did not go through is wrong if the charge in fact succeeded, since the customer has then paid for an order that the shop believes unpaid. To send the charge again is wrong for the same reason, since the customer may then be charged twice.

The correct treatment recognises “unknown” as a legitimate state of a payment, with a name and a procedure of its own.

The steps display 3 practices that are worth stating in general terms.

The payment is recorded as pending in our own system before the network is called. If our process crashes during the call, the record survives to say that a charge was in progress and under what reference, so that it can be followed up on restarting. Had we called the network first and recorded afterwards, a crash between the 2 would leave a customer charged and our system unaware that any payment had been attempted.

The request to the network carries a reference that we generate, and the network supports either the repetition of a request under the same reference without a second charge, or a query on the status of a reference. This is our own idempotency key, presented to the next party along. Without some such facility at the network, the dilemma of the lost reply cannot be resolved at all, and a payment system must select its external partners with this requirement in mind.

And the outcome is determined by asking. A background process takes each pending payment in turn and queries the network until it obtains a definite answer, upon which the payment moves to done or failed and the ledger entries are written. The shop, which was told that the payment was pending, is informed of the final outcome by a call to an address it has registered, the webhook of chapter 13.

The states of a payment thus form a small machine: created, pending, and then either done or failed, with later movements to refunded or disputed. Every transition is recorded with its time and its cause, and certain transitions are prohibited outright. A payment that is done never returns to pending, and a refund is a new movement with entries of its own.

Reconciliation

However carefully all of this is constructed, our records and the bank’s will sometimes differ. A reply was lost and the query that should have resolved it was itself mishandled. A defect in our software caused a step to be skipped. A dispute was raised at the bank and never communicated to us. The bank made an error of its own.

A payment system therefore does not assume that its records are right. Every day it obtains from the bank a statement of what the bank did in fact process, and compares that statement, payment by payment, with its own ledger. This comparison is called reconciliation.

Each discrepancy falls into 1 of a few classes: a payment that the bank has and we lack, a payment that we have and the bank lacks, or a payment present in both with different amounts or states. Each is investigated, automatically where a rule can decide and by a person where it cannot, and is corrected by adding entries to the ledger, in accordance with the rule that nothing already recorded is altered.

Reconciliation is the final safeguard of the whole system. Idempotency keys, atomic transactions and the handling of pending payments are all intended to prevent discrepancies, and reconciliation is what detects those that occur in spite of them, including any that arise from mistakes in the preventive mechanisms themselves. A payment system without it is correct only so long as all of its code is free of defects, which is to say that it is not correct.

Payments that span several services

Placing an order usually requires more than a payment. Stock has to be reserved, the payment taken, and a shipment arranged, and in a system divided into services each of these belongs to a different service with a database of its own. One would wish the 3 to be atomic, so that either all take place or none does, and no single database transaction can span 3 databases.

There is a protocol, called 2-phase commit, that makes several databases commit together. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare and to promise that it will be able to commit, and when all have promised, instructs them all to do so. The protocol achieves atomicity and is seldom used between services, for 2 reasons. Each participant must hold its locks from the moment of its promise until the instruction arrives, and if the coordinator fails in that interval the participants are left holding locks indefinitely, unable to proceed in either direction. And every participant, including external ones such as a card network, must implement the protocol, which external services do not.

The usual alternative gives up atomicity and substitutes for it the assurance that the process will eventually be either completed or undone. The operation is divided into steps, each a local transaction in a single service, and for every step there is defined a compensating action that reverses its effect: releasing the reserved stock, refunding the payment, cancelling the shipment. The steps are executed in order, and if one fails, the compensating actions of those already completed are executed in reverse. A sequence of steps organised in this way is called a saga.

A saga is not a transaction, and the difference is observable. While it is in progress, other parts of the system can see its intermediate states: the stock is reserved before the payment has been taken, and for a short time a customer may have been charged for an order that is about to be cancelled. Compensation, moreover, is not erasure. A refunded payment appears on the customer’s statement as a charge and a refund, and a confirmation email that has been sent cannot be recalled. The design of a saga consists largely in ordering its steps so that those most easily reversed come first and those that cannot be reversed come last.

The mechanisms needed to run a saga dependably are those of earlier chapters. The steps are driven by messages on a queue, as in chapter 11, and each service publishes its message by means of an outbox, in the same transaction as its own change. Every step and every compensating action is idempotent, since the queue delivers at least once.

Keeping card numbers out

A card number, in combination with its expiry date and security code, is all that is required in order to spend someone else’s money, and a system that stores card numbers is a target for theft in exact proportion to the number it holds. The card industry imposes a demanding security standard on any system that handles them, with audits whose burden grows with every component the numbers pass through.

The most effective measure is therefore structural: to arrange that card numbers pass through as little of the system as possible. The form in which the customer enters the card is served by, and submits directly to, a small and isolated service called a vault, whose sole purpose is to hold card numbers. The vault returns a token, a random identifier that stands for the card and has no value outside this system. The remainder of the system, including the shop’s servers, the payment API and the ledger, stores and handles only the token. When a charge is to be made, the token is presented to the vault, which alone communicates the real number to the card network. A breach of any component other than the vault then yields tokens, which are of no use to a thief.

Use cases

Shops charge customers and refund them. Accountants read the ledger, in order to confirm that it balances.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A shop can charge a customer an amount.
1A request that is sent again with the same key has no second effect and returns the first result.
2A shop can refund a payment, in full or in part.
3Every payment is recorded as entries in a ledger, and the entries of a payment add up to 0.
4An accountant can list the entries of any account.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0ConsistencyStrong. Both entries of a payment are written, or neither.
1DurabilityA recorded payment is not lost under any single failure.
2Availability99.99%. When in doubt, the system refuses a payment and does not guess.
3Scale1000 payments per second.

This is the chapter in which strong consistency prevails in every dispute. The 2 entries of a movement, the stored balance and the result recorded under the idempotency key are all written in 1 transaction on a store that confirms a write only when a majority of its replicas hold it. When the store cannot reach a majority, payments are refused. A payment system that is unavailable for a minute loses some sales, and a payment system that is inconsistent loses money and, with it, the confidence of the people whose money it was.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 1000 payments per second are 86 million per day and about 35 GB of ledger entries per day.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Payments per day1000 × 8640086.4 million
Entries per day86.4 million × 2172.8 million
Storage per day172.8 million × 200 bytes34.6 GB

The API

A charge is a new resource and is created with POST, a method that HTTP does not define as idempotent, and this is exactly why the API demands a key with every such request.

Charge a customer

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: pay.example
Idempotency-Key: order-7
Content-Type: application/json

{ "from": "ada", "to": "shop", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/payments/9001
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 9001, "state": "done", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR" }

Amounts are whole numbers of cents. Fractions of a currency are not stored as floating-point numbers, which cannot represent 0.10 exactly.

The same request again

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: pay.example
Idempotency-Key: order-7
Content-Type: application/json

{ "from": "ada", "to": "shop", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR" }

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 9001, "state": "done", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR" }

The same payment comes back with 200, and no money moves.

A charge without enough money

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: pay.example
Idempotency-Key: order-8
Content-Type: application/json

{ "from": "ada", "to": "shop", "amount": 9000, "currency": "EUR" }

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "The account does not hold this amount",
  "status": 422
}

422 is the status for a request that is well formed and cannot be carried out.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Payment APIchecks the key and the requestnoneanother instance answers
Key storeremembers the result of every keykeys, replicateda follower takes over; until then payments are refused
Ledgerwrites the 2 entries of a payment in 1 transactionevery entry, replicateda follower takes over; until then payments are refused
Card networkmoves money between banksoutside our controlthe payment stays pending and is checked again

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 19.7.

  1. A shop sends POST /v1/payments with the key order-7.
  2. The API looks up order-7 in the key store. If a result is stored, it is returned and nothing else happens.
  3. For a new key, the ledger checks the balance and writes 2 entries, minus 4000 for the customer and plus 4000 for the shop, together with the key’s result, in 1 transaction.
  4. The card network is asked to move the money between the banks. Its answer can take seconds, so the payment is first pending and becomes done when the answer arrives.

The design, deployed

By the standards of this book the payment system is small, since 1000 payments per second is a modest load, and its deployment is shaped by correctness and isolation more than by scale. The payment API is stateless. The ledger is a single database with a leader and 2 followers in 3 zones, which confirms a write only when a follower in another zone holds it. The vault that holds card numbers is drawn in red because it is a separate system with its own network, its own access rules and its own audit, which the rest of the system can reach only to exchange a token. The background tier carries the work that follows a payment: publishing events from the outbox, asking the card network about pending payments, and the nightly reconciliation.

How real systems do it

The idempotency key is the centrepiece of Stripe’s public API, and an engineer of that company has published the most detailed account of implementing it. The account divides a request into atomic phases, each a database transaction that ends at a call to an outside service, and records after each phase how far the request has progressed, so that a retry with the same key resumes from the last completed phase and does not start again. This is a more careful version of the pending state described above, generalised to requests with several outside calls. Airbnb has described a similar design for its own payments, in which a request is divided into a phase before the outside call, the call itself and a phase after it, with the rule that no outside call may be made inside a database transaction.

The saga comes from a paper of 1987, which proposed it for transactions that run too long to hold locks. The 2-phase commit protocol and its weakness, the participant left in doubt when the coordinator fails, are described in the classic literature on transaction processing.

For the ledger, several companies have described building append-only stores specifically for double-entry records, with the immutability enforced by the store itself, whatever the application attempts. Whatever the store, the rule of keeping card numbers in an isolated component is not a matter of taste. The security standard of the card industry applies to every system that stores, processes or transmits card numbers, and the tokenising vault exists to keep as much of the system as possible outside its scope.

What this chapter leaves out is considerable. A real card payment involves a standard message format between the parties, further authentication of the cardholder in many countries, the screening of every payment for fraud before it is authorised, the conversion of currencies, and the rules of each card network on disputes. Each is a subject in itself, and none of them changes the 3 ideas on which the chapter rests.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
A charge without an idempotency keyA retry after a lost reply charges the customer twice.Require a key, and record the result of every key.
Recording the key separately from the chargeA crash between the 2 leaves a charge whose retry is treated as new.Write the key, the entries and the result in 1 transaction.
Not recording failures under the keyA retry of a declined charge may succeed after the shop has reported failure.Store every outcome, and return it for every retry.
Amounts in floating-point numbersTotals differ by cents across millions of transactions.Store whole numbers of the smallest unit, with the currency.
Adjusting 1 balance and then the otherA crash in between destroys or creates money.Write both entries of a movement in 1 transaction.
Editing or deleting ledger rowsHistory is lost, and mistakes and fraud leave no trace.Add reversing entries, and never change existing ones.
Reading a balance and then deducting2 simultaneous payments both pass the check and overdraw the account.Lock the account, or make the deduction conditional on the balance.
Treating a timeout as a failureThe customer was charged, and the shop is told otherwise.Keep the payment pending, and ask the network for its outcome.
Sending a timed-out charge again without a referenceThe customer is charged twice.Give every charge a reference by which the network recognises a repeat.
Calling the network before recording the paymentA crash leaves a charge of which the system has no knowledge.Record the payment as pending first.
No reconciliationDifferences from the bank’s records accumulate unnoticed.Compare the ledger with the bank’s statement every day.
Treating a saga as a transactionIntermediate states are seen by others, and some steps cannot be undone.Put reversible steps first and irreversible ones last.
Card numbers in ordinary databases and logsA breach anywhere exposes cards.Confine card numbers to a vault, and use tokens elsewhere.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
The answer to a charge is lostthe shop retriesthe key returns the first result
The card network times outthe payment shows as pendingthe system asks the network about that payment until it gets a definite answer
The ledger’s leader failspayments are refused for about 1 seconda follower is elected, as in chapter 4

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Strong consistency everywheremoney is not lost or duplicatedpayments are refused during a failover
A key on every requestretries are safethe result of every key has to be stored
Entries, with balances computed from themevery balance can be explained and checkedmore data than 1 number per account

Simulation in the repository. The program code/paysim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p paysim in the code directory.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Card networkthe organisation that carries payment messages between banks

Capturethe shop’s confirmation that an authorised amount is to be collected
Settlementthe actual transfer of money between banks
Refunda return of money initiated by the shop

Idempotency keya name the caller gives a request, so that a repeat has no further effect
Ledgerthe append-only list of all entries, which is the record of where money has gone
