Summary

  • A payment system places correctness before availability, and declines to act when it is uncertain.
  • A card payment is an object with a life of days: authorisation, capture, settlement, and possibly refund or dispute.
  • Every request carries an idempotency key, recorded atomically with its result, so that a repeat changes nothing.
  • Money is held as whole numbers of the smallest unit of its currency.
  • Every movement is 2 ledger entries that add up to 0, written together and never altered afterwards.
  • A charge whose reply is lost stays pending until its outcome has been established by asking the network.
  • Reconciliation compares the ledger with the bank’s statement every day and catches what everything else missed.
  • Operations that span several services are run as sagas, with compensating actions in place of atomicity.
  • Card numbers are confined to a vault, and the rest of the system handles tokens.

Ticket Booking: System Design

A booking system sells things of which there is a fixed and usually small supply: the seats of a cinema for a particular showing, the rooms of a hotel for a particular night, the places on a particular flight. Each such thing can be sold once, and the entire purpose of the system is to see that it is not sold twice. 2 travellers who arrive at the airport holding confirmations for seat 14C on the same flight have been failed by the airline’s booking system in the most direct way possible, and no apology alters the fact that 1 of them will not be sitting there.

The requirement sounds elementary, and on a single machine serving 1 customer after another it is. It becomes difficult under the conditions in which booking systems in fact operate. Many customers act at the same time, on many servers, and 2 of them will sooner or later choose the same seat in the same instant. A customer who has chosen a seat needs some minutes in which to pay, and may abandon the purchase without saying so. And demand is sometimes of a different order from supply, as when the tickets for a concert go on sale and 2 million people arrive within a minute to compete for 50000 seats. This chapter is about keeping the 1 essential promise, that a seat belongs to at most 1 buyer, under each of these conditions in turn.

This chapter covers

  • the promise that a seat is sold at most once, and where it has to be enforced
  • 2 buyers choosing the same seat at the same moment
  • 3 ways of making the sale of a seat atomic
  • holding a seat while its buyer pays, and what happens when the buyer does not
  • a payment that arrives after its hold has run out
  • booking several seats together
  • a seat map that is allowed to be slightly wrong
  • selling a number of places without numbered seats
  • a sale for which far more buyers arrive than there are seats

The promise

It is useful to state exactly what the system promises before considering how. The promise is an invariant, a condition that must hold at every moment and that no sequence of events may be allowed to violate: every seat of every showing is in exactly 1 of the states free, held or sold, and when it is held or sold, it is held by or sold to exactly 1 buyer.

Everything else in the system is permitted to be approximate. The picture of the auditorium that a customer sees may be a few seconds out of date. The count of remaining seats shown on the event’s page may be slightly wrong. The confirmation email may arrive a minute late. None of these does lasting harm, and each can therefore be served from caches and queues by the methods of earlier chapters. The state of each seat cannot be approximate, and so the design begins by identifying the single place in which that state is kept and making sure that every change to it passes through an operation that cannot break the invariant.

That place is the seat store, and it is strongly consistent in the sense of chapter

  1. It is replicated by the leader and majority method of chapters 3 and 4, so that a change to a seat is confirmed only when a majority of replicas hold it and no 2 replicas can disagree about who owns a seat.

2 buyers and 1 seat

The simplest implementation of a purchase reads the seat, checks that it is free, and writes the buyer’s name against it. Between the reading and the writing there is an interval, and the entire difficulty of concurrent booking lies in that interval.

Each request, taken alone, behaved correctly. It read the seat, found it free, and wrote. The fault lies in the combination, in which the second request’s decision was based on a reading that the first request’s write had already made obsolete. This is the same race that produced 2 leases for 1 job in chapter 12 and 2 forwarded requests for 1 token in chapter 7, and it will arise in any design that separates a decision from the reading on which the decision rests.

It is also far from rare. The seats in a hall are not chosen uniformly: everybody wants the middle of the front rows, and on the first morning of a popular sale, hundreds of buyers are looking at the same few dozen seats.

Making the sale atomic

The reading and the writing must be joined into a single step that the store carries out in its entirety before attending to anything else. There are 3 established ways of doing so.

The first is a lock taken in advance. The transaction that handles a purchase asks the database to lock the row of the seat before reading it. A second transaction that wants the same row has to wait until the first has finished, by which time the seat is taken, and the second, reading it now, finds it so. This approach, in which a lock is taken on the assumption that a conflict is likely, is called pessimistic. It is straightforward and correct, and its cost is that buyers queue behind one another for popular seats, each holding a database connection while it waits. If the holder of a lock is slow, everyone behind it is slow as well.

The second is a conditional write. The request does not lock anything. It issues a single statement of the form “set this seat to held by Ada, provided that it is currently free”, and the store reports whether the condition was met. Of 2 simultaneous statements for the same seat, the store executes one first, which succeeds, and then the other, whose condition is now false and which therefore changes nothing. This is the compare-and-set of chapter 1, and it is called optimistic, since it proceeds on the assumption that conflicts are unusual and merely detects them when they occur. Nobody waits. A buyer who loses the race is told immediately and chooses again.

The third relies on a uniqueness constraint. Bookings are kept in a table of their own, and the database is instructed that no 2 rows of that table may have the same showing and seat. A purchase is then an attempt to insert a row, and of 2 simultaneous attempts for the same seat the database accepts 1 and rejects the other as a violation of the constraint. The invariant is thereby enforced by the database itself, independently of the application’s logic, and it continues to hold even if some future code path forgets to check.

Lock in advanceConditional writeUniqueness constraint
What a losing buyer experienceswaits, then is refusedis refused at onceis refused at once
Database connections held while waitingyesnono
Behaviour when many want 1 seata queue forms1 wins, the rest retry elsewhere1 wins, the rest retry elsewhere
Protection if application code is wrongnonenonethe database still refuses

Our design uses the conditional write for changes of a seat’s state and, in addition, a uniqueness constraint on confirmed bookings, as a second line of defence that does not depend on every part of the application being correct.

Holding a seat while the buyer pays

A purchase is not instantaneous. The buyer selects a seat, then enters the details of a card, and the payment itself takes some seconds to be authorised, as chapter 19 described. During this time the seat must not be sold to anyone else, since it would be intolerable to take a buyer’s payment and then report that the seat has gone. Yet the seat cannot be marked as sold either, since the buyer may never complete the payment.

The seat is therefore given an intermediate state, held. A hold reserves the seat for 1 buyer for a limited period, commonly between 5 and 15 minutes. If the buyer pays within that period, the seat becomes sold. If not, the hold lapses and the seat is available again. A hold is a lease in the sense of chapter 10, granted on a seat.

The simulation for this chapter plays out these events on a hall of 3 seats and ends with seat 1 sold to Bob, Ada’s late attempt to pay having been refused.

The time limit is what prevents a seat from being lost to sale. Without it, every buyer who closed the browser in the middle of a purchase would leave a seat permanently reserved, and within a few hours of a busy sale the hall would appear full while a large part of it had been paid for by nobody. The hold must carry its expiry time within itself, as a field of the seat’s record, so that its validity can be judged by anyone who reads the record, at any time, by a comparison with the clock.

This last point determines how expiry is implemented. One possibility is a background process, sometimes called a reaper, that periodically searches for holds whose time has passed and sets those seats back to free. The simpler and more dependable method requires no such process for correctness. A held seat whose expiry time has passed is treated as free by every operation that examines it, so that the conditional write for a new hold reads “set this seat to held by Bob, provided that it is free or that its hold has run out”. The seat becomes available at the exact moment of expiry without anything having to happen at that moment. A background process may still tidy the records, and nothing depends on its punctuality.

The length of the hold is a compromise between 2 kinds of loss. A long hold gives buyers ample time and keeps abandoned seats out of circulation for longer, which in a sale that will sell out matters a great deal. A short hold returns seats quickly and causes more buyers to lose their seat while they are still typing. Systems commonly display the remaining time to the buyer, which both informs and hurries.

A further abuse must be anticipated. Someone who wishes to disrupt a sale, or to reserve seats for resale, can request holds on a great many seats with no intention of paying, and so remove them from sale for the duration of each hold. Holds are therefore limited in number for each account and each session, and repeated abandonment by the same party is noticed and restricted.

Payment and the hold

The hold and the payment are separate operations in separate systems, and the interval between them contains a case that has to be decided in advance.

Suppose a buyer submits payment 10 seconds before the hold is due to expire, and the authorisation takes 15 seconds. When the payment system reports success, the hold has lapsed, and the seat may already have been taken by somebody else. The booking system now holds a successful payment for a seat it can no longer deliver.

2 measures deal with this, and a careful system uses both. When the buyer submits payment, the hold is first extended by an amount comfortably longer than a payment can take, in a conditional write that succeeds only if the hold is still valid and still belongs to this buyer. If the extension fails, the buyer is told that the seat is gone and no payment is attempted. And when the payment succeeds, the conversion of the hold into a sale is itself conditional on the seat’s still being held by this buyer. In the rare case that this last write fails nonetheless, the system refunds the payment at once, by the procedure of chapter 19, and informs the buyer. The invariant is never sacrificed to complete a payment: it is always the money that is returned and never the seat that is double-sold.

The whole exchange must also be idempotent, for the reasons given at length in chapter 19. The request that confirms a booking carries a key, and a repetition of it, after a lost reply, returns the original booking and neither charges again nor fails for want of a hold that the first attempt already consumed.

Several seats together

A family books 4 seats and wishes to have all 4 or none. A booking that secured 2 of them and then failed on the third would leave the family with 2 seats it does not want and 2 other buyers refused for no purpose.

The seats of a single showing normally reside in the same shard of the seat store, and the 4 conditional writes can then be made within 1 transaction, which succeeds only if every one of them does. Where a database with locks is used, a hazard arises that is worth describing because it recurs wherever several locks are taken. If 1 request locks seat 5 and then asks for seat 6, while another locks seat 6 and then asks for seat 5, each waits for the other indefinitely. This is a deadlock, and the customary prevention is for every request to take its locks in the same fixed order, by seat number for example, so that no such cycle can form.

The seat map

Before choosing, a buyer looks at a picture of the hall showing which seats are free. This picture is requested far more often than seats are bought, since every buyer looks, most look several times, and many look without buying.

To assemble the picture from the seat store on every request would place the heaviest load on the 1 component that must remain fast and correct for the sake of the sales themselves. The seat map is therefore served from a cache, of the kind described in chapter 9, which is refreshed every second or 2 or updated by messages announcing each change of a seat’s state.

The map is consequently eventually consistent. A buyer may be shown a seat as free that was taken half a second earlier. This is entirely acceptable, and the reason should be clearly understood, since it illustrates a principle of wide application. The map is advisory. It influences which seat a buyer attempts to take, and it decides nothing. The decision is made by the conditional write to the seat store, which is always correct, and a buyer who acts on stale information is refused and shown a fresh map. An approximate display backed by an exact transaction is a combination that appears throughout well-designed systems. It would be a serious error to reverse the roles, allowing a sale to proceed because a cached map showed the seat as free.

Places without numbers

Many events sell admission without assigning seats: 5000 places on the floor of a concert hall, any of which is as good as any other. The inventory is then a count, with no distinct seats, and the invariant becomes that the number sold shall never exceed the capacity.

The same reasoning applies in a simpler form. To read the count, check that it is below the capacity, and write it back increased by 1 is the race already described, and would oversell. The sale must be a conditional update, “increase the number sold by 2, provided that the result does not exceed 5000”, which the store applies atomically.

A single counter for a popular event is, however, a single row that every purchase must modify, and under very heavy demand it becomes a point of contention, the hot key of earlier chapters. A common remedy divides the inventory in advance into several portions, 50 portions of 100 places for example, each a separate counter, and directs each buyer to a portion chosen at random. Purchases then contend only within a portion. The portions empty at different rates, so that a buyer may occasionally be refused by an exhausted portion while places remain in others and must be redirected, and this complication is the price of removing the bottleneck.

It should be mentioned that some businesses sell more places than they possess, by policy. Airlines know from experience that a certain proportion of passengers do not appear, and sell a correspondingly greater number of tickets than there are seats. The invariant has not failed in such a case. It is a different invariant, with a capacity set above the physical number, and the system enforces the limit it is given exactly as before.

A sale with far more buyers than seats

When the tickets for a greatly anticipated event are released, the load on the system bears no relation to anything it experiences at other times. 2 million people may arrive in the first minute for 50000 seats. Of all those requests, at most 50000 can end in a sale, and the remaining 1950000 are certain to be disappointed. The task of the system is to conduct the 50000 sales correctly and to disappoint the others cheaply, without the weight of the crowd bringing down the machinery on which the sales depend.

No amount of capacity in the booking system itself is a satisfactory answer, since the seat store’s rate of work is limited by the need for strong consistency, and provisioning for a peak that lasts for minutes and occurs a few times a year is wasteful. The crowd is therefore kept away from the booking system altogether.

A waiting room is a very simple service placed in front of the sale. Each person who arrives is assigned a position in a queue and shown a page that reports the position and refreshes occasionally. Serving this page requires almost no work and can be done from the edge servers of chapter 17. People are admitted from the queue to the booking system proper at a controlled rate, matched to what that system can serve comfortably, and each person admitted receives a signed token, valid for a limited time, without which the booking system accepts no request. The token is what makes the arrangement enforceable, since a person cannot skip the queue by addressing the booking system directly.

The effect is to convert a peak that the booking system could not survive into a steady load that it handles with ease, the excess being absorbed by a component designed for nothing else. It is the load levelling that chapter 11 attributed to queues, applied to people. It also restores a measure of fairness, since admission follows the order of the queue, where it would otherwise fall to whoever’s request happened to get through an overloaded server.

Whether the order of the queue should be the order of arrival is itself a question of policy. When a sale opens at a known moment, the people who arrive in the first second are separated by network delays and nothing else, and strict order of arrival rewards those with the fastest connections and, above all, automated programs. Many systems therefore gather everyone who arrives before the opening into a pool and assign their positions at random when the sale begins.

Automated purchasing is the abiding adversary of such sales. Programs operated by resellers can submit requests faster than any person and from thousands of addresses. The defences are layered and none is complete: rate limits for each account and each address, as in chapter 7; a limit on the number of tickets for each buyer; challenges that are easy for people and costly for programs; and the requirement of an account with some history. The waiting room is where most of these checks are applied, before a request has cost the booking system anything.

Use cases

A buyer looks at the seats of a showing, holds one, and pays for it.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A buyer can see which seats of a showing are free.
1A buyer can hold a free seat for 5 minutes.
2A buyer can pay for a seat that they hold, upon which the seat is sold to them.
3A hold that is not paid for within its time ends, and the seat is free again.
4A seat is held by, or sold to, at most 1 buyer at any moment.
5A buyer can book several seats together, receiving all of them or none.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0ConsistencyStrong for the state of every seat. Eventual for the seat map.
1Availability99.95% for booking. When the seat store cannot reach a majority, sales stop.
2LatencyA hold is granted or refused within 200 ms.
3Scale100000 showings on sale, and a peak of 2 million arrivals in a minute for a single showing.

Non-functional requirements 0 and 1 belong together. The state of a seat is the 1 thing in this system that may never be wrong, and the design accordingly accepts that when the seat store has lost its majority, no seats can be sold until it is restored. An hour without sales is a loss of revenue. A hall with 2 buyers for 1 seat is a loss of the customers’ trust, and cannot be repaired by restarting anything.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. The seats of 100000 showings fit in a few gigabytes. The difficulty of this system lies in the peak of arrivals. The volume of data is small.

The API

A hold is a resource created within a showing, and a booking is a resource created from a hold. Both are created with POST, and both carry an idempotency key.

See which seats are free

GET /v1/shows/881/seats HTTP/1.1
Host: tickets.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=2

{
  "seats": [
    { "label": "A1", "state": "free" },
    { "label": "A2", "state": "held" },
    { "label": "A3", "state": "sold" }
  ]
}

The header Cache-Control permits this answer to be reused for 2 seconds, which states openly that the map may be that much out of date.

Hold a seat

POST /v1/shows/881/holds HTTP/1.1
Host: tickets.example
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c-hold-1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "seats": ["A1"] }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/shows/881/holds/7730
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 7730, "seats": ["A1"], "expires": "2026-10-14T10:05:00Z" }

Hold a seat that somebody else has taken

POST /v1/shows/881/holds HTTP/1.1
Host: tickets.example
Idempotency-Key: 9a2e-hold-1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "seats": ["A1"] }

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/seat-taken",
  "title": "The seat is no longer available",
  "status": 409,
  "seats": ["A1"]
}

409 Conflict is the status for a request that is valid in itself and cannot be carried out because of the present state of the resource.

Pay for a held seat

POST /v1/bookings HTTP/1.1
Host: tickets.example
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c-book-1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "hold": 7730, "payment_token": "tok_83hf" }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/bookings/55102
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 55102, "show": 881, "seats": ["A1"], "state": "confirmed" }

The payment token stands for the buyer’s card, as chapter 19 explained, so that the booking system never handles a card number.

Booking APIturns requests into conditional writesnoneanother instance serves the request
Seat storeholds the state of every seatseats, holds and bookings, replicateda follower is elected, and sales pause for about a second
Seat map cacheserves the picture of the halla copy, up to 2 seconds oldthe map is rebuilt from the seat store
Payment systemcharges the buyersee chapter 19holds are extended, and bookings wait

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 20.6.

  1. A buyer asks to hold seat A1 of showing 881.
  2. The booking API sends the seat store 1 conditional write: set A1 to held by this buyer until 10:05, provided that A1 is free or its hold has run out. The store answers that the write was applied, and the API returns the hold. Had the condition been false, the API would have answered 409.
  3. The buyer submits payment. The API first extends the hold, conditionally, and then asks the payment system to charge the buyer. When the charge succeeds, the API sends a second conditional write: set A1 to sold to this buyer, provided that it is still held by them.
  4. Independently of any request, holds whose time has passed are cleared from the records. No sale depends on this, since an expired hold is already treated as free.

The design, deployed

The figure shows where the load goes. At the opening of a great sale, 33000 people arrive each second, and they are met by the edge servers and the waiting room, which do almost no work for each of them. Only 500 a second pass through to the booking tier, which is an ordinary arrangement of load balancers, stateless API servers and a cache for the seat map. The seat store at the bottom, 3 replicas of each shard with shards assigned by showing, therefore sees a load that it can serve with strong consistency. The numbers of machines in the lower tiers do not change between an ordinary day and the largest sale.

How real systems do it

The mechanisms of this chapter are those of database practice more than of any 1 published system, and the references are accordingly to the foundations.

Optimistic concurrency control, the method of proceeding without locks and checking at the moment of writing whether anything has changed, was set out in a paper of 1981 that also states the condition for preferring it, which is that conflicts be rare. A sale in which hundreds of buyers want the same seat does not meet that condition for the popular seats, and the consequence is the one this chapter accepts: most of those buyers are refused and choose again. Systems that cannot accept this lock in advance, or avoid the contention altogether by assigning seats to buyers, on the principle of “best available”, so that buyers do not choose.

For sales in which stock is a count, a pattern often described for the largest shopping events takes the deduction out of the database altogether during the peak. The remaining stock of each item is held in an in-memory store, a purchase is a small script that checks and decrements it atomically, and the orders are written to the database afterwards from a queue. This is the conditional update of this chapter, moved to a faster store, at the cost of a period in which the 2 stores have to be reconciled.

The waiting room is offered as a product by several content delivery networks, and their descriptions match the design here: a queue held at the edge, a signed cookie or token for those admitted, a controlled rate of admission, and a choice between admitting in order of arrival and admitting at random from those present when the sale opens. The random choice exists for the reason given above, that order of arrival in the first second measures the speed of connections and of programs.

Deliberate overbooking is studied under the name of revenue management, and the airlines’ practice rests on decades of statistics about how many passengers fail to appear on each route.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Reading a seat and then writing it2 buyers both find it free and both are sold it.Make the write conditional on the seat’s state.
Trusting the seat map to decide a saleA stale map sells a seat that is already taken.Let the map advise, and the conditional write decide.
Selling a seat as soon as it is chosenBuyers who never pay keep seats for ever.Hold the seat for a limited time, and sell it on payment.
Holds without an expiry time in the recordExpiry depends on a background process being punctual.Store the expiry time, and treat an expired hold as free.
Taking payment without checking the holdA buyer pays for a seat that has since gone to someone else.Extend the hold conditionally before charging.
Keeping the money when the final write failsThe buyer has paid and has no seat.Refund at once, and never double-sell to save a payment.
A booking request without an idempotency keyA retry charges twice, or fails because the hold is already used.Require a key, and return the first result for a repeat.
Booking several seats in separate stepsA buyer is left with some of the seats they wanted.Write all of them in 1 transaction.
Locking seats in whatever order they were requested2 requests wait for each other indefinitely.Take locks in a fixed order.
1 counter for a very popular eventEvery purchase contends on the same row.Divide the places into portions with separate counters.
Letting the whole crowd reach the booking systemThe seat store is overwhelmed, and the sales themselves fail.Admit buyers from a waiting room at a controlled rate.
Unlimited holds for each account1 party removes many seats from sale without paying.Limit the holds of each account and session.

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/bookingsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p bookingsim in the code directory.

TermMeaning

Summary

  • The 1 promise of a booking system is that a seat is held by or sold to at most 1 buyer, and everything else may be approximate.
  • Reading a seat and then writing it lets 2 buyers take the same seat, so the write is made conditional on the seat’s state.
  • A seat is held for a limited time while its buyer pays, and an expired hold is treated as free without anything having to act.
  • Before charging, the hold is extended, and if the seat is lost in spite of that, the payment is refunded.
  • The seat map is served from a cache and may be stale, because it advises and the conditional write decides.
  • Places without numbers are sold by a conditional update of a count, divided into portions when demand is extreme.
  • When far more buyers arrive than there are seats, a waiting room admits them at the rate the system can serve.

Ride Hailing: System Design

A ride hailing service brings together 2 people who are moving about a city: a rider who wants to travel from 1 place to another, and a driver who is somewhere nearby and free to take them. The rider opens an application, states a destination, and within a few seconds is told that a particular car will arrive in 4 minutes. Behind that brief exchange the service has had to determine which of the tens of thousands of drivers at present on the road are close to this rider.

The question is unusual because it is about position, and position does not submit to the methods on which the rest of this book has relied. A key-value store finds a record by its exact key, and an ordered index finds the records whose keys lie in a range. Neither is of any direct use for finding the points that lie near a given point, since nearness involves 2 coordinates at once and no ordering of points along a single line keeps neighbours together. The data, moreover, will not keep still. Every driver’s position changes continually and is reported every few seconds, so that the service receives far more writes than reads, and each of those writes makes its predecessor worthless. This chapter develops an index for moving points, and then turns to the second problem that a ride presents, which is to give each ride to exactly 1 driver.

This chapter covers

  • why finding nearby points is unlike any lookup met so far
  • dividing a map into squares, and searching a square together with its neighbours
  • choosing the size of the squares, and what goes wrong at either extreme
  • squares within squares, for cities whose density varies
  • storing positions that are replaced every few seconds
  • drivers who disappear without saying so
  • offering a ride to drivers in turn, and assigning it to exactly 1
  • the states of a ride, and where strong consistency is needed
  • estimating a time of arrival, and dividing the world among servers

Why nearness is hard

Suppose the service keeps the latitude and longitude of 20000 drivers and wishes to find the 3 nearest to a rider. The plain method is to compute the distance from the rider to each of the 20000 and to choose the 3 smallest. This is correct, and it costs 20000 calculations for a single request, a cost that grows in proportion to the number of drivers and has to be paid again for every rider who opens the application. At 1000 requests per second it amounts to 20 million distance calculations a second, nearly all of them for drivers who are on the other side of the city and could have been excluded at a glance.

The ordinary remedy for a slow search is an index, and it is instructive to see why the ordinary index fails. An index on latitude can find, very quickly, all the drivers within a narrow band of latitude around the rider. That band, however, extends right round the world, and within a city it runs the full width of the city from east to west and contains thousands of drivers, nearly all of them distant. An index on longitude has the same defect in the other direction. A database can use the 2 together only by retrieving both bands and intersecting them, which examines far more entries than it finally keeps. The root of the difficulty is that an index orders its entries along 1 dimension, whereas nearness on a map is a property of 2.

What is required is some means of naming regions of the map, such that points which are near each other usually bear the same name or closely related ones. A lookup by name, which every store performs well, would then serve as a search by position.

Dividing the map into squares

The simplest such scheme lays a grid of equal squares over the map. Every position falls in exactly 1 square, and the square can be computed from the coordinates by a division: if squares are 1 km on a side, a point 42.5 km east and 17.5 km north of the map’s origin lies in the square numbered 42 in 1 direction and 17 in the other. The service keeps, for each square, the list of drivers currently within it, in an ordinary table keyed by the square’s number.

To find drivers near a rider, the service computes the rider’s square and retrieves the drivers listed there. Only these few need have their distances measured. The remainder of the city is never examined.

This is very nearly sufficient, and it has 1 flaw that must be corrected.

A rider who stands close to the edge of a square may have a driver a few metres away on the other side of the edge, in the adjoining square, and a search confined to the rider’s own square would overlook that driver and return another who is a kilometre off. The search must accordingly include the 8 squares that surround the rider’s, 9 squares in all. Any driver within the length of 1 side of the rider is then certain to be among those examined, wherever in the square the rider happens to be.

The simulation for this chapter places 20000 drivers at random on a map of 100 by 100 units, with squares of 1 unit, and looks for the 3 nearest to a rider by both methods. Measuring every driver takes 20000 distance calculations. The grid takes 15, that being the number of drivers in the rider’s 9 squares, and both methods return the same 3 drivers, at distances of 0.19, 0.84 and 0.85 units. The work has been reduced by a factor of more than 1000, and it no longer depends on the total number of drivers, only on how many are in the vicinity.

Choosing the size of the squares

The size of the squares is the 1 parameter of this index, and the index performs badly when it is wrong in either direction.

If the squares are too large, each holds many drivers, and the 9 squares of a search return hundreds or thousands of candidates whose distances must all be computed. The index has excluded little, and in the limit of 1 square covering the whole city it excludes nothing.

If the squares are too small, most are empty. A search of 9 tiny squares commonly finds no driver, and the service must widen it to the next ring of 16 squares and then to the ring beyond, issuing many lookups to collect a handful of drivers.

The suitable size is of the order of the distance over which a match is useful. If a driver more than 2 km away is too far to be worth offering, squares of about 1 km give a search area of 3 km by 3 km, which covers the range of interest with a single round of lookups.

No single size, however, suits a whole city. In the centre at midday a square of 1 km may contain 300 drivers, while on the outskirts at night an area of 25 square kilometres may contain 2. A grid fine enough for the centre is nearly empty at the edge, and a grid coarse enough for the edge is crowded in the centre.

Squares within squares

The difficulty of uneven density is met by making the grid hierarchical. The whole map is taken as 1 square and divided into 4. Each of these is divided into 4 again, and the division is repeated to whatever depth is required, so that every square of 1 level contains exactly 4 squares of the next level down, each with half its side.

The squares of such a hierarchy can be given names with a most convenient property. The 4 quarters of the map are named 0, 1, 2 and 3. The quarters of square 2 are named 20, 21, 22 and 23, and so on, each level adding 1 digit. The name of a square then begins with the name of every larger square that contains it. A position can be described by a single name of, say, 15 digits, denoting a very small square, and its first 10 digits name the larger square containing it, and its first 6 a larger one still.

Several consequences follow. Drivers are stored under their full, fine names in a store that keeps its keys in order, such as the key-value store of chapter 1 with its sorted index. All the drivers within any larger square then have names beginning with that square’s name, and since names with a common beginning are adjacent in sorted order, they can be retrieved by a single scan of a range of keys. A search for nearby points has thus been converted into a search by prefix, which is precisely the operation an ordered index is built for.

The level at which to search can be chosen at the moment of searching. In a dense district the service searches small squares, and in a sparse one it searches the larger squares that contain them, by using a shorter prefix, with no change to the stored data. A search may begin fine and move to a coarser level until it has found enough candidates.

One caution applies to every scheme of this family. 2 points whose names share a long prefix are certainly close together, and the converse does not hold. 2 points that are very close may lie on either side of a boundary between 2 large squares and have names that differ from the first digit. The neighbouring squares must therefore still be searched, exactly as with the plain grid, and the neighbours of a square are computed by arithmetic on its position and never by supposing that their names resemble its own.

The squares of such schemes are in practice not always square. Some systems divide the globe into cells bounded by lines of latitude and longitude, which are simple to compute and become narrower towards the poles. Others cover the globe with hexagons, which have the merit that all 6 neighbours of a cell are at the same distance from its centre, whereas a square has 4 near neighbours and 4 that are further off at the corners. The principle is the same in each case: to name regions so that position becomes a key.

Positions that are replaced every few seconds

Each driver’s application reports its position every 4 seconds or so. With 500000 drivers on the road, that is 125000 updates per second, considerably more than the rate of requests from riders, and each update supersedes the last. This pattern of load is very different from that of the stores in earlier chapters, and it justifies a different treatment of durability.

In chapter 2 every write was forced to disk before it was acknowledged, since an acknowledged write that was subsequently lost would have been a broken promise. A driver’s position carries no such obligation. It will be replaced by a fresh report within 4 seconds, and nobody will ever wish to know where a driver was 10 seconds ago for the purpose of matching. Were the entire index of positions to be lost, it would rebuild itself in 4 seconds as the drivers reported again. The index is therefore kept in memory only, without any log on disk and without waiting for copies to be confirmed, and this is what allows it to absorb 125000 writes a second on modest hardware. To have given it the durability of chapter 2 would have multiplied its cost many times and purchased nothing.

An update consists of 2 small steps. The driver’s new position is recorded, and if the driver has crossed into a different square, the driver is removed from the list of the old square and added to that of the new. Most updates find the driver in the same square as before and alter only the stored coordinates.

Positions that must be kept are a separate matter and take a separate path. The route actually driven during a ride is needed in order to calculate the fare and to settle any later dispute, and it is appended to a durable log, through the message queue of chapter 11, apart from the live index.

Drivers who disappear

A driver may cease to be available without informing the service. The phone’s battery is exhausted, the car enters a tunnel, the application is closed. If nothing were done, the driver’s last known position would remain in the index indefinitely, and the service would go on offering rides to a car that is no longer there.

The remedy is the lease, which has now appeared in nearly every chapter. Each position is stored with a time limit of some 15 seconds, several times the interval between reports. Every report renews it, and a driver who stops reporting vanishes from the index when the limit expires. Nothing has to detect the departure, since an entry that is not renewed lapses of its own accord.

Giving a ride to exactly 1 driver

To find nearby drivers is half of the task. The other half is to assign the ride to 1 of them, and here the considerations are of a different kind, since an error is no longer a slightly worse match and becomes 2 cars arriving for 1 rider, or a rider left waiting for a car that is not coming.

The nearest driver in a straight line is not necessarily the best choice. A driver 300 metres away on the far side of a river, or heading in the opposite direction along a road with a central barrier, may need 10 minutes to arrive, while another 800 metres off reaches the rider in 3. Having obtained a short list of candidates from the index, the matching service therefore ranks them by estimated time of arrival along the road network, a calculation discussed further on.

The ride is then offered to the drivers in turn.

2 decisions embodied in these steps merit comment.

The ride is offered to 1 driver and, only if that driver declines or fails to answer in time, to the next. The alternative, to offer it to several at once and take the first acceptance, would assign rides sooner and would leave every driver but 1 having responded to an offer that was then withdrawn, which drivers reasonably resent. An offer has a time limit and is in effect a lease on the ride, so that a driver who does not respond cannot hold it up for more than a few seconds.

The assignment itself is a conditional write to a strongly consistent store, of the form “set the driver of this ride to 7056, provided that it has no driver”. This is the operation that guarantees a ride at most 1 driver. In the last step, a late acceptance from the first driver arrives after the second has been assigned, and the identical conditional write, finding the ride already assigned, is refused. The same operation marks the driver as busy, so that a driver cannot be assigned to 2 rides. It will be recognised as the conditional write that sold a seat to 1 buyer in chapter 20 and gave a job to 1 worker in chapter 12.

In a busy area, to match each ride at the instant it is requested does not give the best result overall. If 2 riders make requests within a second of each other and 2 drivers are nearby, giving the first rider the nearest driver may leave the second rider with a long wait, where the other pairing would have served both tolerably. Services therefore sometimes collect the requests of a small area for a second or 2 and assign the whole batch together, so as to minimise the total waiting time of all the riders concerned.

The states of a ride

A ride, like the payment of chapter 19 and the job of chapter 12, is an object that passes through a series of states: requested, offered, accepted, driver arriving, in progress, completed, and paid, with cancellation possible from several of them. Each transition is caused by an event from the rider’s application, the driver’s application, or the service itself, and each is recorded durably.

This record requires the strong consistency that the index of positions was able to do without. Money depends on it, since the fare is calculated from the recorded beginning and end of the ride, and both parties must be shown the same state, since a rider who is shown “driver arriving” while the driver is shown “cancelled” has been badly served. The ride store is accordingly a replicated database of the kind described in chapters 3 and 4, in which each transition is a conditional write that verifies the current state before altering it, so that a ride cannot, for example, be both cancelled and started.

The design thus contains 2 stores at opposite ends of the range of consistency, each suited to what it holds.

Index of positionsRide store
Contentswhere each driver is at presentthe state and history of every ride
Writes125000 per second, each superseding the lasta few per ride
Durabilitynone: in memory, and rebuilt in 4 secondsfull: stored on a majority
Consistencyeventual, and stale by up to 4 secondsstrong
If it is lostmatching pauses for a few secondsnot permitted

Once a ride has been accepted, the rider wishes to watch the car approach on a map. The driver’s position must then be conveyed to 1 particular rider every few seconds, which is the delivery problem of chapter 18. The rider’s application holds a connection open, and the service forwards on it the positions of the assigned driver.

Estimating the time of arrival

The figure that riders care most about is the number of minutes until the car arrives, and the distance in a straight line is a poor guide to it. The estimate requires a model of the road network, represented as a graph in which the junctions are nodes and the stretches of road between them are edges, each edge carrying the time presently needed to drive along it. The estimated time of arrival is the length of the shortest path through this graph from the driver to the rider.

To compute shortest paths on the road graph of an entire country for every candidate driver of every request would be far too slow by the textbook method, which examines a large part of the graph for each query. Practical systems carry out a great deal of the work beforehand. They identify in advance the major roads that long journeys almost always use and compute the times between the points where such roads meet, so that a query has only to find its way from each end to the nearest major road and then consult a table. The travel times on the edges are revised continually from the movements of the very drivers that the service is tracking, which makes the stream of position reports serve a second purpose as a measurement of traffic.

Dividing the world

Rides are local. A rider in 1 city is never matched with a driver in another, and this affords a natural way of dividing the system among machines, by geography. The map is partitioned into regions, each consisting of a set of the squares described earlier, and each region’s index of positions and matching are served by their own group of servers.

Partitioning by position has the same hazard as partitioning by any other key, namely that the load is unevenly distributed. The centre of a great city on a Friday evening has many times the activity of a rural region, so that regions are made small where the density is high and large where it is low, which the hierarchical naming of squares makes straightforward. Riders and drivers close to the boundary between 2 regions need the search to extend across it, which is once again the matter of neighbouring squares, between servers this time.

Demand also moves in ways that can to some degree be foreseen. When a concert ends or rain begins, requests in a district may increase fivefold within minutes, more quickly than drivers are able to get there. The service has accordingly to guard its own components against such surges, using the rate limiting of chapter 7, and many services raise the price in the affected district for the time being, so as to attract drivers to it and to moderate the demand.

Use cases

A rider requests a ride and watches the car approach. A driver reports a position every few seconds and accepts rides.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A driver’s application reports the driver’s position every 4 seconds.
1A rider can request a ride from a position to a destination.
2The service finds free drivers near the rider and offers the ride to them in turn.
3A ride is assigned to at most 1 driver, and a driver to at most 1 ride.
4The rider can follow the position of the assigned driver.
5Every change in the state of a ride is recorded.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0LatencyNearby drivers are found within 100 ms.
1ConsistencyStrong for rides and their assignment. Eventual for positions, which may be 4 seconds old.
2Availability99.95% for requesting a ride.
3DurabilityThe record of a ride is not lost. A driver’s current position need not survive a failure.
4Scale500000 drivers on the road, 125000 position reports per second, and 1000 ride requests per second.

Non-functional requirements 1 and 3 state the division that runs through this whole design. To hold positions to the standard appropriate to rides would make the index many times more expensive and no more useful, and to hold rides to the standard appropriate to positions would lose customers’ money. The skill lies in recognising which of the system’s data is of which kind.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. The positions of 500000 drivers occupy about 50 MB of memory. The quantity that matters is the rate of updates, 125000 per second.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Position reports500000 drivers ÷ 4 seconds125000 per second
Memory per driverid, position, square, state, expiryabout 100 bytes
Memory for all drivers500000 × 100 bytes50 MB
Drivers in a search9 squares × about 20 driversabout 180
Rides per day1000 per second at the peak, a third of that on averageabout 30 million

The API

Every report of a position creates a new position in the collection of that driver’s positions, with POST. A ride is created with POST as well. A driver accepts by writing the assignment of that driver to the ride, with PUT, so that repeating the request has no further effect.

A driver reports a position

POST /v1/drivers/7056/positions HTTP/1.1
Host: rides.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "latitude": 38.7223, "longitude": -9.1393, "heading": 270 }

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

Reports are sent so frequently that many services convey them over an open connection in a compact binary form, without a separate HTTP request for each. The meaning is unchanged.

A rider requests a ride

POST /v1/rides HTTP/1.1
Host: rides.example
Idempotency-Key: 3f7a-ride-1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "from": { "latitude": 38.7169, "longitude": -9.1399 },
  "to": { "latitude": 38.7742, "longitude": -9.1342 }
}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/rides/501
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 501, "state": "requested" }

The key ensures that a rider whose application retries after a lost reply does not summon 2 cars.

A driver accepts

PUT /v1/rides/501/assignments/7056 HTTP/1.1
Host: rides.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 501, "state": "accepted", "driver": 7056 }

A driver whose offer has ended, or who accepts after another driver has been assigned, receives 409 Conflict.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Location servicereceives position reports and files each driver under a squarenoneanother instance receives the reports
Grid indexholds the drivers of each squarepositions, in memory, with a leaseit is rebuilt from reports within 4 seconds
Matching servicefinds candidates, ranks them, and offers the ride in turnnoneanother instance continues from the ride’s recorded state
Ride storeholds every ride and its staterides, replicateda follower is elected, as in chapter 4

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 21.6.

  1. Every driver’s application reports its position every 4 seconds.
  2. The location service computes the square of the position and updates the grid index, moving the driver from 1 square’s list to another’s when a border has been crossed and renewing the driver’s lease.
  3. A rider requests a ride. The matching service computes the rider’s square, reads the drivers of that square and its 8 neighbours from the grid index, and ranks the free ones by estimated time of arrival.
  4. The matching service offers the ride to the first of them. When a driver accepts, it writes the assignment to the ride store as a conditional write, which succeeds for 1 driver only.

The design, deployed

The system is deployed separately in each region of the world, since no ride crosses between them, and the figure shows 1 region. Drivers and riders hold connections to gateways, as the phones of chapter 18 do. The location service is stateless and turns each of the 125000 reports per second into an update of the grid index, which is divided among 30 machines by area and kept in memory only. The matching service reads the index and writes assignments to the ride store, which is the 1 component here with replicas in 3 zones and durable storage. The picture makes visible the division that the chapter insisted upon, between data that is rebuilt in seconds and data that must not be lost.

How real systems do it

The grid of this chapter corresponds to 3 schemes that are in wide use, and they differ in the shape of the cell and in how the cells are named.

The geohash divides the world by latitude and longitude, halving alternately in each direction, and writes the result as a short string in which every further character selects a smaller cell within the last. It is the hierarchy of names with shared prefixes described above, and several in-memory stores offer queries by radius that are built on it. Its cells are rectangles whose width varies with latitude.

Google’s S2 library projects the sphere onto the faces of a cube and numbers the cells along a space-filling curve, so that a cell is a 64-bit integer and cells that are close on the curve are close on the ground. A region is covered by a small set of cells of mixed sizes, and a search becomes a few scans of ranges of integers.

Uber developed H3, which it published in 2018, and which uses hexagons. The stated reason is the one given above: the centres of all 6 neighbours of a hexagon are at the same distance, which makes it natural to reason about rings of cells around a point and about movement between adjacent cells, where a square has neighbours at 2 different distances. H3 has 16 levels of resolution, each cell containing 7 of the next, and since hexagons do not divide exactly into smaller hexagons, a child cell is only approximately contained in its parent. The surface of a sphere cannot be covered by hexagons alone, and every level contains exactly 12 pentagons, placed where they are least likely to matter.

For the estimate of arrival time, the technique of computing in advance along the important roads is known as contraction hierarchies, and it answers a query on the road network of a continent in about a millisecond. And Uber has described assigning the work for each area to particular servers with a ring of consistent hashing whose membership spreads by gossip, which is the alternative to a coordinator that chapter 1 described.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Measuring the distance to every driverThe cost of each request grows with the size of the whole fleet.Index drivers by the square they are in.
Searching only the rider’s squareA driver just across the border is missed.Search the 8 neighbouring squares as well.
A single size of square for everythingThe centre is crowded, and the outskirts are empty.Use a hierarchy of squares, and choose the level when searching.
Supposing that neighbouring squares have similar names2 nearby points on either side of a major boundary are treated as distant.Compute the neighbours of a square, and search them.
Storing live positions durablyEvery 1 of 125000 writes a second waits for a disk, to no purpose.Keep positions in memory, where they rebuild themselves.
Positions without a time limitDrivers who have gone offline are still offered rides.Store each position with a lease that its reports renew.
Ranking by distance in a straight lineThe nearest driver is across a river and 10 minutes away.Rank by estimated time along the roads.
Offering a ride to many drivers at onceAll but 1 respond to an offer that is then withdrawn.Offer to 1 driver, and move to the next after a time limit.
Assigning a ride by reading and then writing2 drivers are assigned to 1 ride.Assign with a conditional write that requires the ride to have no driver.
Keeping rides in the store used for positionsThe record of a ride is lost in a restart.Keep rides in a durable, strongly consistent store.
Requesting a ride without an idempotency keyA retry summons a second car.Require a key on the request.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Spatial indexa structure that finds the points near a given point without examining them all
Grida division of the map into equal squares
Square, cell1 region of such a division, which serves as a key
Neighbouring squaresthe 8 squares that touch a given square
Hierarchical gridsquares divided into 4 smaller squares, repeatedly
