Summary

  • Finding nearby points is hard for ordinary indexes, which order their entries along 1 dimension.
  • A grid names each region of the map, so that a lookup by square replaces a comparison with every driver.
  • A search covers the rider’s square and its 8 neighbours, since the nearest driver may be just across a border.
  • A hierarchy of squares whose names share prefixes allows the size to be chosen for each search and turns nearness into a scan of a range of keys.
  • Positions are replaced every few seconds and are kept in memory with a lease, since losing them costs 4 seconds.
  • A ride is offered to drivers in turn and assigned by a conditional write, so that it has at most 1 driver.
  • Rides are kept in a durable, strongly consistent store, at the opposite extreme from the index of positions.

Search Autocomplete: System Design

When a person begins to type into a search box, a short list of suggestions appears beneath it, and the list changes with every letter. Typing ka produces “kafka”, “karaoke near me” and “kayak”, and the addition of an f reduces the list to “kafka” and “kafka vs rabbitmq”. The feature is called autocomplete or typeahead, and it spares the user some typing, corrects spelling before it has gone wrong, and shows what other people have looked for.

2 characteristics set this feature apart from the search that it accompanies. It is invoked far more often, once for every letter typed where a search is made once, so that a service handling 100000 searches a second may receive a million requests for suggestions in the same second. And it must be very much faster. A page of search results that takes half a second to appear is acceptable, whereas suggestions that arrive half a second after a keystroke are useless, since the user has by then typed 2 further letters and the suggestions refer to text that is no longer in the box. The practical limit is about 100 ms from the keystroke to the display, of which the network consumes the greater part.

There is no possibility of computing anything substantial within such a limit, and the design is governed by that fact. Whatever can be computed in advance is computed in advance, so that answering a request amounts to a single lookup, and whatever can be answered without reaching the service at all is answered nearer to the user. The interest of the design lies in the question of what exactly should be prepared beforehand, in how the prepared data is kept reasonably up to date, and in a small number of ways in which a feature that looks harmless can cause real embarrassment.

This chapter covers

  • what a suggestion is, and where the candidates come from
  • finding the searches that begin with a prefix: a sorted list, and a tree of letters
  • why the answers are computed before anyone asks
  • how much data that requires, and how it is rebuilt
  • counting what people search for
  • searches that became popular within the last hour
  • what the browser must do: waiting, discarding late answers, and caching
  • suggestions that must not be shown
  • dividing the data among servers

What a suggestion is

A suggestion is a complete search that begins with what the user has typed so far. The text already typed is called the prefix, and the suggestions are completions of it.

The candidates are, for the most part, searches that other people have made. A search engine keeps a record of the searches submitted to it, and the completions of ka are drawn from the searches in that record which begin with ka. There are generally far more of these than can be displayed, since thousands of distinct searches begin with any short prefix, and so they have to be ranked and only the first few shown.

The basic ranking is by frequency. A search that has been made 900 times is preferred to one that has been made 300 times, on the reasoning that what many people have looked for is what the next person is most likely to want. Frequency alone is a serviceable beginning, and the later sections refine it.

The problem can therefore be stated precisely. Given a prefix, return the k most frequent searches that begin with it, where k is a small number such as 5 and the answer is required within a few milliseconds.

Finding the searches that begin with a prefix

A sorted list

The most direct structure is a list of all known searches in alphabetical order, each accompanied by its count. In such a list, all the searches that begin with a given prefix stand together, since alphabetical order groups words by their initial letters. The first of them can be found by binary search, or in an ordered index of the kind used throughout this book, and the remainder follow immediately after it.

The simulation for this chapter is built in this way, with 10 searches held in an ordered map. For the prefix ka it locates the first entry not less than ka, reads forward for as long as the entries begin with ka, which yields kafka, kafka vs rabbitmq, karaoke near me and kayak, sorts these 4 by count, and returns the first 3.

The method is correct and, for long prefixes, perfectly adequate. Its weakness lies in the short prefixes, which are the ones most often requested, since every search begins with a single letter. The number of entries beginning with k may run to millions, and all of them must be read and ranked in order to discover the 5 best. The cost of a request is proportional to the number of matches, and the number of matches is greatest for exactly those requests that are most numerous.

A tree of letters

The traditional structure for prefixes is a tree in which each edge is labelled with a letter and the path from the root to any node spells out a prefix. It is called a trie, or a prefix tree.

To find the completions of ka, one starts at the root, follows the edge labelled k and then the edge labelled a, and arrives at a node beneath which lie all the searches that begin with ka and no others. Reaching that node takes as many steps as the prefix has letters, 2 in this case, however many millions of searches the tree contains.

The trie makes the node easy to find and leaves the main difficulty where it was. The completions lie somewhere in the subtree below the node, and to determine the 5 most frequent it is still necessary to visit the whole subtree, which for a short prefix is a large part of the entire tree. The structure has shortened the search for the beginning of the answer and has done nothing to shorten the collection of the answer itself.

Computing the answers before anyone asks

The observation that resolves the difficulty is that the question “which are the 5 most frequent searches beginning with ka” has the same answer whoever asks it and whenever, until the underlying counts change. There is consequently no reason to work it out at the time of the request. It can be worked out once, in advance, for every prefix, and the results stored.

In terms of the trie, this means that every node carries, in addition to its children, a short list of the best completions that lie beneath it. In terms of a plain table, it means a row for every prefix, containing that prefix’s best completions.

With such a table, a request is a single lookup by key, of the kind that a key-value store or a cache performs in well under a millisecond. Its cost does not depend on the length of the prefix, on the number of searches that match it, or on the size of the collection. The simulation prints the rows of this table for the prefixes of its example: for k, kubernetes with 950, kafka with 900 and karaoke near me with 800; for ka, kafka, karaoke near me and kayak; for kaf, the 2 searches about kafka; and for x, nothing.

Once the answers have been computed in advance, the trie is no longer indispensable. A flat table that maps each prefix, as a string, to its list does everything required and can be held in any key-value store. The trie continues to be of use in building the lists, as will be seen, and in memory it is the more compact representation, since prefixes that share their opening letters share the corresponding nodes. As far as serving is concerned, however, the design has reduced a search problem to a lookup problem, and has done so by the same exchange that chapter 15 made for the news feed, in which work was moved from the moment of reading to the moment of writing.

What this costs

The cost is storage and the labour of construction. Every search of n letters has n prefixes, so that a collection of 100 million distinct searches of 20 letters on average gives rise to as many as 2 billion prefixes. In practice the number is much smaller, since a great many searches share their prefixes and there is only 1 row for k, shared by every search that begins with that letter. It can be reduced further by 2 simple rules. Prefixes beyond a certain length, 20 letters for example, are not stored, since by that point so few searches match that they can be found directly. And searches that have been made only a few times are excluded from the collection altogether, which, as a later section explains, is also required for reasons that have nothing to do with storage.

A row holds 5 completions, which can be stored as references to the searches and need not be full copies. A few hundred million rows of some tens of bytes each come to tens of gigabytes, an amount that can be held in the memory of a small number of machines.

Building the lists

The lists are built from the bottom of the trie upwards. The list for a node is the best 5 drawn from the lists of its children, together with the search that ends at the node itself, if there is one. Since each child’s list contains at most 5 entries, a node with 26 children has to consider at most 131 candidates, and the entire trie is processed in a single pass whose cost is proportional to the number of nodes.

The same property makes it possible to bring the lists up to date without rebuilding everything. When the count of a single search changes, only the lists on the path from that search up to the root can be affected, which for a search of 20 letters is 20 nodes. In practice, most services nevertheless rebuild the whole table at intervals, hourly or daily, from the latest counts, and replace the old table with the new one in a single step. A complete rebuild is simpler to make correct, is done by a batch job that places no load on the servers answering requests, and has the considerable advantage that the previous table remains at hand and can be reinstated at once if the new one proves to be faulty.

Counting what people search for

The counts from which the lists are built come from the record of searches. Every search that is actually submitted, as distinct from every prefix that is typed, is appended to a log, by way of the message queue of chapter 11, so that the recording adds nothing to the time taken by the search itself.

A batch job reads this log at intervals and produces, for every distinct search, the number of times it was made within some recent period. 3 aspects of this counting call for care.

The text of a search has to be normalised before it is counted, since “Kafka”, “kafka” and “ kafka “ are the same search to the person who typed them and would otherwise be counted as 3 separate ones, each with a third of the proper weight. Normalisation ordinarily converts the text to small letters, removes superfluous spaces, and brings accented characters to a standard form. The same normalisation must be applied to the prefix when a request for suggestions arrives, or the lookup will fail to find a row that exists.

Not every search need be counted. At a high volume, a random sample of 1 search in 10 or 1 in 100 yields counts that are proportionally accurate for everything popular enough to appear in a list of suggestions, at a tenth or a hundredth of the work. Sampling loses precision only for rare searches, which are not going to be suggested in any case.

And the counts should favour what is recent. A search that was made a million times 3 years ago and has scarcely been made since ought not to rank above one that has been made 100000 times this week. A common method reduces older counts by a constant factor at each period, halving the weight of every search’s history each week for example, so that popularity has to be sustained in order to be retained. This is the decay that chapter 9 applied to the counts of the least frequently used rule, and it is applied here for the same reason.

What became popular within the hour

A table rebuilt once a day cannot know of anything that happened today. When news breaks and a million people begin to search for a name that nobody had searched for the day before, suggestions built from yesterday’s counts will not include it, and the feature appears conspicuously out of touch at exactly the moment when attention is greatest.

The usual remedy is to maintain a second, much smaller collection alongside the main table. A stream processor reads the log of searches as they arrive and keeps counts over a short sliding window, the last hour for instance, using the windowed counting of chapter 7. Searches whose recent rate far exceeds their historical rate are recognised as trending and placed in a small table of their own, which is brought up to date every minute or so. When a request arrives, the service consults both the main table and the small one and merges the 2 lists.

The division gives each part the method that suits it. The great mass of suggestions changes slowly and is rebuilt at leisure, in bulk, with every opportunity for checking. The few that change quickly are handled by a mechanism that is fast because it is small.

What the browser must do

Much of the performance of autocomplete depends on the behaviour of the client, and a well-constructed service can be made to seem slow and erratic by a carelessly written one.

A user who types quickly produces a keystroke every 100 ms or less. A request sent on every keystroke is mostly wasted, since its answer will be out of date before it has arrived. The client therefore waits for a brief pause in the typing, of perhaps 50 to 100 ms, before sending a request, a technique known as debouncing. A user who types 5 letters in rapid succession and then stops causes 1 request where there would have been 5. Requests are likewise withheld until at least 1 or 2 letters have been typed, according to the language, since the suggestions for a single letter are seldom of any use and such prefixes account for a large share of the load.

A second matter concerns the order in which answers arrive, and it is the source of a defect that is frequently seen.

Requests travel independently over the network and may be answered in an order different from that in which they were sent. If the client displays every answer as it arrives, a slow answer for ka can overwrite the correct answer for kaf, and the user is shown suggestions that do not correspond to the text in the box. The client must therefore remember which prefix each request was for, and display an answer only if that prefix is still the text in the box. Requests that have been overtaken should also be cancelled, which saves the work of answering them.

The third matter is caching, for which autocomplete is exceptionally well suited. The answer for a given prefix is the same for every user, in the absence of personalisation, and remains valid for minutes or hours. It can therefore be cached at every level, with the methods of chapter 9. The browser keeps the answers it has already received, so that a user who deletes a letter sees the previous suggestions again instantly, with no request. The edge servers of a content delivery network, as described in chapter 17, keep the answers for common prefixes close to users, and since requests are heavily concentrated on a small number of short prefixes, a large proportion of them never reach the service. For this to work, a request for suggestions must be an ordinary GET with the prefix in its address, and the reply must state for how long it may be reused.

Suggestions that must not be shown

Autocomplete presents text that the service did not write, taken from what other people have typed, directly beneath the service’s own name. It has in consequence 2 ways of causing harm that are not apparent from the engineering alone.

The first concerns offensive or damaging suggestions. If a sufficient number of people search for a person’s name together with an accusation, the plain frequency ranking will propose that accusation to everybody who starts to type the name, and so lends the authority of the service to a rumour. Suggestions may equally promote abuse, dangerous activity or unlawful content, for no better reason than that many people have searched for it. The service therefore passes candidates through a filter before they enter the table, composed of lists of terms and categories that are never to be suggested, and provides a means by which any particular suggestion can be removed promptly once it has been reported. Because the table is built in advance, the filter is applied during the build and costs nothing when requests are answered, and an urgent removal is effected by a small list of exclusions that is checked as answers are served.

The second concerns privacy. A search may contain a person’s name, an address, a telephone number or a medical question. If a search that only 1 person ever made were to be offered as a suggestion, that person’s private search would be shown to strangers who chanced to type the same opening letters. A search is therefore admitted as a candidate only when it has been made by a sufficient number of different people, some hundreds for example, so that no suggestion can be traced to an individual. This threshold, which was mentioned earlier as a means of saving storage, is in fact required on grounds of privacy, and the number to be counted is that of distinct people, whatever the number of searches, since 1 person may make the same search a great many times.

Dividing the data among servers

The table of prefixes is too large for 1 machine in a big service and has to be divided. The natural key for the division is the prefix itself.

It is tempting to assign prefixes to servers by their first letter, and this distributes the load poorly. Far more searches begin with s than with x, so that some servers would be overloaded and others nearly idle. The division is better based on measured load: the ranges of prefixes are chosen so that each receives roughly the same number of requests, with the consequence that a common letter is spread over several servers by its second letter and several rare letters share 1 server. As an alternative, prefixes may be distributed by a hash, with the consistent hashing of chapter 1, which balances the load without any measurement and gives up the property that neighbouring prefixes reside on the same server.

Since the table is read-only between rebuilds, replicating it is uncomplicated. Every replica of a shard holds an identical copy of the same immutable file, and any of them may answer any request. There is no leader and no question of consistency among the replicas, apart from the short interval during which a new table is being distributed and some replicas have it while others still serve the old one. A user may notice a small change in the suggestions if 2 successive requests fall on either side of that interval, and this is harmless.

Use cases

A person types into a search box, and the service proposes completions.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0For the text typed so far, the service returns up to 5 searches that begin with it.
1Suggestions are ordered by how often they have recently been searched for.
2Searches that have become popular within the last hour appear among the suggestions.
3A suggestion that has been reported can be removed within minutes.
4No suggestion is shown that fewer than a set number of different people have searched for.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0LatencySuggestions are displayed within 100 ms of a keystroke, and the service itself answers within 10 ms.
1Availability99.9%. If suggestions are unavailable, searching still works.
2ConsistencyEventual. Suggestions reflect counts that are up to a day old, or up to a minute old for trending searches.
3Scale1 million requests per second, and 100 million distinct searches.

Autocomplete is an aid, and nothing else depends on it, which is reflected in non-functional requirements 1 and 2. A search box with no suggestions is merely a search box, and suggestions computed from yesterday’s counts are nearly as good as suggestions computed from this minute’s. Both facts are used to the full. The table is built offline and is allowed to be stale, and the client is written so that a slow or failed request for suggestions leaves the user free to type and to search without hindrance.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. The table of prefixes occupies about 25 GB, which is held in memory on a few machines, and most requests are answered by caches before they reach those machines.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Requests per second100000 searches × about 10 letters typed1 million
Requests that reach the service1 million × 20% not answered by caches200000 per second
Rows in the tabledistinct prefixes, after the rules on length and popularityabout 500 million
Size of a rowprefix 12 bytes + 5 references of 8 bytesabout 50 bytes
Size of the table500 million × 50 bytes25 GB

The API

Suggestions are a resource addressed by the prefix, which is passed as a parameter of the query. The request is a plain GET, so that every cache between the user and the service is able to store the answer.

Suggestions for a prefix

GET /v1/suggestions?q=ka HTTP/1.1
Host: search.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300

{
  "prefix": "ka",
  "suggestions": ["kafka", "karaoke near me", "kayak"]
}

The reply repeats the prefix so that the client can verify that the answer belongs to the text now in the box. Cache-Control permits browsers and edge servers to reuse the answer for 5 minutes.

A prefix with no completions

GET /v1/suggestions?q=kafx HTTP/1.1
Host: search.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300

{ "prefix": "kafx", "suggestions": [] }

An empty list is a successful answer and is returned with 200. It is cached like any other, which protects the service against repeated requests for prefixes that lead nowhere.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Suggestion APIlooks up the list for a prefix and applies the list of exclusionsa copy of the table, in memoryanother replica answers
Prefix liststhe table of the best completions for every prefixan immutable file, replaced at each rebuildevery replica holds the same file
Search logrecords every search that is submittedthe log, in a message queueas in chapter 11
Counting jobcounts searches, with decay, at intervalsnone between runsthe job is run again
Search countsthe count of every distinct searchcounts, in a storethe previous counts are still available

One request, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 22.6.

  1. After a pause in the typing, the browser asks for suggestions for the text in the box, unless it already holds the answer.
  2. The suggestion API, if no cache has answered first, normalises the prefix, reads the row for it from the table in its memory, removes any excluded entries, and returns the list.
  3. Independently of this, every search that a user submits is appended to the search log.
  4. At intervals, the counting job reads the log and brings the count of every search up to date, reducing older counts.
  5. A new table of prefix lists is built from the counts, checked, and distributed to the replicas, which begin serving it in place of the old one.

The design, deployed

Most of the million requests per second are answered before they reach this system, by the browser’s own memory of earlier answers and by edge servers that cache each prefix for 5 minutes. The serving tier receives about a fifth of them. It consists of 24 machines, each holding a part of the table in memory, behind load balancers that route by the range of the prefix. Nothing in the serving tier ever writes. The table is produced by the build tier below, from the log of searches, and handed upwards once an hour as a finished file, so that a fault in the building can at worst leave the serving tier with an old table.

How real systems do it

Facebook published an early and clear account of a typeahead in 2010, for the search box that suggests people and pages. Its design starts in the browser, which is loaded with the user’s own friends and pages before a letter is typed and answers from that list first, and which caches every reply so that deleting a letter costs nothing. Only then is the service asked, and the service is a set of indexes, 1 for each kind of result, queried in parallel and merged by an aggregator. The emphasis on the client is the same as in this chapter, and the personal first stage is a form of the personalisation that this chapter mentions only in passing.

The data structure for the general problem, the most frequent completions of a prefix, has been studied as top-k completion. A paper from Microsoft compares several structures and shows that a trie which stores at each node the best score beneath it can find the best completions without visiting the whole subtree, in space close to that of the compressed strings. This is a middle way between the 2 extremes of this chapter, the trie that must be searched and the table that stores every answer, and it is what a system uses when the table would be too large. Search libraries commonly implement completion with a compact automaton that shares both the prefixes and the suffixes of the stored strings.

On what must not be shown, the operators of the large search engines publish policies stating which kinds of prediction they remove, covering violence, sexually explicit and hateful predictions and those that make damaging statements about named people, together with a means of reporting. The existence of these policies is the practical evidence for the section on suggestions that must not be shown. The threshold of distinct users is an application of the idea of k-anonymity, that no released item should be traceable to fewer than k people.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Ranking the matches while the user waitsShort prefixes match millions of searches and cannot be ranked in time.Compute the best completions for every prefix in advance.
Updating the table on every searchThe serving path carries a constant load of writes.Rebuild in batches, and keep a small separate table for what is trending.
A request on every keystrokeMost answers are out of date on arrival.Wait for a brief pause in the typing before asking.
Displaying every answer as it arrivesA slow answer for an earlier prefix overwrites the right one.Display an answer only if it is for the text now in the box.
Requests that caches cannot storeEvery keystroke of every user reaches the service.Use GET with the prefix in the address, and state how long the answer may be reused.
Counting searches without normalisingThe same search is divided among several spellings.Normalise the text before counting and before looking up.
Counts that never decaySearches that were popular years ago keep their places.Reduce older counts at each period.
Suggesting anything that is frequentOffensive or defamatory suggestions appear under the service’s name.Filter candidates during the build, and allow prompt removal.
Suggesting rare searches1 person’s private search is shown to strangers.Admit a search only when enough different people have made it.
Dividing by first letterServers for common letters are overloaded.Divide by measured load, or by a hash.
Making search depend on suggestionsA failure of suggestions blocks the search box.Let the user type and search whether or not suggestions arrive.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
The suggestion service is unreachableno suggestions, and search works as usualcaches continue to answer common prefixes, and the service returns
A newly built table is faultystrange or missing suggestionsthe previous table is reinstated in 1 step
The counting job failssuggestions grow slowly out of datethe job is run again, and the previous table serves meanwhile
An offensive suggestion is reportedit disappears within minutesit is added to the exclusions, and the filter is corrected for the next build
An answer is lost or latethe list fails to update for 1 keystrokethe next keystroke sends a new request

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Answers computed in advance1 lookup per request, whatever the prefixstorage for every prefix, and staleness between rebuilds
Rebuilding in batchessimple, verifiable, and easy to reversenew searches appear late, without the trending table
A separate trending tablefresh suggestions within a minutea second mechanism to operate
Caching at the edge and in the browsermost requests never reach the servicea removed suggestion lingers until the caches expire
A threshold of distinct peopleprivacy, and a smaller tablerare searches that would be legitimate are never suggested

The fourth row conceals a tension that deserves to be noticed. The longer the answers may be cached, the lighter the load, and the longer a suggestion that has been removed continues to be shown from caches that the service cannot reach. The period for which answers are cached is therefore chosen with removals in mind, and it is the reason why 5 minutes is a more usual figure than 5 hours.

Simulation in the repository. The program code/typeahead simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p typeahead in the code directory.

Prefixthe text that has been typed so far
Completiona search that begins with the prefix
Trie, prefix treea tree in which the path to each node spells a prefix
Top kthe k best items by some measure, here the k most frequent
Normalisationbringing text to a standard form before comparing or counting it
Decayreducing the weight of older counts
Trendingrecently far more frequent than in the past
Debouncingwaiting for a pause in the typing before sending a request
Samplingcounting a random fraction of events in place of all of them

Summary

  • Autocomplete is requested for every keystroke and must answer within about 100 ms, which leaves no time to compute anything.
  • A sorted list or a trie finds the searches that begin with a prefix quickly, and ranking them still costs in proportion to their number.
  • The best completions of every prefix are therefore computed in advance, so that a request is a single lookup.
  • The table is rebuilt in batches from counts of submitted searches, normalised, sampled and weighted towards the recent.
  • A small table of trending searches, brought up to date every minute, supplies what the daily rebuild cannot.
  • The client waits for a pause before asking, discards answers that arrive late, and reuses answers it already has.
  • Candidates are filtered for offensive content, and a search is suggested only if enough different people have made it.

Web Crawler: System Design

A web crawler is a program that reads the web as a person would who had unlimited patience and no particular interest in any page. It begins with a few known addresses, downloads the pages at those addresses, extracts from each page the addresses to which it links, and proceeds to download those in their turn. Continued long enough, the process reaches every page that can be reached by following links, and the collection that results is the raw material of a search engine, of an archive, or of any system that needs to know what the web contains.

As an algorithm, this is the traversal of a graph, and an introductory course in programming covers it in a week. What separates the exercise from the system is the nature of this particular graph. It has tens of billions of nodes and can be stored on no single machine. It is not given in advance, each node being discoverable only by fetching another. It changes while it is being traversed. Parts of it are infinite, generated on demand by programs that will produce a new page for every address they are asked for. And every node belongs to somebody, who is paying for the server that answers and who will, quite reasonably, block a crawler that asks too much too quickly. A crawler has therefore to be at once fast in aggregate and gentle towards each individual site, and most of its design follows from the need to reconcile the 2.

This chapter covers

  • the loop at the centre of every crawler
  • the frontier: which address to fetch next, and why it is more than a queue
  • politeness, and a queue for every host
  • what a site asks of crawlers, and why a crawler complies
  • recognising an address that has been seen before
  • recognising a page that has been seen before under another address
  • sites that never end
  • dividing the crawl among many machines
  • returning to pages that change

The loop

Every crawler, whatever its size, repeats the same 4 steps. It takes an address from the collection of those waiting to be fetched, which is called the frontier. It downloads the page at that address. It extracts the links from the page. And it adds to the frontier those of the links that it has not met before.

If the frontier were a simple first-in, first-out queue, this would be a breadth-first traversal. Almost everything of interest in a crawler’s design is a departure from that simple queue, prompted by 1 of 3 matters: the order in which addresses should be taken, given that there are always far more waiting than can be fetched, how soon the same server may be asked again, and how it is known that an address, or a page, has been dealt with already.

Politeness

A crawler with 1000 connections at its disposal could, if it chose, direct all of them at a single web site. For a small site this would be indistinguishable from an attack. The server would be overwhelmed, its ordinary visitors would be turned away, and its owner would respond by blocking the crawler’s addresses permanently, as would the owners of other sites who heard of it. A crawler that is to be tolerated must restrict itself, for each site separately, to a rate that the site will not notice. A usual rule allows 1 request to a given host at any moment, followed by a pause of a second or more before the next.

The difficulty is that this restriction is at odds with the order in which addresses are discovered. A page generally links mostly to other pages of its own site, so that the frontier, at any moment, contains long runs of addresses on the same host. A crawler that took addresses strictly in order would spend nearly all its time waiting for the pause on some host to expire, while thousands of other hosts stood ready.

The standard arrangement resolves this by giving the frontier a structure that mirrors the constraint. There is a separate queue for every host, and with each queue is recorded the earliest time at which that host may next be asked. A fetcher that wants work takes an address from any host whose time has come, and that host’s time is then moved forward by the length of the pause.

The simulation for this chapter crawls a small invented web of 3 hosts under this rule. In 8 seconds it fetches 10 pages, never asking any host twice within 2 seconds, and never standing idle while some host is ready.

The consequence for the performance of a crawler is fundamental and somewhat counter-intuitive. The speed of a crawl is determined by the number of different hosts it has in hand, and hardly at all by how fast any 1 of them answers. With a pause of 1 second, a crawler that knows of a million hosts can fetch a million pages a second, and a crawler confined to a single enormous site can fetch 1. A very large site therefore takes a long time to crawl completely however many machines are available, and the only remedy is an agreement with its owner.

The pause need not be the same for every host. A crawler can measure how long a server takes to answer and wait some multiple of that, which treats a fast server more briskly and backs away from one that is struggling. A server that begins to return errors, or the status 429 of chapter 7, is telling the crawler directly that it is asking too much, and the pause for that host should be lengthened at once.

What a site asks of crawlers

By a convention almost as old as the web, a site may publish a file named robots.txt at its root, stating which parts of the site crawlers are asked to stay out of, and sometimes how long they should wait between requests. A site might exclude its search results, its shopping baskets, or pages that are costly to generate.

Nothing enforces this file. A crawler obeys it because the alternative is to be blocked, and because the exclusions usually serve the crawler’s own interest by steering it away from pages of no value. The file has to be fetched before any other page of the host, and since it applies to every later request it is kept in a cache, with a time limit of perhaps a day, so that it is neither fetched for every page nor relied upon indefinitely after the site has changed it.

A crawler also identifies itself, by a name in the User-Agent header of each request together with an address at which its operators can be reached. An administrator who finds an unfamiliar program in the logs and can discover what it is and whom to write to is far less inclined to block it than one who cannot.

An address seen before

The web is densely connected, and the same address appears as a link on a great many pages. In the small simulation, 7 of the links encountered led to addresses that were already known. On the real web the proportion is far higher, and a crawler that fetched every address every time it was mentioned would never finish. Every address ever added to the frontier is therefore recorded in a seen set, and a newly extracted link is checked against the set before anything else is done with it.

Before the check, the address has to be brought to a standard form, since many different strings denote the same page. The name of the host is not sensitive to case. A port number that is the default may be given or left out. The part of an address after a # refers to a position within the page and is never sent to the server. The parameters of a query may appear in any order, and often include identifiers of a session or of an advertising campaign that have no effect on what is returned. A crawler that failed to normalise its addresses would fetch the same page many times under different spellings.

The seen set is very large. 10 billion addresses of 80 bytes each would occupy 800 GB, and the set is consulted for every link on every page. Storing a fixed-size hash of each address in place of the address reduces this by a factor of 10. A further reduction is possible if occasional errors are tolerated. The Bloom filter that chapter 9 used against cache penetration serves here too: it occupies about 10 bits for each address and answers the question of membership with certainty when the answer is no, and with a small probability of error, around 1 in 100, when the answer is yes. For a crawler the error means that a few addresses in every hundred which are in truth new are taken as seen and are not fetched. Whether that loss is acceptable depends on the purpose of the crawl, and for most purposes a web of which 1% is missed is a perfectly good web.

A page seen before

Normalising addresses does not eliminate duplication, because the same content is very often served at addresses that are truly distinct. A site answers both with and without www. An article is available at a short address and a long one, or in a printable version, or on a second site that reproduces it. Estimates of the share of the web that duplicates some other part of it run to a quarter or more.

Identical copies are detected easily. The crawler computes a checksum of the content of each page it fetches and keeps the checksums, as the object store of chapter 16 does for chunks. A page whose checksum is already present is a duplicate, and is neither stored again nor examined for links.

Copies that are nearly identical are a harder matter, and are much the commoner case. 2 copies of the same article may differ in the date printed at the top, in the advertisements, or in a counter of visitors, and a checksum, which changes completely when a single byte changes, treats them as unrelated. For this purpose a different kind of fingerprint is used, constructed so that similar documents receive similar fingerprints. The page is broken into overlapping sequences of a few words, each sequence is hashed, and the hashes are combined into a short value in such a way that every sequence has a small influence on every bit. 2 pages that share most of their sequences then receive fingerprints that differ in only a few bits, and near duplicates can be found by looking for fingerprints close to one another.

Sites that never end

Some parts of the web are generated by programs and have no boundary. The classic instance is a calendar.

The page for each day contains a link to the following day, and the server will obligingly produce a page for any date whatever. A crawler that follows links faithfully proceeds through the calendar day by day into the indefinite future. A shop with 5 filters that may be combined in any order, a site that embeds a fresh session identifier in every link, and a directory that by mistake contains a link to itself all have the same effect. Such structures are called crawler traps. Most are accidents, and a few are built on purpose to waste the time of crawlers.

No test can tell, for an arbitrary site, whether its pages are endless, and the defences are accordingly limits, since nothing can serve as a detector. A crawler restricts the number of pages it will take from any 1 host, as the simulation does when it stops the calendar at 4. It restricts the depth to which it will follow links from the page at which it entered a site. It restricts the length of the addresses it will accept, since addresses in a trap tend to grow. And it gives a larger allowance to hosts that many other sites link to, on the grounds that a site which the rest of the web considers important is unlikely to be a trap.

Which address next

With far more addresses waiting than can ever be fetched, the order in which they are taken decides what the crawl contains. A crawler that is to feed a search engine wants the important pages first, and has to estimate importance before fetching, from what is known about an address in advance: how many pages link to it, how important those pages are themselves, how near it is to the root of its site, and how valuable the other pages of its host have proved.

Priority and politeness have to be combined, and the usual structure has 2 stages. A set of queues ordered by priority feeds the queues ordered by host. Addresses enter at the front according to their estimated importance, are drawn from the high-priority queues more often than from the low, and are then placed in the queue of their host, from which the rule of politeness releases them. The first stage decides what is worth fetching, and the second decides when it may be fetched.

Many machines

A crawl of billions of pages is carried out by many machines, and the work has to be divided among them in such a way that the constraints still hold. The decisive constraint is politeness, which is a property of a host and must therefore be enforced in 1 place for each host. If 2 machines each held addresses of the same host and each observed the pause on its own account, the host would receive twice the permitted load.

The division is therefore made by host. Each host is assigned to a single crawler machine, by hashing its name, with the consistent hashing of chapter 1 so that the addition of a machine moves only a small share of the hosts. All the addresses of a host are queued on its machine, which alone keeps the host’s waiting time and its robots.txt. When a machine extracts a link to a host that belongs to another machine, it forwards the address there, usually in batches by way of a message queue. Since most links lead to the site on which they are found, most addresses stay where they were discovered.

The frontier must survive failures. It represents days of accumulated discovery and cannot quickly be rebuilt. It is therefore kept on disk, and since it is far larger than memory, each host’s queue is held mostly on disk, with only the next few addresses of each host in memory.

A crawler also depends heavily on the name resolution system, since every host name has to be turned into a network address before the host can be contacted. At thousands of requests a second, the ordinary resolver becomes a bottleneck, and crawlers keep their own cache of resolved names, refreshed as the entries expire.

Returning to pages

The web changes, and a collection that was accurate last month is partly wrong today. A crawler has to revisit, and since it cannot revisit everything as often as it would wish, it has to decide how its limited capacity is best spent.

Pages change at very different rates. The front page of a newspaper changes every few minutes, and a paper published by a scientific journal 10 years ago will never change again. A crawler therefore records, for each page, how often it has found the page changed on its previous visits, and schedules the next visit accordingly: soon for a page that is usually different, and after a long interval for one that is usually the same.

HTTP allows a revisit to be made cheaply. The crawler sends the entity tag that it received with the page on the last occasion, in the If-None-Match header that chapter 1 described, and a server whose page has not changed answers 304 Not Modified with no body. The crawler has confirmed that its copy is current at the cost of a few hundred bytes.

Use cases

An operator starts a crawl and governs it. A consumer, typically the indexer of a search engine, reads the pages that have been fetched.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0Starting from given addresses, the crawler fetches the pages that can be reached by following links.
1No address is fetched more than once in a crawl.
2The crawler observes the rules that each site publishes for crawlers.
3No host is asked more often than once in a configured interval.
4Pages whose content has already been stored are recognised and not stored again.
5Pages are fetched again at intervals that depend on how often they change.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0Scale10 billion pages in a crawl of a month, which is about 4000 pages per second.
1PolitenessAt most 1 request at any moment to a host, with at least 1 second between requests.
2DurabilityThe frontier and the seen set survive the failure of any machine.
3ConsistencyEventual. A small share of addresses may be fetched twice or missed.
4RobustnessNo page, however malformed or large, stops the crawl.

A crawler is unusually tolerant of small errors, and non-functional requirement 3 says so. If 1 address in 100 is skipped because a Bloom filter was mistaken, or fetched twice because a machine failed between fetching and recording, the resulting collection is for all practical purposes as good. This tolerance is what allows the seen set to be approximate and the coordination between machines to be loose. The 1 requirement that admits no approximation is politeness, since the party harmed by a violation is somebody else.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 10 billion pages of 100 KB are 1 PB of content, fetched at 4000 pages per second, which needs about 3 Gbit/s of bandwidth and a few hundred fetching machines.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Pages per second10 billion ÷ (30 × 86400 s)about 3900
Content stored10 billion × 100 KB1 PB
Bandwidth3900 × 100 KB × 8about 3 Gbit/s
Hosts needed to sustain the rate3900 pages per second × 1 s pauseat least 3900 hosts ready at every moment
Seen set as hashes10 billion × 8 bytes80 GB
Seen set as a Bloom filter10 billion × 10 bits12.5 GB

The API

A crawler has few callers. An operator supplies starting addresses and rules, and a consumer reads what has been fetched, in pages, by a cursor.

Give starting addresses

POST /v1/seeds HTTP/1.1
Host: crawler.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{ "addresses": ["https://news.example/", "https://shop.example/"] }

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json

{ "accepted": 2 }

The status is 202, since the addresses have been taken into the frontier and nothing has yet been fetched.

Set the rules for a host

PUT /v1/hosts/calendar.example/rules HTTP/1.1
Host: crawler.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{ "pause_seconds": 5, "page_limit": 1000, "depth_limit": 6 }

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

Read the fetched pages

GET /v1/pages?after=880213&limit=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: crawler.internal

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "pages": [
    { "id": 880214, "address": "https://news.example/a", "fetched": "2026-10-14T09:00:02Z", "status": 200, "content": "/v1/pages/880214/content" },
    { "id": 880215, "address": "https://shop.example/item-1", "fetched": "2026-10-14T09:00:03Z", "status": 200, "content": "/v1/pages/880215/content" }
  ],
  "next_after": 880215
}

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Frontierholds the waiting addresses, in a queue for each hostthe queues and waiting times, on diskits hosts are taken over, with their queues, by another machine
Fetcherdownloads pages, within a time limit and a size limitnonethe address returns to the frontier
Host rulesholds each host’s robots.txt and limitsa cachethe rules are fetched again
Parserextracts and normalises the links of a pagenonethe page is parsed again
Link filterremoves addresses that have been seenthe seen setthe set is restored from its copy
Page storekeeps the content of every pagethe pages, in an object storeas in chapter 16

One page, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 23.5.

  1. The frontier hands a fetcher the next address of a host whose waiting time has passed, and moves that host’s time forward.
  2. The fetcher consults the rules of the host. If the address is excluded, it is dropped. Otherwise the fetcher downloads the page, giving up if the server is too slow or the page too large.
  3. The page passes to the parser.
  4. The content is given a checksum. If no page with that checksum has been stored, the page is stored.
  5. The parser extracts the links, normalises them, and passes them to the link filter.
  6. The filter drops every address that is in the seen set, adds the others to the set, and sends them to the frontier, where each joins the queue of its host.

The design, deployed

A crawler has no users in the ordinary sense, and its deployment is that of a pipeline. The 40 frontier machines are the heart of it. Each owns the hosts whose names hash to it, and holds their queues on disk. The 300 fetchers are stateless and hold thousands of connections each. Parsers, the seen set and the queue that forwards links to the machine owning their host form the processing tier, and the pages themselves go to an object store. Since the frontier is the only state that cannot be rebuilt quickly, it is the part that is replicated.

How real systems do it

The frontier of this chapter, with queues by priority feeding queues by host, is the design of Mercator, a crawler built at Compaq and described in 1999. Mercator’s paper names the 2 stages the front queues and the back queues, keeps exactly 1 back queue for each host being crawled, and holds a heap of the times at which each host may next be contacted. The paper on the original Google crawler, of the year before, describes a simpler arrangement and is of interest chiefly for its account of what went wrong when a crawler first met the real web.

How far a single machine can be taken was shown by IRLbot, which crawled over 6 billion pages in 41 days from 1 server. Its paper is largely about the 2 problems that this chapter treats under the seen set and the endless site. For the first it replaces the in-memory set by a structure on disk that checks addresses in large sorted batches. For the second it gives each site a budget that depends on how many other sites link to it, which is the allowance described above, and it argues that without such a budget any crawler at scale is eventually captured by sites that generate pages without end.

The fingerprint under which similar pages receive similar values is simhash. Google described using it on a collection of 8 billion pages, with fingerprints of 64 bits, treating 2 pages as near duplicates when their fingerprints differ in at most 3 bits, and the paper’s main contribution is a way of finding all fingerprints within that distance of a given one without comparing it with every other.

The convention of robots.txt, in use since 1994, was written down as a standard only in 2022. And the scheduling of revisits according to observed rates of change goes back to a study which showed, among other things, that revisiting every page equally often keeps a collection fresher than revisiting each in proportion to how often it changes, since pages that change constantly can never be kept fresh and absorb the effort.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
1 queue for all addressesThe crawler either overloads a site or waits on 1 host while thousands are ready.Keep a queue and a waiting time for every host.
Enforcing politeness separately on each machineA host served by 2 machines receives twice the permitted load.Assign each host to exactly 1 machine.
Ignoring robots.txtThe crawler is blocked, and fetches pages of no value.Fetch and cache the rules of each host before anything else.
Comparing addresses as raw stringsThe same page is fetched under many spellings.Normalise every address before checking the seen set.
Detecting duplicates by address onlyThe same article is stored from many addresses.Compare checksums of content, and fingerprints for near duplicates.
Following every link without limitA calendar or a set of filters occupies the crawler for ever.Limit the pages and the depth for each host.
No limit on time or size of a download1 slow or endless response holds a fetcher indefinitely.Give every download a time limit and a size limit.
The frontier in memory onlyA restart loses days of discovery.Keep the frontier on disk.
Asking the resolver for every requestName resolution becomes the bottleneck.Cache resolved names.
Revisiting every page equally oftenCapacity is spent on pages that never change.Revisit according to how often each page has changed.
Persisting when a host returns errorsThe host is pushed further into overload, and blocks the crawler.Lengthen the pause for a host that answers with errors or 429.

Failures

A fetcher crashes during a downloadthe page is not storedthe address was not removed from its queue until the page was stored, and is fetched again

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/crawlsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p crawlsim in the code directory.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Crawlera program that fetches pages and follows their links
Frontierthe addresses that are known and have yet to be fetched
Seedan address from which a crawl starts
Hostthe server named in an address, to which politeness applies

Summary

  • A crawler repeats 4 steps: take an address, fetch the page, extract its links, and add the new ones to the frontier.
  • Each host may be asked only at intervals, so the frontier keeps a queue and a waiting time for every host.
  • The speed of a crawl comes from the number of hosts in hand, and no single site can be crawled quickly.
  • Addresses are normalised and checked against a seen set, which may be a Bloom filter where a small loss is acceptable.
  • Duplicate content is found by checksum, and near duplicates by fingerprints that are similar for similar pages.
  • Endless sites cannot be detected, and are contained by limits on pages and depth for every host.
  • Each host is assigned to 1 machine, so that politeness is enforced in a single place.
  • Pages are revisited at intervals that depend on how often they have been found changed.

Metrics and Monitoring: System Design

Every system in this book has been described as doing what its design says. A real system has also to be watched, since machines fail, software is released with defects, and traffic arrives in patterns that nobody foresaw. The people responsible need to know, at every moment, how many requests the system is receiving, how many of them are failing, how long they take, and how close each machine is to the limits of its memory and its disks. They need to see these quantities change over hours and weeks, and they need to be woken at night when one of them goes wrong. The system that provides for this is a monitoring system, and the numbers it collects are called metrics.

A monitoring system has a peculiar workload. It receives an enormous number of very small writes, since every service on every machine reports dozens of numbers every few seconds, and those writes never stop. Its data is of a single shape, a number with a time attached, which permits a degree of compression that no general database approaches. Almost nobody reads the data, and yet when it is read, during an incident, the answer is wanted immediately and may span months. And the system has a responsibility of an unusual kind. It is the means by which every other failure is detected, and it must therefore go on working when the things around it do not.

This chapter covers

  • what a metric is, and the 3 kinds in common use
  • time series, and why their number is the quantity to watch
  • whether services send their measurements or are asked for them
  • storing a number every few seconds for a year in 2 bytes a point
  • reducing old data to 1 point a minute, and what that loses
  • why an average of response times misleads, and what to keep in its place
  • alerts that wake somebody for the right reasons
  • keeping the monitoring system alive when everything else is failing

What a metric is

A metric is a number, measured repeatedly, that describes some aspect of a running system. 3 kinds account for nearly all of them, and they behave differently enough that it matters which is which.

A counter is a number that only ever increases: the requests served since the process started, or the bytes sent. Its value at a single moment is of no interest. What is wanted is its rate of change, obtained by subtracting 2 readings and dividing by the time between them. Counters have the great merit that nothing is lost between readings. If a reading is missed, the next one still includes everything that happened in the interval.

A gauge is a number that rises and falls: the memory in use, the length of a queue, the temperature of a processor. Here the value at a moment is the thing of interest, and whatever it did between 2 readings is unknown. A queue that filled and emptied within 5 seconds leaves no trace in a gauge read every 10.

A histogram records the distribution of a quantity that takes a different value on every occasion, above all the time taken to answer a request. Its treatment needs a section of its own, since the natural way of summarising such a quantity, by its average, turns out to be nearly useless.

Time series

A measurement is identified by the name of the metric and by a set of labels, which are pairs of a key and a value saying what the measurement refers to. The requests served by the payments service on machine 14 with status 500 might be recorded as the metric requests_total with the labels service=payments, machine=14 and status=500. The sequence of values recorded for 1 metric with 1 particular set of label values is a time series.

Labels are what make metrics useful, since they allow the same measurement to be added up or separated out along any dimension: all requests to payments, all requests with status 500, all requests on machine 14. They are also the principal hazard in the operation of a monitoring system, for a reason that follows from simple multiplication.

Every distinct combination of label values is a separate series, to be stored and indexed separately. A metric with the labels service, machine and status, in a system with 20 services, 100 machines and 5 statuses in use, has up to 10000 series, which is entirely manageable. Suppose now that a well-meaning engineer adds a label for the identifier of the user, so as to see which users experience errors. With a million users, the 1 metric has up to 10 billion series. The number of series that a metric gives rise to is called its cardinality, and a single label whose values are unbounded, such as a user identifier, a request identifier or the full text of an address, is enough to exhaust the memory of the system within hours.

The rule that follows is that labels must take a small and bounded number of values. A question about an individual user or request is a legitimate one, and it belongs to a different kind of system: to logs, which record individual events, or to traces, which follow a single request through the services it touches. Metrics answer questions about aggregates, and pay for their cheapness by being unable to answer any other kind.

Sending or being asked

Measurements have to travel from the services to the monitoring system, and there are 2 ways of arranging it.

Under the push model, each service sends its measurements to the monitoring system at regular intervals. Under the pull model, each service exposes its current values at an address of its own, and the monitoring system visits every service at regular intervals to collect them.

PushPull
Who must know whomevery service knows the address of the monitoring systemthe monitoring system knows the address of every service
A service that has diedstops sending, which looks the same as having nothing to reportfails to answer, which is itself a clear signal
A service that lives for secondscan report before it exitsmay be gone before it is visited
Who controls the loadthe services, all at oncethe monitoring system, at its own pace
Services behind a firewallcan send outwardscannot be reached

The second row is the strongest argument for pulling. When the monitoring system does the asking, the absence of an answer is information, and the health of every service is checked as a by-product of collecting its numbers. The third row is the strongest argument for pushing, since a batch job that runs for 5 seconds cannot wait to be visited. Many installations use both, pulling from long-lived services and accepting pushes from short-lived ones. The design of this chapter pulls, with collectors that visit each service every 10 seconds.

Storing a number every 10 seconds

The store receives points, each consisting of a time and a value, and must keep them for months. Stored plainly, as 2 numbers of 8 bytes, a point occupies 16 bytes. A million series sampled every 10 seconds produce 8.6 billion points a day, or 138 GB, and a year of that is 50 TB.

Time series have 2 properties that allow far better. The points of a series arrive in order of time and are never modified afterwards, so that the store only ever appends. And successive points resemble one another closely: the times are evenly spaced, and the values change little from one reading to the next. A number that is close to its predecessor can be stored as the difference between them, and a small difference needs few bits.

For the times, the differences are themselves nearly constant, the interval of collection, so that storing the difference between successive differences yields 0 almost every time. For the values, the difference from the previous value is small whenever the quantity being measured is steady, which most are for most of the time.

The simulation for this chapter stores an hour of a response time measured every second, 3600 points. Stored plainly they occupy 57600 bytes. Stored as changes, with small numbers written in fewer bytes, they occupy 7223, which is 2 bytes for each point and an eighth of the plain size. Production systems encode at the level of individual bits and exploit the structure of floating-point numbers, and commonly reach between 1 and 2 bytes a point. The 50 TB a year computed above becomes about 5.

Compression of this kind has a consequence for the layout of the store. A point encoded as a difference can be decoded only by starting from the beginning of its run and working forwards. Points are therefore grouped into blocks, each covering a fixed span of time for 1 series, 2 hours for example, and each block is encoded and decoded as a unit. The block being written is held in memory, where it can be appended to, and is protected by a write-ahead log of the kind described in chapter 2, and when its span is over it is compressed and written to disk, never to be modified again. Reading a range of time means locating the blocks that cover it, which is quick because blocks are indexed by series and by time.

Keeping less of the past

Even well compressed, points every 10 seconds for a year are more than most questions about the past require. A graph of the last year, drawn on a screen 2000 pixels wide, can show at most 2000 values, and to compute them from 3 million points for each series would be slow and pointless.

Older data is therefore reduced in resolution, a process called downsampling or rollup. A background job reads the raw points of each series and writes 1 point for every minute, and later 1 for every hour. Recent data is retained at full resolution for some days, the 1-minute data for some months, and the hourly data for years. A query chooses the resolution suited to the range it covers.

What is written for each minute has to be chosen with care, since a single number cannot represent 6 or 60 readings without losing something, and what is lost depends on the number chosen.

In the simulation, 1 minute contains 57 seconds in which the response time is about 40 ms and 3 seconds in which it is 900. Kept as its average, that minute is recorded as 83 ms, which suggests a slight slowness and conceals entirely that for 3 seconds the service was nearly unusable. Kept as its largest value, the minute is recorded as 900 ms, which preserves the incident and says nothing of how brief it was. Neither is wrong, and neither is sufficient. A rollup therefore stores several numbers for each interval, usually the smallest value, the largest, the sum and the count, from which the average can be derived and the extremes are not lost.

Why an average of response times misleads

The same example exposes a wider difficulty. The time taken to answer a request is the most important single measure of a service, and its average is a poor description of it.

Response times are not distributed symmetrically about a typical value. Most requests are fast, and a small proportion are very much slower, because they met a busy disk, an expired cache entry or a retry. The average is pulled upwards a little by these slow requests and describes neither group. A service whose requests take 40 ms in 99 cases and 2 seconds in the hundredth has an average of 60 ms, which looks entirely healthy, while 1 user in every 100 waits 2 seconds, and a user who loads a page that issues 50 requests has a chance of 2 in 5 of encountering at least 1 of them.

The quantity that describes experience is the percentile, introduced in chapter 1. The 99th percentile, written p99, is the time within which 99% of requests complete, and it states directly how bad the experience is for the least fortunate 1 in 100.

Percentiles have an awkward property that averages lack, and it shapes how response times must be collected. They cannot be combined. The average of 2 machines can be computed from the average and the count of each. The p99 of 2 machines cannot be computed from the p99 of each: if one machine has a p99 of 50 ms and the other of 2 seconds, the combined p99 may be almost anything between, depending on how the requests were divided. A service that computes its own percentiles and reports them has produced numbers that can never be aggregated across machines or across time.

The histogram solves this. A service does not report a percentile. It counts its requests in buckets by duration, so many under 10 ms, so many under 50 ms, so many under 250 ms and so on, and reports the counts. Counts can be added, across machines and across intervals, and a percentile is estimated from the combined counts at the moment of the query. The estimate is only as fine as the buckets, so the boundaries of the buckets have to be chosen around the durations that matter, but it can be computed for any grouping of machines over any period, which no percentile computed in advance allows.

Alerts

A monitoring system that is only looked at when something is already known to be wrong has done half its work. The other half is to notice the trouble first, by means of alerts. An alert is a rule consisting of a query and a condition, which the system evaluates at regular intervals, notifying somebody when the condition holds.

Rules are easy to write and hard to write well, and the commonest failing of monitoring in practice is too many alerts. An engineer who is woken 3 times a night by alerts that required no action soon ceases to respond with any urgency, and the alert that matters is then lost among the rest. A few principles keep alerts worth answering.

An alert should concern what users experience. What machines are doing is a different matter. “The proportion of failed requests has exceeded 1%” is a statement about harm. “Processor usage is at 90%” is a statement about a machine, which may be working exactly as intended. Alerts on causes multiply endlessly, since there are countless possible causes, while the symptoms that matter are few.

A condition should have to hold for some time before the alert fires. A single reading above a threshold is very often a momentary disturbance, and a rule that requires the condition to persist for 5 minutes ignores the noise at the price of 5 minutes’ delay.

Every alert should demand an action. If the proper response to an alert is to observe it and go back to sleep, it belongs on a dashboard, and nobody should be notified of it.

And related alerts should be grouped. When a database fails, 50 services that depend on it fail too, and 50 alerts arriving together tell the engineer less than 1 that names the database. The notification itself is delivered by the notification service of chapter 13, with escalation to a second person if the first does not acknowledge it.

One further case deserves mention because it is so often overlooked. A rule that tests whether a value is too high does not fire when there is no value at all. If a service stops reporting altogether, its error rate is not high, it is absent, and a naively written alert remains silent during the worst failure of all. Every important series therefore needs a second rule that fires when data has ceased to arrive.

Watching the watcher

The monitoring system is relied upon precisely when other things are failing, and its design has to take account of that.

It must not share the fate of what it monitors. If it runs on the same machines, the same network and the same storage as the services it watches, a single failure may remove both, and the engineers are left without information exactly when they need it most. It is therefore given infrastructure of its own, and kept as simple and as free of dependencies as its function allows. A monitoring system that needs the message queue, the coordinator and the object store all to be healthy before it can display a graph will be unavailable in most serious incidents.

It must also withstand the load that incidents themselves produce. When something breaks, many engineers open many dashboards together, each issuing dozens of queries over long ranges, at the very moment when the stream of incoming measurements may also be surging. The paths for writing and for querying are separated, so that a flood of queries cannot delay the storing of new points, and queries are bounded in the time and memory they may consume.

Finally, something has to watch the monitoring system itself. The usual arrangement is a second, minimal instance that checks nothing except whether the first is alive and evaluating its rules, and that raises its own alert through an independent channel when it is not.

Use cases

Services report measurements. Engineers look at graphs, define alerts and are notified.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0The system collects measurements from every service at a fixed interval.
1An engineer can query any series, or a combination of series selected by labels, over any range of time.
2Percentiles of durations can be computed across any group of machines.
3An engineer can define alerts, each a query, a condition and a duration.
4When an alert fires, the people responsible are notified.
5Data is kept at full resolution for 15 days and at lower resolution for 2 years.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0Scale10 million series, sampled every 10 seconds: 1 million points per second.
1Latency of queriesA dashboard covering the last 6 hours loads within 1 second.
2FreshnessA point is visible in queries within 30 seconds of being measured.
3Availability99.9%, and independent of the systems that are monitored.
4DurabilityThe loss of a few seconds of points in a failure is acceptable. The loss of history is not.
5ConsistencyEventual. 2 queries moments apart may differ in the most recent points.

Non-functional requirement 4 distinguishes 2 things that are often run together. A single point of a metric is nearly worthless: if 10 seconds of 1 series are lost, a graph shows a small gap and no decision is affected. The accumulated history is valuable, since it is what allows this week to be compared with the same week of last year. The design accordingly accepts weak durability for incoming points, which keeps the write path cheap, and stores completed blocks with the full protection of the object store of chapter 16.
