The API

Under the pull model, a service takes no action to report. It answers a request from a collector with its current values. The API of the monitoring system itself is used by dashboards and by the people who define alerts.

What a collector receives from a service

GET /metrics HTTP/1.1
Host: payments-14.internal

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain

requests_total{service="payments",status="200"} 918234
requests_total{service="payments",status="500"} 417
queue_length{service="payments"} 12
request_duration_bucket{service="payments",le="0.05"} 880112
request_duration_bucket{service="payments",le="0.25"} 915540
request_duration_bucket{service="payments",le="+Inf"} 918651

Each line is the present value of 1 series. The lines of request_duration_bucket are a histogram: le is the upper bound of a bucket in seconds, and each count includes every request that took no longer than that.

Query a series over a range

GET /v1/series?query=rate(requests_total{service="payments",status="500"})&from=2026-10-14T08:00:00Z&to=2026-10-14T09:00:00Z&step=60 HTTP/1.1
Host: metrics.internal

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "step": 60,
  "points": [
    { "time": "2026-10-14T08:00:00Z", "value": 0.02 },
    { "time": "2026-10-14T08:01:00Z", "value": 0.03 }
  ]
}

Define an alert

PUT /v1/alerts/payments-errors HTTP/1.1
Host: metrics.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "rate(requests_total{service=\"payments\",status=\"500\"}) / rate(requests_total{service=\"payments\"})",
  "condition": "> 0.01",
  "for_seconds": 300,
  "notify": "payments-on-call"
}

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

The rule fires when more than 1% of the requests to payments have failed continuously for 5 minutes.

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Collectorvisits each service and reads its valuesthe list of servicesits services are visited by another collector
Series storeappends points, and compresses finished blockscurrent blocks in memory, with a log, and finished blocks on diska replica that received the same points answers
Rollup jobreduces old points to 1 per minute and 1 per hournoneit is run again
Query servicereads blocks and computes what a graph or a rule asks fora cache of recent resultsanother instance answers
Alert evaluatorevaluates every rule once a minutewhich alerts are firinga second evaluator runs the same rules

One measurement, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 24.5.

  1. Every 10 seconds, a collector asks each of its services for its current values.
  2. The collector attaches the time to each value and sends the points to the series store, which appends each to the current block of its series.
  3. A dashboard sends a query. The query service finds the blocks that cover the range, decodes them, and computes the result.
  4. In the background, the rollup job reads blocks that are some hours old and writes 1 point for each minute.
  5. Once a minute, the alert evaluator runs the query of every rule, and notifies the people named when a condition has held for long enough.

So that the loss of 1 machine of the series store leaves no gap, every point is sent to 2 machines, each of which builds its own blocks independently. The 2 copies are not kept identical by any protocol, and may differ by a point here and there. For this data that is acceptable, and the query service merges whatever it receives.

The design, deployed

The system watches 100000 service instances with 60 collectors, arranged so that every group of services is visited by 2 of them. Each collector sends its points to 2 nodes of the series store, which build their blocks independently, and finished blocks are copied to an object store. The reading tier is kept apart from the writing tier, with its own machines, so that a flood of queries during an incident cannot delay the storing of new points. The last box is the smallest and among the most important: a second, minimal monitor in another place, which checks nothing except that the first is alive.

How real systems do it

The compression described in this chapter is that of Gorilla, an in-memory store that Facebook described in 2015. The paper introduced the 2 techniques together: storing each timestamp as the difference between successive differences, and storing each value as the result of combining its bits with those of the previous value, which for a floating-point number that changes little leaves mostly zeros. It reports an average of 1.37 bytes for each point against 16 uncompressed, a reduction of 12 times, which is somewhat better than the 2 bytes of the simulation here, whose encoding works on whole bytes. The paper also argues for the priorities adopted in this chapter, that a monitoring store should favour availability for writing and for recent reads over consistency, and should tolerate the loss of a small amount of data.

Prometheus is the widely used system that collects by pulling, and its storage engine adopts Gorilla’s encoding, with blocks of 2 hours that are written once and merged into larger blocks as they age. Google’s Monarch, described in 2020, is a system on a far larger scale that receives pushes and keeps recent data in memory in every region, and its paper gives as a design principle the independence from other systems that this chapter set out under watching the watcher.

The advice on alerts is drawn from Google’s book on site reliability engineering, which distinguishes symptoms from causes and proposes 4 signals to watch for any service that answers requests: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. The danger of the average, and the way in which a small proportion of slow requests comes to affect most users of a service built from many parts, is the subject of a well known article by Dean and Barroso.

For percentiles, fixed buckets are the simplest histogram, and better ones exist. More recent structures choose their buckets so that the relative error of any percentile is bounded, and can still be merged across machines, which removes the need to guess the boundaries in advance.

Summary

  • Metrics are numbers measured repeatedly, of 3 kinds: counters, gauges and histograms.
  • Every combination of label values is a separate series, and a label with unbounded values will exhaust the system.
  • Pulling lets the monitoring system notice a service that has fallen silent, and pushing suits jobs that live for seconds.
  • Points arrive in order and resemble their predecessors, so that storing each as its change from the one before takes about 2 bytes.
  • Old data is reduced to 1 point for each minute or hour, keeping the smallest value, the largest, the sum and the count.
  • An average of response times hides the slow requests that users notice, and percentiles must be computed from histograms because they cannot be combined.
  • An alert should concern what users experience, hold for some time before firing, demand an action, and have a companion that fires when data stops.
  • The monitoring system runs on infrastructure of its own, and is itself watched by something independent.

File Sync: System Design

A file synchronisation service keeps the same folder on several devices. A person saves a document on a laptop, and a few seconds later the same document, with the same changes, is on their phone and their desktop computer, without anything having been copied by hand. If a device is switched off or out of reach at the time, it receives the changes when it next connects. From the user’s side the service is nearly invisible, a folder that is the same everywhere.

Behind that simplicity lies a problem of replication with a feature that the replicated stores of earlier chapters were spared. In chapter 3 a single leader accepted all the writes of a shard, and the followers had only to copy what the leader decided. Here every device is a place where writes originate, and devices write while they are disconnected, sometimes for days. A laptop on a flight and a phone in the mountains may each change the same file, in different ways, with neither able to learn of the other until both return. No arrangement of leaders can prevent this, since the devices cannot reach any leader at the time. The service has to accept that conflicting changes will be made, detect them reliably when they come to light, and resolve them without destroying anybody’s work.

The other half of the design is economy. Files are large, the connections of mobile devices are slow and often charged by volume, and a service that transferred a whole file of 500 MB because 1 paragraph of it had changed would be unusable. Much of the engineering lies in transferring exactly what has changed and nothing else.

This chapter covers

  • a file as a list of chunks, with the bytes in 1 place and the list in another
  • transferring only the chunks that have changed
  • why cutting a file at fixed positions fails when a byte is inserted
  • cuts that depend on the content
  • versions, and detecting that 2 devices have changed the same file
  • what to do with a conflict
  • how a device learns that something has changed
  • how a device catches up after being offline
  • deleting, renaming, and the order in which things are uploaded

A file as a list of chunks

The service does not store a file as a single object. It follows the practice of the object store in chapter 16: a file is cut into chunks of moderate size, each chunk is identified by a checksum of its contents, and the file itself is represented by the list of the checksums of its chunks, in order.

The representation divides the data into 2 parts of very different character. The chunks are large, immutable and without structure, and are kept in a chunk store, which is an object store. The lists, together with the names of the files, their versions and their positions in folders, are the metadata. They are small, frequently changed, and have to be strongly consistent, and they are kept in a replicated database.

Several properties that the service needs follow from this division with little further effort. Identical chunks have identical checksums and are stored once, whether they occur in 2 versions of a file, in 2 files, or in the folders of 2 different users. The previous versions of a file cost almost nothing to retain, since an old version is merely an old list, most of whose chunks are shared with the new one. And a transfer that is interrupted can be resumed, since the chunks that arrived are already in the store and need not be sent again.

Transferring only what changed

When a file is modified, the device cuts the new contents into chunks, computes their checksums, and compares the resulting list with the list of the version it previously held. The chunks whose checksums already appear are in the store and need not be sent. Only the chunks with new checksums are uploaded, followed by the new list.

A device that receives the change proceeds in the mirror image. It obtains the new list, compares it with the chunks it holds locally, downloads those it lacks, and assembles the new version of the file from old and new chunks together.

If a paragraph is altered in the middle of a document of 100 MB that has been cut into chunks of 4 MB, 1 chunk of the 25 has changed, and 4 MB are transferred in place of 100. The scheme has, however, a weakness that depends on how the file is cut, and it is serious enough to determine the design.

Where to cut

The obvious way of cutting a file is at fixed positions, after every 4 MB. This serves well when a file is modified by overwriting some of its bytes in place, and very badly when bytes are inserted or removed.

Suppose that a single byte is added at the very beginning of a file. Every byte that follows is now 1 position later than it was. The first chunk consists of the new byte and the first 4 MB less 1 byte of the old content, the second chunk begins 1 byte earlier in the old content than it used to, and so on to the end. Although the content is all but unchanged, every chunk contains different bytes from before and has a different checksum, and the entire file is uploaded again. Inserting text near the start of a document, which is among the commonest of all edits, defeats the scheme completely.

The remedy is to let the content itself determine where the cuts fall. The device passes a small window, of a few dozen bytes, along the file, computing at each position a hash of the bytes in the window. Wherever the hash satisfies some fixed condition, for instance that its lowest 22 bits are all 0, a cut is made. Since the condition is met on average once in every 4 million positions, the chunks have an average size of 4 MB, though they vary in length. This technique is called content-defined chunking.

Its value lies in the fact that a cut now depends only on the few bytes around it. When a byte is inserted at the start of the file, the positions of all later cuts shift by 1 along with the content, and each still falls between the same 2 pieces of content as before. The chunks after the first therefore contain exactly the bytes they contained previously and have the same checksums.

The simulation for this chapter makes the comparison on a file of 64 KB, with small chunks so that the effect is visible. After 1 byte is added at the start, cuts every 1024 bytes leave all 65 chunks to be uploaded again, and cuts that depend on the content leave 1 of 62.

The hash of the window has to be computed at every position in the file, and would be slow if it were calculated from nothing each time. A rolling hash is designed so that when the window advances by 1 byte, the new value is obtained from the old by removing the contribution of the byte that has left and adding that of the byte that has entered, in a constant number of operations. Limits are also set on the size of a chunk in both directions, so that an unlucky stretch of content yields neither a swarm of tiny chunks nor a single enormous one.

Versions and conflicts

Every file has a version, a number that the metadata store increases by 1 each time the file is changed. A device records, for each file, the version on which its local copy is based.

When a device uploads a change, it states that version: “here is a new list of chunks for this file, which I produced by modifying version 3”. The service compares the stated version with the current one. If the file is still at version 3, nobody else has changed it in the meantime, and the upload is accepted as version 4. If the file is by now at version 4 or beyond, some other device has changed it since this device last looked, and the upload is rejected as a conflict.

This is the conditional write of chapter 1, the If-Match header under another name, and it is the foundation on which the correctness of the whole service rests. Without it, the later of 2 uploads would silently replace the earlier, and one person’s work would vanish with no indication that it had ever existed.

The comparison and the update have to be a single atomic operation in the metadata store. If 2 devices upload within the same instant, exactly 1 must succeed, and this is the principal reason why the metadata is held in a strongly consistent database.

What to do with a conflict

Detecting a conflict is a precise matter. Deciding what to do about it is a question of policy, on which reasonable designs differ.

The simplest policy is that the last writer prevails, the later upload replacing the earlier. It needs no intervention from the user and silently discards somebody’s work, and it is acceptable only for data whose loss nobody would mind.

The policy adopted by most services for ordinary files is to keep both. The version that arrived first remains under the original name, and the other is saved beside it under a name that marks it as a conflicting copy, with the device and the date. Nothing is lost, and the user, who alone knows what the 2 edits were meant to achieve, combines them by hand. It is a slightly awkward outcome and an honest one.

For certain kinds of content the 2 changes can be merged automatically. If 2 people have edited different paragraphs of a text, both edits can be applied. This requires the service to understand the structure of the content, and is the subject of chapter 26. A service that synchronises arbitrary files treats them as opaque bytes and cannot attempt it, since 2 edits to a spreadsheet or an image cannot be combined by anything that does not know what a spreadsheet or an image is.

Learning that something changed

A device has to find out that a file was changed elsewhere. It could ask the service at regular intervals, and this is the polling that chapter 18 examined and found wanting: frequent polling wastes requests and battery when nothing is happening, and infrequent polling delays every change.

The service therefore uses the remedy of chapter 18. Each device keeps a connection open to a notification service, and when a change is accepted, the service informs the other devices of the same account over their connections. The message carries no content. It says only that something has changed, and the device, on receiving it, asks the metadata service what.

That question is answered by means of a cursor, exactly as in chapter 18. The metadata store keeps for each account an ordered list of every change, each with a sequence number: file 7 changed to version 4, file 12 deleted, folder 3 renamed. A device remembers the number of the last change it has applied and asks for everything after that. The same request serves a device that was told of a change a second ago and one that has been switched off for a month, and the service keeps no record of which device has received what.

The design of chapter 18 thus reappears almost unaltered: a signal to attract attention, which is permitted to be lost, and a cursor from which the true state is recovered, which is not. It is among the most reusable patterns in this book.

Deleting, renaming and order

A few matters of detail cause a disproportionate share of the defects in services of this kind.

A deletion has to be synchronised like any other change, and it cannot be represented by the mere absence of a file. Were a device to see only that a file is missing from the list, it could not distinguish a file that was deleted elsewhere from a file that it has itself created a moment ago and has yet to upload. A deletion is therefore recorded as an explicit entry in the list of changes, sometimes called a tombstone, and the file’s chunks are retained for a time so that the deletion can be undone.

A rename should be recorded as a rename, an operation on the metadata alone. If it were treated as the deletion of one file and the creation of another, every device would download again a file whose bytes it already held. With chunks identified by their checksums, even that naive treatment would in fact transfer nothing, since the “new” file consists of chunks that are already present, which is a further dividend of content addressing.

The order of an upload matters for the same reason that it did in chapter 16. The chunks are uploaded first, and the new list is committed to the metadata store last. The list is what makes the new version exist for other devices, and at that moment every chunk it refers to must already be in the store. An upload interrupted halfway leaves a few chunks that nothing refers to, to be collected later as garbage, and never a version that other devices are told of and cannot assemble.

Finally, a file that is still being written should not be uploaded. An application saving a large file writes it over several seconds, and a device that began uploading at the first change would send a partial file, followed at once by another. Devices wait until a file has been unchanged for a short period before treating it as modified.

Use cases

A person changes files on 1 device, sees the changes on another, and occasionally has to settle a conflict.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A change made to a file on 1 device appears on the user’s other devices.
1A device that was offline receives every change made in its absence when it reconnects.
2Only the parts of a file that have changed are transferred.
3When 2 devices change the same file independently, neither change is lost.
4Earlier versions of a file can be restored for 30 days.
5A deleted file can be restored for 30 days.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0DurabilityA file whose upload was confirmed is not lost.
1ConsistencyStrong for metadata: of 2 uploads based on the same version, exactly 1 is accepted. Eventual between devices.
2LatencyA change reaches a connected device within 5 seconds.
3EconomyThe bytes transferred are proportional to the size of the change and not to the size of the file.
4Scale100 million users, 10 billion files, 1 EB of content.

Non-functional requirement 1 sets 2 consistency models side by side, and it is worth being clear about where each applies. Among the devices, the system is eventually consistent by necessity, since a device that is switched off cannot possibly have the latest version. The metadata store that arbitrates among them is strongly consistent, and it has to be, because the detection of conflicts depends on every upload being compared with the true current version. The service as a whole can tolerate devices that are far behind precisely because, at its centre, there is 1 place that is never in doubt about what the latest version is.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 1 EB of content in chunks of 4 MB is 250 billion chunks, and the metadata for 10 billion files comes to about 5 TB.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Chunks1 EB ÷ 4 MB250 billion
Metadata per filename, version, folder, and 25 checksums of 16 bytes on averageabout 500 bytes
Metadata for all files10 billion × 500 bytes5 TB
Open connections100 million users × 2 devices × 20% online40 million
Changes per second100 million users × 20 changes a day ÷ 86400about 23000

The API

A device first learns which chunks the store lacks, uploads those, and then commits the new version, stating the version it started from.

Ask which chunks are missing

POST /v1/chunk-queries HTTP/1.1
Host: sync.example
Content-Type: application/json

{ "checksums": ["9f2c", "41aa", "c07e"] }

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "missing": ["c07e"] }

The resource created is a query, which is why the request is a POST to a collection of queries and the answer comes back at once. Only the chunk c07e has to be uploaded.

Upload a chunk

PUT /v1/chunks/c07e HTTP/1.1
Host: sync.example
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Length: 4194304

(4194304 bytes)

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

The address of a chunk is its checksum, so that uploading the same chunk twice is harmless and PUT is the proper method.

Commit a new version of a file

PUT /v1/files/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: sync.example
If-Match: "3"
Content-Type: application/json

{ "path": "notes.txt", "chunks": ["9f2c", "41aa", "c07e"] }

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "4"
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 7, "version": 4 }

The same commit from a device that is behind

PUT /v1/files/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: sync.example
If-Match: "3"
Content-Type: application/json

{ "path": "notes.txt", "chunks": ["9f2c", "77b0", "c07e"] }

HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/version-conflict",
  "title": "The file has been changed by another device",
  "status": 412,
  "current_version": 4
}

Fetch the changes since a cursor

GET /v1/changes?after=5120 HTTP/1.1
Host: sync.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "changes": [
    { "number": 5121, "file": 7, "kind": "modified", "version": 4, "chunks": ["9f2c", "41aa", "c07e"] },
    { "number": 5122, "file": 12, "kind": "deleted" }
  ],
  "next_after": 5122
}

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Devicewatches a folder, cuts files into chunks, uploads and downloadsthe files, and a cursorit catches up from its cursor when it returns
Chunk storekeeps chunks by checksumevery chunk, as in chapter 16as in chapter 16
Sync servicecompares versions and commits changesnoneanother instance serves the request
Metadata storeholds files, versions, chunk lists and the list of changesall metadata, replicateda follower is elected
Notifierholds a connection to every online deviceconnections, in memorydevices reconnect and fetch from their cursors

One change, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 25.5.

  1. The laptop notices that a file has changed and has been still for 2 seconds. It cuts the file into chunks, asks which of them the store lacks, and uploads those.
  2. It sends the new list of chunks to the sync service, together with the version on which its change was based.
  3. The sync service asks the metadata store to replace the list if the file is still at that version. The store does so, increases the version, and appends an entry to the account’s list of changes.
  4. The sync service tells the notifier that the account has a change.
  5. The notifier passes the signal to the phone over its open connection. The phone asks for the changes after its cursor, downloads the chunks it lacks from the chunk store, assembles the file, and moves its cursor forward.

The design, deployed

The deployment separates 3 kinds of traffic that have nothing in common. Small requests about metadata go through load balancers to the 100 instances of the sync service and from there to the metadata store, which is sharded by account with 3 replicas of each shard. Long-lived connections, 1 for every online device, are held by 400 notifiers, a tier of the same kind as the gateways of chapter 18. And the bytes of the files travel directly between the devices and the chunk store, without passing through either of the other tiers, which is what keeps them small.

How real systems do it

Dropbox has described the protocol of its service, and it matches the outline of this chapter closely. A file is divided into blocks of 4 MB, each named by a cryptographic hash of its contents, and the list of those hashes identifies the contents of the file. To upload, a client sends the list to a metadata server. If the server lacks some of the blocks, it says which, the client sends them to a separate block server, and the commit is then repeated and recorded in a journal of changes for the account, which is the ordered list of changes from which other clients read with a cursor.

In 1 respect the published design differs from the recommendation of this chapter, and the difference should be stated plainly. Dropbox’s blocks are of fixed size. Cutting at positions determined by the content, which this chapter presents as the remedy for insertions, is the method of the Low-Bandwidth File System, a research system of 2001, and it is used today mainly by backup programs, for which deduplication across many versions matters most. A fixed block size is simpler, and a service can limit the damage of an insertion by other means, notably by transferring within a changed block only the differences from its previous version. That technique comes from rsync, whose rolling checksum is the original of the rolling hash described above.

The cost of the rolling hash has itself been reduced. A method published in 2016 replaces the traditional fingerprint by a much cheaper one and adjusts the condition for a cut so as to avoid very small and very large chunks, and reports chunking several times faster with nearly the same deduplication.

For the storage of the blocks, Dropbox built its own system of the kind described in chapter 16, holding exabytes, and has described rewriting its client’s synchronisation engine after concluding that the hardest part of the problem is the client, which has to reconcile the server’s view with a local file system that other programs are changing all the time.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Uploading whole filesA small edit to a large file transfers all of it.Cut files into chunks and upload only the new ones.
Cutting at fixed positionsAn insertion near the start changes every chunk.Let the content determine the cuts.
Accepting an upload without its base versionThe later of 2 edits silently replaces the earlier.Require the version the change was based on, and compare it atomically.
Resolving conflicts by letting the last writer prevailSomebody’s work is discarded without notice.Keep both versions, and let the user decide.
Committing the list before the chunksOther devices are told of a version they cannot assemble.Upload the chunks first and commit the list last.
Polling for changesBattery and requests are wasted, or changes arrive late.Signal over an open connection, and fetch from a cursor.
Trusting the signal to carry the changeA lost signal is a lost change.Treat the signal as a hint, and recover from the cursor.
Representing a deletion by absenceA device cannot tell a deleted file from one it has just created.Record deletions as explicit entries.
Treating a rename as delete and createThe history of the file is broken, and work may be repeated.Record a rename as a change to metadata.
Uploading a file while it is being writtenPartial files are synchronised, followed by more partial files.Wait until the file has been still for a moment.
Deleting chunks as soon as a file is deletedChunks shared with other files or needed for restoring are lost.Collect unreferenced chunks later, after a period of grace.

Failures

FailureWhat users seeHow the system recovers
A device loses its connection during an uploadthe file shows as still synchronisingthe chunks already uploaded are kept, and the upload resumes with the rest
2 devices change the same filea second file marked as a conflicting copyboth versions are kept
The signal of a change is lostthe change appears a little laterthe device also fetches from its cursor at intervals and on reconnecting
A device is offline for a monthnothing, until it reconnectsit fetches every change after its cursor
The reply to a commit is lostthe device tries againthe retry finds the file already at the new version with the same chunks, and treats it as success
The metadata store’s leader failscommits fail for about 1 seconda follower is elected

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Chunks identified by checksumsmall transfers, shared storage, cheap old versionsmetadata for every chunk, and garbage to collect
Cuts that depend on the contentinsertions change 1 chunkchunks of uneven size, and a hash at every byte
Strong consistency for metadataconflicts are always detectedcommits wait for a majority
Keeping both versions in a conflictnothing is lostthe user has to combine them
A signal and a cursorprompt delivery that survives lost signalsa connection for every online device

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/syncsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p syncsim in the code directory.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Synchronisationbringing copies of the same data on several devices into agreement
Chunka piece of a file, identified by a checksum of its contents
Metadatathe names, versions, folders and chunk lists of files
Content-defined chunkingcutting a file where its content satisfies a condition
Rolling hasha hash of a moving window that is updated in constant time as the window advances
Versiona number that increases with every change to a file
Conflict2 changes to the same file, each made without knowledge of the other
Conflicting copythe second of 2 conflicting versions, kept under another name
Cursorthe number of the last change a device has applied
Tombstonean explicit record that something was deleted

Summary

  • A file is a list of chunks identified by checksum, with the chunks in an object store and the lists in a strongly consistent metadata store.
  • A device uploads only the chunks that the store does not already hold.
  • Cuts at fixed positions make an insertion change every chunk, and cuts that depend on the content confine the change to 1.
  • Every upload states the version it was based on, and an upload based on an old version is a conflict.
  • In a conflict both versions are kept, since the service cannot know which edit the user would prefer.
  • Devices are signalled over an open connection and fetch changes from a cursor, so that a lost signal delays a change and loses nothing.
  • Chunks are uploaded before the list that refers to them, and deletions are recorded explicitly.

Collaborative Editing: System Design

In a collaborative editor, several people work on the same document at once. Each sees the others’ changes appear as they are made, character by character, with a coloured cursor marking where each person is typing, and nobody has to save, send or merge anything. The experience is that of several pens writing on a single sheet of paper.

The previous chapter dealt with 2 devices that had changed the same file, and resolved the matter by keeping both versions and asking the user to choose. In an editor that answer is not available. Conflicting changes are here the ordinary condition, by no means an occasional accident: whenever 2 people type within the same fraction of a second, each has changed the document without knowledge of the other’s change, and this happens many times a minute. The editor cannot present a conflict for a human to settle on every keystroke. It has to combine concurrent changes automatically, in a way that keeps every participant’s intention, and it has to do so in such a manner that everybody ends with exactly the same document.

That last requirement, known as convergence, is the difficult one. Each person’s own keystrokes must appear on their own screen at once, since nobody will tolerate typing into an editor that waits for a server before showing a letter. Every participant therefore applies their own changes first and the others’ afterwards, which means that different participants apply the same changes in different orders, and the result must nevertheless be identical for all of them. This chapter explains why the obvious representation of a change fails that test, and then the 2 families of solution that are in use.

This chapter covers

  • why each person’s changes must take effect at once on their own screen
  • changes described by position, and how 2 of them go wrong
  • operational transformation, which adjusts a change for what its author had not seen
  • the role of a central server in ordering changes
  • conflict-free replicated data types, which give every character a name
  • deleting, and why deleted characters cannot disappear
  • cursors, presence and working offline
  • storing a document as a log of operations with snapshots

Changes that take effect at once

The simplest way of building a shared editor would be to treat the document as a value in a strongly consistent store. A keystroke would be sent to the server, the server would apply it, and the new document would be returned to everybody. All participants would see the same thing, because there would be only 1 copy.

It would also be unusable. Every character would appear on the typist’s own screen only after a round trip to the server, some 50 to 200 ms later, and on a poor connection later still. People notice a delay of that size in their own typing within a few characters, and find it intolerable.

An editor therefore applies each change to the local copy of the document immediately, and sends it to the others afterwards. This is the same decision that chapter 18 took when it displayed a sent message before the server had confirmed it, and it has a far-reaching consequence. Each participant now holds a copy of the document that is momentarily ahead of everyone else’s in respect of their own changes, and behind in respect of the others’. The copies are replicas in the full sense, every one of them accepts writes, and the system is one of replication with many writers and no possibility of coordination before a write.

2 changes by position

A change to a text is most naturally described as an operation on a position: insert this character at position 5, or delete the character at position 9. This is how a single-user editor works internally, and it is entirely adequate so long as every operation is applied to the same text that its author was looking at.

With 2 people editing concurrently, that condition fails, and the consequences can be followed in a small example.

Ada inserted an h at position 1, and Bob an s at position 3, which at the time was the end of the word. When Bob’s operation reaches Ada, her text has already changed: her own h has moved every later character 1 place to the right, and position 3 no longer means what it meant to Bob. The operation is applied faithfully and lands in the wrong place. Ada’s operation, arriving at Bob’s copy, is unaffected, since nothing before position 1 has moved. The 2 copies now read chast and chats.

The simulation for this chapter runs exactly this case and prints the 2 different results. The copies have diverged, and the fault will never correct itself, since each later operation is applied to 2 different texts and can only compound the difference.

The root of the trouble is that a position is not a stable way of referring to a place in a text. It is meaningful only relative to a particular state of the document, and an operation that travels to another replica arrives at a different state. The 2 families of solution correspond to the 2 possible remedies. One may keep positions and correct them on arrival, or one may abandon positions for something that does not go out of date.

Adjusting a change for what its author had not seen

The first remedy is called operational transformation, usually abbreviated OT. Before an operation that was made concurrently with others is applied, it is transformed so as to take account of them.

In the example, Bob’s insertion at position 3 was made without knowledge of Ada’s insertion at position 1. Ada’s character was placed before position 3 and so displaced it by 1. The transformed operation is therefore an insertion at position 4, and applied to Ada’s text it yields chats. Ada’s operation is transformed against Bob’s in turn. Bob’s character was placed after position 1 and displaced nothing before it, so Ada’s operation is unchanged, and Bob’s text becomes chats as well. The last step of the picture above shows the outcome, and the simulation confirms it.

For insertions the rule is short. An insertion is moved 1 place to the right for every concurrent insertion that was made at an earlier position. A further rule is needed for the case in which 2 people insert at the very same position, where some fixed convention, such as giving precedence to the participant with the smaller identifier, must decide which character comes first, and must decide it identically on every replica.

Deletions add further cases. An insertion after a concurrently deleted character moves 1 place to the left. 2 participants who both delete the same character must between them delete it once. An insertion in the middle of a range that somebody else is deleting must survive. For each pair of kinds of operation there is a transformation, and the difficulty of OT lies in the number of these cases and in the requirement that they agree with one another: whichever order a replica happens to receive 2 concurrent operations in, transforming and applying them must lead to the same text. Published algorithms have been found, years afterwards, to violate this requirement in obscure combinations.

What a central server contributes

The difficulty is greatly reduced by a decision about architecture. If participants exchanged operations directly with one another, each might see the operations in a different order, and the transformations would have to be correct for every possible order among any number of participants. Nearly all practical systems avoid this by routing every operation through a central server.

The server gives the document a single, agreed history. It maintains a revision number, which counts the operations applied so far. A participant sends each operation together with the revision of the document on which it was based. The server compares that revision with its current one. If others have been applied since, the server transforms the incoming operation against each of them in order, applies the result, assigns it the next revision number, and sends the transformed operation to all the other participants. Each participant, meanwhile, transforms the operations it receives from the server against any of its own that the server has not yet acknowledged.

With this arrangement, every transformation involves only 2 sequences: what the server has applied, and what 1 client has pending. The server is the single place at which order is decided, exactly as the leader of a shard was in chapter 3 and the message store was in chapter 18, and the general lesson holds here too, that a problem of ordering among many parties becomes tractable when 1 of them is appointed to decide the order.

The price is the usual one. The server must be reachable for collaboration to proceed. A participant who is offline can continue to type, and the operations accumulate locally, but they are merged only on reconnection, by transformation against everything that has happened in the meantime.

A name for every character

The second remedy removes the cause of the trouble. If positions go out of date, characters can be referred to by something that does not.

In this approach every character is given, at the moment it is typed, a unique identifier that it keeps for ever. The identifiers are chosen so that they can be ordered, and the text is defined as the characters arranged in the order of their identifiers. An insertion no longer says “at position 3”. It says “a new character with this identifier”, and the identifier is chosen to fall between those of the 2 characters where the author placed it.

An operation of this form has a remarkable property. It refers to nothing that another operation can alter, and applying it consists merely in adding 1 element to a sorted collection. 2 such operations can be applied in either order with the same result, and an operation applied twice has the same effect as once. No transformation is required, and no server is needed to decide an order, since order is irrelevant.

A data structure whose operations can be applied in any order, any number of times, with every replica arriving at the same state, is called a conflict-free replicated data type, or CRDT. In the simulation, the same 2 insertions are applied in both orders to a text represented in this way, and both replicas read chats. When both participants insert at the same place, the identifiers are distinguished by the identity of the device, and both replicas read carnt, with the characters in the same order on each.

The identifiers have to satisfy 2 conditions. They must be unique, which is arranged by including the identity of the device in each. And it must always be possible to create a new identifier between any 2 existing ones, however close together. Whole numbers do not suffice, since nothing lies between 1500 and 1501. Practical schemes use sequences of numbers of variable length, compared as the entries of a dictionary are, so that between any 2 a longer one can be found, or else define each character’s place by reference to the identifier of the character it was typed after.

The cost of a name

The simplicity of the operations is bought with metadata. A plain text of 10000 characters occupies 10000 bytes. The same text as a CRDT carries an identifier for every character, which may be 10 or 20 times the size of the character itself, and identifiers of the dictionary kind grow longer wherever a great deal of text has been inserted in the same place. Much of the engineering in CRDT libraries is devoted to compressing this, for instance by storing a run of characters typed in succession by 1 person as a single unit with 1 identifier and a length.

Automatic merging has a further limit, which applies to both families and which no algorithm can remove. Convergence guarantees that all replicas end with the same text. It does not guarantee that the text is what anybody meant. If 2 people correct the same misspelt word simultaneously, each by deleting it and typing it again, the merged document contains the corrected word twice. The result is consistent and wrong, and what collaborative editors rely upon in practice is that people can see each other’s cursors, and tend not to edit the same word at the same moment.

Deleting

Deletion presents a difficulty of its own in a CRDT. Suppose that Ada deletes a character at the same moment that Bob inserts a new one immediately after it, his operation saying in effect “after the character with identifier 2000”. If Ada’s replica had removed that character altogether, Bob’s operation would arrive referring to something that no longer exists there.

A deleted character is therefore not removed. It is marked as deleted and hidden from view, and its identifier remains in the structure to serve as a point of reference. Such a marker is the tombstone of chapter 25. The consequence is that a document which has been heavily edited contains far more tombstones than visible characters, and they can be discarded only when it is certain that no replica anywhere still holds an operation that refers to them, which, with participants who may be offline for weeks, is difficult to establish.

The 2 approaches compared

Operational transformationCRDT
How an operation refers to a placeby positionby the identifier of a character
What makes replicas convergetransforming operations against concurrent onesoperations that give the same result in any order
Central serverrequired, to fix the ordernot required
Working offline, or peer to peerawkward: everything is transformed on returnnatural: operations are merged whenever they meet
Size of the documentclose to the plain textseveral times the plain text, with tombstones
Where the complexity liesin the transformation rulesin the identifiers and their compaction

Services in which a server is always in the path, and in which documents are large and long-lived, have mostly used operational transformation. Applications that must work offline for long periods, or without any central server, have mostly used CRDTs. The design in the remainder of this chapter uses a central server with operational transformation.

Around the text

A collaborative editor conveys more than the text. Each participant sees where the others’ cursors and selections are, and who is present in the document. This information is ephemeral: it is forwarded to the other participants as it changes and is stored nowhere, since a cursor position that is lost is replaced by the next one a moment later. It is the presence of chapter 18, with the same loose guarantees.

Cursors are nonetheless subject to the central problem of this chapter. A cursor is a position in the text, and when another participant inserts characters before it, it has to move. A cursor is therefore transformed against incoming operations in the way that an operation would be, or, in a CRDT, is attached to the identifier of a character, which does not move.

Undo also needs rethinking. In an editor for 1 person, undo reverses the most recent change. In a shared document the most recent change may be somebody else’s, and to reverse it would be bewildering. Undo is accordingly made to reverse the most recent change of the person who invokes it, which requires the inverse of an operation that is no longer the latest and has to be transformed against everything that came after.

Storing the document

The server retains every operation, in order, in a log, each with its revision number. The document at any revision is the result of applying the operations up to that point, so that the log is the authoritative record and the current text is derived from it. This is the relation between records and entries from chapter 1, and it yields the complete history of the document, by which an author can see what it contained at any earlier moment and who changed what.

To replay the whole log each time a document is opened would grow slower with every keystroke ever made. The server therefore saves a snapshot of the text at intervals, every few hundred operations, and a document is opened by loading the latest snapshot and applying the operations that follow it. The operations before a snapshot are kept as long as history is wanted and are not needed for opening.

Each document is served, at any moment, by a single server process, which holds its current text in memory and decides the order of its operations. Documents are assigned to servers by hashing their identifiers, and every participant in a document is connected, through a gateway of the kind described in chapter 18, to that document’s server. The operation is appended to the log before it is acknowledged and broadcast, so that if the process fails, another can take over the document from the log without losing anything that was confirmed.

Use cases

An author types in a shared document, sees what the others type, and may continue while offline.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0Several authors can edit the same document at the same moment.
1An author’s own change appears on their screen immediately.
2A change by another author appears within 200 ms.
3When all changes have been delivered, every author sees the same document.
4An author sees the cursors of the other authors.
5An author who is offline can continue to edit, and the changes are merged on reconnection.
6The history of a document can be viewed, and an earlier state restored.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0ConvergenceAll replicas reach the same state once every operation has been delivered, in whatever order they were applied locally.
1DurabilityAn operation that the server has acknowledged is not lost.
2ConsistencyEventual between authors. Strong for the order of operations in the server’s log.
3LatencyA local change takes effect in under 16 ms, and a remote one within 200 ms.
4Scale10 million documents open at once, with up to 100 authors in a document.

Non-functional requirement 2 has the form that has now appeared in several chapters. The replicas that people look at are eventually consistent, each running ahead with its own changes. At the centre is a log whose order is strongly consistent and never in dispute, and the eventual consistency of the edges is made safe by the certainty of the centre. Convergence, non-functional requirement 0, is the precise statement of what “eventual” promises here.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. 10 million open documents with 2 authors typing in each produce about 10 million operations per second at the peak, and far fewer in practice, since people pause.

Skip to the high-level design

Show the calculation
QuantityCalculationResult
Authors typing at any moment10 million documents × 2 authors × 10% actually typing2 million
Operations per second2 million × 5 keystrokes per second10 million
Size of an operation in the logdocument, author, revision, position, characterabout 30 bytes
Log growth10 million × 30 bytes300 MB per second at the peak
Memory for open documents10 million × 50 KB500 GB, across the session servers

In practice operations are sent in small batches, several keystrokes together, which reduces the number of messages by a large factor without any perceptible delay.

The API

A document is opened with an ordinary request, which returns the text and its revision. From then on, operations travel in both directions over an open connection.

Open a document

GET /v1/documents/8812 HTTP/1.1
Host: docs.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 8812, "revision": 4410, "text": "cat" }

An operation sent by a client, over the open connection

{ "document": 8812, "client_id": "ada-17", "based_on": 4410, "insert": { "at": 1, "text": "h" } }

based_on is the revision that the author was looking at. client_id identifies the operation, so that if it is sent a second time after a lost acknowledgement, the server recognises it.

The server’s acknowledgement to the sender

{ "document": 8812, "client_id": "ada-17", "revision": 4412 }

The same operation as broadcast to the other authors

{ "document": 8812, "author": "ada", "revision": 4412, "insert": { "at": 1, "text": "h" } }

The operation broadcast is the transformed one, and its revision is the position it was given in the log. Revision 4411 belonged to an operation by another author that reached the server first.

Read the history of a document

GET /v1/documents/8812/operations?after=4400&limit=100 HTTP/1.1
Host: docs.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operations": [
    { "revision": 4411, "author": "bob", "insert": { "at": 3, "text": "s" } },
    { "revision": 4412, "author": "ada", "insert": { "at": 1, "text": "h" } }
  ],
  "next_after": 4412
}

High-level design

ComponentRoleState it holdsWhen 1 instance fails
Clientapplies the author’s changes at once, and transforms incoming onesits copy of the document, and operations not yet acknowledgedit reopens the document and sends its pending operations again
Session serverorders the operations of a document, transforms them, and broadcaststhe current text of each of its documents, in memoryanother server loads the document from its snapshot and log
Operation logevery operation of every document, in orderthe log, replicateda follower is elected
Snapshotsthe text of a document at intervalssnapshots, in an object storeas in chapter 16

One operation, step by step

The steps follow the arrows of figure 26.5.

  1. Author A types a character. The client applies it to its own copy at once, and sends the operation to the session server with the revision on which it was based.
  2. The session server transforms the operation against every operation applied since that revision, appends the result to the log under the next revision number, and acknowledges it to A.
  3. The server sends the transformed operation to author B, whose client transforms it against any operations of its own that the server has not yet acknowledged, and applies it.
  4. Every few hundred operations, the current text is saved as a snapshot.

The design, deployed

Authors hold connections to gateways, as in the chat service. What is particular to this system is the tier below. Each open document is owned by exactly 1 of the 300 session servers, which holds its text in memory and decides the order of its operations, and a small directory records which server owns which document, so that the gateways can route every author of a document to the same place. The session servers are therefore not interchangeable in the way that stateless servers are. If 1 fails, each of its documents is taken over by another server, which loads the latest snapshot and replays the log from there.

How real systems do it

Operational transformation was introduced in 1989, in a paper on a group editor that exchanged operations directly among its participants. The arrangement with a central server, in which each client synchronises with the server alone and the server fixes the order, is that of the Jupiter system of 1995, and it is the form that Google adopted for its collaborative documents. Its attraction is the one given in this chapter: with a server in the middle, the transformation functions have to satisfy only the simpler of the 2 correctness conditions that the general case requires. The warning that published algorithms have been found faulty refers to the other condition, needed when there is no server, for which several algorithms were shown by formal analysis to diverge in particular cases, years after they were published.

Conflict-free replicated data types were given their name and a systematic theory in 2011. For text, the scheme of this chapter, in which each character has a position drawn from a dense ordered set, is that of a family of early designs. It has a defect that should be mentioned, since the simulation does not show it. When 2 people type whole words at the same place at the same time, their characters can become interleaved letter by letter, because the positions that each chooses fall among the other’s. Designs in which a new character names the character it was typed after, and ties are broken consistently, keep each person’s run together, and the libraries in common use today work in that way.

Not every collaborative product uses either method in its pure form. The makers of Figma have described a design in which a central server orders changes, as with operational transformation, while each property of each object is a simple register in which the last write prevails, as in a basic CRDT. Their argument is that a design tool’s documents are trees of objects with properties, for which that is enough, and that the full generality of either method serves the editing of long texts and is not needed elsewhere.

Mistakes to avoid

MistakeWhat goes wrongWhat to do
Waiting for the server before showing a keystrokeTyping feels delayed and becomes unusable on a slow connection.Apply every local change at once, and reconcile afterwards.
Applying operations by position as they arriveReplicas diverge, and never recover.Transform them, or use identifiers in place of positions.
Exchanging operations between clients directlyEvery client sees a different order, and the transformations must be right for all of them.Route every operation through a server that fixes the order.
No fixed rule for 2 insertions at the same placeReplicas order the 2 characters differently.Break the tie by a rule that every replica applies alike.
Removing deleted characters from a CRDTA concurrent operation refers to a character that is gone.Keep a tombstone.
Acknowledging an operation before logging itA crash loses an edit that the author believes is saved.Append to the log first.
Replaying the whole log to open a documentOpening grows slower with every edit ever made.Save snapshots, and replay from the latest.
Storing cursors durablyA flood of writes for information that is worthless a second later.Forward cursors, and store nothing.
Undo that reverses the latest operationAn author undoes somebody else’s work.Undo the author’s own latest operation, transformed against what followed.
Assuming that convergence means correctness2 simultaneous corrections of 1 word leave it doubled.Show cursors, so that people avoid editing the same place.

Failures

FailureWhat authors seeHow the system recovers
An author’s connection dropstheir own typing continues, and others’ changes stop arrivingon reconnection, pending operations are sent and missed ones fetched from the log
The acknowledgement of an operation is lostnothingthe client sends it again, and the server recognises its identifier
A session server failsa pause of a second or 2another server loads the snapshot and the log, and the clients reconnect to it
An author is offline for a daytheir copy and the shared one differevery local operation is transformed against the day’s operations and merged
2 authors edit the same worda result that neither intended, the same on both screensthe authors see it and correct it

Trade-offs

DecisionWhat it gainsWhat it costs
Local changes applied at oncetyping with no delayreplicas that differ for a moment, and the whole problem of merging
A central servera single order, and far simpler transformationno collaboration without the server
Operational transformationdocuments close to the size of their textintricate rules that are hard to get right
A log with snapshotsfull history, and fast openingstorage that grows with every keystroke
Automatic mergingno conflict is ever put to the authorresults that are consistent and sometimes unintended

The simulation

Simulation in the repository. The program code/editsim simulates this design. To run it, clone the repository and type cargo run --release -p editsim in the code directory.

Terms introduced in this chapter

TermMeaning
Operationa description of 1 change to a document
Concurrentmade without knowledge of each other
Convergenceall replicas reaching the same state once every operation has been delivered
Divergencereplicas that hold different states and will not come together
Operational transformation, OTadjusting an operation to take account of concurrent ones
Revisionthe number of operations that the server has applied to a document
Conflict-free replicated data type, CRDTa data structure whose operations give the same result in any order
Tombstonea deleted element that is kept, hidden, as a point of reference
Ephemeralforwarded and not stored
Snapshotthe state of a document at 1 revision, saved so that earlier operations need not be replayed

Summary

  • Each author’s changes are applied to their own copy at once, so that every copy is a replica that accepts writes without coordination.
  • An operation described by position is wrong on a replica where earlier concurrent changes have moved the text, and the replicas diverge.
  • Operational transformation adjusts each operation for the concurrent ones its author had not seen.
  • A central server fixes a single order of operations, which reduces transformation to a manageable problem.
  • A CRDT gives every character an unchanging identifier, so that operations can be applied in any order and no server is needed.
  • Deleted characters are kept as tombstones, since concurrent operations may refer to them.
  • Convergence makes all copies equal, and does not make the result what anybody intended.
  • The document is a log of operations with periodic snapshots, served for each document by a single process.

Stock Exchange: System Design

A stock exchange is a place where people who wish to buy a share and people who wish to sell it are brought together. Each states the price at which they are willing to trade, and whenever a buyer’s price meets a seller’s, a trade is made. The program at the centre of a modern exchange, which keeps the outstanding orders and decides who trades with whom, is the matching engine.

The requirements laid on this program are unlike those of any other system in this book, and they lead to a design that at first sight contradicts much of what the book has recommended. An exchange must be fair, in a precise and legally enforceable sense: of 2 orders at the same price, the one that arrived first must trade first, with no exception and no ambiguity about which was first. It must be fast, answering an order in well under a millisecond, since the participants are themselves programs that compete on speed. And it must be deterministic, so that its every decision can be reconstructed afterwards and shown to a regulator.

The preceding chapters have met demands for throughput by dividing work among many machines and many threads. A matching engine does the opposite. The trading of each share is handled by a single thread on a single machine, with all its data in memory and no database in its path. This chapter explains why that is the right design for this problem, and how such a system, which appears to have a single point of failure at its heart, is nevertheless made to survive the loss of any machine.

This chapter covers

  • orders, the order book, and the rule of price and time
  • matching an incoming order against the book
  • why fairness requires a single agreed order of events
  • why the engine is 1 thread, and why that is fast
  • the journal, and recovering by replaying it
  • a standby that is ready to take over
  • the gateway, and the checks that precede matching
  • publishing prices to everybody at the same moment
  • what happens after a trade

Orders and the book

A participant expresses a wish to trade by submitting an order. The commonest kind, the limit order, names a side, a quantity and a price: buy 100 shares at 10.05 or less, or sell 50 shares at 10.10 or more. The price is a limit beyond which the participant will not go, and a better price is always acceptable.

An order that cannot be satisfied at once waits. The collection of waiting orders for 1 share is its order book, and it has 2 halves. The buy side holds the orders to buy, of which the most attractive to a seller is the one with the highest price. The sell side holds the orders to sell, of which the most attractive to a buyer is the one with the lowest. The highest price that any buyer is offering is the best bid, the lowest that any seller is asking is the best ask, and the difference between them is the spread. So long as the best bid is below the best ask, nobody is willing to trade with anybody, and the book is at rest.

Within each half the orders are ranked by a rule called price-time priority. An order at a better price ranks ahead of an order at a worse one. Among orders at the same price, the one that arrived earlier ranks ahead. The rule rewards a participant for offering a better price, and, at a given price, for having committed to it sooner, and it is the definition of fairness on which the exchange rests.

Prices are held as whole numbers of the smallest unit in which the share is quoted, for the reasons set out in chapter 19. 10.05 is the integer 1005.

Matching

When a new order arrives, the engine compares it with the best order on the opposite side of the book. If their prices meet, which for an incoming buy means that its limit is at or above the best ask, a trade is made between them, for the smaller of their 2 quantities. The trade takes place at the price of the order that was waiting in the book, and this is why an incoming order may obtain a better price than its limit. If the incoming order has quantity remaining, the engine turns to the next best waiting order and repeats. When the prices no longer meet, or the opposite side is exhausted, whatever remains of the incoming order is placed in the book to wait.

The simulation for this chapter processes these 7 orders. The first 4 rest in the book, since the cheapest seller asks 1005 and the only buyer offers 1000. Order 5, to buy 50 at 1005, trades with the 2 orders waiting at that price in the order of their arrival, taking 30 from order 2 and 20 from order 3. Order 6 takes the remainder of order 3 and all of order 1, and its unfilled 30 shares become the best bid. Order 7, a sale at 995 or better, trades at 1010 and at 1000, the prices of the buyers who were waiting. 200 shares change hands, and 10 remain in the book.

Several other kinds of order are built from the same mechanism. A market order names no price and trades at once with whatever is best on the other side, until it is filled. A cancellation removes a waiting order from the book. An order may be marked to trade immediately as far as it can and to cancel the rest, without ever resting in the book. None of these changes the essential structure.

The book has to support 3 operations efficiently: finding the best price on a side, adding an order at a price, and removing an order from anywhere within it, since most orders on a real exchange are cancelled before they trade. A usual arrangement keeps, for each side, a map from price to the queue of orders at that price, ordered by price, together with an index from order identifier to the order’s place in its queue, so that a cancellation finds its target directly.

One agreed order of events

The rule of price and time presupposes that, of any 2 orders, it is known which arrived first. On a single machine with a single connection this is trivial. On a real exchange, orders arrive over thousands of connections at several gateway machines, within microseconds of one another, and the question of which was first is by no means settled by the fact of their arrival.

The clocks of different machines cannot settle it, as chapter 8 explained at length. 2 gateways that each stamp their orders with the time will disagree by more than the interval that separates competing orders, and whichever gateway’s clock runs slow will systematically favour its own participants.

The exchange therefore establishes the order of events by decree, at a single point. Every order, cancellation and other input passes through a component called the sequencer, which assigns to each the next number in a single sequence. That number, and nothing else, defines the order in which events are deemed to have occurred. An order is “first” if the sequencer numbered it first.

This is the fourth appearance in this book of the same idea. The leader of a shard assigned sequence numbers to records in chapter 3, the message store numbered the messages of a conversation in chapter 18, and the session server numbered the operations on a document in chapter 26. In each case a question about order among many parties, which could not be answered by comparing clocks, was resolved by appointing a single party to decide.

Why the engine is a single thread

Given a single sequence of inputs, the matching of a share is an inherently sequential computation. Whether order 6 trades, and at what price, depends on exactly what the book contained after order 5, which depends on order 4, and so on to the beginning. 2 orders for the same share cannot be matched in parallel, since the result for the second depends on the first.

One might still be tempted to use several threads, protecting the book with locks. This would be both slower and worse. It would be slower because the work for each order is very small, a few lookups and updates in memory, and the cost of taking and releasing locks and of moving data between processor cores would exceed the cost of the work itself. It would be worse because the order in which threads acquire a lock is decided by the operating system’s scheduler and varies from run to run, so that the same inputs could produce different trades on different occasions.

The engine is therefore a single thread that takes inputs from the sequence one after another and processes each to completion before looking at the next. It holds the entire book in memory, waits for no disk and no network during matching, and takes no locks, since nothing else touches its data. An engine of this kind can process several hundred thousand orders a second on 1 core, with a response time of a few microseconds, which is far more than a design with locks and threads achieves. The general lesson, which applies well beyond exchanges, is that for work which is small, sequential by nature and entirely in memory, a single thread is the fastest arrangement, and no limitation that calls for apology. Chapter 6 reached a related conclusion when it gave the store to a single committer thread.

Capacity beyond 1 core is obtained by partitioning. Each share has its own book, and the books of different shares are independent of one another. Shares are divided among engines, each engine a single thread serving some hundreds of shares, and a share that is exceptionally busy can be given an engine to itself. This is sharding by share, with the order book as the unit that must not be divided.

The journal and the replay

An engine that keeps everything in memory loses everything when its machine fails, and an exchange cannot lose its order book. The apparent conflict is resolved by a property that the design has been careful to preserve.

The engine is deterministic. Its output depends on its sequence of inputs and on nothing else. It consults no clock, generates no random numbers, and is not affected by the timing of threads, there being only 1. From this it follows that the state of the engine can always be recomputed by starting from an empty book and applying the same inputs again in the same order.

It is therefore sufficient to make the inputs durable. The sequencer writes every input to a journal on disk, in sequence, before the engine processes it. This is the write-ahead log of chapter 2, and it is kept on several machines by the replication of chapter 3, so that it survives the loss of any 1 of them.

If the engine’s machine fails, a replacement reads the journal from the beginning and arrives at exactly the book that the failed engine held, having made exactly the same trades. The state was never the thing that needed protecting. The inputs were, and the state follows from them.

To replay a whole day’s journal would take too long to be acceptable, and in practice a standby engine runs continuously on another machine, reading the same journal and applying the same inputs a moment behind the primary. It holds an identical book at all times and suppresses its outputs. When the primary fails, the standby is promoted and begins to publish, and the changeover takes milliseconds. Since the 2 engines processed the same inputs deterministically, there is no question of their disagreeing about the state of the book.

The same property serves purposes other than recovery. A regulator who asks why a particular order did not trade can be answered by replaying the journal to that moment and examining the book. A new version of the engine can be tested by feeding it yesterday’s journal and comparing its trades with those that were actually made. And a defect that occurred in production can be reproduced exactly, as often as required, on a developer’s machine.

Determinism has to be defended deliberately, since it is easily lost. An engine that reads the time from the system clock in order to stamp a trade has made its output depend on something outside the journal, and its replay will produce different stamps. The time must therefore itself be an input, assigned by the sequencer and recorded in the journal. Iterating over a hash table whose order varies between runs, or performing arithmetic in floating point that differs between processors, would break determinism in the same way.

The gateway

Participants do not communicate with the engine directly. They connect to gateways, which authenticate them, check the syntax of what they send, and apply the checks that have to be made before an order is allowed to reach the book.

The most important of these are the checks of risk. A participant must have the funds to pay for what they buy and the shares to deliver what they sell, and must be within the limits their broker has set. An order of obviously mistaken size or price, such as a sale at a hundredth of the current price, is rejected, since such errors have on more than one occasion caused very large losses within seconds. And each participant is limited in the rate at which they may send orders, by the rate limiter of chapter 7.

It matters where these checks are made. They are performed before the sequencer, so that an order which fails them never enters the journal and never affects the book. Checks that depend on the state of the book itself, on the other hand, must be made by the engine, after sequencing, since only there is the state well defined.

Since the gateways lie before the sequencer, there is a subtle demand of fairness on them as well. If 1 gateway were consistently faster than another, the participants connected to it would have their orders sequenced earlier. Exchanges go to considerable lengths to equalise the path from every participant to the sequencer, to the extent of giving all participants network cables of the same length.

Publishing prices

Every change to the book is of interest to all participants: each trade, and each change in the best bid and ask. The engine publishes a stream of these events, the market data, and participants decide what to do next on the basis of it.

The demand of fairness applies here with particular force. A participant who learned of a trade a millisecond before the others could act on it first, to their profit and at the others’ expense. Market data is therefore published to all participants simultaneously, by a mechanism designed to deliver the same message to every recipient at as nearly the same instant as can be arranged.

The engine does not wait for the market data to be delivered, or even to be sent. It hands each event to a separate publishing component and proceeds to the next input. Every event carries its sequence number, and a participant who notices a gap in the numbers requests the missing events again, which is the recovery by sequence number that chapter 18 used for messages.

After the trade

A trade made by the engine is an agreement, and the exchange of shares for money that it calls for happens later. The record of each trade passes to a clearing system, which works out what each participant owes and is owed, and thence to settlement, in which shares and money actually change hands, typically 1 or 2 days afterwards.

These later stages have requirements of the kind that chapter 19 described. They must be exact, every movement must be recorded twice in a ledger, and nothing may be lost, while speed is of little account. They are built on ordinary strongly consistent databases, and they receive the trades from the engine through a durable queue, so that the engine is never made to wait for them. The architecture of an exchange is thus divided at the trade: before it, a path built for speed and determinism, in memory and on a single thread, and after it, a path built for exactness and durability, with databases and reconciliation.

Use cases

A trader places orders, cancels them, and watches the prices.

Functional requirements

No.Functional requirement
0A participant can place an order to buy or sell a quantity of a share at a limit price.
1A participant can cancel an order that has not been completely filled.
2An incoming order trades with waiting orders on the other side whose prices meet its own, best price first, and earliest first at each price.
3A trade is made at the price of the order that was waiting.
4What remains of an order waits in the book.
5Every trade and every change in the best prices is published to all participants.

Non-functional requirements

No.PropertyNon-functional requirement
0FairnessEvents are processed in the order of a single sequence, which is the same for every participant.
1DeterminismThe same sequence of inputs always produces the same trades.
2LatencyAn order is answered within 1 ms, 99% of the time.
3DurabilityNo input that was sequenced is lost.
4Availability99.99% during trading hours, with a changeover of under 1 second when a machine fails.
5ConsistencyStrong. There is exactly 1 order book for each share.

The system is strongly consistent in the most literal sense available. For each share there is 1 sequence of events and 1 book, and no participant can ever be shown a state that another participant’s view contradicts. Where earlier chapters accepted eventual consistency in order to gain availability or speed, an exchange cannot, since 2 books that disagreed about who had bought what would be a failure of the exchange’s entire purpose. It obtains its speed by other means, namely by keeping the consistent part small enough to be executed by a single thread.

Core entities

Capacity estimate

Arithmetic ahead. A busy share receives a few thousand orders per second at its peak, which a single thread handles with a great deal to spare, and a day’s journal for the whole exchange is some tens of gigabytes.
